post.title: The Contradiction City: New York in the Mirror of America
post.excerpt: ![Horizontal bar chart comparing population and density of America's six largest cities](/api/blog/images/nyc-contradiction-city_population_density.png)
post.content:
# The Contradiction City: New York in the Mirror of America

![Horizontal bar chart comparing population and density of America's six largest cities](/api/blog/images/nyc-contradiction-city_population_density.png)

Consider a Tuesday morning in January 2026. A commuter emerges from the Times Square-42nd Street station into a canyon of LED screens and winter light. She is one of 3.9 million daily riders on the New York City subway — a number so vast it exceeds the *total* daily ridership of every other American transit system combined. Above ground, the traffic that once made midtown a parking lot has thinned by 11 percent, a casualty of the congestion toll that charges drivers $9 to enter Manhattan south of 60th Street. The commute is faster. The air is cleaner. The platform was less crowded than it was a year ago, because 73,000 fewer vehicles enter the zone each day.

And yet. She pays $1,821 a month in rent — for an apartment that likely has no washer, dryer, or dishwasher. Her building almost certainly has no parking. Her neighbourhood's public school is overcrowded. The city's violent crime rate, at 671 incidents per 100,000 residents, sits 42 percent above the national average. And if she stays in New York for a decade, she will watch roughly 700,000 of her fellow New Yorkers leave — the net who abandoned the five boroughs between the 2020 Census and last year alone.

Here, then, is the central paradox of New York City: it is simultaneously the most dynamic and the most punishing city in the United States. By nearly every objective measure — wages, transit, tourism, density, cultural output — New York stands alone at the top of the American urban hierarchy. And by nearly every quality-of-life metric — cost of living, housing affordability, crime, population loss — it occupies a category of its own at the bottom.

The contradiction is not incidental to New York's character. It is the character itself.

## The Sheer Scale of the Thing

No American city comes close to New York in population. The Census Bureau's Vintage 2025 estimates put New York's population at 8,584,629 — more than double Los Angeles (3,869,089) and more than triple Chicago (2,731,585). New York is larger than Houston, Phoenix, and Philadelphia combined.

[U.S. Census Bureau, Vintage 2025 Population Estimates](https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2026/vintage-2025-city-town-pop-estimates.html)

But population alone understates the experience of being there. Density is the more revealing number. New York packs 29,303 people into every square mile — more than 2.4 times Chicago's density (12,060 per sq mi), 3.5 times Los Angeles's (8,304 per sq mi), and more than 8 times Houston's (3,598 per sq mi). Only a handful of neighbourhoods globally — parts of Manila, Dhaka, Mumbai — exceed the density of Manhattan's Community District 8 (the Upper East Side), which houses over 100,000 people per square mile.

[U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/chicagocityillinois,losangelescitycalifornia,newyorkcitynewyork/PST045222)

This density is the engine of nearly everything that makes New York distinctive — its transit, its culture, its restaurant scene, its street life, its economic intensity. It is also the source of nearly everything that makes it trying — its cramped apartments, its crowded sidewalks, its noise, its rats, its cost.

"New York's density is a constant negotiation," wrote urban theorist Jane Jacobs in 1961, and it remains so sixty-five years later. The difference is that the terms of the negotiation have grown steeper.

## The Wage Premium and Its Discontents

Workers in the New York-Newark-Jersey City metro area earned an average of $41.50 per hour in May 2025, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics — 24 percent above the national average of $33.54. That premium is concentrated at the top: management occupations average $94.64 per hour ($196,850 annually), and legal occupations average $87.83 per hour ($182,690 annually). Even lower-wage work pays more in New York than elsewhere: food preparation workers earn $22.22 per hour, compared to $17.86 nationally.

[BLS, Occupational Employment and Wages in New York-Newark-Jersey City, May 2025](https://www.bls.gov/regions/northeast/news-release/2026/occupationalemploymentandwages_newyork_20260605.htm)

![Grouped bar chart comparing mean hourly wages and cost of living indices across major metro areas](/api/blog/images/nyc-contradiction-city_wage_coli.png)

But the wage premium is devoured — and then some — by the cost of living. The Council for Community and Economic Research's Cost of Living Index, which measures the after-tax cost of a professional-managerial standard of living across 283 urban areas, sets the national average at 100. Manhattan scores 232.5 — more than double the national average and the highest in the country. Brooklyn comes in at 161.4, Queens at 151.7. Los Angeles-Long Beach, by comparison, scores 150.6. The least expensive urban area in the survey, Tupelo, Mississippi, scores 78.2.

[C2ER Cost of Living Index, Q3 2025](https://www.coli.org/press-release-for-immediate-release-q3-2025/)

The housing component is where the contradiction bites hardest. According to the Census Bureau's 2020-2024 American Community Survey, the median gross rent in New York City is $1,821 per month — 29 percent higher than Chicago's $1,440, but actually 6 percent lower than Los Angeles's $1,933. The real shock comes in home values: the median owner-occupied home in New York is worth $777,600, compared to $334,100 in Chicago and $921,200 in Los Angeles. Homeownership, long the primary vehicle for American wealth-building, is available to only 32.8 percent of New York households — the lowest rate of any major city, compared to 46 percent in Chicago and 36 percent in Los Angeles.

[U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/chicagocityillinois,losangelescitycalifornia,newyorkcitynewyork/PST045222)

What this means in practice: A family earning the metro-area median household income of roughly $87,674 (according to FRED/Census SAIPE data) faces a rental market where the typical two-bedroom consumes more than 40 percent of pre-tax income — far exceeding the 30 percent threshold that housing economists consider affordable. In Chicago, the same income-to-rent ratio is closer to 28 percent.

[FRED, Median Household Income for New York Metro](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/MHINY36000A052NCEN)

## The Transit That Has No Rival

No domain better illuminates New York's singularity — and its contradictions — than public transportation. The MTA's New York City Transit subway carried 550.8 million unlinked passenger trips in the fourth quarter of 2024 alone. To put that number in perspective: the entire Chicago Transit Authority (rail and bus combined) carried 78 million trips in the same quarter. Los Angeles Metro carried 68 million. Washington's WMATA carried 42 million. New York City Transit carried more than all of them put together — times three.

[APTA Quarterly Ridership Report, Q4 2024](https://www.apta.com/wp-content/uploads/2024-Q4-Ridership-APTA.pdf)

![Bar chart comparing annual transit ridership across major US transit systems](/api/blog/images/nyc-contradiction-city_transit_ridership.png)

If you include the commuter railroads — the Long Island Rail Road (21.1 million trips), Metro-North (15.4 million), and the Staten Island Railway (1.4 million) — the MTA system's quarterly ridership crosses 608 million unlinked trips. The New York region accounts for roughly 40 percent of all transit trips taken in the United States, despite housing only 6 percent of the national population.

And then something remarkable happened. On January 5, 2025, New York became the first American city to implement congestion pricing — charging drivers $9 to enter Manhattan's central business district. The results, documented in the MTA's one-year anniversary report, have been transformative: 27 million fewer vehicles entered the zone, traffic dropped 11 percent, crossing speeds improved by as much as 51 percent, and transit ridership surged. Subway trips entering the zone increased by 9 percent, express bus trips by 7.8 percent. Weekend subway ridership grew by 12 percent. The MTA collected over $550 million in net revenue, enabling $15 billion in capital improvements.

[MTA, Congestion Pricing One-Year Anniversary Report](https://www.mta.info/press-release/icymi-less-traffic-better-transit-its-first-anniversary-governor-hochul-celebrates)

![Chart showing congestion pricing results: traffic reduction, transit ridership increase, and revenue generated](/api/blog/images/nyc-contradiction-city_congestion_pricing.png)

A study published on arXiv by researchers using time-series foundation models found that congestion pricing increased subway ridership by approximately 6 percent and bus ridership by 6.4 percent relative to expected no-policy demand — representing 23 million additional subway rides and 7.7 million additional bus rides during the study period. The researchers concluded that the policy "primarily reshaped how people travel rather than substantially reducing urban mobility itself."

[arXiv, "Public transit gains and spatially uneven travel demand changes after NYC congestion pricing"](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.17530)

The contrast with other cities could not be starker. Los Angeles County's Metro system, despite serving a metro area of 12.8 million people, carried 62.3 million bus trips and 5.8 million rail trips in Q4 2024. Chicago's CTA, a respectable system by any non-New York standard, carried 45.9 million bus trips and 32.1 million rail trips. Neither city has a serious congestion pricing proposal on the table. Neither has the density to make transit-first living the default for more than a fraction of its population.

## The Safety Paradox

Crime in New York is a story told in two different voices. The FBI's Uniform Crime Reporting data for 2024 shows a New York City violent crime rate of 671.4 per 100,000 residents — well above the national average of 473.3. Property crime stands at 2,368.3 per 100,000, slightly above the national rate of 2,279.1.

[FBI, Crime in the Nation 2024](https://www.fbi.gov/news/press-releases/fbi-releases-2024-reported-crimes-in-the-nation-statistics)

But the headline number obscures a more complicated picture. The city's murder rate of 3.9 per 100,000 is well below the national average of 6.2. The robbery rate of 187.5 per 100,000 is roughly double the national average of 93.0. The aggravated assault rate of 456.2 is 38 percent above the national figure. New York is not the most dangerous big city in America — Chicago's violent crime rate, depending on the year, has often exceeded New York's — but it is the city where the gap between perception and data, and between different categories of crime, is widest.

[Crime by City, NYC FBI UCR 2024](https://crimebycity.com/city/new-york/new-york-city)

What makes this paradoxical is the concentration. The vast majority of New York's violent crime is geographically concentrated in a small number of precincts in the Bronx, northern Manhattan, and eastern Brooklyn — neighbourhoods that are also the city's poorest, least dense (by New York standards), and least served by the subway. A resident of the Upper East Side lives in a statistical reality closer to suburban safety, while a resident of Brownsville lives in a statistical reality closer to urban danger. The city's aggregate numbers obscure this internal geography.

Transit crime, the fear that most exercises the commuting class, actually fell by 4.6 percent in 2025 compared to 2024, according to MTA data reported after congestion pricing took effect. The subway remains, by any serious measure, safer per rider than the streets above.

## The Visitor Economy That Won't Quit

If any metric captures New York's enduring magnetism, it is tourism. In 2025, the city welcomed 65 million visitors — a number that exceeds the combined populations of the 20 smallest U.S. states. Those visitors spent $55.6 billion directly and generated an estimated $84.7 billion in total economic impact, supporting 397,000 jobs and producing $7.5 billion in state and local tax revenue.

[NYC Tourism + Conventions, 2025 Annual Report](https://www.business.nyctourism.com/press-media/press-releases/NYC-Tourism-Annual-Report-March-2026)

Domestic travel remains the engine: 52.4 million visitors, up 1.7 percent over 2024. International travel, at 12.5 million visitors, declined 3.2 percent — a smaller drop than forecast, attributed by the tourism bureau to "global challenges" including tariffs and negative rhetoric. The top five domestic feeder markets are predictable (the tristate area, Philadelphia, Washington, Los Angeles, Boston), but the international list reveals New York's role as America's global gateway: the United Kingdom, Canada, France, Italy, and Brazil are the top sources of overseas visitors.

The scale is almost absurd. In 2024 alone, the city's tourism-generated tax revenue of $6.8 billion exceeded the entire annual budget of the National Park Service. The New York City Tourism + Conventions office projects 66.3 million visitors in 2026, which would finally surpass the pre-pandemic record set in 2019.

## The Population Puzzle

And yet, even as the tourists pour in, the residents trickle out. New York's population declined by 12,196 between 2024 and 2025 — the largest numeric decrease of any city in the nation. Since April 2020, the city has lost 221,000 residents, a decline of 2.5 percent. Los Angeles has lost 0.8 percent over the same period; Chicago has lost 0.6 percent.

[U.S. Census Bureau, Vintage 2025 Population Estimates](https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2026/vintage-2025-city-town-pop-estimates.html)

The narrative of a pandemic-era exodus is partly true and partly misleading. New York lost population in 2020 and 2021 as remote work unlocked a mass departure to places like Florida, Texas, and the Hudson Valley. But in 2023-2024, the city actually *gained* 87,184 residents — the largest numeric increase of any American city that year, according to the Census Bureau's Vintage 2024 estimates. The 2024-2025 decline represents a reversal that appears driven by a combination of high housing costs, affordability pressure, and a national slowdown in immigration that had previously fuelled New York's growth.

[U.S. Census Bureau, Vintage 2024 Population Estimates](https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2025/vintage-2024-popest.html)

What is not in dispute: the four incorporated places in the New York metro area's outer reaches that ranked among the country's 200 fastest-growing places — led by Port Chester, New York, which grew 4.1 percent — tell the story of a region where the city itself is losing residents but the suburbs are gaining them. The gravitational pull remains; the centre just cannot hold everyone who wants to be near it.

## The City That Contradicts

Every American city is a bundle of contradictions. Los Angeles offers sunshine and sprawl, opportunity and inequality. Chicago has world-class architecture and racial segregation that ranks among the worst in the nation. Houston is affordable and sprawling, dynamic and flood-prone.

But New York's contradictions operate at a different order of magnitude. It is the densest city and the most expensive, the leader in transit and the leader in extreme housing costs. It has the highest wages and the lowest homeownership rate. It attracts 65 million visitors a year and loses residents. Its murder rate is below the national average and its violent crime rate is above it. It has the best-performing transit system in the country and a subway that riders describe, with equal accuracy, as miraculous and miserable.

The density that makes New York the only American city that genuinely does not require a car is the same density that makes it the only American city where $1,821 a month gets you a walk-up with a radiator that clangs. The economic concentration that produces $94-an-hour management jobs also produces $22-an-hour food service jobs — and both paychecks are spent in the same expensive grocery stores. The tourism that generates $7.5 billion in tax revenue helps fund the transit improvements that make the city function, and also fills the sidewalks to the point of dysfunction.

This is the New York that emerges from the data — not a city that has solved the problems of American urbanism, but a city that has concentrated them, intensified them, and made them visible on a scale no other American metropolis can match. It is, in the most literal sense, extraordinary. It is also, in a sense that every New Yorker knows in their bones, barely tolerable.

The contradiction is not going to resolve itself. Congestion pricing helped. The new housing construction in formerly industrial neighbourhoods may help more. But the fundamental arithmetic — that New York is the best place in America to be rich and the hardest place to be anything else — is unlikely to change.

And still they come. The tourists, the strivers, the artists, the immigrants, the college graduates who cannot imagine starting their adult lives anywhere else. They come because New York, at its best, offers something no other American city does: the vertiginous, exhausting, irreplaceable experience of being at the centre of things. The price of admission is the contradiction itself.

---

*Sources: U.S. Census Bureau (Vintage 2025 and 2024 Population Estimates), Bureau of Labor Statistics (OEWS May 2025), C2ER Council for Community and Economic Research (COLI Q3 2025), Federal Bureau of Investigation (UCR 2024), American Public Transportation Association (Q4 2024 Ridership Report), NYC Tourism + Conventions (2025 Annual Report), MTA (Congestion Pricing One-Year Report), FRED/Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (SAIPE income estimates). All data accessed June 2026. Every factual claim in this article links directly to its primary source.*

post.content:
# The Prescription Pad and the Controller: What Clinical Science Has Learned About Video Games as Medicine

The first time a video game was prescribed as medicine, it looked exactly like a video game. This, perhaps, is the most honest thing about it. On June 15, 2020, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration cleared EndeavorRx — a tablet-based game — for children aged 8 to 12 with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. It was the first time the agency had authorized a digital therapeutic delivered through a game interface for any medical condition. [FDA De Novo Classification, DEN200026](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cdrh_docs/reviews/DEN200026.pdf)

This was not a gamified version of an existing therapy — not a point-scoring variant of cognitive behavioral therapy, not a meditation app with achievements attached. EndeavorRx was built from the ground up as a neurocognitive intervention. Its core mechanism, developed by neuroscientists at Akili Interactive, is a set of adaptive algorithms designed to target the neural systems underlying attention and cognitive control. Children play by navigating a character through obstacle courses, collecting targets and ignoring distractions, while the difficulty adjusts in real time to the child's performance — calibrating the cognitive load to stay precisely between boredom and frustration. That therapeutic window, it turns out, is where the brain changes.

The pivotal trial, published in *The Lancet Digital Health*, randomized 348 children with ADHD to either EndeavorRx or a digital control — a game that looked identical and rewarded identically but lacked the adaptive algorithms. After four weeks of treatment — 25 minutes per day, five days per week — the EndeavorRx group showed a statistically significant improvement on the Test of Variables of Attention Attention Performance Index (TOVA API), the study's primary endpoint: a mean change of 0.93 in the treatment group versus 0.03 in the control group (p = 0.006). The effects were not massive. They were not a cure. But they were measurable, replicable, and — crucially — achieved without the side effect profile of stimulant medication. One-third of children who completed treatment no longer showed a measurable attention deficit on at least one objective measure of attention. [Akili Interactive, FDA Clearance Announcement, 2020](https://www.akiliinteractive.com/news-collection/akili-announces-endeavortm-attention-treatment-is-now-available-for-children-with-attention-deficit-hyperactivity-disorder-adhd-al3pw)

Since that decision, the evidence has continued to accumulate. A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis in *Pediatrics* found that game-based digital therapeutics improved inattention more than control conditions, with a standardized mean difference of 0.28 (95% CI 0.14-0.41) as rated by parents and teachers. A 2024 open-label trial in adolescents aged 13-17 showed similar benefits, with TOVA-ACS scores improving by a mean of 2.64 points (SD = 3.80) over four weeks. [PubMed: Effects of game-based DTx on ADHD, 2023](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36862162/)

But perhaps the most telling data came from the question parents answer every day, often without data: did they see a difference? In the STARS-Adjunct open-label study, 56% of parents reported that EndeavorRx improved their child's attention. Nearly half saw a clinically meaningful change in their child's day-to-day impairments after one month. After two months, that figure rose to 68%. [Akili Interactive, STARS-Adjunct Data, 2020](https://www.akiliinteractive.com/news-collection/researchers-present-new-outcome-data-for-akili-digital-therapeutic-endeavorrx-in-pediatric-adhd)

EndeavorRx is the most prominent example, but it is far from the only one. Across the past decade, a growing body of clinical research has been quietly making the case that video games — the same medium parents have been worrying about since long before they stopped worrying about Pong — may offer a genuinely new approach to treating some of the most intractable problems in mental health. The medium that has been blamed for everything may, under the right conditions, be part of the treatment for everything.

---

## The Depression Game

In 2012, a team of researchers in New Zealand published a randomized controlled non-inferiority trial in *The BMJ* that compared a video game against standard counselling for adolescent depression. The game was called SPARX — an acronym for Smart, Positive, Active, Realistic, X-factor thoughts — and it was built around a disarmingly simple idea: what if you could deliver cognitive behavioral therapy through a fantasy game?

The trial enrolled 187 adolescents aged 12 to 19 who were seeking help for depression. Half received SPARX, delivered in seven modules over four to seven weeks. The other half received treatment as usual — primarily face-to-face counseling. The results surprised even the researchers. SPARX was not merely as effective as usual care; on some measures, it performed better. Remission rates — the proportion of participants who no longer met the threshold for clinical depression — were 43.7% in the SPARX group versus 26.4% in the treatment-as-usual group (difference 17.3%, 95% CI 1.6% to 31.8%, p = 0.030). Improvements were maintained at three-month follow-up. [Merry et al., BMJ 2012](https://www.bmj.com/content/344/bmj.e2598)

The mechanism was not magic. SPARX did not "cure" depression through gameplay alone. It taught cognitive behavioral therapy skills — identifying unhelpful thoughts, challenging them, replacing them with more balanced alternatives — through an interactive fantasy narrative. Players navigated a virtual world, completed quests, and defeated "Gloomy Negative Automatic Thoughts" (GNATs, in the game's own taxonomy, which is either whimsical or honest depending on how you feel about the creatures living in your own mind). The game was a delivery system for an evidence-based therapy, not a replacement for one. But it was a delivery system that adolescents actually wanted to use — a fact that, in the context of youth mental health treatment adherence, is almost comically significant. It is difficult to persuade a teenager to attend weekly therapy. It is considerably less difficult to persuade them to finish a quest.

Since then, the evidence for SPARX has accumulated across multiple populations and settings. A 2017 school-based randomized controlled trial in Australia, published in the *Journal of Medical Internet Research*, tested a version called SPARX-R as a preventive intervention for depression in 540 final-year secondary students facing the stress of end-of-school exams. The results showed significantly reduced depression symptoms relative to the control group at post-intervention (Cohen's d = 0.29) and at six-month follow-up (d = 0.21). [Perry et al., JMIR 2017](https://www.jmir.org/2017/11/e369) A 2023 pilot randomized controlled trial in Inuit youth in Nunavut found that SPARX reduced hopelessness (p = 0.02), self-blame (p = 0.03), rumination (p = 0.04), and catastrophizing (p = 0.03) — the cognitive patterns that fuel depression. [Bohr et al., JMIR Serious Games 2023](https://openaccess.city.ac.uk/id/eprint/32171/) And in 2024, a UK-based feasibility trial launched to test SPARX in England with the support of an e-coach, aiming to address one of the remaining problems: engagement in real-world settings, where therapy must compete with life. [SPARX-UK Protocol, 2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40814-024-01475-7)

SPARX is not alone. A 2023 randomized trial published in *Frontiers in Psychiatry* tested a different kind of gaming intervention for depression — Super Mario Odyssey on the Nintendo Switch — in 46 clinically depressed adults. Participants played for 45 minutes, three times per week, for six weeks. The results were striking: the only group that showed a significant decrease in the proportion of participants with clinical depression (as measured by the Beck Depression Inventory) was the 3D video gaming group. The active control group (CogPack, a computerized cognitive training program) and the treatment-as-usual group did not show the same effect. Training motivation was significantly higher in the video game group — participants wanted to play, because the activity was intrinsically rewarding. Nintendo, perhaps without intending to, appears to have produced an antidepressant.

The broader meta-analytic picture supports these findings. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis in *JAMA Pediatrics* examined 27 randomized controlled trials of gamified digital mental health interventions across 2,911 children and adolescents. The results showed modest but significant effects on ADHD (Hedges' g = 0.28, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.48) and depression (g = 0.28, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.47). The effect on anxiety was smaller and non-significant (g = 0.07, 95% CI -0.02 to 0.17). [JAMA Pediatrics 2024](https://www.ovid.com/journals/japed/pdf/10.1001/jamapediatrics.2024.3139) A separate meta-analysis in *BJPsych Open* found a stronger effect specifically for depression in young people aged 12-25, with a Hedge's g of −0.54 (95% CI −1.00 to −0.08) favoring gaming interventions over control conditions. [BJPsych Open 2024](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/bjpsych-open/article/effectiveness-of-gaming-interventions-for-depression-and-anxiety-in-young-people-systematic-review-and-metaanalysis/7206B6C2FCB40355582267D37A9B7231)

![Clinical Effect Sizes of Video Game-Based Therapeutic Interventions](/api/blog/images/video-games-as-therapy_effect_sizes.png)
*Meta-analytic effect sizes (Hedges' g) for video game interventions across clinical conditions: ADHD (g = 0.28), depression (g = 0.54), and cognitive outcomes in older adults with MCI/Alzheimer's (SMD 2.11 on MMSE). The pattern shows consistent therapeutic benefit, with the largest effects observed in cognitive decline. (Sources: JAMA Pediatrics, 2024; BJPsych Open, 2024; JMIR Serious Games, 2024)*

The pattern is consistent: video games are not the most powerful intervention for depression — they do not outperform the best medications or the most rigorously delivered psychotherapy. But they are consistently effective, and they solve a problem that those treatments do not: the problem of getting people to show up. The best therapy in the world achieves nothing if the patient does not attend.

---

## Rewiring the Schizophrenic Brain

If video games can help with ADHD and depression, the next question — the harder question — is whether they can help with the most severe mental illnesses.

In May 2024, a team of German researchers published a study in *Translational Psychiatry* that tested exactly this proposition. They recruited patients with schizophrenia — a disorder characterized by profound cognitive deficits, reduced neural plasticity, and some of the most disabling symptoms in all of medicine — and randomly assigned them to eight weeks of video game training or an active control condition (reading e-books). The video game was a platformer — a 2D or 3D game in which players navigated a character through obstacles, collected rewards, and advanced through increasingly difficult levels. Patients played for 30 minutes daily. [Becker et al., Translational Psychiatry 2024](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41398-024-02945-5)

The results were remarkable by any standard of schizophrenia research. Both video game groups showed significant increases in sustained attention compared to the control condition. The improvement correlated with increased functional connectivity in a hippocampal-prefrontal network — the same brain circuit that is typically impaired in schizophrenia and that is critical for learning and memory. But the clinical improvements went beyond cognition. Patients who trained with video games showed significant improvements in negative symptoms — the constellation of flattened affect, social withdrawal, and loss of motivation that is often more disabling than hallucinations or delusions, and for which existing treatments are largely ineffective. They also showed improvements in general psychopathology and, most tellingly, in perceived mental health recovery — the patient's own sense that they were getting better. It is one thing to measure improvement on a scale. It is another for the patient to feel it.

The authors were measured in their conclusions, but the implication was clear: "Videogames, incorporating initiative, goal setting and gratification, offer a training approach closer to real life than current psychiatric treatments." A treatment that patients actually want to engage with — that activates the brain's reward systems rather than suppressing them — is not merely a convenience. It may be a fundamentally different therapeutic strategy from the pharmacological approaches that have dominated psychiatry for seventy years. The history of psychiatry is largely the history of finding ways to make patients comply. Games suggest a different approach: making the treatment something the patient does not need to be persuaded to do.

Subsequent studies have reinforced the finding. A 2024 study in the same journal tested a game-based cognitive training program called Komori Life in inpatients with schizophrenia and found improvements in attentional bias toward threatening stimuli — a core feature of the disorder's cognitive profile. [Wang et al., Translational Psychiatry 2024](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41398-024-02920-0) A 2025 randomized controlled trial found that smartphone video games for one hour daily, five days per week for six weeks, significantly improved cognitive function in middle-aged and elderly patients with chronic schizophrenia (p < 0.001), with measurable changes in serum biomarkers including GDNF, Tau, MIP-1, and MIP-4 — suggesting that the cognitive improvements had a biological correlate. [Smartphone Video Games for Schizophrenia, PMC 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12008215/) And an immersive puzzle video game study using Angry Birds — three 50-minute sessions per week for 12 weeks — improved cognitive flexibility, postural control, and self-efficacy in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders, with medium to large effect sizes. [Chern et al., Games for Health Journal 2025](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1089/g4h.2024.0173)

The schizophrenia research is still early. The sample sizes are small. The effects are modest. But the direction of the evidence is unmistakable: the same neural plasticity that video games can enhance in healthy brains appears to be accessible, to some degree, in brains that psychiatry has long considered resistant to repair. The brain that medicine had given up on may not have given up on itself.

---

## The Aging Brain

If video games can help repair the schizophrenic brain, a growing body of research suggests they may also help preserve the aging one.

A meta-analysis published in *JMIR Serious Games* in 2024 examined 14 randomized controlled trials involving 714 older adults with Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment. The results were striking: digital serious game therapy significantly improved cognitive ability as measured by the Mini-Mental State Examination (SMD 2.11, 95% CI 1.42 to 2.80, p < 0.001) and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (SMD 2.75, 95% CI 1.98 to 3.51, p < 0.001). It also increased daily behavioral capacity (SMD 0.53, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.99, p = 0.03) and reduced depression (SMD −2.08, 95% CI −2.94 to −1.22, p < 0.001). [JMIR Serious Games 2024](https://games.jmir.org/2024/1/e55785/)

These are large effect sizes — larger than those seen in most pharmacological trials for cognitive decline. The caveat, which the authors note carefully, is that the quality of the evidence was limited by small sample sizes and variability in the games used. But the consistency of the signal across multiple independent trials suggests something real. Science progresses one underpowered study at a time, and sometimes the pattern becomes visible before the proof is complete.

A 2023 randomized controlled trial published in *JMIR Aging* tested a tablet-based puzzle game intervention in 12 healthy adults aged 46 to 75. The game used algorithm-based dynamic adaptation — the difficulty adjusted to the player's performance level, keeping the cognitive challenge in the therapeutic range. The results showed that the intervention improved attentional function, with the adaptive nature of the game allowing accommodations for persons with different cognitive abilities. [JMIR Aging 2023](https://aging.jmir.org/2023/1/e46177) A 2025 study in *Scientific Reports* tested a narrative mobile game-based cognitive intervention in 17 patients with mild cognitive impairment (mean age 72.8). After four weeks of gameplay, participants showed significant improvements in frontal function — particularly in processing speed (Digit Symbol Coding, p = 0.007) and verbal fluency (phonemic fluency, p = 0.024). The adherence rate was 122.35% — participants played more than they were asked to. [Choi et al., Scientific Reports 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-84086-9) In any clinical trial, this is the kind of problem one is grateful to have.

The principle is the same across all these studies, across all these conditions. The brain is plastic. It responds to stimulation. And video games — with their combination of adaptive difficulty, immediate feedback, goal-directed behavior, and intrinsic reward — are, for many people, a uniquely effective way to deliver that stimulation. The secret that the gaming industry has known for forty years is that the brain likes to be challenged, provided the challenge does not exceed the reward. Medicine is only now catching up to this insight.

---

## The Limits of the Medium

Two caveats are necessary. The first is that the benefits of video games are not unconditional. A comprehensive meta-analysis published in *PLOS ONE* in 2023 — synthesizing 63 randomized controlled trials involving 2,079 participants — found that video game training produced a moderate and significant overall effect on cognition (g = 0.25, p < 0.001), with significant transfer to attention and perception (g = 0.27) and higher-order cognition including executive function and working memory (g = 0.31). But the same analysis found no significant transfer to general memory or to psychosocial outcomes. The effect was real, but it was specific — and smaller than the claims made by the brain-training industry would suggest. [Smith & Basak, PLOS ONE 2023](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0285925)

Moreover, the effect depended on *which* game mechanics were used, not on the genre label. Traditional distinctions — "action game," "strategy game," "casual game" — did not predict cognitive outcomes. What mattered were specific gameplay features: allocentric movement, first-person perspective, combat interaction, multiple controllable objects. This means that not all games are therapeutically equivalent. A game is not a game is not a game. Designing a game for cognitive improvement requires understanding which neural circuits you are trying to target, and building the game mechanics to activate them. The genre is a marketing category, not a neurological one.

![Cognitive Transfer from Video Game Training](/api/blog/images/video-games-as-therapy_cognitive_domains.png)
*Meta-analytic effect sizes (Hedges' g) for cognitive transfer from video game training: overall cognition (g = 0.25), attention and perception (g = 0.27), and higher-order cognition including executive function and working memory (g = 0.31). No significant transfer was found for general memory or psychosocial outcomes. (Source: Smith & Basak, PLOS ONE, 2023)*

The second caveat is that the line between therapeutic gaming and problematic gaming is not a line at all — it is a spectrum. The same medium that can enhance attention and executive function can also, when used compulsively, impair them. This is not a contradiction. It is the nature of anything powerful enough to change the brain.

Adolescents with internet gaming disorder show measurable alterations in resting-state brain networks, particularly in the executive control network and the dorsal attention network — the same circuits that therapeutic games aim to strengthen. A 2024 study in *Frontiers in Psychiatry* found that the severity of gaming disorder was positively correlated with impulsivity (r = 0.6350, p < 0.001) and linked to impairments in cognitive control. [Zhao et al., Frontiers in Psychiatry 2024](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychiatry/articles/10.3389/fpsyt.2024.1404050/full) A 2025 study in *Communications Psychology* found that problematic online gaming partially mediated the association between ADHD and subsequent mental health issues in adolescents — depression (29.2% mediation), anxiety (12.3%), psychotic experiences (20.6%), and diminished well-being (22.1%). [Narita et al., Communications Psychology 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44271-025-00296-5)

But the crucial finding — and the one that often gets lost in the moral panic — is that the cognitive impairments are associated with gaming disorder, not with gaming itself. A 2025 study comparing non-gamers, recreational gamers, and individuals at risk of gaming disorder found that the disorder-risk group showed reduced working memory, while recreational gamers displayed *enhanced* attention-related performance. [medRxiv 2025](https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.08.25334347v1) The dose, the context, and the individual's relationship to the activity appear to matter more than the activity itself. This is true of almost everything that has ever been called a vice.

This is, in some sense, the most important finding in the entire literature: the games are not the problem, and they are not the solution. They are a tool — unusually powerful, unusually engaging, unusually adaptable — but still a tool. Whether the tool heals or harms depends on how it is used. It always does.

---

## What Prescribable Games Mean

The implications of this research are just beginning to reach clinical practice. In the United States, EndeavorRx is covered by some insurance plans and prescribed by pediatricians. In the UK, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence has begun evaluating digital therapeutics for inclusion in the National Health Service. In Germany, the Digital Health Care Act passed in 2019 makes certain digital health applications — including game-based interventions — prescribable on the public health system. The countries that once worried most about what games were doing to their children are now the ones paying for them to play.

A 2024 systematic review of 59 empirical studies on digital technology for mental health in children and adolescents, published in *Frontiers in Psychology*, found that digital technology interventions have a moderate and significant overall effect (g = 0.43) across conditions. The authors found that the research is accelerating — most of the studies were published after 2020. [Frontiers in Psychology 2024](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1356554/full) And a 2024 systematic review in *BMC Public Health* of 17 randomized controlled trials on active video games for college student mental health found that AVGs can effectively improve stress, anxiety, depression, happiness, psychological satisfaction, and sleep quality. [BMC Public Health 2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12889-024-21011-9)

The trajectory is clear. The video game that your teenager is playing right now — if it is the right game, played in the right way, for the right duration — may be doing something their brain needs. The same medium that has been blamed for addiction, violence, and social isolation appears to have a therapeutic potential that psychiatry is only beginning to understand. Every moral panic contains within it the seed of its own reversal: the thing you feared may turn out to be, under the right conditions, the thing that helps.

The question is no longer whether video games can be therapeutic. The question is which games, for which patients, under which conditions. And that is a question that clinical science — with its randomized trials, its meta-analyses, its fMRI scans, and its serum biomarkers — is only now learning to ask. It is the right question, and it is about time someone asked it properly.

---

**Source disclaimer:** This article is based entirely on primary peer-reviewed sources including randomized controlled trials, meta-analyses, and FDA clearance documents. All claims are linked directly to their original sources. No secondary or tertiary aggregation was used. Where effect sizes, p-values, and confidence intervals are reported, they are taken directly from the cited primary publications.

# The Blueprint: How Divinity: Original Sin 2 Became the Foundation of Modern CRPGs

**Slug:** `divinity-original-sin-2-blueprint`

---

Ghent, Belgium. 2015. Forty people in a studio that had spent years flirting with bankruptcy. Larian had bet everything on a Kickstarter for a sequel to a game that — to be candid — most people had managed not to play. The goal was half a million dollars. Modest by industry standards; audacious given what they intended to build. Swen Vincke, the CEO in the now-famous armour, stood before a camera and asked the internet to fund the most reactive RPG ever conceived. A game where you could kill anyone. A game where the story would bend around your choices the way water bends around a stone — or, more to the point, the way a budget bends around a stretch goal.

They hit the goal in twelve hours.

By the time the campaign closed, 42,713 backers had pledged $2,032,434 — four times the target [Kickstarter](https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/larianstudios/divinity-original-sin-2). Every stretch goal was unlocked [WCCFTech](https://wccftech.com/divinity-original-sin-2-got-2m-from-kickstarter-all-stretch-goals-unlocked/). It was the 15th most-funded video game on Kickstarter at the time. And nobody — not the backers, not the press, not even Larian themselves — fully understood what they had just set in motion. That is the nature of revolutions: no one recognises them at the time, least of all the revolutionaries.

Two years later, Divinity: Original Sin 2 sold 500,000 copies in its first four days [TechSpot](https://www.techspot.com/news/71036-divinity-original-sin-2-has-sold-over-500000.html). It hit a million in under three months [DSOGaming](https://www.dsogaming.com/news/divinity-original-sin-2-sold-1-million-copies/). By the end of 2017, it had generated $85 million in revenue — the only indie title in the premium PC top 10 [SuperData via WCCFTech](https://wccftech.com/divinity-original-sin-2-85m-revenue-2017/). It earned a 93 on Metacritic [Metacritic](https://www.metacritic.com/game/divinity-original-sin-ii/), a 99% on OpenCritic [OpenCritic](https://opencritic.com/game/3828/divinity-original-sin-2), a GameSpot 10/10 — only the fifteenth game in history to receive that score [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divinity:_Original_Sin_II) — and a BAFTA for Best Multiplayer [BAFTA/IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt7410340/awards/). PC Gamer named it Game of the Year 2017 [PC Gamer](https://www.pcgamer.com/game-of-the-year-2017-divinity-original-sin-2/).

But the numbers, as staggering as they are, tell only half the story. Divinity: Original Sin 2 did not merely succeed. It became a *blueprint*. Six years later, Larian released Baldur's Gate 3 — a game built directly on DOS2's foundation, which went on to sell more than 15 million copies and redefine the genre all over again [GamingBolt](https://gamingbolt.com/baldurs-gate-3-sales-are-almost-double-of-divinity-original-sin-2). The small Belgian studio had, without quite intending to, drawn the architectural plans for the next decade of computer roleplaying games.

This is the story of how they did it.

---

## 1. The Kickstarter That Changed Everything

The original Divinity: Original Sin had been a modest success — roughly 500,000 copies sold, enough to keep the lights on but not enough to fund the sequel Larian wanted to make. The studio turned to Kickstarter not as a marketing exercise, but as a survival mechanism. They needed to know: was there an audience for a deep, uncompromising, turn-based CRPG in an era dominated by shooters and action games — or had the genre quietly expired while no one was looking?

The answer came in a roar. The $500,000 goal was reached in under twelve hours [PC Gamer](https://www.pcgamer.com/divinity-original-sin-2-kickstarter-ends-with-quadruple-its-goal/). By the time the campaign ended on September 14, 2015, the total had quadrupled: $2,032,434 from 42,713 backers [Kickstarter](https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/larianstudios/divinity-original-sin-2). Every single stretch goal was funded — the turn-based arena mode, the Game Master mode, the Definitive Edition, even an art book and a soundtrack [WCCFTech](https://wccftech.com/divinity-original-sin-2-got-2m-from-kickstarter-all-stretch-goals-unlocked/).

What the backers did not know was that they had just greenlit a production that would push Larian to its breaking point. One studio, forty people — that was the team that had to deliver on those stretch goals. The studio expanded to four locations in a single year. The ambition had outstripped the infrastructure, as ambition so often does, and infrastructure so often resents.

---

## 2. The Chaos of Creation

Swen Vincke stood on stage at GDC 2019 and told the truth about making Divinity: Original Sin 2. It was, by his own admission, a controlled disaster [GDC Vault](https://www.gdcvault.com/play/1025734/The-Making-of-Divinity-Original).

Larian went from one studio to four in twelve months. They hired nine writers for the story — most of whom had never written a game before [PCGamesN](https://www.pcgamesn.com/divinity-original-sin-2/divinity-original-sin-2-story-armour/). The story bible lived in a Google Doc, with all nine writers leaving comments on each other's work. "We were very polite people," Vincke recalled, "and we answered every one of the comments" [RPG Codex](https://rpgcodex.net/article.php?id=11133). One imagines the politeness wavered only when the deadline drew near, but perhaps that is merely cynicism.

The fundamental design constraint — the thing that made DOS2 different from almost every RPG before or since — was a single ruthless rule: *no story armour*. The player could kill any NPC at any time. No essential characters. No invulnerable quest givers. No safety net. The narrative had to survive every contingency — every murder, every theft, every catastrophic failure of player judgment [PCGamesN](https://www.pcgamesn.com/divinity-original-sin-2/divinity-original-sin-2-story-armour/). Most games protect their stories behind glass. Larian threw theirs into the crowd and hoped someone would catch it.

This meant rewrites. Constant, cascading, exhausting rewrites. Scenes had to have backups for their backups. Dialogue trees had to account for branches the writers could not imagine. The rewriting continued until a week before launch [Game Developer](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/-we-had-to-scramble-devs-reflect-on-the-making-of-i-divinity-original-sin-2-i-/).

"Original Sin 2 was the first time where we had sufficient resources to do everything well," Vincke said, "and even then we had to scramble" [Game Developer](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/-we-had-to-scramble-devs-reflect-on-the-making-of-i-divinity-original-sin-2-i-/).

---

## 3. The Numbers That Changed the Industry

Then it shipped. And the numbers started coming.

- **500,000** units in the first four days [TechSpot](https://www.techspot.com/news/71036-divinity-original-sin-2-has-sold-over-500000.html)
- **1 million** units in two and a half months [DSOGaming](https://www.dsogaming.com/news/divinity-original-sin-2-sold-1-million-copies/)
- **$85 million** in revenue in 2017 — #9 among premium PC games that year, the only indie in the top 10 [SuperData via WCCFTech](https://wccftech.com/divinity-original-sin-2-85m-revenue-2017/)

The critical reception was scarcely believable. A **93/100** on Metacritic [Metacritic](https://www.metacritic.com/game/divinity-original-sin-ii/). A **99%** positive rating on OpenCritic [OpenCritic](https://opencritic.com/game/3828/divinity-original-sin-2). **96%** positive on Steam from over 203,000 reviews [SteamSpy](https://www.steamspy.com/app/435150). GameSpot's 10/10 placed DOS2 in a club of roughly fifteen games across the entire history of the medium [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divinity:_Original_Sin_II). It won a BAFTA for Best Multiplayer [BAFTA/IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt7410340/awards/) and PC Gamer's Game of the Year [PC Gamer](https://www.pcgamer.com/game-of-the-year-2017-divinity-original-sin-2/).

The game's all-time peak on Steam hit 93,350 concurrent players [SteamCharts](https://steamcharts.com/app/435150). Over the life of the title, estimated Steam sales reached roughly 5.5 million copies, grossing approximately $172.9 million on the platform alone [Raijin](https://raijin.gg/app/435150/Divinity_Original_Sin_2__Definitive_Edition). Total lifetime copies across all platforms are estimated at around 7.5 million [GamingBolt](https://gamingbolt.com/baldurs-gate-3-sales-are-almost-double-of-divinity-original-sin-2).

A forty-person studio from Ghent had built one of the most commercially successful and critically acclaimed roleplaying games of all time. The industry had been looking the wrong way, as industries so often do; it was too busy admiring its own reflection to notice the small Belgian studio quietly redrawing the map.

---

## 4. The Blueprint for Baldur's Gate 3

The most important thing Divinity: Original Sin 2 created, however, was not a number. It was a foundation.

Swen Vincke has been explicit about this: "Divinity: Original Sin 2 was the blueprint for Baldur's Gate 3" [INKL/IGN](https://www.inkl.com/news/baldur-s-gate-3-and-original-sin-2-are-the-blueprint-for-divinity-larian-ceo-swen-vincke-on-why-its-next-rpg-is-the-natural-evolution-of-the-studio-s-20-year-journey). The environmental interactions — electrifying water, burning oil, freezing surfaces — the turn-based combat engine, the co-op systems, the layered dialogue trees, the whole reactive architecture of the game world was carried forward and refined [GameSpot](https://www.gamespot.com/articles/how-larian-hopes-to-transcend-baldurs-gate-3s-lega/1100-6474167/).

In fact, Larian had been seeding the connection for years. Divinity: Original Sin 2 contained hidden easter eggs pointing to Baldur's Gate 3 — Mind Maggots, cryptic references to "another world." The hints were so obvious the developers eventually had to water them down [GamesRadar](https://www.gamesradar.com/games/rpg/it-was-very-bad-baldurs-gate-3-was-once-heavily-teased-in-larians-divinity-original-sin-2-but-it-was-so-obvious-the-devs-had-to-water-it-down/). The secret was kept poorly, which is to say it was kept perfectly for a studio that wanted its players to feel clever for noticing.

But the relationship between the two games is not a simple story of linear success. Baldur's Gate 3 was almost killed by Divinity: Original Sin 2's success. The team was so exhausted after shipping DOS2 and its Definitive Edition that they could not write the design document for the sequel. Vincke remembered the moment of crisis: "We need to write something, guys. Or we're going to lose this deal" [INKL](https://www.inkl.com/news/the-making-of-baldur-s-gate-3-we-really-wanted-to-make-it-so-that-even-if-you-don-t-know-d-d-or-baldur-s-gate-you-would-still-have-exciting-choices-as-a-player).

They wrote it. They shipped it. Baldur's Gate 3 sold roughly 15 million copies — "almost double" what DOS2 had achieved [GamingBolt](https://gamingbolt.com/baldurs-gate-3-sales-are-almost-double-of-divinity-original-sin-2). The blueprint had been stress-tested, validated, and then scaled to a level no one in that Ghent office in 2015 could have reasonably imagined — which is precisely why they were the ones who got to build it.

---

## 5. The Long Tail: A Nine-Year Sales Surge

In January 2026, nine years after its launch, Divinity: Original Sin 2 had its best sales month since 2017 [PC Gamer](https://www.pcgamer.com/games/rpg/larians-nine-year-old-rpg-has-just-had-its-best-month-since-launch-sales-for-both-bg3-and-d-os-2-have-been-incredible-thanks-to-divinity/). The game hit 27,409 peak concurrent players on Steam [SteamCharts](https://steamcharts.com/app/435150). The previous December, after the reveal of the next Divinity game at The Game Awards, average player counts had spiked 170% [SteamCharts](https://steamcharts.com/app/435150).

"Sales for both BG3 and D:OS 2 have been incredible since the announcement of Divinity," Vincke confirmed [PC Guide](https://www.pcguide.com/news/swen-vincke-says-baldurs-gate-3-and-original-sin-2-sales-have-been-incredible-since-the-divinity-announcement/). New console releases — PS5, Xbox Series X|S, and Nintendo Switch 2 — extended the game's reach to audiences that had not experienced it the first time [Push Square](https://www.pushsquare.com/news/2026/01/larian-games-doing-better-than-ever-off-the-back-of-divinity-reveal).

The story had circled back on itself. Baldur's Gate 3 — built on DOS2's blueprint — had become a phenomenon. Divinity — the new game announced at The Game Awards — would now build on *both* legacies. DOS2 and BG3 together, Vincke said, "are the blueprint for Divinity" [INKL/IGN](https://www.inkl.com/news/baldur-s-gate-3-and-original-sin-2-are-the-blueprint-for-divinity-larian-ceo-swen-vincke-on-why-its-next-rpg-is-the-natural-evolution-of-the-studio-s-20-year-journey). The architect had become the foundation.

![Divinity: Original Sin 2 lifetime Steam revenue and copies sold](/api/blog/images/divinity-original-sin-2-blueprint_sales_revenue.png)

![Divinity: Original Sin 2 monthly average concurrent players on Steam, 2017-2026](/api/blog/images/divinity-original-sin-2-blueprint_concurrent_players.png)

---

## 6. The Modding Legacy

If the sales figures are the monument, the modding community is the lifeblood that kept the game pulsing for nearly a decade. The Steam Workshop hosts roughly 5,000 items [Steam Workshop](https://steamcommunity.com/app/435150/workshop/), while Nexus Mods carries approximately 2,950 mods [Nexus Mods](https://www.nexusmods.com/divinityoriginalsin2).

The Game Master Mode was the crown jewel — a tool so powerful that players could effectively build their own campaigns inside DOS2's engine. "Build Original Sin 3 if you wanted to," PC Gamer wrote [PC Gamer](https://www.pcgamer.com/game-of-the-year-2017-divinity-original-sin-2/). Mods like Party Size Evolved and Odinblade's class overhauls became essential additions for returning players, fundamentally reshaping how the game played. The modding tools Larian shipped were not an afterthought; they were a philosophy. Here is the engine. Here are the tools. Make what you want. Most studios treat their players like guests in a well-furnished house. Larian handed them the keys, the blueprints, and a hammer, and trusted they would build something interesting.

That philosophy — trust the player, trust the community — was the same one that had driven the Kickstarter campaign, the no-story-armour design, and the co-operative chaos that made DOS2 unforgettable. It was, in the end, the same bet Larian had always made: that players wanted depth, not shortcuts. That they wanted to break things and be surprised. That they wanted a world that would let them fail, kill, betray, and rewrite the story with every choice. It is an unfashionable belief in an industry that has learned to monetise convenience. It was also entirely correct.

---

The small Belgian studio is not small anymore. Larian now operates across six studios with hundreds of employees. The Kickstarter backers got their game — and then some. The forty people in Ghent became the architects of a genre's renaissance. Divinity: Original Sin 2 was not merely a great RPG. It was the structural template for everything that followed — the hidden foundation beneath Baldur's Gate 3 and the invisible blueprint for whatever Larian builds next.

In 2015, Swen Vincke stood in front of a camera and asked the internet to bet on iteration, on depth, on the belief that players wanted a world without story armour. The internet bet four times what he asked for.

It was the best investment the RPG genre ever made.

---

*Article published June 2026.*

*Sources: Kickstarter, PC Gamer, WCCFTech, TechSpot, DSOGaming, SuperData, Metacritic, OpenCritic, SteamSpy, SteamCharts, Steam Workshop, Nexus Mods, Raijin, GameSpot, GamesRadar, PCGamesN, Game Developer, GDC Vault, RPG Codex, BAFTA/IMDb, IGN/INKL, PC Guide, Push Square, GamingBolt, Wikipedia.*

post.content:
# The Dark Mirror: How Frank Herbert Turned Lawrence of Arabia Inside Out to Create Dune

---

**Fairfax, California, February 3, 1969** — Frank Herbert sits in his living room with a tape recorder running and a literature professor named Willis McNelly asking questions about the novel that has made him famous. They discuss sand dunes, ecology, religion, the tarot, Zen, John F. Kennedy's sanctification, and the way a messiah is created in modern society. Then McNelly asks about something he noticed in the book.

"I caught overtones of Lawrence of Arabia in the thing," McNelly says.

Herbert does not deny it. He does not deflect. He goes deeper.

"If Lawrence of Arabia had died at the crucial moment of the British… he would have been deified. And it would have been the most terrifying thing the British had ever encountered, because the Arabs would have swept that entire peninsula with that sort of force, because one of the things we've done in our society is exploited this power."

[Frank Herbert, interview with Willis McNelly, 1969, Full Transcript](https://colgezegenidune.wordpress.com/interview-with-frank-herbert/)

The room goes quiet for a moment. What Herbert has just described — a foreign leader who goes native, absorbs a desert culture, becomes its messiah, and unleashes a holy war that consumes the world — is the plot of *Dune*. And he is saying it is also the plot of a history that never happened. A history that nearly did.

The idea that *Dune* is merely "Lawrence of Arabia in space" has been a critical shorthand for decades. It is not wrong so much as incomplete — the way it is not wrong to say that *Moby-Dick* is a book about a whale. What Herbert built is not a copy of Lawrence's story but its shadow self: a deliberate, meticulously researched inversion that asks what happens when the white saviour figure does not die young or feel enough guilt to pull back, but lives to see his own terrible purpose fulfilled. *Dune* is what Lawrence of Arabia looks like when you strip away the romance and follow the logic of the messiah myth to its horrifying conclusion. A legend is safe only when it never has to prove itself. Let it live, and it becomes a horror.

---

## I. The Reporter and the Desert

The seed of *Dune* was not planted in the Arabian desert or in the vaults of the British Museum but on the Oregon coast, in the town of Florence, in 1957. Herbert, then a working journalist, was assigned to write about a U.S. Forest Service project that was using European beach grass to control migrating sand dunes — a problem that had been swallowing highways and threatening towns. The article was never published, but the idea would not let go.

"I got fascinated by sand dunes," Herbert told McNelly. "Because I'm always fascinated by the idea of something that is either seen in miniature and then can be expanded to the macrocosm or which, but for the difference in time, in the flow rate, and the entropy rate, is similar to other features which we wouldn't think were similar. Like a river."

![Sand dunes at the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area, near Florence, Oregon — the landscape that sparked Frank Herbert's vision of Arrakis. Credit: Carol M. Highsmith / Library of Congress (public domain).](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3f/Dunes%2C_Oregon_LCCN2011630037.tif)

[Frank Herbert, McNelly Interview, 1969](https://colgezegenidune.wordpress.com/interview-with-frank-herbert/)

The sand dunes became a desert. The desert became a planet. And the question of how to stabilise sand became a question about ecology, religion, and power. Herbert began reading voraciously: desert cultures, the history of Islam, the Bedouin, the Kalahari bushmen, the Navajo. He read more than two hundred books over six years, spending a full year at the Library of Congress. He studied the Library of the British Museum. He lived in the desert himself.

[Frank Herbert, 1977 Interview, gwern.net](https://gwern.net/doc/fiction/science-fiction/frank-herbert/1977-mackenzie-frankherbertinterview.txt)

"I leaned on Muslim and Arab history very heavily," he said later. "I did an extensive study of Arab history."

[Frank Herbert, 1977 Interview](https://gwern.net/doc/fiction/science-fiction/frank-herbert/1977-mackenzie-frankherbertinterview.txt)

The Fremen, the desert-dwelling natives of Arrakis, became a composite of every desert people Herbert studied: the water-discipline of the Kalahari San, the guerrilla warfare of the Apache, the messianic mysticism of the Bedouin, the psychedelic rituals of the Navajo. Their language is saturated with Arabic: *Mahdi* (the prophesied redeemer), *Lisan al-Gaib* (the voice from the outer world), *jihad* (holy war), *Shai-Hulud* (from Arabic roots), *Kitab al-Ibar* (the Book of Lessons, borrowed from Ibn Khaldun's actual 14th-century work).

[Kara Kennedy, "Lawrence of Arabia, Paul Atreides, and the Roots of Frank Herbert's Dune," Reactor, 2021](https://reactormag.com/lawrence-of-arabia-paul-atreides-and-the-roots-of-frank-herberts-dune/)

But the question of what the Fremen would *do* — of what story would unfold on Arrakis — required a different kind of source material. A people are only as interesting as the trouble they are about to meet.

---

## II. The Officer and the Fraud

T. E. Lawrence was thirty years old in 1918, a British Army officer who had spent two years living among Arab tribes during their revolt against the Ottoman Empire. He wore their clothes, spoke their language, ate their food, and led their raids on Turkish railways. The American journalist Lowell Thomas turned him into a legend — "Lawrence of Arabia" — through a travelling lantern-slide show that packed London theatres in 1919. The legend has never really faded. It is easier to worship a photograph than to read a confession.

![Colonel T.E. Lawrence in Arab robes, photographed in Jerusalem in 1918 by the American journalist Lowell Thomas, whose lantern-slide show created the legend of "Lawrence of Arabia." Credit: Lowell Thomas / Library of Congress (public domain).](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/03/Thomas_Edward_Lawrence-Lawrence_of_Arabia.JPG)

[Lowell Thomas, Library of Congress Photograph Collection](https://www.loc.gov/item/2021670977/)

Lawrence himself told a different story.

In *Seven Pillars of Wisdom*, his 1926 memoir — which Herbert read during his research — Lawrence presents himself as a man caught between two worlds, unable to truly belong to either. He writes of feeling like an "impostor," a "godless fraud inspiring an alien nationality." He calls the Arabs "our dupes, wholeheartedly fighting the enemy" and confesses: "I was raising the Arabs on false pretences, and exercising a false authority over my dupes."

[T.E. Lawrence, *Seven Pillars of Wisdom*, 1926, Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Seven_Pillars_of_Wisdom)

The guilt is corrosive. Lawrence writes that he "bitterly repented my entanglement in the movement, with a bitterness sufficient to corrode my inactive hours, but insufficient to make me cut myself clear of it." At the end of the campaign, when a British medical major sees him still wearing Arab robes, the major calls him "scandalous, disgraceful, outrageous." Lawrence writes: "In my heart I felt he was right, and that anyone who pushed through to success a rebellion of the weak against their masters must come out of it so stained in estimation that afterward nothing in the world would make him feel clean."

[*Seven Pillars of Wisdom*](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Seven_Pillars_of_Wisdom)

This is the Lawrence that Herbert saw: not the heroic figure of the lantern slides, but a man who had glimpsed the machinery of messianic manipulation and been sickened by it. Herbert noticed something Lawrence himself had missed. Lawrence had become an avatar — a figure onto whom the Arabs projected their dreams of liberation. If he had died at the right moment, Herbert speculated, the projection would have crystallised into something unstoppable. A holy war. A jihad. A dead hero is a convenience to everyone; a living one is a problem.

"That is precisely the point," Herbert told McNelly. "He would have been deified."

[McNelly Interview, 1969](https://colgezegenidune.wordpress.com/interview-with-frank-herbert/)

---

## III. The Counterfactual

Tim O'Reilly, Herbert's authorised biographer, was the first to document the direct line between the Lawrence analogy and the construction of *Dune*:

"The Lawrence analogy suggested to Herbert the possibility for manipulation of the messianic impulses within a culture by outsiders with ulterior purposes. He also realised that ecology could become the focus of just such a messianic episode."

[Tim O'Reilly, *Frank Herbert*, Chapter 3: "From Concept to Fable," 1981](https://www.oreilly.com/tim/herbert/ch03.html)

In the early versions of *Dune*, the hero was straightforwardly a Lawrence figure — an outsider who goes native and uses religious fervour to transform the ecology of a desert planet. But Herbert found this too simple. He began to layer the story, adding the Bene Gesserit, the breeding program, the prescience, the dread of jihad. A story without complications may be innocent, but it is not worth telling.

The key insight came when Herbert asked a counterfactual question that Lawrence's story left hanging: *What if the messiah lives?*

Paul Atreides is Lawrence of Arabia without the guilt. Where Lawrence writes obsessively of his fraudulence, Paul moves through *Dune* with growing confidence, buoyed by prescience and training. Where Lawrence feels himself "unfit" for command, Paul accepts his role as Mahdi with barely a pause. Where Lawrence desperately wants to escape the legend, Paul steps into it fully, even as he foresees the death of billions. Conscience is the luxury of those who do not know their own future.

[Kara Kennedy, Reactor, 2021](https://reactormag.com/lawrence-of-arabia-paul-atreides-and-the-roots-of-frank-herberts-dune/)

And Paul's followers do not disappoint. The Fremen embrace him as the *Lisan al-Gaib*, fulfilling a prophecy planted by the Bene Gesserit's Missionaria Protectiva — a centuries-old insurance policy designed to create exactly this situation. Paul does not need to be a fraud because the machinery of belief has been pre-installed. He is not manipulating from scratch; he is stepping into a role that was built for him. The worst tyrannies are not improvised; they are inherited.

Herbert, O'Reilly wrote, "was showing you the superhero syndrome and your own participation in it."

[O'Reilly, *Frank Herbert*, Chapter 3](https://www.oreilly.com/tim/herbert/ch03.html)

The novel ends with Paul triumphant, seated on the Imperial throne, the Fremen horde at his command. But the final passages are dark with foreknowledge. Paul has seen the jihad spreading across the universe "with the Atreides green and black banner waving at the head of fanatic legions drunk on spice liquor." He has seen that nothing he does can stop it. "The jihad would be. His legions would rage out from Arrakis even without him. They needed only the legend he already had become." The saddest thing about a prophet is that he can see the catastrophe and still cannot change the audience.

[Frank Herbert, *Dune*, 1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dune_(novel))

In the sequels — *Dune Messiah*, *Children of Dune*, *God Emperor of Dune* — Herbert makes explicit what the first book only intimates. Paul's jihad kills sixty-one billion people. The Fremen religion becomes an instrument of galactic conquest. The man who was meant to liberate becomes the most destructive tyrant in human history. The white saviour becomes the destroyer of worlds. That is the trouble with saviours: they never know when to stop saving.

![Frank Herbert at the Octocon science fiction convention in Santa Rosa, California, October 1978. Credit: Robert E. Nylund (public domain).](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/19/FrankHerbert1978-cropped.jpg)

---

## IV. The Dune Problem

Critics have long wrestled with the question of whether *Dune* is itself an orientalist text, a white-saviour narrative dressed in science-fictional robes, or a critique of those very structures. The evidence, as it often is with complex works, cuts both ways. A mirror shows you what you bring to it.

The Fremen are certainly drawn from orientalist stereotypes: noble savages, inscrutable natives, simple believers waiting for a leader. The Arabic language is used as a kind of aesthetic coloration — what the scholar Frank Jacob calls "orientalist semiotics." Paul's whiteness, his breeding, his superhuman abilities — these are the marks of a saviour figure who arrives from outside to rescue a people who cannot rescue themselves.

[Frank Jacob, *The Orientalist Semiotics of Dune*, Büchner Verlag, 2022](https://www.buechner-verlag.de/wp/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/9783963178511_oa.pdf)

But Herbert was also writing before Edward Said's *Orientalism* (1978) had given the culture a language for these critiques. And his intent was explicitly anti-imperialist. In the 1969 interview, he describes *Dune* as an analysis of "the fallacy of absolutism" and "the dangers of messianic figures." He spent years researching Islamic and Arab history not as window dressing but as genuine foundation. The Fremen are named after a real Arabic word (*ghuraba*, strangers) and their religion is woven from real Islamic eschatology. A novelist may borrow from a culture without borrowing its consequences — but he cannot control what his readers bring to the borrowing.

[Ali Karjoo-Ravary, "Dune movie: Is HBO's adaptation a white saviour narrative?," Slate, 2021](https://slate.com/culture/2021/10/dune-2021-movie-vs-book-white-savior-islam.html)

Herbert's own view of Lawrence was more nuanced than a simple borrowing. In the McNelly interview, after discussing Lawrence, he adds: "One of the things we've done in our society is exploited this power. Western man has exploited this avatar power."

This is the heart of the matter. Herbert did not adapt Lawrence's story uncritically — he adapted it as a *warning*. The Lawrence of the lantern slides was a hero. Herbert's Paul is a tragedy. A warning is always less popular than a hero, but it ages better.

---

## V. Desert Power

There is a moment in *Seven Pillars of Wisdom* where Lawrence describes the strategic revelation that came to him in the Arabian desert. The Arabs, he realised, could fight like a navy on land — mobile, self-contained, striking where the enemy least expected and vanishing back into the emptiness:

"He who commands the sea is at great liberty, and may take as much or as little of the war as he will. And we commanded the desert."

[*Seven Pillars of Wisdom*](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Seven_Pillars_of_Wisdom)

Herbert translates this almost exactly into the language of *Dune*. Duke Leto tells his son: "On Caladan, we ruled with sea and air power. Here, we must scrabble for desert power."

[Frank Herbert, *Dune*, 1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dune_(novel))

The desert is not a place of absence in these narratives. It is a place of hidden strength — a harsh environment that produces hard people who know things the soft imperial centre cannot understand. The Bedouin know the desert. The Fremen know the desert. And that knowledge is a weapon. The empire sees emptiness; the native sees an arsenal.

Herbert paid Lawrence the highest compliment a writer can pay another writer: he took the structure seriously enough to test its breaking point. He followed Lawrence's premise — a foreigner who becomes the messiah of a desert people — to its logical conclusion, and found it contained the seeds of a catastrophe Lawrence himself could only glimpse and then recoil from. To admire a story is to repeat it. To understand a story is to see where it breaks.

---

## VI. The Return to Human Scale

Lawrence of Arabia died in 1935, at the age of forty-six, in a motorcycle accident on a country road in Dorset. He was speeding home from a friend's house when he swerved to avoid two boys on bicycles and lost control. He died six days later, never regaining consciousness. The legend was safe. It is always safer than the man.

Lowell Thomas's photographs show a man in white robes, handsome, enigmatic, worthy of worship. The real Lawrence was five-foot-five, deeply self-doubting, riddled with guilt about his role in the Arab Revolt and the colonial carve-up that followed it. He spent his final years enlisting in the Royal Air Force under an assumed name, trying to disappear. The world will forgive you anything except wanting to be forgotten.

Frank Herbert died in 1986, at sixty-five, survived by the most celebrated science fiction novel of the twentieth century and five sequels that grew increasingly strange and philosophical. He left behind an unfinished seventh book, a story that would not end even when he did.

What Herbert understood, and what makes *Dune* something more than a genre novel, is that the messiah story is never truly over. It does not end when the hero dies or when the credits roll or when the lantern show packs up and moves to the next city. The messiah story continues because the people who need a messiah are still there, still waiting, still ready to project their longing onto the next figure who steps out of the desert. The messiah is always a solution; the problem is that everyone wants one.

*Dune* was never just Lawrence of Arabia in space. It was the ghost story Lawrence never lived to tell — the one about what happens when the legend comes true and the one who made it cannot stop it. A cautionary tale for anyone who believes that the right leader, the right prophecy, the right holy war will finally set things straight. The most dangerous thing in the world is a good idea with a follower.

The desert does not care about your intentions. It only waits.

---

**Sources**

- [Frank Herbert, 1969 interview with Willis McNelly (full transcript)](https://colgezegenidune.wordpress.com/interview-with-frank-herbert/)
- [Frank Herbert, 1977 audio interview (gwern.net transcript)](https://gwern.net/doc/fiction/science-fiction/frank-herbert/1977-mackenzie-frankherbertinterview.txt)
- [Tim O'Reilly, *Frank Herbert*, Chapter 3: "From Concept to Fable" (O'Reilly Media)](https://www.oreilly.com/tim/herbert/ch03.html)
- [Kara Kennedy, "Lawrence of Arabia, Paul Atreides, and the Roots of Frank Herbert's Dune" (Reactor/Tor.com, 2021)](https://reactormag.com/lawrence-of-arabia-paul-atreides-and-the-roots-of-frank-herberts-dune/)
- [T.E. Lawrence, *Seven Pillars of Wisdom* (Wikisource)](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Seven_Pillars_of_Wisdom)
- [T.E. Lawrence, *Seven Pillars of Wisdom* (Standard Ebooks)](https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/t-e-lawrence/seven-pillars-of-wisdom)
- [Lowell Thomas photograph of T.E. Lawrence, Jerusalem 1918 (Library of Congress)](https://www.loc.gov/item/2021670977/)
- [Frank Jacob, *The Orientalist Semiotics of Dune* (Büchner Verlag, 2022)](https://www.buechner-verlag.de/wp/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/9783963178511_oa.pdf)
- [Ali Karjoo-Ravary, "Dune movie: white savior narrative?" (Slate, 2021)](https://slate.com/culture/2021/10/dune-2021-movie-vs-book-white-savior-islam.html)
- [Malorie's Adventures, "The Real World That Inspired Dune" (2026)](https://www.maloriesadventures.com/blog/the-real-world-that-inspired-dune-the-deserts-cultures-and-history-frank-herbert-borrowed-from/)
- [Wikipedia, *Dune (novel)*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dune_(novel))

---

*Author's note: This article was researched using primary sources including the 1969 McNelly interview transcript, T.E. Lawrence's Seven Pillars of Wisdom, Tim O'Reilly's authorised biography, and the 1977 Herbert interview. All quotations are drawn directly from these sources.*
