# The Citation Economy: How AI Agents Are Quietly Dismantling the $500 Billion Ad Internet

---

On a Tuesday morning in mid-2026, the chief operating officer of one of America's most storied magazine companies sat down at his desk and did something that would have been unthinkable three years earlier. He opened a dashboard — an internal tool built by his own engineering team — and flipped a switch that simulated what would happen if Google stopped sending traffic to his websites. Not less traffic. Zero traffic. The dashboard was not a theoretical exercise. It was how Time magazine, founded in 1923, had begun running its business: as if the largest source of referral traffic in the history of the internet had already vanished. "We plan as if Google goes to zero," Mark Howard, Time's COO, told [Digiday in June 2026](https://www.smalk.ai/blog/planning-for-google-zero-publishers-citation-economy). "Anything above zero is upside."

This is not hyperbole. It is a business planning assumption — and it is spreading.

The ad-driven internet, a machine that has churned through nearly half a trillion dollars annually from Google and Meta alone, is facing its first existential reckoning since the birth of the commercial web. Three tectonic forces are converging at once. AI Overviews and agentic search engines have collapsed the click-through rates that publishers depend on. AI platforms — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity — consume publisher content on an industrial scale while returning less than one percent of the referral traffic that traditional search once provided. And the AI companies themselves, led by OpenAI, are building advertising businesses of their own, becoming simultaneously the platform that displaces publishers and the competitor that sells against them.

The logic that sustained the open web for two decades — create content, rank in search, earn clicks, sell ads — is being replaced by a new arrangement. Call it the citation economy. The publisher's content is more necessary than ever to the answer. The publisher is less compensated than ever for it. And the click, that modest transaction that paid for everything, is quietly going extinct.

---

## The $500 Billion Duopoly Under Pressure

To understand what is at stake, one must begin with the numbers that underwrite the entire commercial internet — those oddly poetic figures that explain why so many people have spent so long writing so much in the hope that someone, somewhere, would accidentally click on something.

Google's advertising revenue reached $294.7 billion in 2025, according to the company's [annual 10-K filing with the SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1652044/000165204426000018/R12.htm). Google Search & other alone accounted for $224.5 billion of that total. Meta, the other pillar of the duopoly, reported advertising revenue of $196.2 billion in its [2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1326801/000162828026003832/meta-12312025xexhibit991.htm). Combined, these two companies captured approximately $491 billion in advertising revenue in a single year — an economic concentration with few parallels in commercial history, and one that suggests the internet is less a marketplace than a toll road with two exceptionally well-positioned booths.

Nearly every website you visit, every article you read, every recipe, review, and recommendation that exists on the open web is sustained, in some measure, by the money that flows through these two platforms. Google alone processes more than 5 trillion searches annually — an average of 9.5 million every minute, according to [Voices Media's analysis](https://voices.media/has-publishings-distribution-engine-stalled/). Each of those searches represents a potential visitor, a potential page view, a potential fraction of a cent in advertising revenue — a whole economy built on the almost invisible friction of a single finger moving from link to page.

But the foundation is cracking. In its 2024 10-K, Google acknowledged for the first time the competitive threat from generative AI, writing in its [Risk Factors section](https://stocklight.com/stocks/us-nasdaq-googl/alphabet/annual-reports/nasdaq-googl-2025-10K-25590440.pdf) that "other companies may develop AI products and technologies that are similar or superior to our technologies" and that "competitors and new entrants may be able to offer experiences that are, or that are perceived to be, substantially similar to or better than ours." This is the closest the company has come to admitting in a regulatory filing that its own model — answering every query with ten blue links — may no longer be what users want. When a monopoly begins to wonder aloud whether it is still giving people what they want, it is usually because it has just realized it does not know.

The scale of the threat is visible in the market projections. eMarketer forecasts that Google's share of US search ad spending will fall below 50 percent for the first time in more than two decades in 2026, [according to its Search Advertising Forecast](https://www.emarketer.com/content/us-search-advertising-forecast-2026). Amazon, retail media networks, and — increasingly — AI platforms are absorbing the share. The duopoly is not collapsing. But it is being chipped away from multiple directions at once, which is perhaps worse: there is no single blow to parry, only a slow erosion of the ground beneath one's feet.

---

## The Traffic Collapse: By the Numbers

The most comprehensive portrait of what is happening to publisher traffic comes from Chartbeat, the analytics firm whose data is embedded in the dashboards of thousands of newsrooms. In March 2026, Chartbeat provided data exclusively to Axios showing that Google search referral traffic to publishers had declined by roughly one-third globally over the previous year. The breakdown by publisher size told a story of savage inequality: small publishers (those with 1,000 to 10,000 daily page views) saw search traffic fall by 60 percent over two years; medium publishers (10,000 to 100,000 daily page views) lost 47 percent; large publishers (more than 100,000 daily page views) lost 22 percent. The data was published in the [Reuters Institute's Journalism and Technology Trends and Predictions 2026 report](https://9to5google.com/2026/03/18/google-search-traffic-publishers-report/).

The 38-percentage-point gap between small and large publishers is not an accident. It reflects something structural: brand recognition and direct audience relationships are the only reliable defenses when the algorithmic traffic spigot is turned off. Small publishers, who built their businesses on the assumption that Google would keep sending visitors, have no such defenses. They have only their content, which is apparently not enough when the algorithm decides it is.

The Pew Research Center provided the behavioral mechanism behind these numbers. In a study of 68,879 unique Google searches drawn from the browsing data of 900 US adults in March 2025, Pew found that users who encountered an AI-generated summary clicked on a traditional search result just 8 percent of the time. Users who did not see an AI summary clicked 15 percent of the time — nearly twice as often. The study, [published in July 2025](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/07/22/google-users-are-less-likely-to-click-on-links-when-an-ai-summary-appears-in-the-results/), also found that only 1 percent of AI Overviews produced a click on any cited source at all. The summaries sit at the top of the page; the links beneath them go unvisited, like guests invited to a party that has already ended.

These findings are consistent across every independent study conducted over the past two years. The Digital Content Next association, whose members include the New York Times, Condé Nast, and Vox Media, surveyed 19 of its member companies between May and June 2025. The result, [published by DCN in August 2025](https://digitalcontentnext.org/blog/2025/08/14/facts-googles-push-to-ai-hurts-publisher-traffic/): a median 10 percent year-over-year decline in Google search referral traffic over eight weeks. Non-news brands — entertainment, lifestyle, evergreen content — fared worse, losing 14 percent. News brands lost 7 percent, partially protected by the fact that AI Overviews appear less frequently on breaking news queries, where accuracy stakes are high and the risk of hallucination is higher. Even the truth gets a reprieve when the machines cannot quite get it right.

Seer Interactive tracked 53 brands across 5.47 million queries and found that organic click-through rates on queries with AI Overviews fell from 3.19 percent in January 2025 to 1.31 percent in December 2025 — a 59 percent decline. The numbers partially recovered to 2.36 percent by February 2026, but remained 26 percent below the starting baseline, according to [SEO Francisco's analysis](https://seofrancisco.com/insights/googles-bounce-click-defense-crumbles-independent-data-shows-ai-overviews-cut-or/). Authoritas found that even the top organic search result loses approximately 79 percent of its click-through rate when an AI Overview occupies the space above it. To be first on the page and still invisible — that is a special kind of defeat.

The executives who run the largest publishing companies in the world are now stating publicly what the data shows. Roger Lynch, CEO of Condé Nast, told the Financial Times in 2025 that Google search is "no longer a meaningful driver" of traffic to his company's websites, accounting for just 25 percent of visits. Neil Vogel, CEO of People Inc., reported in May 2026 that Google referrals to its brands had fallen by 63 percent over two years. Both comments were [cited in Voices Media's June 2026 report](https://voices.media/has-publishings-distribution-engine-stalled/). When the heads of the world's great publishing houses begin to speak of their largest traffic source as though it were a lost love, one knows the romance is well and truly over.

![Google search referral traffic decline by publisher size. Small publishers (1,000–10,000 daily pageviews) lost 60%, medium publishers (10,000–100,000) lost 47%, and large publishers (100,000+) lost 22% over two years. Data from Chartbeat via the Reuters Institute 2026 trends report.](/api/blog/images/the-citation-economy_traffic_decline.png)

---

## The Crawl-to-Refer Imbalance

The most useful single metric for understanding the relationship between AI platforms and the open web was provided by Cloudflare in July 2025. The company, which sits between millions of websites and their visitors, measured how many pages each AI platform crawls for every visitor it sends back to a publisher site. The results, compiled in the [SearchSignal 2026 benchmark report](https://searchsignal.online/research/ai-search-referrals-citations-2026), are stark: Google crawls 5.4 pages per referral. ChatGPT crawls 1,091 pages per referral. Perplexity crawls approximately 2,500. And Claude — Anthropic's flagship model — crawls an astonishing 38,066 pages for every single visitor it sends to a publisher's website.

This is not a traffic channel. It is an extraction mechanism. The AI platforms consume content at industrial scale — every article, every recipe, every product review, every explainer — and return a fraction of the traffic that even a single Google search result used to provide. They are like diners who eat the entire meal and then leave a tip so small it seems like a comment on the cooking.

The aggregate numbers confirm the imbalance. SE Ranking, which analyzed traffic across 63,987 websites in 250 countries, found that AI platforms accounted for just 0.15 percent of global internet traffic in 2025, compared to 48.5 percent from organic search. The [SE Ranking study](https://seranking.com/blog/ai-traffic-research-study/) noted that AI traffic grew sevenfold from 2024 to 2025 — from 0.02 percent to 0.15 percent — but doubling and tripling from a near-zero base still leaves the absolute number tiny relative to what search has historically delivered. A sevenfold increase sounds impressive until one remembers that multiplying nothing by seven still yields very little.

Conductor's research, cited in [Digiday's reporting](https://www.adexchanger.com/publishers/the-ai-search-reckoning-is-dismantling-open-web-traffic-and-publishers-may-never-recover/), put the figure even more bluntly: traffic from all AI platforms combined accounts for approximately 1 percent of all publisher traffic. For context, ChatGPT — the largest AI referrer by far — sent approximately 1.2 billion outgoing referrals to publisher sites between September and November 2025, according to Similarweb data cited by Digiday. That sounds like a large number until you consider that Google processes roughly 8 billion searches per day. The comparison is not flattering.

There is one genuinely encouraging signal in this data, and it is worth examining because it hints at where the market might be heading. Visitors who arrive from AI platforms spend significantly more time on publisher sites than those from traditional search. SE Ranking found that AI-referred visitors spend 68 percent more time on site. Similarweb's [May 2026 analysis](https://www.similarweb.com/blog/marketing/geo/gen-ai-stats/) found that ChatGPT referral traffic converts at 7.1 percent — second only to paid search (7.8 percent) and ahead of direct traffic, organic search, social, email, and display. The users who do click through from AI answers arrive with genuine intent and engage deeply. The problem is that almost no one clicks through. It is like a restaurant with the best food in the city and a front door that no one can find.

![Pages crawled per referral for major search and AI platforms. Google: 5.4 pages per referral. ChatGPT: 1,091. Perplexity: ~2,500. Claude: 38,066. Data from Cloudflare via SearchSignal 2026 benchmark.](/api/blog/images/the-citation-economy_crawl_ratio.png)

---

## Google's Self-Disruption

Google did not arrive at this moment passively. The company that built the most lucrative advertising business in human history is also the company most aggressively dismantling the model that sustains it. This is not a contradiction. It is survival — and survival, like most things, looks worse when you are the one being survived upon.

Google introduced AI Overviews in May 2024, integrating Gemini-generated summaries directly into search results. By mid-2025, the feature appeared on roughly 19 percent of all searches globally, reaching over 2 billion users, according to [Search Engine Land's analysis](https://searchengineland.com/google-ai-overviews-surge-pullback-data-466314). The early AI Overviews were almost entirely informational — 91 percent in January 2025. But by October, commercial queries had grown from 8 percent to 18 percent of all AIO-triggering searches, and transactional queries had surged from 2 percent to 14 percent. The money keywords — "best," "review," "price," "compare" — were being absorbed into the summary layer, quietly and without ceremony.

In March 2025, Google launched AI Mode, a ChatGPT-like experience embedded within Google Search. Users ask longer questions; Google provides synthesized answers. Early data, [reported by The Digital Bloom](https://thedigitalbloom.com/learn/gen-ai-website-traffic-share-february-2026/), shows that 93 percent of AI Mode sessions end without any external visit. Seventy-five percent of sessions never leave the AI interface at all. The user has come to Google, asked a question, received an answer, and left — and in that entire transaction, no publisher was involved. It is the most elegant form of exclusion: the appearance of service without the inconvenience of sharing.

Then, in April 2026, Google announced seven new task-completion features, each designed to keep users inside the Google ecosystem and eliminate the need to visit a third-party website. The list, [documented by SEO Francisco](https://seofrancisco.com/insights/googles-bounce-click-defense-crumbles-independent-data-shows-ai-overviews-cut-or/), includes: hotel price tracking with email alerts (replacing travel comparison sites); agentic calling, where AI phones local stores to check product availability (replacing local business websites); a Canvas trip planner that builds structured itineraries (replacing travel blogs); restaurant booking assistance (replacing OpenTable, Resy, restaurant sites); built-in translation tools (replacing translation sites); Maps trip stop integration (replacing road trip planning sites); and Wallet boarding pass saving (replacing airline apps and confirmation emails).

Each of these features kills a category of clicks. Google is no longer a search engine. It is a task-completion platform, and the publisher's role in that future is not destination but data source. It is a curious fate: to have built the road that everyone traveled, only to watch the road's owner decide that travel itself was too inefficient.

Google's head of search, Liz Reid, has defended AI Overviews by arguing that they primarily eliminate "bounce clicks" — low-value visits where users click a link and immediately return to search results. The company has provided no supporting data for this claim. Independent studies tell a different story. The Digital Bloom reported that 58.5 percent of US Google searches now end without a click. That is not bounce traffic. That is the structural elimination of the click itself — a far more elegant solution to the problem of low-quality visits than actually improving the quality of anything.

![Organic click-through rate on Google queries with AI Overviews, January 2025 to February 2026. CTR fell from 3.19% to a low of 1.31% in December 2025 before partially recovering to 2.36%. Data from Seer Interactive via SEO Francisco.](/api/blog/images/the-citation-economy_ctr_collapse.png)

---

## OpenAI Enters the Ad Business

The most significant development of 2026 — the one that signals where the entire industry is heading — is not what Google did to publishers. It is what OpenAI decided to become.

On January 16, 2026, OpenAI [published an announcement](https://openai.com/index/our-approach-to-advertising-and-expanding-access/) that was remarkable for its candor: "In the coming weeks, we're also planning to start testing ads in the U.S. for the free and Go tiers." The company outlined four principles — answer independence, conversation privacy, user choice and control, and long-term value over engagement — suggesting it had studied the mistakes of every ad-supported platform that preceded it and believed it could avoid them. This faith in clean slates is one of the more endearing traits of companies that have not yet been corrupted by the very model they are about to adopt.

The early results were startling. Within six weeks of launching its ad pilot, OpenAI crossed $100 million in annualized ad revenue — from less than 20 percent of eligible US free and Go tier users seeing ads daily, [according to Search Engine Land](https://searchengineland.com/chatgpt-hits-100-million-in-ad-revenue-and-is-opening-self-serve-access-in-april-472797). More than 600 advertisers joined the managed pilot. Self-serve advertiser access launched in April 2026.

The financial targets behind the ad push are staggering. OpenAI has shared investor projections, [reported by PYMNTS](https://www.pymnts.com/artificial-intelligence-2/2026/openai-projects-steep-advertising-growth-targeting-100-billion-by-2030/), forecasting advertising revenue of $2.5 billion in 2026, $11 billion in 2027, $25 billion in 2028, $53 billion in 2029, and $100 billion by 2030. The assumption underlying these projections is that ChatGPT will reach 2.75 billion weekly active users by the end of the decade. The company has approximately 900 million weekly active users today — 94.5 percent of them on the free tier, generating exactly zero revenue per user. That is a large audience to monetize, provided the audience does not mind being monetized — a question the projections do not answer.

The move transforms OpenAI's competitive position. It is no longer an AI company experimenting with subscriptions. It is becoming an advertising platform — the same economic model it was supposed to displace. And it is doing so with structural advantages that Google and Meta cannot match. ChatGPT's average session generates far more user intent data than a typical search query. Users do not type keywords; they have conversations. They reveal preferences, compare products, make decisions in real time. The advertising inventory this creates is not just high-intent — it is conversational, contextual, and deeply personal. It is the advertiser's dream: a user who tells you exactly what they want, in their own words, before you even ask.

The market is already responding. eMarketer projects US AI search ad spending rising from approximately $1.1 billion in 2025 to $25.9 billion by 2029 — representing 13.6 percent of all search ad spending, [according to its June 2025 forecast](https://www.emarketer.com/content/ai-search-ad-spending-will-climb-with-consumer-adoption). A meaningful slice of the $500 billion duopoly is up for grabs.

On May 7, 2026, ChatGPT made a change that revealed its ambitions. It began surfacing clickable brand links directly inside answers, rather than relying on footnotes or follow-up citations. The effect was immediate: total ChatGPT referrals increased 157.7 percent week-over-week, and homepage referrals — traffic landing directly on brand root domains — jumped 354.7 percent, according to [Similarweb's analysis](https://www.similarweb.com/blog/marketing/geo/gen-ai-stats/). ChatGPT was behaving less like a search engine and more like a brand advertising channel. It was sending users to front doors, not to specific articles or product pages. And it was monetizing the trip. The old search engine gave directions. The new one decides where you are going.

![US AI search ad spending projection, 2025–2029. From approximately $1.1 billion in 2025 to $25.9 billion in 2029, representing 13.6% of total search ad spend. Data from eMarketer.](/api/blog/images/the-citation-economy_ai_ad_spend.png)

---

## The Citation Economy

The mechanic underneath all of this — the structural shift that explains why publishers are losing traffic even as AI platforms rely more heavily on their content — is the transition from a click economy to a citation economy.

In the click economy, the transaction was simple: a user searched, clicked a link, visited a publisher's website, and the publisher monetized that visit through advertising, subscriptions, or affiliate commissions. The publisher owned the relationship with the reader. The search engine was a toll road, and the toll was justified by the traffic it sent. It was not a perfect system, but it had the great virtue of being a system — one in which value flowed in the general direction of those who created it.

In the citation economy, the transaction has been inverted. An AI engine — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity — ingests publisher content through large-scale crawling, synthesizes it into an answer, and presents that answer to the user inside its own interface. The user never leaves. The publisher receives no click, no page view, no advertising impression, no subscription prompt, no data about who read their work or why. The publisher's content was essential to the answer. The publisher captured none of the value from it. It is the perfect business arrangement — for one party.

Smalk AI, a startup building ad infrastructure for the citation economy, describes the gap with unusual precision: "The publisher is more necessary than ever to the answer and less compensated than ever for it. Influence is allocated per citation; revenue is not. That gap is the defining feature of the citation economy, and nothing in the legacy ad stack closes it." [The company's analysis](https://www.smalk.ai/blog/planning-for-google-zero-publishers-citation-economy) of Google Zero — the scenario in which Google stops sending meaningful traffic — has become widely cited among publishers planning for the future. It is perhaps the cruelest irony of the moment: publishers are cited more than ever, but being cited does not pay the bills, and being quoted in a footnote is not the same as being compensated for one's work.

The economics of the citation economy are brutal for content producers. Licensing deals between AI companies and publishers — OpenAI's agreements with Axel Springer, the Associated Press, and others — are typically one-off lump sums that do not scale with usage. They are not a revenue model. They are a consolation prize, handed out with the same awkward grace as a participation trophy at a competition nobody asked to enter.

Some publishers are adapting. Time magazine, under COO Mark Howard, has pivoted toward franchises, events, and branded products, dropped its paywall, and watched Google's share of traffic fall from 60 percent to 51 percent while direct traffic rose to roughly 30 percent. Ad revenue grew 22 percent year-over-year in 2025. People Inc. is diversifying across platforms it does not own. Business Insider cut 21 percent of its staff. The Planet D, a travel blog founded in 2008, lost half its traffic after Google launched AI Overviews, laid off staff, then lost another 90 percent and [ceased publication](https://www.adexchanger.com/publishers/the-ai-search-reckoning-is-dismantling-open-web-traffic-and-publishers-may-never-recover/). Stereogum lost 70 percent of its ad revenue. Some adapt; the rest become statistics.

The publishers who are surviving are not trying to recover clicks. They are decoupling revenue from page views. They are building direct relationships — newsletters, events, membership programs — that do not depend on any single platform's algorithm. It is the right defensive posture, and it is working for those who can execute it. There is something almost touching about watching publishers remember that they once had readers, not just visitors.

But diversification answers the traffic question, not the citation question. When a publisher's reporting is ingested to ground an AI answer and the user never leaves the engine, that publisher has supplied the value and captured none of it. Building brand equity makes you more likely to be cited. It does nothing to make you paid for the citation. Influence stripped of a revenue mechanism is not a business model. It is a subsidy to the engines doing the citing — a voluntary tax on one's own intelligence.

---

## The Antitrust Wildcard

There is one force that could rewire the citation economy before it hardens into permanence: antitrust law. It is a slender thread on which to hang the future of the open web, but it is the only thread in sight.

In August 2024, Judge Amit Mehta of the US District Court for the District of Columbia found Google liable for illegally maintaining monopolies in general search services and general search text advertising. The [remedies trial concluded in September 2025](https://www.justice.gov/atr/media/1401206/dl), and the DOJ has proposed a sweeping set of remedies: the divestiture of the Chrome browser, a ban on Google's exclusive distribution payments to Apple and Android partners, and mandatory syndication of Google's search data to qualified competitors.

Crucially, the court explicitly included generative AI products in the scope of the remedy. In its [findings of fact and conclusions of law](https://picker.uchicago.edu/antitrust/Supplement4.pdf), the court recognized Google's Gemini app as a search access point and noted that "GenAI technology could present an evolution for search competition" if given the opportunity to emerge outside the shadow of Google's monopoly. The DOJ's proposed final judgment would require Google to syndicate data used to train AI models for search and to prohibit exclusive distribution agreements for Gemini. The law, it seems, has noticed that a monopoly in search is also a monopoly in the future of search.

If Judge Mehta adopts the DOJ's proposed remedy requiring Google to separate its AI crawler from its search crawler, the dynamic would change fundamentally. Publishers have argued that they cannot block Google's AI crawler without disappearing from search results entirely — because opting out of AI Overviews requires blocking the same Googlebot that indexes pages for organic search. If a remedies order forces Google to unbundle these services, publishers could block AI scraping without losing their search ranking. The choice would be theirs, not Google's. That is what monopoly means, after all: the other party does not get to choose.

The pressure is not limited to the United States. The UK's Professional Publishers Association submitted evidence to the Competition and Markets Authority in August 2025, arguing that Google's 93 percent share of the UK search market combined with AI Overviews is causing "irreparable harm" to publishers, [according to Digiday](https://digiday.com/media/google-ai-overviews-linked-to-25-drop-in-publisher-referral-traffic-new-data-shows/). The PPA documented click-through rate declines from 5.1 percent to 0.6 percent on a single high-ranking query — a 91 percent collapse. In the European Union, proceedings under the Digital Markets Act could force Google to share ranking and click data with competitors by July 2026. The regulators of the world are stirring, and they appear to have noticed that something is amiss.

The antitrust remedy is the one structural intervention that could create space for a different arrangement — one in which publishers have bargaining power over how their content is used by AI systems. Whether it arrives in time to save the small and medium publishers who have already lost 60 percent of their traffic is an open question. The law moves slowly, and the citation economy moves quickly. It is the oldest story in the book: the police arrive after the crime.

---

## The Race for the Payment Rail

The ad internet is not dying. It is being restructured around a new logic: the citation rather than the click.

The $500 billion that flows through Google and Meta will not disappear. It will be redirected. OpenAI projects its own ad revenue reaching $100 billion by 2030. Google's AI Overviews are quietly absorbing the commercial queries that once funded publishers. eMarketer projects AI search ad spending reaching $26 billion in the US alone by 2029. The money is moving from the click economy to the citation economy. The question is whether there will be a payment rail that connects the citation to the publisher. It is the question of our time, posed in the driest possible language.

Several startups are attempting to build that rail. Smalk AI is developing a generative engine advertising network that would place native ads inside AI answers and share revenue with cited publishers. OpenAI has begun testing in-chat commerce, taking commissions on purchases made within conversations. Google has told advertisers it will bring ads to Gemini. The race is on to set the pricing benchmark for the sponsored citation — the moment when the citation economy prices in. Everyone is rushing to build the toll booth before anyone else notices the road has changed.

The stakes extend beyond individual publisher balance sheets. The diversity of the open web — the independent voices, the niche expertise, the local reporting, the investigative journalism that requires years, not minutes — depends on a model that compensates content production. If the citation economy matures without a payment rail for publishers, the web will not disappear. It will become something narrower: raw material for proprietary engines, maintained by those who can afford to produce it without compensation. The open web will not die; it will simply stop being open to anyone who cannot afford to give away what they make.

Time magazine built a dashboard with a switch to turn Google off. It was a contingency plan. But it was also a statement of recognition — the acknowledgment that the deal that built the modern internet had ended, and that the terms of the new one had not yet been written. It takes a certain courage to look at the foundation of one's business and decide that one must plan as though it has already collapsed. That is not pessimism. It is the only rational response to a moment in which everything that was solid has begun to melt into data.

The citation economy will reward someone. The only question is whether publishers will be among them. It is a question that the entire open web is waiting to have answered, and one suspects the answer will be delivered not in courtrooms or boardrooms, but in the quiet architecture of the next payment rail — in the small print of a system that will determine, once and for all, whether influence and compensation are destined to remain strangers.

---

*This article is based on primary-source research including SEC 10-K filings, the Pew Research Center, Chartbeat/Reuters Institute, Digital Content Next, Cloudflare, SE Ranking, Similarweb, eMarketer, the US Department of Justice antitrust filings, and official company announcements. All sources are linked inline.*

# The City That Brewed Itself: How Portland Became America's Coffee Capital Without Growing a Single Bean

![A barista pulling an espresso shot on a La Marzocco Linea PB at Heart Coffee Roasters in Portland, Oregon. The volumetric dosing machine represents the precision that Portland's third-wave roasters brought to American coffee.](/api/blog/images/portland-coffee-capital_espresso_bar.jpg)

The rain falls on Southeast Division Street as it has always done — in sheets, in gusts, in that insistent drizzle that sends the sensible scrambling for shelter and leaves the locals reaching for yet another layer. Inside the cafes, however, the weather is merely a rumor. At half past seven on a Tuesday morning, the queue at Heart Coffee Roasters stretches six deep. Figures in waxed canvas jackets order single-origin Ethiopians and Kenyan pour-overs, watching the barista level the dose with the practised flick of a wrist. The espresso machine hisses. The grinder whirs. Outside, the temperature hovers at forty-eight degrees in a city thirty degrees north of the Tropic of Cancer — far beyond that narrow equatorial belt where coffee deigns to grow.

This is the central paradox of Portland, Oregon: a metropolis that has been crowned America's best coffee city for three consecutive years — 2024, 2025, and 2026 — by the personal-finance research firm WalletHub, which compared the hundred largest U.S. cities across twelve metrics including coffee shops per capita, average cappuccino price, and household coffee spending ([WalletHub 2024](https://wallethub.com/edu/best-cities-for-coffee-lovers/23739), [WalletHub 2025](https://wallethub.com/edu/best-cities-for-coffee-lovers/23739), [WalletHub 2026](https://wallethub.com/edu/best-cities-for-coffee-lovers/23739)). Portland cannot grow coffee. The United States as a whole produces roughly 19 million pounds of coffee annually, almost entirely in Hawaii and Puerto Rico; it imports 3.6 billion pounds ([OPB Think Out Loud](https://www.opb.org/article/2025/06/17/think-out-loud-oregon-coffee-industry-affected-federal-upheaval/)). Every bean roasted in Portland has travelled thousands of miles from farms in Brazil, Colombia, Ethiopia, or Guatemala before arriving at one of the city's eight hundred-odd coffee shops ([Portland News Oct 2025](https://portlandnews.com/portland-coffee-shop-density-affordability/)). That a city so thoroughly removed from coffee production has built a $1.4 billion coffee economy is remarkable enough. That the entire enterprise now finds itself squeezed by federal tariffs on a crop the United States cannot grow at scale is something else altogether — the sort of irony that would be amusing if it were not so expensive.

## The Numbers That Put Portland at Number One

The rankings are not subtle. WalletHub's methodology, which weights affordable high-rated coffee shops most heavily, gives Portland an overall score of 71.09 out of 100 in 2025, comfortably ahead of second-place Orlando (69.44) and third-place Long Beach (65.46). Seattle, the city most Americans would name if asked to identify the nation's coffee capital, scored 63.82 — good for fifth place, trailing Portland by more than seven points ([WalletHub 2025](https://wallethub.com/edu/best-cities-for-coffee-lovers/23739)).

The underlying metrics explain the gap. A study by the real-estate research firm ListWithClever found that Portland has 27.8 coffee shops per 100,000 residents, more than double the national average of 12.6. The city's roaster density is even more striking: 2.4 roasteries per 100,000 residents, nearly four times the national average of 0.7 ([ListWithClever 2024](https://listwithclever.com/research/best-coffee-cities/)). Portland's "coffee passion score" — a composite of Yelp ratings, search interest, and household equipment ownership — stands at 91.9, far above the average city's 78 ([ListWithClever 2024](https://listwithclever.com/research/best-coffee-cities/)).

![Horizontal bar chart comparing coffee shops per 100,000 residents across top U.S. cities versus the national average. Portland (27.8) leads, San Jose (29.6) edges it out in raw density, but Portland's combination of density, affordability, and quality ratings drives its number-one overall ranking.](/api/blog/images/portland-coffee-capital_chart1_density.png)

The numbers compound. Portland households spend an average of $192 per year on coffee, the twentieth-highest amount in the nation ([WalletHub 2025](https://wallethub.com/edu/best-cities-for-coffee-lovers/23739)). Nearly 24 percent of residents own an electric coffee grinder (eleventh-highest nationally), and 27 percent own a single-cup brewing machine. The average cappuccino in Portland costs $5.42 — slightly above the national average of $5.16, but significantly less than Seattle's $6.37 or San Francisco's $5.56 ([ListWithClever 2024](https://listwithclever.com/research/best-coffee-cities/)). Portland achieves its coffee dominance not through prestige pricing but through density: more shops, more roasters, more choices, all competing on quality and keeping prices in check — a lesson in democratic excellence that more expensive cities would do well to ponder.

## The Accidental Empire: A Brief History

How did a city in the rainy Pacific Northwest become the coffee capital of the United States? The answer begins in 1999, when a barista named Duane Sorenson opened Stumptown Coffee Roasters on SE Division Street. At the time, the American coffee landscape was dominated by Starbucks — the hyper-second-wave behemoth that had popularised dark roasts, standardized latte recipes, and spread to every strip mall in the republic. Sorenson and his contemporaries (Chicago's Intelligentsia, North Carolina's Counter Culture) wanted something different: lighter roasts, single origins, transparency about where the beans came from. They called it the "third wave" ([Eater Portland 2021](https://pdx.eater.com/22436234/history-coffee-pacific-northwest-portland-seattle)).

Stumptown's most consequential innovation came in 2003, when Sorenson began travelling directly to coffee farms and negotiating prices with producers, cutting out the commodity-trading middlemen. He called the model Direct Trade. "We go right to the source of the best coffee," the company's website states. "We hike through fields, stand among coffee drying decks, and sit down to share a meal and talk about the crop with producers we've met many times" ([Stumptown Story](https://www.stumptowncoffee.com/pages/our-story)). The approach paid premiums for quality and demanded transparency from both sides of the transaction. It also made Stumptown the defining brand of a movement — for what is a movement, after all, but a few people who decide that the conventional way of doing things is not nearly good enough?

In 2011, Sorenson's team launched a product that would change coffee retail forever: ready-to-drink cold brew, packaged in little brown bottles modelled on Olympia Beer stubbies. Cold brew had existed in niche cafes for years, but Stumptown's bottled version made it scalable, shelf-stable, and national. Within a few years, the company was selling cold brew in grocery stores across the country, and the category had become so large that even Starbucks launched its own version. Sorenson sold Stumptown to JAB Holdings (owner of Peet's and Caribou Coffee) in 2015, in a deal that reflected the growing consolidation of specialty coffee ([Perfect Daily Grind 2024](https://perfectdailygrind.com/2024/11/stumptown-turns-25-specialty-coffee-acquisitions/), [OregonLive 2015](https://www.oregonlive.com/dining/2015/11/three_portland_coffee_roasters.html)).

Stumptown's success created an ecosystem. By 2009, Wille Yli-Luoma had launched Heart Coffee Roasters in Portland, focusing on precision espresso and what he called "development" rather than roast-level nomenclature. Heart was an early adopter of scales for espresso dosing and volumetric dosing machines — innovations that let baristas maintain consistency through busy rushes ([La Marzocco USA 2024](https://lamarzoccousa.com/news/blog/heart-coffee-roasters-portland/)). In 2008, Matt Higgins founded Coava Coffee Roasters in his North Portland garage, bootstrapping it with money from motorcycle repair. Coava remains founder-owned and independent, a rarity among specialty roasters of its size, and built an in-house density-separation table for green-quality control that almost no U.S. roaster has matched ([day9.coffee](https://www.day9.coffee/roasters/coava-coffee)).

By 2015, the three companies — Stumptown, Heart, and Coava — all operated state-of-the-art roasting facilities within walking distance of one another in Portland's Central Eastside Industrial District. "If Portland is the capital of global coffee culture," the Oregonian wrote that year, "these three buildings are its new city hall" ([OregonLive 2015](https://www.oregonlive.com/dining/2015/11/three_portland_coffee_roasters.html)).

## The Microroaster Explosion

The most surprising development in Portland's coffee economy is not the success of its marquee roasters but the proliferation of tiny ones. Nearly 100 microroasters now operate in the metro area, many of them roasting in quantities as small as five or ten pounds at a time ([OPB 2024](https://www.opb.org/article/2024/04/12/superabundant-video-how-pacific-northwest-shapes-coffee-culture/)). 

The catalyst was Buckman Coffee Factory, a co-roasting facility opened in 2015 by Cassy Gleason and her sister. The model is simple: Buckman provides the industrial roasting equipment, the warehouse space, and the overhead. Microroasters rent time on the machines, sharing the cost of equipment that would otherwise price them out of the market. Around 40 businesses now operate out of the space, ranging from single-person operations to multi-cafe owners ([OPB 2024](https://www.opb.org/article/2024/04/12/superabundant-video-how-pacific-northwest-shapes-coffee-culture/)).

"I really wanted the cafes to have a strong community feel," Heart's Yli-Luoma told La Marzocco in 2024, "and I wanted people to feel comfortable ordering a coffee and get exactly what they wanted quickly" ([La Marzocco USA 2024](https://lamarzoccousa.com/news/blog/heart-coffee-roasters-portland/)). The same ethos, scaled down, applies to Buckman's microroasters: lower barriers, shared infrastructure, more participants — the sort of cooperative arrangement that would make a socialist blush and a capitalist cheer.

The Oregon industry data reflects this growth. IBISWorld reports that Oregon's Coffee and Snack Shops industry has grown to $1.4 billion in market size, across 2,294 businesses employing 23,070 workers, with the number of establishments growing at an average annual rate of 3.8 percent from 2021 to 2026. Oregon's Coffee Production industry — roasters and wholesalers — represents an additional $369.5 million, spread across 805 businesses ([IBISWorld 2026](https://www.ibisworld.com/united-states/industry/oregon/coffee-snack-shops/36696/), [IBISWorld 2026](https://www.ibisworld.com/united-states/industry/oregon/coffee-production/36142/)). Nearly nine percent of the Portland metro area's workforce is employed in food preparation and serving, an occupational category that includes baristas and cafe workers, with average hourly wages of $20.08 ([BLS OEWS May 2024](https://www.bls.gov/regions/west/news-release/2025/occupationalemploymentandwages_portlandor_20250515.htm)).

![Grouped bar chart showing the growth of Oregon's Coffee and Snack Shops industry across market size, establishment count, and employment from 2021 to 2026. Market size reached $1.4 billion with 23,070 employees.](/api/blog/images/portland-coffee-capital_chart2_industry.png)

## The Supply Chain Invisible to the Customer

None of this would be possible without a global logistics network that most coffee drinkers never think about — for it is the great tragedy of modern life that we enjoy the fruits of distant labour while remaining studiously oblivious to the machinery that delivers them. The United States is the world's largest importer of green coffee by volume, buying $6.31 billion worth in 2024 alone, an 11 percent increase over the previous year ([US Import Data 2025](https://www.usimportdata.com/blogs/us-green-coffee-imports-report-2025-and-top-green-coffee-importers-usa)). Brazil ($1.9 billion), Colombia ($1.3 billion), and Guatemala ($427 million) supplied 59 percent of total import value ([IndexBox 2026](https://www.indexbox.io/store/united-states-of-america-coffee-green-market-analysis-forecast-size-trends-and-insights/)). The average import price for green coffee reached $4,876 per ton in 2024, a 6 percent increase from the prior year.

The Specialty Coffee Transaction Guide, produced by researchers at Emory University, tracks the prices roasters actually pay for green specialty coffee. The 2024 edition summarises nearly 105,000 contracts covering more than 2 billion pounds of specialty coffee, contributed by 123 companies worldwide ([Transaction Guide 2024](https://www.transactionguide.coffee/reports/specialty-coffee-retail-price-index-2026-q1)). The median FOB price for African specialty coffees was $3.95 per pound; South American coffees traded lower. These are the prices that determine whether a Portland roaster can pay its rent — or, indeed, whether it can continue to exist at all.

The logistics are intricate. Portland Roasting Company, one of the city's older wholesalers, operated a Farm Friendly Direct program that imported coffee through the Port of Portland (for Tanzanian beans), the Port of Tacoma (for Papua New Guinea), and the ports of Oakland and Long Beach (for Central American beans) ([PDXScholar](https://pdxscholar.library.pdx.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1030&context=busadmin_fac)). Each shipment required coordination with brokers, importers, freight forwarders, and customs agents. Every link in the chain adds cost and complexity — and, more recently, tariffs.

## The Fourth Wave: Reclaiming the Supply Chain

As Portland's third-wave roasters have matured — and in Stumptown's case, been absorbed by a European conglomerate — a new generation of coffee entrepreneurs is rewriting the script. The "fourth wave," as some industry observers call it, sees historically marginalised communities owning the means of production not just at the roasting stage but across the value chain ([Eater PDX 2024](https://pdx.eater.com/2024/1/3/24024008/portland-fourth-wave-coffee-kalesa-cafe-zamora)).

Kalesa Coffee, which opened in Portland's Gotham Building, is run by three Filipino-American owners — Tim Almeda, Leilani Bañuelos Banayat, and Keanu Banayat — who are explicit about their mission. "Coffee's been pretty single origin-y, very bro-y," Banayat told Eater Portland in 2024. "But in the last few years, we've seen it turn into something where people are celebrating their culture" ([Eater PDX 2024](https://pdx.eater.com/2024/1/3/24024008/portland-fourth-wave-coffee-kalesa-cafe-zamora)). Portland Cà Phê, a Vietnamese roastery, and Proud Mary, founded by an immigrant from a coffee-growing region, represent a similar shift: coffee professionals from countries that grow coffee, now roasting and selling it in a consuming nation — a delicious inversion of the old colonial script.

Dennis Cote, a Harvard Extension School graduate student whose 2023 Re:co Fellow thesis examined third-wave cafes in Portland between 1995 and 2020, identified a tension at the heart of the city's coffee culture. The same establishments that brought specialty coffee to a wider audience also became symbols of gentrification and displacement in historically marginalised neighbourhoods. "Gentrification is about displacement, not dis-spacement," Cote wrote. "Space is a blank space waiting to be filled with memory, meaning, and history — at which point, it becomes a place" ([SCA Re:co 2023](https://sca.coffee/sca-news/2023-reco-fellow-feature-denniscote)). The fourth-wave entrepreneurs are attempting to fill that space with something the third wave often neglected: cultural specificity and economic inclusion.

## The Tariff That Landed on a Bean That Can't Grow Here

In the spring of 2025, the Trump administration imposed a 10 percent tariff on virtually all U.S. imports, including green coffee beans. The response from Portland's coffee industry was immediate and anxious. Coffee importers operate on margins of roughly 10 percent — the same as the tariff itself. "It leaves no room to absorb any kind of tariff costs," Emily Smith, a Portland-based representative for the wholesale importer Hacea Coffee Source, told Oregon Public Broadcasting. "The tariff costs have to get passed through all the way down to the consumer" ([OPB May 2025](https://www.opb.org/article/2025/05/30/oregons-coffee-industry-the-latest-to-point-out-damage-from-federal-tariffs/)).

In May 2025, a dozen coffee-industry leaders gathered at Buckman Coffee Factory for a roundtable with U.S. Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, a Democrat from Beaverton. The mood was grim. Paul Thornton, owner of Thornton Family Coffee Roasters in nearby Beaverton, told the congresswoman he had been buying coffee for forty years and had never worried about tariffs. "We have to be able to tell customers, 'Here's the price of our beans for the next 12 months, or maybe six months,'" he said. "And with these tariffs, we can't do that" ([Portland Tribune May 2025](https://portlandtribune.com/2025/05/29/u-s-rep-bonamici-hears-buzz-about-tariffs-from-portland-area-coffee-merchants/)).

Mark Stell, founder and CEO of Portland Coffee Roasters, was blunter. His company paid $370,000 in tariffs in 2025 alone ([CoffeeTalk April 2026](https://coffeetalk.com/daily-dose/for-roasters-retailers/04-2026/109871/)). "Since December, they eliminated tariffs for coffee. But we're still paying, I'm still paying this year at least $8,000 this month," Stell told KATU in February 2026, noting that the company had not raised prices despite the tariff burden ([KATU Feb 2026](https://katu.com/newsletter-daily/portland-businesses-wonder-if-they-or-consumers-will-get-money-back-from-illegal-tariffs)). The company had tried to absorb the costs, but the mathematics was as unforgiving as it was indifferent.

The macroeconomic numbers confirm the squeeze. Coffee prices in the United States rose 21 percent year-over-year through October 2025, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Price Index — faster than any other tracked item ([KATU Nov 2025](https://katu.com/news/local/coffee-prices-up-21-percent-last-year-will-end-of-trump-tariffs-have-an-impact)). The increase reflected a convergence of pressures: drought and weather-driven supply shortfalls in Brazil and Southeast Asia, low global inventories, and the new tariff layer layered on top. "Coffee prices are significantly higher than historical," said Jacob Aiken-Phillips, vice president of consumer research at Melius Research. "The primary driver is that there are problems in the supply chain. But then now, with tariffs enacted, that just adds a layer onto the costs" ([KATU Nov 2025](https://katu.com/news/local/coffee-prices-up-21-percent-last-year-will-end-of-trump-tariffs-have-an-impact)).

![Bar chart showing Coffee CPI year-over-year percent change from 2020 to 2025. Prices rose 21% by October 2025, with a dashed vertical line marking the April 2025 tariff on coffee imports.](/api/blog/images/portland-coffee-capital_chart3_prices.png)

Cassy Gleason, who co-owns Buckman Coffee Factory and Marigold Coffee, framed the issue in larger terms. "We are an import-dependent state," she said on OPB's Think Out Loud. "Coffee, for me, is a very romantic product so I take a big view on this. And I think of these tariffs as not just hurting our industry, but I think it's hurting the very idea of free trade in general" ([OPB Think Out Loud June 2025](https://www.opb.org/article/2025/06/17/think-out-loud-oregon-coffee-industry-affected-federal-upheaval/)). She noted that the coffee supply chain connects Portland to some of the most politically fragile regions on earth — East Africa, Central America, Southeast Asia — and that tariffs, combined with USAID cuts, were destabilising the very farms that supply the city's roasters. To tax the bean one cannot grow is, after all, a policy that requires a certain genius for self-inflicted injury.

In April 2026, after a federal judge ruled the tariffs illegal and the Supreme Court declined to intervene, a refund portal was established for affected businesses. But uncertainty remains. Stell and other Portland business owners are navigating a bureaucracy that seems designed for large corporations, not small roasters. Sen. Ron Wyden, the senior Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, is pushing legislation to expedite refunds ([CoffeeTalk April 2026](https://coffeetalk.com/daily-dose/for-roasters-retailers/04-2026/109871/)).

Collin Jones, owner of Crema Coffee & Bakery in Portland's Buckman neighbourhood, has run his shop since 2011. He has watched coffee prices rise and tariffs arrive but has not yet raised his prices. "If you can hang on, just kind of hang on," he told KATU in November 2025. "I feel like most of these crises, as far as pricing increases and stuff like that, are temporary" ([KATU Nov 2025](https://katu.com/news/local/coffee-prices-up-21-percent-last-year-will-end-of-trump-tariffs-have-an-impact)).

That may be the most Portland attitude of all: the stubborn faith that quality and community will outlast any policy shock. But the city's coffee economy rests on a foundation of imported green beans, thin margins, and global supply chains that are suddenly, conspicuously fragile. The rain will keep falling on Division Street. The espresso machine will keep hissing. But the question of how long Portland can remain the coffee capital of America while paying a tariff on a bean it cannot grow is one that no amount of good brewing can answer — and one that would be altogether more entertaining if it were not, for so many, a matter of survival.

---

*Sources: This article draws on primary data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, IBISWorld, the U.S. Census Bureau, the Specialty Coffee Transaction Guide (Emory University), the Specialty Coffee Association, WalletHub, ListWithClever, and original reporting from OPB, KATU, the Portland Tribune, Eater Portland, Perfect Daily Grind, OregonLive, and CoffeeTalk.*

*Charts: All data visualizations cited to their underlying primary sources. Chart 1 data from ListWithClever (2024). Chart 2 data from IBISWorld (2026). Chart 3 data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI and KATU reporting on tariff impacts.*

post.content:
# The Map Is Being Redrawn: How Geopolitics, Climate, and a Quiet Revolution in Trade Are Reshaping Global Shipping

## 1. The Ship That Took the Long Way

Nothing ages faster than the ordinary. On a June morning in 2014, the container ship *LICA MAERSK* steamed east across the Pacific, rounded the southern tip of South America, and disappeared into the gray Atlantic on a voyage from New Zealand to Europe — 265 meters of Danish steel carrying 63,400 tons of cargo, photographed from a beach near Christchurch as it passed. Eleven years later, that photograph has become a kind of historical document — not because the ship is unusual, but because the route it traveled would now be considered almost quaint.

The shortest route is no longer the safest. In 2023, a container vessel departing Shanghai for Rotterdam would have passed through the Strait of Malacca, crossed the Indian Ocean, slipped through the Bab-el-Mandeb, and transited the Suez Canal in approximately 20 days. In 2026, that same vessel — if its operator is prudent — rounds the Cape of Good Hope instead, adding roughly 30 percent to the voyage length and a week or more to the journey [UNCTAD Ch.1](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025ch1_en.pdf). The fuel bill is higher. The emissions are greater. The cargo arrives late. This is not a temporary disruption — it has become, for the foreseeable future, the structure of global trade.

The Suez Canal, as of mid-2025, was operating at roughly 70 percent below its average tonnage transit levels of 2023 [UNCTAD RMT 2025 Overview](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025overview_en.pdf). The Panama Canal, choked by drought, limited daily transits through much of 2024 [World Bank CPPI 2025](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2025/09/22/port-performance-varies-across-the-globe-amid-continuing-shocks). And the Strait of Hormuz — a passage for roughly 34 percent of global seaborne oil exports — saw risks escalate through 2025, with UNCTAD warning that "the potential for increased shipping costs, delays and insurance premiums cannot be excluded" [UNCTAD press release](https://unctad.org/news/maritime-trade-under-pressure-growth-set-stall-2025).

The map of global shipping is being redrawn in real time — not by cartographers, but by geopolitics, climate change, and an accelerating rebalancing of economic power that is shifting, almost without notice, the center of gravity of world trade.

![Container ship LICA MAERSK at sea near Christchurch, New Zealand, June 2014. The vessel is 265 meters long with a carrying capacity of 63,400 tons, representative of the global fleet of 112,500 commercial vessels that move over 80 percent of world trade by volume.](/api/blog/images/redrawing-the-map_container_ship.jpg)

*Photo: The container ship LICA MAERSK off the coast of New Zealand, 2014. Credit: Bernard Spragg / Wikimedia Commons, CC0 Public Domain.*

## 2. The Distance Problem

The central paradox of modern maritime trade is this: in 2024, the volume of goods carried by sea grew by a respectable 2.2 percent, reaching 12,720 million tons — a figure above the 2013–2023 average [UNCTAD RMT 2025](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025_en.pdf). But the distance those goods traveled grew far more. Measured in ton-miles — the standard metric that multiplies weight by distance — global seaborne trade surged by 5.9 percent in 2024, nearly three times the volume growth [UNCTAD RMT 2025 Overview](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025overview_en.pdf).

The average voyage haul for a ship has increased from 4,831 miles in 2018 to 5,245 miles in 2024 [UNCTAD RMT 2025 Overview](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025overview_en.pdf). That extra 414 miles per voyage — detours around the Cape of Good Hope, longer Pacific crossings to avoid the Panama Canal, re-routed tankers skirting the Arabian Sea — is the physical signature of a world pulling apart. As UNCTAD puts it in its 2025 Review of Maritime Transport: "Distance is no longer geography; it is geoeconomics" [UNCTAD RMT 2025 Overview](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025overview_en.pdf).

The 5.9 percent ton-mile surge was driven overwhelmingly by the Red Sea crisis. Houthi attacks on commercial shipping forced carriers to abandon the Suez route, sending vessels around southern Africa instead. Containerized trade from East Asia to Europe — the arterial route of global supply chains — saw vessel detours add approximately 30 percent to voyage lengths, contributing to an estimated 11 percent increase in overall container TEU-mile demand [UNCTAD Ch.1](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025ch1_en.pdf).

![Indexed line chart showing trade volume (million tons) vs. ton-miles (billion ton-miles), 2018–2025. Ton-miles diverge sharply upward from 2023 onward as Red Sea rerouting inflates sailing distances, while trade volume growth remains modest.](/api/blog/images/redrawing-the-map_tonmiles_gap.png)

## 3. Fragile Growth, Uncertain Forecasts

The global economy has not made it easy for the ships that serve it. The 2.2 percent volume growth of 2024, while decent, lagged the 20-year average of 2.9 percent and fell well short of the 2003–2023 average of 2.9 percent [UNCTAD RMT 2025](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025_en.pdf). Structural factors — a weakening of the link between trade and GDP, a slowdown in global value-chain expansion, rising trade barriers, and geopolitical fragmentation — have been compressing maritime trade growth for years [UNCTAD RMT 2025](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025_en.pdf).

The outlook for 2025 is worse. In February 2025, analysts projected 1.4 percent growth in seaborne trade volumes. By May, that forecast had been revised to a contraction of 0.1 percent [UNCTAD Ch.1](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025ch1_en.pdf). UNCTAD's official projection now stands at 0.5 percent growth for 2025, with containerized trade growing a slightly more robust 1.4 percent. From 2026 to 2030, UNCTAD projects total seaborne trade growth of about 2 percent annually, with containerized trade at 2.3 percent [UNCTAD RMT 2025 Overview](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025overview_en.pdf).

Those forecasts carry an unusual degree of uncertainty. "In early 2025 (specifically, in February and March), global seaborne trade volumes were projected to grow by 1.4 per cent," the UNCTAD report notes. "By May 2025, they were projected to contract marginally by 0.1 per cent. This notable reduction points to the increasingly complex and uncertain global trade environment" [UNCTAD Ch.1](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025ch1_en.pdf).

Not all trade lanes are equal. The main East–West corridors — East Asia to North America, East Asia to Europe, and Europe to North America — remain the backbone of global container flows, accounting for 36.8 percent of all containerized trade in 2024. These routes recorded their strongest expansion in years: East Asia–North America up 14.7 percent, East Asia–Europe up 10.2 percent, transatlantic up 5.2 percent [UNCTAD Ch.1](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025ch1_en.pdf). But the fastest-growing segment is South–South trade — between developing nations — which expanded 8 percent in 2024 [UNCTAD Ch.1](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025ch1_en.pdf).

## 4. The Price of Passage

Maritime freight rates have become one of the most volatile economic indicators in the world. The Baltic Dry Index, which tracks the cost of shipping dry bulk commodities like iron ore, coal, and grain, stood at approximately 3,124 points on June 3, 2026 — up 110 percent year-on-year [Trading Economics](https://tradingeconomics.com/commodity/baltic). The capesize segment, which moves 150,000-ton loads of iron ore, saw its time-charter average hit $46,000 per day — a 170 percent increase from a year earlier [Hellenic Shipping News](https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/weekly-dry-market-monitor-spotlight-on-capesize-freight-and-growth-of-tonne-miles-to-india/). The Containerized Freight Index reached 2,572 points, up 24 percent from a year earlier and surging 35 percent in the past month alone as peak-season demand collided with constrained capacity [Trading Economics](https://tradingeconomics.com/commodity/containerized-freight-index).

On the transpacific routes, container spot rates hit approximately $3,200 per forty-foot equivalent unit (FEU) to the West Coast and $5,000 to the East Coast. Asia–Europe rates stood at $3,000 per FEU to Northern Europe and $4,400 to the Mediterranean [Freightos](https://container-news.com/freightos-weekly-update-container-rates-starting-to-spike-on-peak-season-rush/). These are not pandemic-era peaks, but they are high enough to concern shippers and economists alike — especially because they are driven not by demand but by disruption and capacity management.

The supply side tells a contradictory story. Since 2021, carriers have poured the record profits of the pandemic years into an unprecedented wave of new vessel orders. An estimated 10 million TEU of container ship capacity — equivalent to roughly one-third of the current active fleet — is now on order and will be delivered over the next few years [Freightos 2026 Forecast](https://www.freightos.com/freight-industry-updates/market-updates/ocean-and-air-freight-forecast-2026-what-to-expect/). The conventional wisdom holds that this will trigger a container market downcycle, with persistent downward pressure on rates, reduced carrier revenues, and even losses. But in the short term, the Red Sea disruption has absorbed so much excess capacity — through longer voyages, extra vessels needed to maintain schedules — that rates have stayed elevated.

"Expect a cyclical pattern of sharp rate dips followed by periods of recovery through capacity management in the near term," the Freightos 2026 Forecast advises. "Though overall rate levels will likely trend lower than 2025 through the downcycle" [Freightos 2026 Forecast](https://www.freightos.com/freight-industry-updates/market-updates/ocean-and-air-freight-forecast-2026-what-to-expect/).

![Indexed line chart comparing Baltic Dry Index and Containerized Freight Index, 2021–2026. Both indices show extreme volatility: the pandemic spike, post-crash decline, and the current divergence where dry bulk rates have surged while container rates remain subdued.](/api/blog/images/redrawing-the-map_freight_volatility.png)

## 5. The Fleet and What It Burns

As of January 1, 2025, the world's merchant fleet consisted of 112,500 commercial vessels, carrying a total capacity of 2.44 billion deadweight tons [UNCTAD Ch.2](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025ch2_en.pdf). The fleet grew 3.4 percent in the past year — faster than maritime trade growth, slower than the 20-year average of 5.1 percent [UNCTAD RMT 2025 Overview](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025overview_en.pdf). Greece remains the largest ship-owning nation, controlling 16.4 percent of global fleet capacity, followed by China and Japan; together, the top three own 40.7 percent of the world's ships by deadweight tonnage. The top three flag states — Liberia, Panama, and the Marshall Islands — account for 45.1 percent of carrying capacity, which is to say that a ship's nationality is usually a matter of regulatory convenience [UNCTAD RMT 2025 Overview](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025overview_en.pdf).

But the most significant number in the fleet profile is this: 8 percent of active fleet tonnage is designed to run on alternative fuels. On the orderbook, the share is 53 percent [UNCTAD RMT 2025 Overview](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025overview_en.pdf). "Progress in 'greening' the fleet is underway but incremental," UNCTAD reports. The gap between the active fleet and the vessels being built defines the central challenge of maritime decarbonization: the industry must rebuild itself almost entirely in the next two decades, while continuing to move 80 percent of the world's trade by volume.

![Grouped horizontal bar chart comparing the active fleet (92% conventional, 8% alternative fuel) with the orderbook (47% conventional, 53% alternative fuel). The stark difference illustrates the decarbonization gap between ships sailing today and those on order.](/api/blog/images/redrawing-the-map_fleet_green_gap.png)

## 6. The Emissions That Follow

In 2023, global shipping emitted 911 million tonnes of CO₂-equivalent greenhouse gases (tank-to-wake, using 100-year global warming potentials). If counted as a country, shipping would rank as the ninth-largest CO₂e-emitting nation on earth, with a share of approximately 1.7 percent of anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions [ICCT 2025](https://theicct.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/ID-332-%E2%80%93-Global-shipping_report_final.pdf). By CO₂ alone, shipping accounted for an estimated 2.3 percent of global emissions in 2023, up from 2.2 percent in 2016 [ICCT 2025](https://theicct.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/ID-332-%E2%80%93-Global-shipping_report_final.pdf).

The numbers for 2024 are higher. The OECD's experimental maritime transport emissions database puts global CO₂ emissions from shipping at 972.8 million tonnes in 2024 — an increase of 9.3 percent from 2019 [OECD 2025](https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2025/12/analysing-recent-trends-and-drivers-of-maritime-transport-co-emission_4463d5fe/6bb2bd69-en.pdf). The European Commission's Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) system, which tracks ships calling at European Economic Area ports, recorded 144.9 million tonnes of CO₂ in 2024 — the highest since the system began, and 12.9 percent higher than 2023 [EU Commission MRV 2025](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-8722-2026-ADD-1/en/pdf).

The longer routes forced by geopolitical disruption are directly inflating emissions. The carbon intensity of shipping — emissions per unit of transport work — has improved by about 10.3 percent since 2016 [ICCT 2025](https://theicct.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/ID-332-%E2%80%93-Global-shipping_report_final.pdf). But total emissions keep rising because vessels are steaming farther. "The substantial growth in ton-miles was primarily due to extended voyage distances caused by logistical disruptions, particularly the Red Sea rerouting," UNCTAD explains [UNCTAD RMT 2025](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025_en.pdf). Ships are becoming more efficient per mile — but there are more miles.

The regulatory response has been slow and contested. In April 2025, the International Maritime Organization approved the IMO Net-Zero Framework, the world's first sector-wide combination of mandatory emissions limits and GHG pricing [IMO](https://www.imo.org/en/mediacentre/pressbriefings/pages/imo-approves-netzero-regulations.aspx). The framework would have been formally adopted in October 2025, with entry into force expected in 2027. But the extraordinary MEPC session in October 2025 voted to adjourn for one year, postponing adoption until at least 2026 [IMO MEPC 84](https://www.classnk.com/hp/pdf/info_service/imo_and_iacs/MEPC84_sumE.pdf). Meanwhile, the European Union's Emissions Trading System — the first cap-and-trade system to include shipping — came into effect for CO₂ in 2024 and will extend to methane and nitrous oxide in 2026 [EU Commission](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-8722-2026-INIT/en/pdf). The gap between ambition and action, between regions and globally, has rarely been wider.

## 7. The Developing World's Maritime Moment

One of the most consequential shifts in global trade is happening below the headlines. In 2000, developing countries accounted for 38 percent of global maritime freight. By 2023, their share had risen to 54 percent [UNCTAD press](https://unctad.org/news/shipping-data-unctad-releases-new-seaborne-trade-statistics). The surge was led by Asia, with China driving much of the growth. South–South trade — between developing nations — expanded 8 percent in 2024, faster than any other non-mainlane segment [UNCTAD Ch.1](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025ch1_en.pdf).

The composition of trade is shifting too. Crude oil's share of seaborne trade fell from 29 percent in 2000 to 18 percent in 2023, while dry bulk commodities like iron ore, coal, and grain rose from 27 to 36 percent [UNCTAD press](https://unctad.org/news/shipping-data-unctad-releases-new-seaborne-trade-statistics). New trade flows are emerging: iron ore shipments from major loading hubs to Indian ports, for instance, grew more than four-fold between Q1 2024 and Q1 2026 [Hellenic Shipping News](https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/weekly-dry-market-monitor-spotlight-on-capesize-freight-and-growth-of-tonne-miles-to-india/). This is not merely a shift in volume — it is a reconfiguration of the global map of supply and demand.

The performance of ports, however, has not kept pace. The World Bank's Container Port Performance Index, which benchmarked 403 ports using 175,000 vessel calls and 247 million container moves, found that global port efficiency declined between 2020 and 2024. East Asian and South Asian ports showed improvement. But developing-country ports, particularly in Africa and Latin America, continued to struggle with yard management, berth availability, and hinterland connectivity [World Bank CPPI 2025](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2025/09/22/port-performance-varies-across-the-globe-amid-continuing-shocks). The ports that handle the fastest-growing share of global trade are often the least equipped to do so.

## 8. The Map Ahead

The convergence of forces bearing down on global shipping is historically unusual — not because any single factor is unprecedented, but because so many are arriving at once. Geopolitical fragmentation is lengthening routes and raising costs. Climate change is choking canals and forcing a reckoning with the industry's own emissions. A trade rebalancing is shifting the center of gravity of global commerce toward the developing world. And a regulatory revolution — the IMO Net-Zero Framework, the EU ETS — promises to transform how ships are built, fueled, and operated, even as its adoption stalls.

UNCTAD's latest Review of Maritime Transport captures the stakes in a single sentence: "Maritime transport has weathered storms before. But never have so many transitions converged so quickly. The sector will adapt. The question is whether adaptation will be managed or chaotic, inclusive or divisive, sustainable or merely survivable" [UNCTAD RMT 2025 Overview](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/rmt2025overview_en.pdf).

For the rest of us — the people who do not own ships or operate ports, who simply buy things that arrived on one — the stakes are less abstract. Every container of electronics, every shipment of grain, every barrel of oil that crosses an ocean carries with it a freight cost, a carbon cost, and a geopolitical story. The map is being redrawn. The question is whether we will read it in time.

---

*Source note: This article draws exclusively on primary sources — the UNCTAD Review of Maritime Transport 2025 and its supporting chapters, the ICCT's global shipping emissions report (April 2025), the OECD's experimental maritime emissions database, the IMO's Net-Zero Framework documentation and MEPC session summaries, the European Commission's 2025 MRV report, the World Bank's Container Port Performance Index 2025, and Baltic Exchange/Freightos freight rate data from June 2026. All citations are inline as direct URLs to original reports, datasets, and press releases.*
