# The Two Berkshires: $839 Million in Visitor Spending and the Towns Still Waiting

## 1. The Lawn at Dusk

The gates open at five, but those who take their pleasures seriously arrive by mid-afternoon. They come through the Lion Gate at Tanglewood with their picnic baskets and folding chairs, their bottles of Sancerre wrapped in linen, their cheese boards composed with the care of a Dutch still life. By the time the Boston Symphony Orchestra's first violins begin tuning, the lawn holds 18,000 people — more than the entire year-round population of Lenox, Stockbridge, and Richmond combined.

On a July evening in 2024, when James Taylor played his annual Fourth of Weekend show, the Koussevitzky Music Shed and its surrounding acres reached exactly that capacity. The license plates told the story the Berkshires, on its best days, likes to tell about itself: New York, Connecticut, New Jersey, Florida, a scattering of California. The hotel rooms within a twenty-mile radius were booked solid weeks in advance. At the nearby Red Lion Inn, guests paid peak-season rates and considered themselves fortunate to have secured a cancellation.

The 2024 season at Tanglewood drew 304,000 ticketed visitors across 121 performances — up nearly 4 percent from the year before [Berkshire Eagle — Tanglewood 2024 attendance](https://www.berkshireeagle.com/news/central_berkshires/tanglewood-season-attendance-2024/article_9f4c71f6-75d1-11ef-a975-e34a568b7c0a.html). The 2025 season, now underway, is the largest in the venue's history: 187 performances, with Paul Simon, Brandi Carlile, Hugh Jackman, and Carrie Underwood among the headliners [Live 959 — Tanglewood security changes / record season](https://live959.com/tanglewood-lenox-security-bag-check/).

This is the Berkshires the outside world knows: "America's Premier Cultural Resort," the summer home of the Boston Symphony, a landscape of world-class museums and Gilded Age estates where the air smells of pine and the sound of a cello drifts across a lake at sunset.

But there is another Berkshire County, and it tells a different story.

![Koussevitzky Music Shed at Tanglewood, summer home of the Boston Symphony Orchestra, designed by Eliel Saarinen and opened in 1938. The venue drew 304,000 visitors in 2024 — more than twice the year-round population of Berkshire County.](/api/blog/images/the-two-berkshires_tanglewood_shed.jpg)

*Photo: The Koussevitzky Music Shed at Tanglewood. Credit: Chamberednautilus / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.*

## 2. The Paradox, in Numbers

In 2024, visitors to Berkshire County spent $839.3 million. That money supported 6,530 direct tourism jobs, generated $202.2 million in earnings, and produced $72.4 million in state and local tax revenue [Dean Runyan Associates / Mass.gov MOTT — 2024 Economic Impact of Travel](https://www.visitma.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/2024p_MA_TravelImpacts_8.22.25.pdf). The county's concentration of arts, entertainment, and recreation employment is more than double the national average — a location quotient of 2.39 [MassHire Berkshire Regional Workforce Blueprint, 2024](https://www.mass.gov/doc/berkshire-regional-workforce-blueprint/download). For hotels and accommodations, the concentration is nearly triple: 2.89.

By any measure a tourist board would think to apply, the cultural economy is thriving.

And yet Berkshire County is shrinking. The 2020 Census counted 129,026 residents. By July 2025, the U.S. Census Bureau estimates the population had fallen to 128,224 — a decline of 0.6 percent in just five years [U.S. Census Bureau — Berkshire County QuickFacts (V2025)](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/berkshirecountymassachusetts/PST045224). The decade before that was no better: the county lost 2,193 people between 2010 and 2020 [Berkshire Benchmarks — 2020 Census Summary](https://berkshirebenchmarks.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/2020-Census-Summary.pdf).

The median age in Berkshire County is 47.8 — significantly older than the national median of 38.8. In the town of Alford, the median age is 61.3. In Stockbridge, it is 59.6 [Berkshire Benchmarks — 2020 Census Summary](https://berkshirebenchmarks.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/2020-Census-Summary.pdf). The arithmetic is unsparing: people are dying faster than babies are being born, and natural decrease — more deaths than births — is the primary driver of population loss [USAFacts — Berkshire County population](https://usafacts.org/answers/is-the-population-growing-or-shrinking/county/berkshire-county-ma/).

The region's own workforce blueprint projects 8 percent population growth by 2033, but that projection depends on attracting thousands of new residents and building 23,000 housing units — neither of which is happening at the required pace [MassHire Berkshire Blueprint, 2024](https://www.mass.gov/doc/berkshire-regional-workforce-blueprint/download).

The gap between the Berkshires the world sees and the Berkshires that year-round residents inhabit is not a contradiction. It is a transformation — from an industrial economy to a cultural one — that remains incomplete.

![Berkshire County visitor spending (bars) versus population (line), 2019–2024. Visitor spending has grown 24.5 percent over five years while the county has lost population.](/api/blog/images/the-two-berkshires_spending_vs_population.png)

## 3. From Mills to Museums

The transformation did not happen overnight. To understand what the Berkshires have become, one must first reckon with what they were.

In 1957, manufacturing accounted for 59.3 percent of all nonagricultural employment in Berkshire County. Nearly six out of every ten workers made things — textiles, paper, electrical equipment, shoes, machinery [Massachusetts State Archives — "Tourism industries in Berkshire County, 1979"](https://archives.lib.state.ma.us/server/api/core/bitstreams/4f0d11be-f3fa-4a4d-8221-18d55cdbc036/content). The Housatonic River, which had powered sawmills and woolen mills since the eighteenth century, still drove the economy.

General Electric arrived in Pittsfield in 1903, drawn by the same water power and rail access that had built the textile mills before it. By mid-century, GE's Pittsfield Works employed more than 13,000 people — roughly a quarter of the city's workforce — manufacturing power transformers shipped around the world [Berkshire Eagle — GE demolition, 2024](https://www.berkshireeagle.com/news/central_berkshires/general-electric-plans-to-demolish-building-12-building-14-at-power-transformer-site/article_8788afb0-beef-11ee-a223-2375ca9712bf.html); [ETHW — "Transformers at Pittsfield"](https://ethw.org/Archives:Transformers_at_Pittsfield,_part_1).

In North Adams, Sprague Electric Company grew from a wartime manufacturer of gas masks, bomb casings, and atomic bomb components into a major electronics research and development center. At its peak in the 1970s and early 1980s, Sprague employed over 4,000 people at its 28-building, 16-acre complex on Marshall Street [CLUI — Mass MoCA / Sprague Electric site](https://clui.org/ludb/site/mass-moca-sprague-electric-site).

The paper mills of Lee and the textile mills of Adams gave the county an industrial identity that lasted 150 years. Berkshire-Hathaway's Mill Number Four in Adams — the last cotton mill in western Massachusetts — had employed 1,000 people until it closed in 1958 [MassMoments — Berkshire-Hathaway mill closing](https://www.massmoments.org/moment-details/berkshire-hathaway-announces-mill-closing.html).

Then, in the space of a few decades, almost all of it was gone.

The decline was not gradual in any terms that matter to the people who lived through it. Between 2001 and 2011 alone, manufacturing employment in Berkshire County fell by 45 percent — worse than the national decline of 30 percent [UMass Donahue Institute — Berkshire Advanced Manufacturing Study](https://donahue.umass.edu/documents/Berkshire_Advanced_Manufacturing_Study..pdf). Over 18 manufacturing companies closed their doors, eliminating 2,700 more jobs. GE's power transformer division shut down in 1986. Sprague Electric ceased operations in 1985.

By 2011, manufacturing provided just 8.8 percent of all employment in the Berkshires [UMass Donahue — Advanced Manufacturing Study](https://donahue.umass.edu/documents/Berkshire_Advanced_Manufacturing_Study..pdf).

What filled the void — slowly, deliberately, over the course of three decades — was the creative economy.

The Massachusetts Museum of Contemporary Art opened in 1999 in the abandoned Sprague Electric complex in North Adams, transforming 26 brick mill buildings into one of the largest contemporary art museums in the world. Joseph Thompson, MASS MoCA's founding director, had spent years raising money from public and private sources, winning a keystone state grant in 1988, surviving a recession, and reimagining the museum through what he later described as "a seemingly interminable birthing process" [MASS MoCA — "Transition Decade of Decision"](https://massmoca.org/transition-decade-of-decision-1989-1999-sprague-electric-mass-moca/).

By the time it opened, MASS MoCA had become a national model of post-industrial reinvention. A Williams College economic impact study estimated that the museum's annual expenditures combined with visitor spending generated approximately $16.7 million in economic activity and supported about 209 local jobs [Williams College — MASS MoCA Economic Impact Summary](https://web.williams.edu/Economics/ArtsEcon/library/pdfs/MassMocaSummary.pdf).

Tanglewood had been drawing audiences since 1937. The Clark Art Institute in Williamstown opened in 1955. The Norman Rockwell Museum in Stockbridge followed in 1969. Slowly, the Berkshire economy — once built on what people made — was being rebuilt on what people came to see.

## 4. The Jobs That Replace Jobs

No one disputes that tourism supports a significant number of Berkshire residents. The 6,530 direct tourism jobs span hotels, restaurants, retail, transportation, and the arts. Total tourism-related earnings reached $202.2 million in 2024 [Dean Runyan / MOTT 2024 Report](https://www.visitma.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/2024p_MA_TravelImpacts_8.22.25.pdf).

But the arithmetic of replacement is unsparing. GE's Pittsfield plant alone employed more than twice the number of people that the entire tourism sector in Berkshire County now supports — and those were union-scale manufacturing jobs with benefits and middle-class wages.

The average tourism job in the Berkshires pays approximately $31,000 annually — more than a minimum-wage service job, but less than what you need to buy a home in a county where the median house price reached $318,000 in 2024 [UMass Donahue — Berkshire housing study](https://donahue.umass.edu/news-events/media-coverage/berkshire-edge-study-reveals-berkshire-county-and-western-massachusetts-have-long-way-to-go-toward-solving-housing-crisis). The median household income is $76,013 — well below the Massachusetts state median of $104,828 [Census Reporter — Berkshire County](http://censusreporter.org/profiles/05000US25003-berkshire-county-ma/).

Maynard Seider, an activist sociologist who spent decades studying the region, distilled the central question into the title of his book: *The Gritty Berkshires*. In its final chapter, he examines MASS MoCA as a case study and asks: "Can a tourist-service economy provide a meaningful and economically sustainable life for its residents?" [The Gritty Berkshires — Maynard Seider](http://www.thegrittyberkshires.com/)

The evidence, so far, is mixed.

![Manufacturing employment share (1957–2011) versus tourism visitor spending (2017–2024) in Berkshire County. The two lines crossed somewhere in the late 1990s or early 2000s.](/api/blog/images/the-two-berkshires_mfg_vs_tourism.png)

## 5. The Second Berkshire

Drive forty minutes north from Tanglewood, and you arrive in North Adams. The city of 13,000 sits in a mountain bowl where the Hoosic River cuts through the northern Berkshires — isolated by the same geography that once made it an industrial center.

North Adams lost 3.6 percent of its population between April 2020 and July 2024 — one of the steepest declines of any municipality in Massachusetts [UMass Donahue Institute — V2024 Municipal Population Estimates](https://donahue.umass.edu/documents/UMDI_Census_V2024_Massachusetts_MCD_Pop_Estimates_Summary.pdf). Its median age of 42.6 is younger than the county average but still older than the national figure. And the jobs that Sprague Electric once provided — 4,000 at the company's peak — have not been replaced by anything comparable.

MASS MoCA is a triumph of adaptive reuse — a stunning museum that has drawn international attention and become a cultural anchor for the region. But a museum that primarily attracts visitors from beyond the county — 80 percent of its attendees come from outside Berkshire County — cannot function as a local employer the way a factory once did. Its total economic impact of $16.7 million and 209 jobs, while significant, remains a fraction of what Sprague provided [Williams College — MASS MoCA Economic Impact](https://web.williams.edu/Economics/ArtsEcon/library/pdfs/MassMocaSummary.pdf).

Across the county, the pattern repeats. Of Berkshire County's 32 towns and cities, only 25 percent gained population in the 2024 estimates. The fastest-growing towns are the rural retreats favored by second-home owners; the declining ones are the former mill and factory towns where year-round residents actually live [UMass Donahue Institute — V2024 Estimates](https://donahue.umass.edu/documents/UMDI_Census_V2024_Massachusetts_MCD_Pop_Estimates_Summary.pdf).

The pandemic briefly interrupted this trajectory. Between 2020 and 2021, a wave of remote workers and second-home buyers moved to the Berkshires, drawn by space and scenery and the sudden ability to work from anywhere. The population ticked upward. USPS data showed a more than doubling of moves into the region [Berkshire Regional Planning Commission — 2023-2027 CEDS](https://berkshireplanning.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/2023-2027-Berkshire-County-CEDS.pdf).

But by 2023, the trend had reversed. Domestic migration returned to its pre-pandemic patterns. In the 2023-2024 estimate year, Berkshire County lost another 137 residents [UMass Donahue — 2024 County Population Summary](https://donahue.umass.edu/documents/UMDI_2024_County_Pop_Summary_2025.03.13.pdf).

The pandemic bump was a sugar high. The underlying condition — an aging population, a shortage of younger workers, a housing market that serves the wealthy far better than it serves the employed — remained untreated.

## 6. The Housing Trap

The same tourism economy that generates $839 million in spending also generates a housing crisis.

Nearly 9,000 homes in Berkshire County are classified as second homes — properties occupied only part of the year by people whose primary residence lies elsewhere [Berkshire Regional Planning Commission — Survey of Second Homeowners](https://berkshireplanning.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/Survey-of-Second-Homeowners-Results-220825.pdf). Another 2,700 short-term rental units are active in western Massachusetts, two-thirds of which are located in Berkshire County [UMass Donahue — Berkshire housing study](https://donahue.umass.edu/news-events/media-coverage/berkshire-edge-study-reveals-berkshire-county-and-western-massachusetts-have-long-way-to-go-toward-solving-housing-crisis). Every short-term rental is a long-term rental that does not exist.

The result is entirely predictable. Rents in Berkshire County increased 35 percent between January 2021 and October 2024. The median sale price of a single-family home, adjusted for inflation, rose from $225,260 in 2014 to $318,000 in 2024 — a 41 percent increase [UMass Donahue — Berkshire housing study](https://donahue.umass.edu/news-events/media-coverage/berkshire-edge-study-reveals-berkshire-county-and-western-massachusetts-have-long-way-to-go-toward-solving-housing-crisis). Homeowner vacancy dropped from 1.6 percent in 2018 to 0.7 percent in 2023, meaning virtually every available home was occupied or sold.

In December 2024, the state of Massachusetts designated eight Berkshire County towns — Alford, Becket, Hancock, Monterey, Mount Washington, Otis, Stockbridge, and Tyringham — as "seasonal communities," a formal acknowledgment that seasonal housing units comprise more than 40 percent of their total housing stock [Berkshire Eagle — Seasonal communities designation](https://www.berkshireeagle.com/news/local/seasonal-communities-berkshire-county/article_80f7ba9e-b8ac-11ef-bd9f-2f5fc983fc35.html). The designation grants access to specialized policies and grants, but it also acknowledges a fundamental imbalance: in these towns, housing exists primarily for people who do not live here year-round.

The Berkshire Regional Planning Commission's Survey of Second Homeowners in 2022 provided a revealing portrait. The typical second-home owner is wealthy, educated, and white, with a primary residence in New York City. Forty percent come from the New York metropolitan area. Over half are employed full-time outside Berkshire County. Only 3 percent work for a county employer [BRPC — Survey of Second Homeowners](https://berkshireplanning.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/Survey-of-Second-Homeowners-Results-220825.pdf).

Twenty percent of second-home owners said they plan to move to the Berkshires permanently in the future, most of them as retirees. But retirees do not fill workforce gaps. They do not staff the restaurants, clean the hotel rooms, or become the next generation of public school students.

![Berkshire County median home sale price (adjusted to 2024 dollars), 2014–2024. The price has risen 41 percent while the county's working-age population has declined.](/api/blog/images/the-two-berkshires_housing_costs.png)

## 7. The Question That Remains

In April 2026, the 1Berkshire Economic Development team reported that they had held nearly 100 business consultations so far that year, written 31 letters of support that helped secure $460,000 in funding for local businesses, and hosted 189 unique job postings [1Berkshire — 2025 Economic Development Update](https://1berkshire.com/2025-update-from-economic-development-team/). They also launched "Belong Berkshires," a program designed to help transplants make social connections so they do not leave.

"Much like any rural place, this area has many tight-knit friend groups and families, and for someone without those connections, this can be a hard place to feel like you belong," the update noted. "That makes it harder for those people to find their niche here, and tends to result in some of them leaving despite the quality of life the region offers."

The region's challenges are not unique. Post-industrial communities across the Northeast — from upstate New York to western Pennsylvania to northern New England — are asking the same questions. Can cultural tourism replace manufacturing? Can a place built on making things survive on welcoming people? Can the creative economy support a middle class?

The Berkshires may be the best test case in America. The cultural assets are world-class. The natural beauty is genuinely spectacular. The marketing machine — 1Berkshire's 410 million visitor impressions in FY24 — is effective [1Berkshire — Marketing page](https://1berkshire.com/marketing/). The state is investing: $6.34 million in Destination Development Grants in FY26, including $180,000 for Berkshire Natural Resources Council trail improvements and $90,000 for the Berkshire Botanical Garden [Mass.gov — FY26 DDC Grants](https://www.mass.gov/news/massachusetts-awards-634-million-to-65-organizations-through-fy26-destination-development-grants).

But the fundamental question — "Can a tourist-service economy provide a meaningful and economically sustainable life for its residents?" — remains unanswered.

## 8. The Sound of What Comes Next

On a summer evening at Tanglewood, the question recedes. The music begins. The wine is poured. The sun sets behind Monument Mountain, and Stockbridge Bowl catches the last light.

This is the Berkshires that 304,000 people came to see in 2024. This is the Berkshires of the marketing campaigns, the guidebooks, the memories that visitors carry home with them.

It is real. The orchestra plays beautifully. The grass is soft. For a few hours, the place makes perfect sense.

But forty miles north, in the empty lots where General Electric's Building 12 and Building 14 were demolished earlier this year, the only sound is the wind through the chain-link fence. In Adams, where Berkshire-Hathaway's Mill Number Four has been converted into luxury apartments, the photographs of long-dead mill workers still line the hallways. And in North Adams, where Sprague Electric's 4,000 jobs became MASS MoCA's 209, the question hangs unanswered, as persistent as a half-remembered melody — what comes next for the people who live in the place that everyone visits?

*Source note: This article draws on primary data from the U.S. Census Bureau, the Massachusetts Office of Travel and Tourism (Dean Runyan Associates economic impact reports), the UMass Donahue Institute, the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, the Berkshire Regional Planning Commission, 1Berkshire, the Boston Symphony Orchestra, and the Williams College Center for Creative Community Development. All citations are inline as direct URLs to original reports and datasets.*

# The Thread of Power: A 400-Year Story of Who Controls What You Wear

*In a garment factory on the outskirts of Dhaka, a woman stitches a shirt destined for a mall outside Chicago, where it will sell for $39.99. She earns roughly $3,000 a year. The brand that ordered the shirt will book more than that in revenue before its morning coffee has cooled. This arrangement is not an accident of commerce. It is the latest chapter in a 400-year struggle for control of the oldest, most globalized, and most volatile supply chain on earth: the one that clothes humanity. The players have been replaced. The architecture of power remains standing.*

---

**I. The Indian Century**

For most of recorded history, the world's finest cotton textiles came from the Indian subcontinent. The muslins of Bengal, the calicoes of the Coromandel Coast, the chintzes of Gujarat — these were never mere commodities. They were signals of status, traded across the Indian Ocean, through the Middle East, into the Mediterranean, and finally, inevitably, to London. Indian weavers practiced a level of refinement that European artisans could admire and envy in equal measure, but never match. As the economic historians Stephen Broadberry and Bishnupriya Gupta have documented, India was "the world's main producer of cotton textiles" throughout the early modern period, with a substantial export trade. [Broadberry & Gupta, "Cotton Textiles and the Great Divergence" (2005), CEPR Discussion Paper, via University of Warwick](https://wrap-test.warwick.ac.uk/id/eprint/1708/1/WRAP_Broadberry_CEPR-DP5183%5B1%5D.pdf)
![A Tantee (Indian weaver) in Dhaka, 1827. Etching from Sir Charles D'Oyly's Antiquities of Dacca, showing a Bengali weaver at his handloom.](/api/blog/images/the-thread-of-power_indian_weaver.jpg)
>*A Tantee (weaver) in Dhaka, 1827. Bengali muslin weavers like this one supplied the finest cotton cloth in the world — until Lancashire's mechanized mills destroyed their market. Source: Sir Charles D'Oyly / British Library (Public Domain). [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:A_Tantee_or_Indian_weavers.jpg)*

When the British East India Company began importing Indian cottons in serious volume during the late 17th century, the effect on British consumers was electrical. Here was fabric that was lightweight, washable, and brilliantly coloured — everything that domestic wool and linen were not, and everything that an empire in a hurry could desire. By 1720, Parliament had passed the Calico Acts, banning most Indian cotton imports to protect the domestic wool and silk interests. Britain wanted the product but not the producer. Here, already, was the pattern that would define the next three centuries: the consuming nation using political power to dictate the terms of the textile trade, and calling it protection.

The Acts did not extinguish the appetite for cotton. They merely redirected it. As the economic historian Robert Allen has argued, they helped create a "high wage economy" in Britain — a system of incentives that made mechanization not merely attractive but inevitable. British wages were roughly six times those of Indian weavers, a ratio confirmed by contemporary accounts cited in Chaudhuri's study of the trade. [Broadberry & Gupta, op. cit.](https://wrap-test.warwick.ac.uk/id/eprint/1708/1/WRAP_Broadberry_CEPR-DP5183%5B1%5D.pdf) If Britain was to have cotton, it would have to be spun and woven by machines. The human hand had priced itself out of the market.

---

**II. The Lancashire Revolution**

Between 1764 and 1830, a cascade of mechanical inventions transformed cotton production from a domestic craft into an industrial conquest. James Hargreaves' spinning jenny (1764) multiplied a single spinner's output eightfold. Richard Arkwright's water frame (1769) substituted water power for human muscle. Samuel Crompton's spinning mule (1779) combined the jenny's fineness with the water frame's strength. And Edmund Cartwright's power loom (1785) began the mechanization of weaving — a process that took decades longer to perfect, as weaving, it turned out, was less willing to be tamed.

The numbers invite disbelief. In 1700, Great Britain consumed roughly 2 million pounds of raw cotton. By 1830, it consumed 270 million pounds. [Baines, "History of the Cotton Manufacture in Great Britain" (1835), reprinted Cambridge University Press](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/history-of-the-cotton-manufacture-in-great-britain/0CF3C5233C9F06CE3CA287C9E91F3166) Between 1780 and 1800 alone, output grew at 10.8 percent per year; exports expanded at 14 percent per annum. [Broadberry & Gupta via Deane & Cole (1969) and Farnie (1979)](https://wrap-test.warwick.ac.uk/id/eprint/1708/1/WRAP_Broadberry_CEPR-DP5183%5B1%5D.pdf) By the 1830s, Britain had done what three centuries of trade had not: it was now exporting cotton textiles to India — the very nation that had taught the world how to make them.

The productivity gains were unprecedented. As C. Knick Harley's archival research into the account books of three Manchester-area firms shows, the price of even the coarsest cotton yarn fell to a third of its early-1780s level by 1815. [Harley, "Cotton Textile Prices and the Industrial Revolution" (1998), Oxford University Working Paper](http://www.nuff.ox.ac.uk/economics/history/Paper81/harley81.pdf) Andrew Ure, an admiring chronicler of the factory system, wrote in 1835 that the new machines had "achieved a mighty revolution not only in the structure of British society, but in the fortunes of the world at large." [Ure, "The Philosophy of Manufactures" (1835)](https://historyofeconomicthought.mcmaster.ca/ure/PhilosophyManufactures.pdf)

Ure was not wrong. He was merely selective — and the side he chose happened to be the one that owned the machines.
![Interior of a steam-powered Lancashire weaving shed, 1914. Rows of power looms driven by overhead line shafts and steam engines.](/api/blog/images/the-thread-of-power_lancashire_mill.jpg)
>*Inside a Lancashire cotton mill, 1914. Power looms driven by steam engines replaced handloom weavers and concentrated textile production in vast factories. Source: E.L. Hoskyn / *More Pictures of British History* (Public Domain). [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cotton_mill.jpg)*

---

**III. The Spinners Who Paid the Price**

The human cost of the textile revolution was not distributed evenly. It fell, as such costs generally do, on women and children. The new evidence assembled by Jane Humphries and Benjamin Schneider overturns the long-held assumption that hand spinners were part of a "high wage economy." By combing through parish account books, spinning school records, farm ledgers, and workers' commonplace books, they reconstructed what female spinners actually earned from the late 16th to the early 19th century.

The picture that emerges is grim. In 1615, married spinners earned 1 shilling 4 pence per week — about 2.7 pence per day. [Humphries & Schneider, "Spinning the Industrial Revolution," *Economic History Review* 72(1), 2018](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ehr.12693) Productivity was low: a wool spinner could produce around 2.1 pounds per week. The mechanization of spinning did not liberate these women. It destroyed their livelihood. A single child operating a spinning jenny could produce what it took one hundred hand wheels to accomplish. Progress, as it was then called, had arrived.

A pamphlet from 1794 captures the desperation with an intimacy that no economic history can match:

> "To tell a poor woman with three, four or five children… to set her children to work, where no Wool is to be had is a mockery of misery… The scanty fare it enables them to eat when the day's work is done, with want of firing makes her at length prefer breaking a hedge for her own fuel."

[Fordham University Internet History Sourcebook, "Observations on the Loss of Woollen Spinning" (c. 1794)](https://sourcebooks.web.fordham.edu/mod/1794woolens.asp)

The mills that replaced the cottages were not sanctuaries. They had their own particular horrors. Children as young as five worked 14-hour days in rooms "many stories high" with no woman presiding, the pamphlet's anonymous author noted with alarm. The Factory Act of 1833 — restricting child labour — was the first legislative acknowledgment that the textile industry's hunger for power had a moral limit, however faint a one. By then, of course, the wheel — literal and figurative — had already turned. Textile power had migrated from the weavers of Bengal to the mill owners of Manchester, and it was not inclined to return.

---

**IV. The Cotton Empire and American Slavery**

The Lancashire mills did not run on British cotton. They ran on American cotton, grown by enslaved hands in the American South — a fact the industry preferred to treat as a logistical detail rather than a moral accusation. Eli Whitney's cotton gin (1793) made short-staple cotton profitable to process, and the plantation system expanded violently across the Deep South. By 1860, the United States was producing two-thirds of the world's cotton, and the British textile industry was utterly dependent on slave-grown fiber. [USDA Economic Research Service, Cotton and Wool Yearbook (historical data)](https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/cotton-wool-and-textile-data/cotton-and-wool-yearbook)

This was the second great transfer of power in the textile story: first from Indian artisans to British machines, then from British mills to American fields. The American Civil War and the abolition of slavery disrupted the supply chain — the "Lancashire Cotton Famine" of 1861–1865 threw hundreds of thousands of British mill workers out of work — but the underlying structure held. Cotton production in the American South recovered under sharecropping and tenant farming, a system that had the decency to rename what it continued to practice. The textile industry has never found itself at a loss for a captive labour supply.
![Women workers at sewing machines in a Bangladeshi ready-made garment factory, 2011.](/api/blog/images/the-thread-of-power_garment_factory.jpg)
>*Women working at sewing machines in a Bangladeshi garment factory, 2011. Bangladesh is today one of the world's largest garment exporters — but the workers who stitch the clothes earn a fraction of their selling price. Source: Tareq Salahuddin, CC-BY-2.0. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Garment_factory_in_Bangladesh_Women_working.jpg)*

---

**V. The Great Asian Reversal**

The 20th century witnessed the slow unraveling of Western dominance. The Japanese textile industry modernized in the Meiji era and by the 1930s was competitive on the global stage. After World War II, the centre of gravity shifted again: first to Japan, then to Hong Kong, South Korea, and Taiwan, then to China — each move a reminder that the industry's loyalty lies with the cheapest labour, not the most grateful nation.

The mechanism of control was the Multi-Fibre Arrangement (MFA), established in 1974, which imposed quotas on textile exports from developing countries to rich ones. The MFA was, in essence, a coordinated attempt by the United States and Europe to stretch the decline of their domestic textile industries across decades rather than admit it in a season. It did not prevent the decline. It merely orchestrated its migration. When the MFA was finally dismantled in 2005 under the WTO's Agreement on Textiles and Clothing, production consolidated swiftly around the most efficient producer available — which is to say, China. [WTO, "Global Value Chain Sectoral Profiles: Textiles and Clothing" (2024)](https://www.wto.org/english/res_e/statis_e/miwi_e/gvc_sectoral_profiles_textiles_clothing24_e.pdf)

Today, Asia accounts for 70.6 percent of world textile and clothing exports, up from 59.4 percent in 2017. China alone accounts for more than 40 percent of the value-added in global textile exports. Its domestic supply chains cover every stage — from fiber creation to finished garment — giving it an integration that no other country matches. India has similarly high domestic content (83.2 percent). Bangladesh and Vietnam concentrate in labor-intensive assembly, relying on imported raw materials. [WTO TiVA analysis, op. cit.](https://www.wto.org/english/res_e/statis_e/miwi_e/gvc_sectoral_profiles_textiles_clothing24_e.pdf)

The geography of control is now unmistakably Asian. But the raw materials tell an entirely different story.

---

**VI. The Synthetic Shift**

In 1996, natural fibres still held more than half of the global fibre market. By 2023, the situation had reversed itself with an efficiency that would impress a fashion editor. Synthetic fibres — overwhelmingly polyester, made from fossil fuels — now account for 72.7 percent of global fibre production. Natural fibres, led by cotton, have fallen to about 27 percent. [UNCTAD, "Trends in Natural and Man-made Fibres Trade" (2025)](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/ditccom2025d2_en.pdf)

The numbers are extraordinary. Global fibre production has more than doubled since 2000, from 58 million tonnes to a record 132 million tonnes in 2024. Polyester alone reached 78 million tonnes in 2024 — 59 percent of all fibre produced. [Textile Exchange, "Materials Market Report 2025"](https://textileexchange.org/knowledge-center/reports/materials-market-report-2025/) Production is on track to hit 169 million tonnes by 2030 if current trends hold.

This shift represents a quiet but decisive transfer of power from the cotton farmers of the United States, India, China, and Brazil to the petrochemical companies of China. The control of what we wear has passed from agriculture to industry, and ultimately to the fossil fuel sector — an irony that would be devastating if it were not so profitable. The implications for geopolitics and the environment are, as one might expect, profound.

![Global fiber production growth, 1975–2030, showing the dramatic rise of synthetics and the stagnation of natural fibers.](/api/blog/images/the-thread-of-power_fiber_production.png)
>*Global fiber production by type, 1975–2030. Synthetic fibers have risen from under half of total production to dominate nearly three-quarters of the market. Cotton's relative share has fallen by half, even as absolute production has grown. Source: Textile Exchange Materials Market Report 2025; UNCTAD Fibre Trade Report 2025.*

---

**VII. The Environmental Reckoning**

The modern textile industry is among the most accomplished polluters on earth. Total greenhouse gas emissions from textile production reached 1.2 billion tonnes of CO₂ equivalent in 2015 — more than the emissions of all international flights and maritime shipping combined. [Ellen MacArthur Foundation, "A New Textiles Economy" (2017)](https://content.ellenmacarthurfoundation.org/m/6d5071bb8a5f05a2/original/A-New-Textiles-Economy-Redesigning-fashions-future.pdf) Production uses roughly 93 billion cubic meters of water annually, and 20 percent of industrial water pollution globally comes from textile dyeing and treatment. [UNEP, "Sustainability and Circularity in the Textile Value Chain" (2020)](https://wedocs.unep.org/handle/20.500.11822/34184)

The waste is, by any reasonable standard, obscene. Every second, the equivalent of one garbage truck of textiles is landfilled or burned. Less than one percent of material used to produce clothing is recycled into new clothing — a loss of more than $100 billion in materials each year, which the industry has learned to describe as the cost of doing business. [Ellen MacArthur Foundation, op. cit.](https://content.ellenmacarthurfoundation.org/m/6d5071bb8a5f05a2/original/A-New-Textiles-Economy-Redesigning-fashions-future.pdf) The Circularity Gap Report found that of all materials the textile industry uses, just 0.3 percent come from recycled sources. Over 99 percent come from virgin sources. [Circularity Gap Report: Textiles (2024)](https://circularity-gap.world/textiles)

![Environmental footprint of the textile industry, showing GHG emissions, water use, and waste across the value chain.](/api/blog/images/the-thread-of-power_environmental_footprint.png)
>*The textile value chain's environmental footprint spans climate, water, and waste. Fiber production and wet processing are the hottest hotspots. Source: Ellen MacArthur Foundation (2017); UNEP (2020); Circularity Gap Report (2024).*

The cheapness of synthetic fibres is the root cause, as cheapness so often is. Polyester is cheaper to produce than cotton, and virgin polyester is cheaper than recycled polyester. The economic incentive runs directly against the environmental imperative, and in the textile industry, the economic incentive has rarely lost a contest. The structure of power — with production concentrated among a small number of giant brands and fibre manufacturers — makes systemic change a matter of will, and the industry has never been particularly willing.

"The same creativity that defines the industry is what will transform it," the Ellen MacArthur Foundation argues. [Ellen MacArthur Foundation, "Circular Fashion" overview](https://www.ellenmacarthurfoundation.org/topics/fashion/overview) One hopes they are right. But creativity operates within constraints, and the primary constraint is the profit margin of a system built on volume. The industry's annual 2–8 percent share of global greenhouse gas emissions is projected to rise. Sector CO₂ emissions could hit 2.7 billion tons per year by 2030. [UNEP, "Sustainability and Circularity in the Textile Value Chain: Global Roadmap" (2023)](https://circulareconomy.europa.eu/platform/sites/default/files/2023-12/Full%20Report%20-%20UNEP%20Sustainability%20and%20Circularity%20in%20the%20Textile%20Value%20Chain%20A%20Global%20Roadmap_0.pdf)

---

**VIII. The Next Thread**

The future of textiles is dividing into two roads, as futures so often do when the present has become untenable. On one track lies the continuation of the synthetic, linear model — ever-cheaper polyester, ever-faster fashion, ever more waste. On the other lie two alternative visions: the circular economy and smart textiles.

The circular economy vision — championed by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation, UNEP, and a growing number of brands — imagines a system in which clothes are designed to last, to be repaired, remade, and eventually reborn as new garments. It is a vision that sounds almost quaint in an industry built on making things that fall apart just after they cease to be fashionable. Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) policies are being introduced in France, the Netherlands, and other European countries, requiring brands to fund the collection and recycling of the textiles they sell. [Ellen MacArthur Foundation, "Pushing the boundaries of EPR policy for textiles" (2024)](https://www.ellenmacarthurfoundation.org/epr-policy-for-textiles) Six scenarios identified by the Circularity Gap Report could triple the industry's circularity while reducing environmental impacts by up to 50 percent. [Circularity Gap Report, op. cit.](https://circularity-gap.world/textiles)

The smart textiles vision is something else entirely, and considerably more seductive to the sort of person who invests in futures. Valued at roughly $2.4 billion in 2025, the smart fabrics market is projected to reach between $5.6 billion and $21.2 billion by 2030, depending on the estimate — growth rates range from 18 to 31 percent annually. [MarketsandMarkets, "Smart Textiles Market Report 2025–2030"](https://www.marketsandmarkets.com/Market-Reports/smart-textiles-market-13764132.html); [Grand View Research, "Smart Fabrics Market 2030"](https://www.grandviewresearch.com/industry-analysis/smart-textiles-industry) These are fabrics that can sense, react, and adapt: graphene-coated fibres that monitor heart rate, carbon-nanotube threads that harvest energy from movement, AI-enabled textiles that function as human-machine interfaces.

A recent review in the *Journal of Electronic Materials* describes the field as "a fundamental materials design problem rather than a simple integration problem." [Hossain et al., "Nanomaterial-Enabled Smart Textiles," *J. Electron. Mater.* 55, 4899–4925 (2026)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11664-026-12806-0) The technological frontier is real — but so is the question of who will control it. Today's smart textile patents are concentrated in the United States, Japan, and South Korea. The next generation of textile power may belong not to the country with the cheapest labour or the largest mills, but to the one that masters the materials science — and the old pattern of control will simply have found a new disguise.

![Projected growth of the smart textiles market, 2025–2030, by application segment.](/api/blog/images/the-thread-of-power_smart_textiles_market.png)
>*The smart textiles market is projected to grow at 18.2% CAGR through 2030, with sensing applications and healthcare leading adoption. Source: MarketsandMarkets (2025); Grand View Research (2023).*

---

**Closing**

The woman stitching shirts in Dhaka has never heard of graphene, nor the Multi-Fibre Arrangement. She knows the piece rate for a finished garment, the cost of the bus ride to the factory, the rent for the room she shares with three other women. Her great-grandmother might have spun cotton by hand in a village in Bengal, before the British mills destroyed that market. Her granddaughter may work in a factory automated by robots and monitored by smart fabrics. The thread that connects them across centuries is not made of cotton or polyester or graphene. It is made of power.

Whoever controls the thread controls more than cloth. They control the terms on which billions of people are clothed, the conditions under which millions work, the environmental burden the planet bears, and the direction of technological change. For four hundred years, that power has moved — from weavers to mill owners to plantation owners to petrochemical companies — always promising liberation, always delivering a new master. Where it goes next — toward circularity or deeper into the linear economy, toward smart materials that serve human needs or toward still more concentrated control — is not a question of technology. It is a question of power. And as the history of textiles makes abundantly clear, power is never surrendered. It is only taken. Or lost.

---

**Source Notes**

- Broadberry & Gupta (2005). *Cotton Textiles and the Great Divergence*. CEPR Discussion Paper. [Source](https://wrap-test.warwick.ac.uk/id/eprint/1708/1/WRAP_Broadberry_CEPR-DP5183%5B1%5D.pdf)
- Humphries & Schneider (2018). *Spinning the Industrial Revolution*. Economic History Review 72(1). [Source](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ehr.12693)
- Harley (1998). *Cotton Textile Prices and the Industrial Revolution*. Oxford Economics. [Source](http://www.nuff.ox.ac.uk/economics/history/Paper81/harley81.pdf)
- Baines (1835). *History of the Cotton Manufacture in Great Britain*. Cambridge. [Source](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/history-of-the-cotton-manufacture-in-great-britain/0CF3C5233C9F06CE3CA287C9E91F3166)
- Ure (1835). *The Philosophy of Manufactures*. [Source](https://historyofeconomicthought.mcmaster.ca/ure/PhilosophyManufactures.pdf)
- Fordham Sourcebook. *Loss of Woollen Spinning* (1794). [Source](https://sourcebooks.web.fordham.edu/mod/1794woolens.asp)
- WTO (2024). *GVC Sectoral Profiles: Textiles and Clothing*. [Source](https://www.wto.org/english/res_e/statis_e/miwi_e/gvc_sectoral_profiles_textiles_clothing24_e.pdf)
- UNCTAD (2025). *Trends in Natural and Man-made Fibres Trade*. [Source](https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/ditccom2025d2_en.pdf)
- Textile Exchange (2025). *Materials Market Report 2025*. [Source](https://textileexchange.org/knowledge-center/reports/materials-market-report-2025/)
- Ellen MacArthur Foundation (2017). *A New Textiles Economy*. [Source](https://content.ellenmacarthurfoundation.org/m/6d5071bb8a5f05a2/original/A-New-Textiles-Economy-Redesigning-fashions-future.pdf)

- Circularity Gap Report (2024). *Textiles*. [Source](https://circularity-gap.world/textiles)

post.content:
# The Coast and the Quiet: New England's Internal Distance

The man boarding the 7:15 Red Line train at Braintree, Massachusetts, on a June morning is not thinking about the fact that he lives in the fourth-most-densely-populated state in the union — because he is too busy standing (there are no seats), pressed against a stranger's backpack, his phone counting down a 32-minute arrival at South Station. He pays $2,726 a month for a mortgage on a house whose median value in his area has climbed past $562,100 [Census Bureau QuickFacts: Massachusetts](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/massachusetts). He shares his car-free commute with a transit system that moves 1.2 million people daily. His neighbors include families from Brazil, China, Haiti, and the Dominican Republic. A quarter of the households in his state speak a language other than English at home [Census Bureau QuickFacts: MA, ME, NH](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/ME,MA,NH/PST040216). Density, in his experience, is not an abstraction. It is the polite name for having a stranger's backpack pressed into your ribs at 7:15 in the morning.

Three hundred miles north, on a gravel road in Aroostook County, Maine, a woman in a Ford F-150 checks her mailbox at the end of a driveway that is a mile and a half long. She knows her nearest neighbor's name, the make of their truck, and how many cords of wood they stacked last fall — a degree of intimacy that the man on the T could not achieve with the person currently occupying his personal space. The median home value in her state is $296,600 — barely half what the man on the T is paying [Census Bureau QuickFacts: Maine](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/ME/POP060220). She drives 45 minutes to the grocery store. The population density of the county she lives in is 3.9 people per square mile — roughly the same as central Montana [Census Bureau QuickFacts: Maine Geography](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/ME/POP060220). Her state's population is one-fifth the size of the transit system that carries the man to work. Solitude, for her, is not a vacation. It is the natural state of things.

They live in the same region. They vote in the same presidential primary. They pay the same highest-in-the-nation electricity rates. And they might as well inhabit different centuries. They do.

---

New England occupies the peculiar position of being both one of the smallest and one of the most culturally coherent regions in the United States — six states united by colonial history, town-meeting governance, high educational attainment, Democratic presidential voting habits, and residential electricity bills that exceed those of every other region in the continental country [EIA 2024 Average Retail Price](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/sales_revenue_price/pdf/table_4.pdf). It is roughly the size of Washington state — 71,992 square miles — yet the internal gaps between its states rival the disparities between entire American regions [Census Bureau QuickFacts: All six states](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/table/PST045216/50,44,33,23,25,09). Rhode Island packs 1,061 people into every square mile; Maine gets by on 44. A household in Massachusetts earns a median of $103,960 per year; a household in Maine, $74,733. Vermont's population (644,663) could fit inside Boston's metropolitan statistical area with room to spare [Census Bureau QuickFacts: Vermont](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/50/PST045216). These are not subtle gradients. They are structural chasms hiding in plain sight, masked by the shared accent, the common red-brick-and-white-clapboard aesthetic, and the mutual exasperation with Interstate 95 — the great unifier of inconvenience.

---

## The Scale of the Small

The first thing to understand about New England's geography is that Maine is lying — not deliberately, but because the state is physically larger than the other five states combined. Maine's land area of 30,845 square miles exceeds the total of Connecticut, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, Vermont, and New Hampshire added together (31,848 square miles) [Census Bureau QuickFacts: All six states](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/table/PST045216/50,44,33,23,25,09). You could drop Rhode Island into Aroostook County — the northernmost chunk of Maine — and still have room to wander. Northern Maine is geographically part of the Canadian Maritimes in every way that matters except the passport check, a fact its residents do not find nearly as amusing as the map suggests.

This produces a density gradient that has no equivalent in any other comparably sized American region. The three coastal states — Rhode Island, Massachusetts, and Connecticut — form a continuous urbanized arc stretching from New Haven to Providence to Boston. Their combined population density is 902 people per square mile. The three interior states — Vermont, New Hampshire, and Maine — are largely rural. Their combined density is 69 people per square mile [Census Bureau QuickFacts: All six states](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/table/PST045216/50,44,33,23,25,09). The factor of thirteen between these two numbers is not a gradient. It is a wall — one that is entirely invisible from an airplane and entirely inescapable from the ground.

At the extremes, the contrast becomes almost absurd. Rhode Island, the second-most-densely-populated state in the nation after New Jersey, packs 1,061 people per square mile [Census Bureau Population Density Data Table](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/decennial/2020/data/apportionment/population-density-data-table.pdf). Maine, the least-densely-populated state east of the Mississippi, packs 44. The human experience of space in these two states — the proximity of neighbors, the availability of sidewalks, the ambient noise level of daily life — is not merely different. It is inverted. Rhode Islanders, one suspects, have never understood what Mainers mean by "quiet." Mainers, one knows, have never needed to.

And yet: the interior states are growing faster. Between the 2020 Census and the July 2025 estimates, Maine added 3.8 percent to its population — the fastest growth rate in New England and the 15th-fastest nationally. New Hampshire added 2.7 percent, Connecticut 2.2 percent. Vermont, astonishingly, grew by only 0.2 percent — effectively flat, a demographic stagnation that has become a subject of growing concern in Montpelier [Census Bureau State Population Estimates 2025](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/table/PST045216/50,44,33,23,25,09). Vermont's population of 644,663 is smaller than the city of Boston's metropolitan population growth since 2010. The state, it seems, is not so much losing people as declining to acquire them.

The conventional wisdom — that the rural north is emptying out while the coastal south swells — is, for now, exactly backward. The pandemic-era migration to the northern forest has not fully reversed.

---

![Population density comparison across the six New England states — Rhode Island exceeds 1,000 people per square mile while Maine, the largest state, falls below 50.](/api/blog/images/new-england-coast-quiet_density.png)

*Caption: Population density (people per square mile, 2020 Census) for the six New England states and the U.S. average. Rhode Island is second-densest nationally; Maine is the least-dense state east of the Mississippi. Data: U.S. Census Bureau.*

---

## The Demography of Difference

The coastal states are not merely denser. They are qualitatively different places — which is to say, they are inhabited by qualitatively different people.

Connecticut is 19.2 percent Hispanic, 13.3 percent Black, and 5.5 percent Asian. Its foreign-born population stands at 15.7 percent. A nearly identical profile describes Rhode Island (18.8 percent Hispanic, 9.5 percent Black, 4.1 percent Asian) and Massachusetts (14.0 percent Hispanic, 9.9 percent Black, 8.3 percent Asian), where 18 percent of residents were born outside the United States [Census Bureau QuickFacts: CT](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/09/PST045216). [Census Bureau QuickFacts: RI](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/44/PST045216). [Census Bureau QuickFacts: MA](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/massachusetts).

Vermont is 93.2 percent White alone. Maine is 93.2 percent White alone. New Hampshire is 92.3 percent White alone. The Hispanic population of Vermont (2.7 percent) is roughly one-seventh the size of Connecticut's. The foreign-born share of Maine (4.1 percent) is less than a quarter of Massachusetts's [Census Bureau QuickFacts: VT, RI, NH, ME, MA, CT](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/table/PST045216/50,44,33,23,25,09). The northern states, one might say, are not so much un-diverse as extraordinarily consistent — consistent in a way that the coastal states, with their Babel of languages and cuisines, could never manage.

What this means, in practical terms, is that a child growing up in Bridgeport, Connecticut, or Providence, Rhode Island, or Boston, Massachusetts — cities where no single racial or ethnic group constitutes an overwhelming majority — inhabits a fundamentally different social landscape than a child growing up in Burlington, Vermont, or Portland, Maine, or rural Grafton County, New Hampshire. The difference is not theoretical. It shapes everything from the languages heard on the school bus to the cuisines available on the high street to the informal networks of opportunity that young people absorb by osmosis — which is to say, everything a census cannot capture but a life cannot escape.

Twenty-five percent of Massachusetts households speak a language other than English at home. In Vermont, the figure is 5.5 percent. In Maine, 6.0 percent [Census Bureau QuickFacts: MA, ME, NH](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/ME,MA,NH/PST040216). [Census Bureau QuickFacts: VT](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/50/PST045216). These numbers trace not merely a demographic difference but a difference in worldview — the difference between a society that regularly confronts its own pluralism and one that largely does not. One learns, in the interior, to recognize one's own kind. One has no choice, on the coast, but to learn the ways of everyone else's.

---

![Racial and ethnic composition of each New England state — showing the stark contrast between the diverse coastal tier (CT, RI, MA) and the predominantly White interior (VT, NH, ME).](/api/blog/images/new-england-coast-quiet_demographics.png)

*Caption: Racial and ethnic composition by state, 2020-2024 American Community Survey estimates. The southern coastal states are among the most diverse in the Northeast; the three northern states rank among the least diverse in the nation. Data: U.S. Census Bureau.*

---

## The Knowledge Premium

If demography divides New England, then education is what paradoxically unites it — even as it exposes a different kind of internal distance, which is always the most insidious kind.

All six New England states rank among the top 20 in the nation for bachelor's degree attainment [FRED: Bachelor's Degree or Higher by State](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/release/tables?eid=391444&rid=330). Massachusetts ranks second nationally, behind only the District of Columbia, with 47.3 percent of adults holding a bachelor's degree or higher. Vermont ranks fourth (43.8 percent), Connecticut seventh (42.5 percent), New Hampshire ninth (40.6 percent), Rhode Island 14th (37.7 percent), and Maine 18th (36.2 percent). By comparison, the national average is 33.7 percent [U.S. Data Explorer: Bachelor's Degree by State 2024](https://usdataexplorer.com/ranking/bachelors-degree-or-higher/states/). Every New England state exceeds the national rate — a uniformity that is, by American standards, extraordinary, and by the same standards entirely insufficient to prevent the region from arguing about everything else.

But the gap between Massachusetts and Maine — 11 percentage points — is larger than the gap between Maine and Mississippi (12 points). The region's educational advantage is real, but it is not evenly distributed. It concentrates in the Boston metropolitan corridor and radiates outward, dissipating as the road miles accumulate. Education, like wealth, follows the laws of physics: it pools in the lowest point, which in this case happens to be Cambridge.

The Federal Reserve Bank of Boston quantified this dynamic in a January 2026 study of four decades of administrative wage records. The finding was striking: per capita personal income in New England grew from $10,731 to $87,655 between 1980 and 2024 — the largest increase of any U.S. census division [Boston Fed: Educational Attainment and Wage Growth](https://www.bostonfed.org/publications/new-england-public-policy-center-research-report/2026/educational-attainment-wage-growth-in-new-england.aspx). As of 2024, 53 percent of New England workers aged 25 to 64 held at least a bachelor's degree, and 23 percent possessed advanced degrees — well above national averages of 44 percent and 17 percent, respectively. The region's economic success, the study concluded, is inseparable from its educational intensity. The flywheel works. But it works best in places that already have momentum — which is to say, it works best in places that least need the help.

The income gap that results is the most tangible measure of New England's internal distance. Massachusetts's median household income of $103,960 is the fourth-highest in the nation [Census Bureau ACS 2024](https://www.census.gov/library/publications/2025/acs/acsbr-025.html). New Hampshire follows at $99,031, then Connecticut at $95,781, Rhode Island at $87,796, and Vermont at $81,203. Maine, at $74,733, ranks 33rd nationally — a position closer to Missouri than to Massachusetts [Census Bureau QuickFacts: ME](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/ME/INC110221). The difference of $29,227 between the region's richest and poorest median household incomes is, in raw terms, larger than the gap between California ($100,205) and West Virginia ($57,872) — two states separated by 2,500 miles and a continent of political and cultural difference.

The region's poorest state and its richest state are separated by a five-hour drive on Interstate 95. They are separated by $29,000 in annual income. They are separated by very little else, which is precisely what makes the distance so striking. Proximity, one learns, has nothing to do with closeness.

---

## The Cost of Being Coastal

If income flows from education, then housing costs flow from density — and on this measure, the coastal tier exacts a punishing premium.

The median home value in Massachusetts is $562,100. In Rhode Island: $404,200. In New Hampshire: $402,500. In Connecticut: $366,900. In Vermont: $316,600. In Maine: $296,600 [Census Bureau QuickFacts: All six states](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/table/PST045216/50,44,33,23,25,09). The pattern is not random. It maps almost perfectly onto the population density gradient, with one instructive anomaly: New Hampshire, which is less dense than Connecticut, has more expensive housing — because it sits in the Boston commuter shed, absorbing spillover demand from a state whose own housing supply cannot keep pace. The lesson is clear: even the desire to escape Massachusetts exacts a Massachusetts toll.

The cost of a mortgage tells the same story in monthly terms. Massachusetts homeowners with a mortgage pay a median of $2,726 per month — among the highest in the nation, exceeded only by California, Hawaii, New Jersey, and the District of Columbia [Census Bureau: The Cost of Homeownership Continues to Rise](https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2025/acs-1-year-estimates.html). Rhode Island homeowners pay $2,234, New Hampshire $2,367, Connecticut $2,429. Vermont drops to $1,907, and to $1,729 in Maine — still substantial, but less than two-thirds of the Massachusetts burden [Census Bureau QuickFacts: Housing data](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/table/PST045216/50,44,33,23,25,09). One pays, it seems, for the privilege of being where other people are. One saves by going where they are not.

Rent tells a parallel story. The median gross rent in Massachusetts ($1,762) exceeds Maine's ($1,139) by more than $600 per month — an annual rent differential of more than $7,400. That $7,400 is, in effect, the annual premium on being coastal: the price of proximity to everything except affordability.

Yet homeownership rates invert the pattern. Maine has the highest rate in New England (74.3 percent), followed by Vermont (73.2 percent) and New Hampshire (72.8 percent). Massachusetts has the lowest (62.5 percent), followed by Rhode Island (63.6 percent) and Connecticut (66.5 percent). The coastal tier, where housing costs the most, is where the fewest people own their homes. The interior, where housing is cheaper, is where ownership is the norm. Affordability and ownership track each other closely. Density and ownership are inverse. One might almost say that the closer one gets to the American Dream, the less likely one is to own a piece of it.

And then there is electricity. New England as a whole pays the highest residential electricity rates in the contiguous United States — an average of 27.68 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2024, compared to a national average of roughly 15.5 cents [EIA Table 4: Average Retail Price 2024](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/sales_revenue_price/pdf/table_4.pdf). Massachusetts residents pay 29.35 cents; Connecticut, 28.75; Rhode Island, 28.65. But Maine pays 24.29 cents, New Hampshire 23.40, and Vermont — the state with the lowest residential rate in New England — pays 21.90 cents, nearly a third less than Massachusetts. The interior is marginally more affordable not just in shelter but in keeping the lights on — though "affordable" is, in this context, a relative term used by people who have never seen a bill from any other region.

The Boston Fed study notes that New England's per capita income growth has been the highest in the nation over four decades. But that growth has been captured disproportionately by those who could afford the coastal premium. The region's economic success is real. It is also regionally concentrated and increasingly stratified by housing cost. The rich get richer, and everyone else gets a longer commute.

---

![Median household income versus median home value across the six New England states — the coastal tier clusters in the expensive upper right, while the interior occupies the more affordable lower left.](/api/blog/images/new-england-coast-quiet_income_housing.png)

*Caption: Median household income (2024 dollars) versus median home value, 2020-2024 ACS estimates. Massachusetts leads both measures; Maine trails on both. The spread between the region's richest and poorest states ($29,227) exceeds the spread between California and West Virginia. Data: U.S. Census Bureau.*

---

## The Politics of Proximity

Politically, New England presents a united front to the rest of the country — a front that is, like most united fronts, considerably more united in appearance than in reality. All six states voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. The region's electoral votes — 33 in total — have gone to the Democratic nominee in every presidential election since 1992, with two exceptions (New Hampshire voted for George H.W. Bush in 1988, and for George W. Bush in 2000 — the only electoral votes a Republican has taken from New England in the 21st century) [FEC 2024 Official Presidential Results](https://www.fec.gov/resources/cms-content/documents/2024presgeresults.pdf).

But the margins tell a more interesting story than the outcomes. Harris won Vermont by roughly 30 points — her strongest performance in the region. She won Massachusetts by 25 points. Connecticut by 14.5. Rhode Island by 12. Maine by 6.9. New Hampshire by approximately 2.4 points [Elections Daily: Analyzing the 2024 Election in New England](https://elections-daily.com/2025/02/12/analyzing-the-2024-election-results-in-new-england/). The spread from Vermont to New Hampshire — the range of Democratic performance within a single region — is nearly 28 percentage points. The region appears to vote as a bloc only if one does not look too closely at the numbers, which is, of course, exactly what everyone does.

New Hampshire functions, in effect, as New England's swing state. It has the region's most independent electorate, the shortest coastline (18 miles), and the deepest attachment to its "Live Free or Die" identity — an identity its residents take seriously enough to exercise in both directions simultaneously. It voted for a Republican governor (Kelly Ayotte, elected in 2024 with 53 percent of the vote) while simultaneously casting its four electoral votes for Harris. The state's second congressional district — the western and northern reaches — voted for Harris by a margin barely exceeding 3 points. New Hampshire, in short, is the region's conscience: it cannot decide what it believes, and it believes in that indecision wholeheartedly.

Maine, too, splits its electoral sovereignty: its statewide vote went to Harris by 6.9 points, but the 2nd Congressional District — the vast, rural northern and eastern portion of the state — awarded one electoral vote to Donald Trump, as it did in 2016 and 2020. Maine is one of only two states (Nebraska is the other) that allocate electoral votes by congressional district. This system, which elsewhere produces only mathematical curiosity, in Maine generates a genuine political schism: the state is of two minds, and it has arranged its electoral machinery to prove it.

Vermont, meanwhile, is the most consistently Democratic state in the union by presidential voting margin — yet in 2024, Republicans posted their strongest gains in the state relative to any other in New England. Trump flipped Orleans County, a first for the GOP since 2000. Republicans gained 19 seats in the state Senate and six in the state House, breaking Democratic supermajorities. Senator Bernie Sanders, the state's independent icon, posted his weakest reelection margin to date [Elections Daily](https://elections-daily.com/2025/02/12/analyzing-the-2024-election-results-in-new-england/). Even in the most reliably blue state in the union, it seems, the ground shifts — slowly, but perceptibly, like a glacier that has decided to become a mudslide.

Voter turnout, too, tells a revealing story. Maine had the highest voter turnout as a percentage of voting-age population in New England (72.9 percent), followed by New Hampshire (72.2 percent) — both among the highest rates in the nation. Massachusetts (61.8 percent) and Connecticut (61.7 percent) had some of the lowest [Dave Leip's Atlas: 2024 Turnout](https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/data.php?datatype=national&f=0&year=2024). The interior states vote in higher proportions than the coastal states — a pattern that holds across every election cycle and that suggests a civic culture in which the act of voting is more deeply embedded in community identity, perhaps because community identity is harder to come by and therefore more actively maintained. In the interior, one votes because one belongs. On the coast, one votes because one has been reminded to by a text message.

---

## The Unifying Threads

Given the scale of these internal differences, one might reasonably ask what holds New England together at all. The answer, as with most answers, is a set of structural commonalities that run deeper than the disparities — though "deeper" does not necessarily mean "more interesting."

Educational attainment is the most significant. Every New England state exceeds the national average for bachelor's degree attainment — and by substantial margins. The region as a whole educates its population at a level that would be the envy of any country in Europe, and that, in this context, is the highest compliment one can pay to a group of American states.

Employment is consistently strong. The New England division had an average unemployment rate of 3.6 percent in 2024, below the national average of 4.0 percent. Vermont (2.3 percent) had the second-lowest unemployment rate among all states, behind only South Dakota [BLS: Geographic Profile of Employment 2024](https://www.bls.gov/opub/geographic-profile/home.htm). [BLS: Unemployment rates 2024](https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2025/unemployment-rates-averaged-1-8-percent-in-south-dakota-5-6-percent-in-nevada-in-2024.htm). The region, whatever its internal arguments, has not yet resorted to the indignity of widespread joblessness.

Health insurance coverage is nearly universal. Massachusetts, with only 3.3 percent of adults under 65 uninsured, has the lowest uninsured rate in the nation — the legacy of its 2006 healthcare reform, the model for the Affordable Care Act. The highest uninsured rate in New England is Maine's 7.1 percent — still below the national average of roughly 8.3 percent [Census Bureau QuickFacts: All six states](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/table/PST045216/50,44,33,23,25,09). The region has decided, collectively, that health is a right rather than a luxury — a position that puts it at odds with roughly half the country and entirely at peace with itself.

Broadband access is uniformly high. Between 90.3 percent of Maine households and 92.9 percent of New Hampshire households subscribe to broadband internet — a narrow range that speaks to the region's relatively even infrastructure investment [Census Bureau QuickFacts: MA, ME, NH](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/ME,MA,NH/PST040216). Even the most remote farmhouse, it seems, is not too remote for Netflix.

And, everywhere in New England, the electricity bill arrives with a number that surprises — a shared burden of infrastructure age, fuel import dependence, and regional market design that unites the six states in a collective grumble. The average New England household paid 27.68 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2024 — 78 percent above the national average [EIA 2024](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/sales_revenue_price/pdf/table_4.pdf). In this, at least, the commuter on the T and the woman in Aroostook County are true equals. Nothing unites people quite like a shared grievance, and nothing generates a grievance quite like a New England electricity bill.

---

## The Distance Between

New England is not one thing. It is six things that happen to share a border, a colonial history, a surprising number of Dunkin' Donuts locations, a collective astonishment at the price of electricity, and a presidential voting pattern that makes the rest of the country regard it as a single liberal bloc — a bloc whose internal fractures are visible only from the inside, and only to those who care to look.

The density gradient from Providence to Presque Isle is not merely a matter of how many people occupy a square mile. It predicts educational attainment, income, housing costs, racial diversity, foreign-born population, homeownership rates, and the likelihood that a household speaks a language other than English at home. Within a region smaller than Washington state, these six variables shift by more than they do across entire swaths of the American interior. New England, in other words, contains multitudes — and the multitudes do not always get along.

And yet the things that bind them are not trivial. The educational intensity that puts all six states in the national top 20. The labor market that keeps unemployment below the national average. The universal healthcare coverage that leaves almost no one behind. The broadband cable that connects the most remote farmhouse to the same network as the Back Bay brownstone. The shared exasperation with a power grid that charges twice what the rest of the country pays. The historical memory of mill strikes, town meetings, covered bridges, and leaf-peeping season. These are not small things. They are the threads from which a region's identity is woven, even when the fabric is more patched than patterned.

The commuter on the T and the woman in Aroostook County share a region. They share an accent — or close enough. They share a set of assumptions about what constitutes a good life, a fair society, a proper town common. But the ground beneath their feet — the density of opportunity, the price of shelter, the face of the crowd on the street, the distance to the nearest neighbor — could not be more different. They are cousins, not siblings; the family resemblance is there, but the lives are their own.

New England's homogeneity is real. Its internal distance is equally real. The region does not need to be resolved into a single story. It needs to be seen clearly for what it is: a small place with very large differences, held together by history, habit, and the gravitational pull of its dominant city — a city that nearly half its population has never lived within a hundred miles of, and whose influence they nonetheless feel every time they open an electric bill, look at a home listing, or watch a presidential candidate try to figure out which New England they are actually campaigning in. Boston, it turns out, does not need to be loved to be felt. It only needs to exist.

The distance between the two New Englands is not a problem to be solved. It is a condition to be described. And the description, once made, raises a question the region is only beginning to confront: whether a place this internally varied can continue to function as a single political and economic unit — or whether the coast and the quiet are destined to drift further apart, connected only by the roads that run between them, the power lines that bind them, and the shared memory of the winters that shaped them both.
