# The Roads You've Never Driven: America's Hidden Byway Empire

---

On a September morning in 1935, more than one hundred men gathered at the North Carolina-Virginia line, where a two-lane dirt track crossed between Lowgap and Sparta. They came from the unemployment rolls of Alleghany County — farmers without farms, millworkers without mills, fathers who had not worked in years. Their first job: clear a two-hundred-foot-wide swath of timber off a mountainside. A diesel-powered shovel that had cost twenty-five thousand dollars sat waiting. The nation was in its sixth year of the Great Depression. The Blue Ridge Parkway was about to begin.

They worked with picks, shovels, and the quiet desperation of men who had been told, over and over, that there was no work for them. They built stone bridges by hand. They drilled holes for blasting charges into granite that had sat untouched since the last ice age. They lived in Civilian Conservation Corps camps — tidy rows of tents organized in military fashion, nicknamed the "tree army." They planted trees to hold the soil, built retaining walls, and carved a road along the crests of the Southern Appalachians where no road had ever been. They were building something they could not yet see: the most visited unit in the entire National Park System, which would one day draw nearly seventeen million visitors a year [Blue Ridge Parkway construction, September 1935 - Mt. Airy News via superscenic.com](https://superscenic.com/omeka/items/show/5); [CCC camp at Black Camp Gap, August 1935 - UNC DocSouth](https://docsouth.unc.edu/blueridgeparkway/content/4650/).

![Early construction on the Blue Ridge Parkway, Section 2-A-1, 1936 — men and machinery carving a road through the Appalachian mountains.](/api/blog/images/byways_blueridge_construction.jpg)
*Blue Ridge Parkway construction, Section 2-A-1, 1936. W.D. Stanton, National Park Service. Public domain, courtesy Library of Congress HAER collection.*

---

![Civilian Conservation Corps camp at Black Camp Gap, North Carolina, August 20, 1935 — tents organized in military rows before the Parkway was built.](/api/blog/images/byways_ccc_camp.jpg)
*Civilian Conservation Corps camp at Black Camp Gap, North Carolina, August 20, 1935. Edward H. Abbuehl, National Park Service — Blue Ridge Parkway. Public domain, courtesy NPS via UNC DocSouth.*

---

Ninety years later, that road — the Blue Ridge Parkway, a 469-mile ribbon of asphalt that follows the spine of the Appalachian Mountains from Shenandoah National Park to the edge of the Great Smoky Mountains — generates $1.52 billion in visitor spending every year and supports 15,679 jobs across Virginia and North Carolina. This is not an incidental side effect. It is, and always was, the point. The parkway was conceived during the Depression as an economic stimulus — a way to channel federal money into the most impoverished region of the eastern United States, paying unemployed mountaineers to build a road that would, in turn, deliver tourists and their dollars back into the same hollows and coves. It worked so well that the National Park Service now calls it "the most heavily visited unit of the National Park System." It draws more people than Yellowstone, Yosemite, and the Grand Canyon combined [NPS 2024 Visitor Spending Effects report](https://www.nps.gov/nature/customcf/NPS_Data_Visualization/docs/NPS_2024_Visitor_Spending_Effects.pdf); [HAER Blue Ridge Parkway significance statement, Library of Congress](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/nc0478/).

The Blue Ridge Parkway is the crown jewel of a national program so obscure that most Americans have never heard of it, though it touches nearly every state in the union. The National Scenic Byways Program, established by Congress in 1991 under the Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act, has quietly designated 184 roads across 48 states as "America's Byways" — a collection that includes National Scenic Byways and the elite All-American Roads. The criteria for designation are exacting: a road must possess at least one of six "intrinsic qualities" — archaeological, cultural, historic, natural, recreational, or scenic — and must be nominated by the state or an Indian tribe before it can even be considered for federal recognition. The U.S. Secretary of Transportation personally signs off on each designation [FHWA National Scenic Byways Program](https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/hep/scenic_byways/); [FHWA Designations page](https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/hep/scenic_byways/designations/).

And yet: ask the average American how many National Scenic Byways exist, and they will guess zero. Ask them to name one, and they might mention Route 66 — which is, indeed, a National Scenic Byway in multiple states. But Route 66 is the exception that proves the rule of invisibility. There are roads in this collection that wind through the most spectacular landscapes on the continent, roads that trace the path of freedom seekers escaping slavery, roads that follow the route of the Lewis and Clark expedition, roads that climb to nearly eleven thousand feet through the Beartooth Highway in Montana and Wyoming — roads that could change the way you see the country, if only you knew they were there.

---

## The Road You Have Driven

Route 66 is the only byway that needs no introduction — a 2,448-mile highway from Chicago to Santa Monica that John Steinbeck called "the Mother Road" and that Americans have elevated to something approaching mythology. In 2026, it celebrates its centennial, and the occasion has prompted a wave of reexamination. The Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, of all institutions, published "The Byways Report: The Scenic Route to Rural Prosperity" in February 2026, focused on the 432 miles of Route 66 that cross Oklahoma and the small towns that have rebuilt themselves around the Mother Road's enduring appeal [Kansas City Fed Byways Report, Feb 2026](https://www.kansascityfed.org/community/the-byways-report/).

The report's conclusion is bracing in its practicality: "Tourism is an efficient form of economic development for towns and regions, as it doesn't require building infrastructure such as schools or hospitals to support new residents." You can build a tourism economy on what already exists — a historic motel, a diner that has served hamburgers since 1953, a filling station repurposed as a museum, a roadside attraction of such magnificent oddity that people will drive five hundred miles to photograph it and post it on social media. The Blue Whale of Catoosa, Oklahoma — a concrete whale emerging from a pond, with a slide built into its mouth — has been doing precisely this since 1972 [Kansas City Fed Byways Report photos](https://www.kansascityfed.org/community/the-byways-report/).

But the Kansas City Fed's report is about something more than kitsch. It is about a fundamental insight into American economic geography: the roads built to connect places also create the possibility of staying in them. "When linked along a route — a byway — small towns use what makes them special to enchant visitors and boost prosperity, improving the quality of life for their residents," the report's foreword reads. Among the ten themes it outlines for strengthening byway economies, the first is: "Take an appreciative view of what your town has to offer visitors."

---

![Dust Bowl refugees camped alongside the highway near Bakersfield, California, November 1935 — the road as both escape route and destination.](/api/blog/images/byways_route66_dustbowl.jpg)
*Along the highway near Bakersfield, California. Dorothea Lange, 1935. Farm Security Administration, Library of Congress. Public domain.*

---

The economic data makes it clear why appreciation matters. The Route 66 Economic Impact Study, conducted by Rutgers University in collaboration with the National Park Service and the World Monuments Fund, found that travelers on the Mother Road spend $132 million per year in the communities along its path — eighty-five percent of them visiting historic places and museums. Those dollars support 2,400 jobs, generate $127 million in gross domestic product, and produce $37 million in tax revenue annually [Route 66 Economic Impact Study, NPS](https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/route-66-economic-impact-study.htm); [WMF Synthesis of Findings](https://www.wmf.org/sites/default/files/press_releases/Rt%2066%20Econ%20Impact%20Study.pdf). The restored Route 66-themed motels, restaurants, and gift shops that anchor downtowns in towns like Vinita, Oklahoma and Galena, Kansas are not quaint relics. They are the economy.

## The Road You Should Drive

The Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad Byway is a 125-mile driving tour of forty-five historic sites across Maryland's Eastern Shore, following the landscape where Tubman was born into slavery around 1822 and from which she escaped to freedom. It is a road that runs through the same marshes, farm fields, and tidal creeks that Tubman navigated on her thirteen rescue missions, during which she led approximately seventy enslaved people to freedom — and, by her own account, "never lost a single passenger." The byway connects sites where she was enslaved, where she hid, where she received assistance, and where she found safety. It ends at the Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad Visitor Center, a 10,000-square-foot LEED-certified building that opened in 2017 on seventeen acres of parkland, complete with a meditation garden and nature trails [Scenic America, History of the Harriet Tubman Byway](https://www.scenic.org/2022/06/22/the-history-of-the-harriet-tubman-underground-railroad-byway/); [Harriet Tubman Byway travel guide](https://harriettubmanbyway.org/newhtbw/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/TubmanBywayGuide_2017.pdf).

What makes this byway remarkable is not merely its historical significance — though it is difficult to overstate the power of driving a road that follows the literal path taken by one of the most extraordinary figures in American history. It is that the byway functions simultaneously as a memorial, an educational tool, and an economic engine. A 2016 study by the economic development firm Camoin 310 found that the 251,155 net new visitors drawn to the byway each year contribute $23 million in annual sales to Dorchester and Caroline Counties, supporting 363 jobs and $9.9 million in earnings. A separate analysis from the same study found that Maryland residents who use the byway for recreation derive an additional $187,000 per year in direct use benefit — the value of having a beautiful road to drive [Harriet Tubman Byway Economic Impact Study, via visitdorchester.org](https://visitdorchester.org/media/markets/dor-co/links-information/full-report.pdf).

There is, in other words, a business case for remembering who you are.

The same principle applies to roads with less freighted histories. The Paul Bunyan Scenic Byway in Minnesota generates $21.2 million in economic output and supports 331 jobs. The Lake Country Scenic Byway, also in Minnesota, generates $31.7 million and supports 512 jobs — or $344,000 per mile. The Beartooth Highway in Montana and Wyoming, which reaches nearly 11,000 feet and is open only four months a year, generates more than $50 million in that short season. Florida's twenty-six scenic highways collectively produce $63.1 million in direct economic impact, supporting 1,070 jobs [University of Minnesota Tourism Center, Paul Bunyan and Lake Country Byways study](https://conservancy.umn.edu/items/a5d481ff-afe5-4c43-9149-7350f0060966); [Florida Scenic Highways study, ROSA P](https://rosap.ntl.bts.gov/view/dot/54531/dot_54531_DS1.pdf); [Beartooth Highway thesis, University of Montana](https://scholarworks.umt.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2146&context=etd).

None of these figures include the most staggering statistic in the entire byway system: the 184 designated roads are a subset of a much larger phenomenon. The National Park Service units that overlap with or function as scenic byways — the Blue Ridge Parkway, the Natchez Trace Parkway, the George Washington Memorial Parkway — generated a combined $29 billion in visitor spending in 2024, supporting 340,100 jobs across the country. The Blue Ridge Parkway alone accounts for $1.52 billion of that total, making it the second most economically valuable unit in the entire Park Service, behind only the Great Smoky Mountains National Park [NPS 2024 VSE report](https://www.nps.gov/nature/customcf/NPS_Data_Visualization/docs/NPS_2024_Visitor_Spending_Effects.pdf).

Why does virtually no one know this? There is no single answer. Part of it is that the National Scenic Byways Program has never had the marketing budget of the National Park Service, which itself struggles for visibility. Part of it is that roads are so ordinary — so much a part of the background of daily life — that the idea of a "designated" road sounds bureaucratic rather than thrilling. The program's funding has also been erratic: authorized at $74.3 million under ISTEA in 1991, it was cut to $16 million in the 2021 appropriations, then partially restored to $27.5 million by 2024. It is a program that has always done more with less, and that has paid for its efficiency in obscurity [FHWA Reauthorization page](https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/hep/scenic_byways/byway_quality/projects/reauthorization_phases.cfm); [FHWA NSBP page](https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/hep/scenic_byways/).

---

## The Roads That Almost Were

The idea of a national scenic highway system did not spring from nowhere in 1991. Its roots reach back to the earliest days of the automobile. In 1922, the Bronx River Parkway opened in Westchester County, New York, the first road in America designed not for speed or commerce but for pleasure — a winding, landscaped drive with moderate speeds, intended to let motorists enjoy the scenery. It was followed in 1932 by the Mount Vernon Memorial Highway, linking Washington, D.C. to George Washington's estate, the first federally built scenic parkway. In 1935, the Blue Ridge Parkway began its fifty-two-year construction odyssey, a New Deal project that would employ thousands of men through the Great Depression [FHWA History of Scenic Road Programs](https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/infrastructure/scenichistory.cfm).

---

![Cars on the Bronx River Parkway, October 22, 1922 — the first road in America designed for pleasure driving.](/api/blog/images/byways_bronx_river_parkway.jpg)
*Cars on the Bronx River Parkway, October 22, 1922. Bronx Parkway Commission Photograph Collection, Westchester County Archives.*

---

![Aerial view of a bridge underpass on the Mount Vernon Memorial Highway, 1932 — the first federally constructed scenic parkway in America.](/api/blog/images/byways_mount_vernon_parkway.jpg)
*Mount Vernon Memorial Highway bridge underpass, 1932. Historic American Engineering Record, Library of Congress. Public domain.*

President John F. Kennedy established the Recreation Advisory Council in 1962, which recommended the development of a national program of scenic roads and parkways. The resulting 1966 interagency study, "A Proposed Program for Scenic Roads and Parkways," remains the most exhaustive review of the subject ever conducted. It cited five reasons for a national scenic road program: driving for pleasure was one of America's most popular recreational pursuits; automobile ownership and leisure time were increasing; urban growth was consuming open space; tourism generated substantial economic benefits; and road planning and design could produce aesthetic and recreational gains. The study recommended a minimum program and an expanded program, with financing, administration, and planning mechanisms [FHWA History of Scenic Road Programs](https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/infrastructure/scenichistory.cfm).

It took another twenty-five years for Congress to act.

When ISTEA finally passed in 1991, it created the National Scenic Byways Program as a "grass-roots collaborative effort" to "recognize, preserve, and enhance selected roads throughout the United States." The program's structure was deliberately bottom-up: roads are nominated by states or Indian tribes, not by the federal government. Local communities must develop corridor management plans that spell out how they will preserve the road's intrinsic qualities while promoting tourism. The federal role is limited to designation and grant funding — a light touch that has proved remarkably durable [FHWA US Code page](https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/hep/scenic_byways/us_code.cfm); [Interim Policy, Federal Register 1995](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-1995-05-18/html/95-12211.htm).

## The Map

What does the collection look like? It is stranger and more wonderful than you might imagine.

You can drive the Selma to Montgomery March Byway in Alabama, which traces the route of the 1965 voting rights march — a road that is not merely historic but actively didactic, teaching the geography of the civil rights movement mile by mile. You can drive the San Juan Skyway in Colorado, a 236-mile loop through the San Juan Mountains that passes through the old mining towns of Ouray, Silverton, and Telluride, offering views of fourteen-thousand-foot peaks and the remnants of a silver boom that ended 130 years ago. You can drive the Kancamagus Scenic Byway in New Hampshire through the White Mountain National Forest, a 34.5-mile ribbon of pavement that is so spectacular in autumn that traffic jams form at overlooks, and so remote that there are no gas stations, restaurants, or lodges along its entire length — by design, to preserve what the Abenaki called the "fearless place" [FHWA complete list of America's Byways, 2021](https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/hep/scenic_byways/designations/designated_byways.cfm).

You can drive the Florida Keys Scenic Highway, an All-American Road that crosses forty-two bridges over 113 miles of open ocean. You can drive Utah's Scenic Byway 12, which the Federal Highway Administration has called "a journey through time," winding through red rock canyons, alpine forests, and the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument. You can drive the Trail of the Ancients in Colorado and Utah, which follows the archaeological traces of the Ancestral Puebloans — a road that requires you to see not just the landscape but the civilization that lived in it a thousand years before your own. You can drive the Journey Through Hallowed Ground in Maryland, Pennsylvania, and Virginia, which passes through more historic sites per mile than any other road in America, including Gettysburg, Harper's Ferry, and Monticello.

In 2021, the last round of designations, the U.S. Department of Transportation added forty-nine new roads to the collection — fifteen All-American Roads and thirty-four National Scenic Byways in twenty-eight states. Among the new designations: the Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad Byway was elevated to All-American Road status. The St. John Valley Cultural Byway in Maine, which traces the border with Canada through Acadian communities that have preserved their French language and culture since the eighteenth century, was added as a National Scenic Byway. The Sandhills Journey Scenic Byway in Nebraska, which runs through the largest sand dune formation in the Western Hemisphere — grass-stabilized dunes that stretch for 20,000 square miles — was also added. The Battle Road Scenic Byway in Massachusetts, which follows the route of the British retreat from Concord on April 19, 1775, was designated an All-American Road [FHWA 2021 Designations booklet](https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/hep/scenic_byways/designations/); [2021 Designated Byways list](https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/hep/scenic_byways/designations/2021_designated_byways.cfm).

---

## The Mother Road at One Hundred

In 2026, Route 66 turns one hundred years old. It will be celebrated, photographed, and driven by thousands of people who will post photographs of the Wigwam Motel in Holbrook, Arizona, of the Blue Whale in Catoosa, Oklahoma, of the neon sign of the Hi-Way Cafe in Vinita that was relit in a ceremony in 2023. It will be the most famous road in America for a year, and then it will settle back into its accustomed role as the most famous road that very few people actually drive — at least, not end to end.

But the centennial is an occasion worth marking for a reason that goes beyond nostalgia. Route 66 is the road that taught America what scenic byways could be. It demonstrated, over the course of a century, that a road could be more than a conduit for commerce and commuting — that it could be a destination in itself, a place where the journey matters as much as the arrival. The National Scenic Byways Program took that lesson and multiplied it across the continent, creating a network of roads that preserve the best of what America has been, even as the country hurtles toward whatever it is becoming.

The question is whether Americans will discover them in time. The roads are there — 184 of them, in 48 states, waiting. The archives and studies are full of numbers proving their value. What is missing is not infrastructure or funding, but attention. We drive past them every day, on our way to somewhere else, not knowing that we are already there.

---

*This article was researched using primary sources from the Federal Highway Administration, the National Park Service, the Library of Congress, the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, the University of Minnesota Tourism Center, the World Monuments Fund, state historical archives, and academic journals. All economic figures are drawn from government or peer-reviewed studies cited inline.*

# The Transparent Eyeball and the Ecomyth: How New England Poets Learned to See

*From Emerson's "transparent eyeball" to Mary Oliver's daily walks to David Crews climbing Monadnock with Abenaki names in his pocket — a 190-year arc of poets who learned to see the natural world, and the climate-changed landscape that now demands a new kind of seeing.*

---

On a morning in October 2023, the poet David Crews stood on the summit of Mount Monadnock in southern New Hampshire — the second-most-climbed mountain on Earth after Mount Fuji, which tells you less about the mountain than about the species that climbs it — and tried to hold two ways of seeing the same place at once. In his notebook he carried the Abenaki name for the mountain — *Mônadenok*, "the place of the unearthed mountain" — and the 408-line poem that Ralph Waldo Emerson had written about the same peak in 1847, also titled "Monadnock." Crews was writing his own 408-line response, a revision and a reckoning. The mountain had not changed. The language around it had. And the climate that shaped the spruce and fir on its upper slopes had begun to shift in ways that would make Emerson's nineteenth-century vision, and perhaps Crews's twenty-first-century one, into a record of what had already passed [David Crews, Mônadenok](https://www.davidcrewspoetry.com/monadenok).

It is easy to mistake this for a local story — one poet, one mountain, one echo across 176 years. It is not. It is the story of a whole way of being in the world, born on a specific patch of North American ground, that has now run up against its own material limit. New England nature poetry — the tradition that runs from Emerson's ecstatic dissolution of self into landscape, through Thoreau's patient catalogues, through Dickinson's slanted natural history, through Frost's farmer's-eye negotiations with a rocky field, through Mary Oliver's exultant daily attention — is not merely a literary genre. It is a protocol for relationship. And the forests, ponds, birds, and seasons that gave it shape are now in retreat.

---

## I. The Transparent Eyeball (1836–1862)

The founding document of American nature poetry is not a poem at all. It is an essay published in 1836, when Ralph Waldo Emerson was thirty-three years old and still searching for a voice that could hold both the granite of New England and the ether of spirit. He called it simply *Nature*, and on its first page he issued a challenge to his generation: "Why should not we also enjoy an original relation to the universe? Why should not we have a poetry and philosophy of insight and not of tradition?" [Emerson, Nature (1836)](https://archive.vcu.edu/english/engweb/transcendentalism/authors/emerson/essays/naturetext.html).

The question was revolutionary. American literature in the 1830s was still derivative, still looking toward Europe for permission — a colony of the mind long after it had ceased to be a political one. Emerson proposed that a man walking in a New England wood could have an experience as valid as any Greek's on Parnassus — that the "mean and lowly things" of the Concord landscape were worthy of the same attention that Virgil had given to the Italian vales. "The sun shines to-day also," he wrote. "There is more wool and flax in the fields. There are new lands, new men, new thoughts. Let us demand our own works and laws and worship."

This was the seed. But the flower belonged to Henry David Thoreau, who took Emerson's philosophy and walked it into the woods — as philosophy always should be walked, if it is to be of any use. In *Walking*, his great essay on wildness, Thoreau wrote: "I wish to speak a word for Nature, for absolute Freedom and Wildness, as contrasted with a freedom and culture merely civil — to regard man as an inhabitant, or a part and parcel of Nature, rather than a member of society" [Thoreau, Walking (1862)](https://gutenberg.org/files/1022/1022-h/1022-h.htm). He wanted a poetry that would "nail words to their primitive senses, as farmers drive down stakes in spring, which the frost has heaved."

Thoreau got his wish in a way he could not have anticipated. The poetry that came out of New England over the next century did exactly what he asked — it nailed words to the visible world with such precision that the landscape itself became a language. When he surveyed Walden Pond in 1846 with "compass and chain and sounding line," he produced the first accurate map of that small, deep body of water [Walden Pond Survey, Concord Free Public Library](https://concordlibrary.org/special-collections/walden/list). He was making a map of a place. He was also, without knowing it, mapping a tradition.

---

![Walden Pond, circa 1908 — Thoreau's Cove, photographed by the Detroit Publishing Company more than four decades after Thoreau's death.](/api/blog/images/emerson_ecomyth_walden_pond.jpg)
*Walden Pond, Thoreau's Cove, circa 1908. Detroit Publishing Company, Library of Congress. Public domain.*

---

## II. The Slanted Naturalist (1862–1886)

Emily Dickinson never left Amherst. She was born in 1830 in the same house where she would die fifty-six years later, in the Connecticut River Valley, a temperate deciduous forest of oak, maple, beech, and elm. From her window she watched the birds of that valley — robins, bobolinks, sparrows, phoebes, hummingbirds, orioles, crows — and she wrote about them with a precision that was both scientific and mystical, as if the microscope and the séance had somehow agreed upon a single method. Of the more than 250 bird species that nest in or pass through the Connecticut River Valley, she named a relatively small number. But she listened to all of them, and she understood that birdsong was "place-making" — a way of orienting a creature in space and time [Dickinson's Birds, Adagia](https://birds.adagia.org/project/about-overview).

Living on her father's fourteen-acre estate with its perennial gardens, orchard, conservatory, and woods, Dickinson was an observer of nature in an age before field recording. Her poems register seventy species of wildflower ("New feet within my garden go"), the behavior of winter snow ("It sifts from leaden sieves"), the precise aerodynamics of a hummingbird ("A Route of Evanescence"). She is sometimes called a nature poet, but the label misses the strangeness of her project. She was not celebrating nature. She was interrogating it — asking what the natural world could tell her about the nature of consciousness, the existence of God, and the meaning of death, as though nature were a witness she was cross-examining rather than a landscape she was admiring. As literary scholar Grace Mei-shu Chen has observed, Dickinson "did not remain a passive receiver or advocate of [transcendental] influences; rather, she balanced assimilation with interrogation, skepticism, disruption, and exploration" [Chen, "Coda: Natural Messages and Aesthetic Pleasure in Emily Dickinson's Nature Writing," Dickinson Electronic Archives](https://www.emilydickinson.org/emily-dickinson-lyrical-ecologies-forays-into-the-field/coda-natural-messages-and-aesthetic-pleasure-in-emily-dickinson-s-nature-writing).

Her poetry reminds us that the New England nature tradition was never merely pastoral. It was always shadowed by awareness — of time passing, of winter coming, of the small death that waits in every beautiful thing. She saw a train cut through Amherst in 1853, its jarring hiss a "strange stimulus for birdsong," and wrote: "A train went through a burial gate, / A bird broke forth and sang" [Dickinson Electronic Archives](https://birds.adagia.org/project/about-overview). The tension between industrial violence and natural persistence would only deepen in the century after her death.

---

## III. The Farmer Poet (1900–1915)

Robert Frost came of age in the shadow of these New England writers. Born in San Francisco in 1874, he moved east as a young man and spent eight and a half years as a farmer on a thirty-acre lot in Derry, New Hampshire, where he wrote the poems that would make him famous. The Derry years — roughly 1900 to 1915 — were formative: Frost was broke, his farm was rocky and unproductive, and he was writing about the everyday labor of living on a piece of New England land that had already been farmed out and abandoned once [Harvard Thesis, Frost's Ecopoesis](https://dash.harvard.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/7312037d-ca0c-6bd4-e053-0100007fdf3b/content). It is the perfect biography for a poet whose subject would be the steady pressure of the real on the ideal.

Frost's New England was not Emerson's. It was not a temple of spirit. It was a place where people made choices — "Two roads diverged in a yellow wood" — and had to live with them. His woods were lovely, dark and deep, but they were also a practical problem: "Whose woods these are I think I know. / His house is in the village though." The nature in Frost's poetry is active, not passive; it pushes back against human intention. A wall falls down. Birches bend under ice. Snow fills a pasture. A mountain dominates the horizon, indifferent to the people who live at its foot. Nature, for Frost, was not a backdrop but an adversary — the sort you respect precisely because you cannot defeat it.

Critics have sometimes treated Frost as a minor poet of regional charm. The assessment has aged poorly — as most condescensions do, once they have had time to ripen into embarrassment. As scholar Priscilla Paton has noted, Frost's best poems refuse the pastoral tradition's easy idealization: "Frost rarely extols the breath-taking vista. The poem refigures the unprofitable New England landscape as a moralized scene of limits" [Paton, "Robert Frost and the American Landscape"](https://files01.core.ac.uk/download/pdf/61163255.pdf). Frost himself described his method in a letter to Walter Prichard Eaton in 1915, the year his breakout collection *North of Boston* appeared: he wanted a poem that "ends in a momentary stay against confusion" [Frost, Letters](https://dash.harvard.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/7312037d-ca0c-6bd4-e053-0100007fdf3b/content).

What Frost was describing was a new relationship between observer and observed. If Emerson had dissolved the self into nature, and Dickinson had watched nature like an experimental subject, Frost was the first New England poet to stand *beside* nature — to treat it as a neighbor, difficult and worth knowing. The literary scholar Astrid Galbraith has called this "the New England poetic landscape" — a place where the land itself becomes a conversation partner [Galbraith, *New England as Poetic Landscape* (Peter Lang, 2010)](https://www.ijfmr.com/papers/2023/5/7876.pdf).

---

## IV. The Daily Walk (1964–2019)

Mary Oliver moved to Provincetown, Massachusetts, in 1964 and lived there for fifty years, at the very tip of Cape Cod, where the land frays into shifting dunes and the Atlantic meets the bay in a collision of currents and light. She walked every morning, usually before dawn, carrying a hand-bound notebook. Over the course of her life, she filled more than 130 of these notebooks — small, unlined books that she kept during her daily rambles, recording what she saw: the arrival of migratory birds, the condition of the tide, the behavior of a single grasshopper or bear or whale [Library of Congress, Mary Oliver Papers](https://hdl.loc.gov/loc.mss/eadmss.ms024014.3). She understood what most writers discover only too late — that the body must be in motion before the mind will consent to do its work.

The Library of Congress, which holds her papers, describes these notebooks as the wellspring of her published work: "over 130 small, bound notebooks, some handbound, Oliver kept during her daily walks on Cape Cod." They contain her birding sight lists, her observations of the natural world, and "various trial lines and general musings on the natural and spiritual world." She was, in a very literal sense, a poet who composed by walking — a practice that connected her directly to Thoreau's sauntering, Emerson's wandering, and the long tradition of New England poets who understood that the body must be in motion before the mind can settle into attention.

Oliver's poetry was widely loved — she became the best-selling poet in the United States, a fact that bemused her and continues to puzzle critics who prefer difficulty to accessibility. In a review for the Poetry Foundation, one critic described her work as "easy to digest, smooth and slightly sweet like pap" — a dismissal that misses the radical discipline underneath the ease [Poetry Foundation, Mary Oliver and the Nature-esque](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/articles/69656/mary-oliver-and-the-nature-esque). Oliver was not writing comfort poetry. She was writing a sustained argument that attention is the highest form of devotion. "I could not be a poet without the natural world," she wrote. "Someone else could. But not me. For me the door to the woods is the door to the temple" [Cape Cod Times, Oliver Obituary](https://www.capecodtimes.com/story/news/2019/01/18/person-in-community-people/6252584007/).

In a 2016 essay for the Boston Globe, Oliver looked back at the Provincetown she had known since the 1960s — a fishing town that had been transformed by tourism, overfishing, and climate change. "The great rafts of fish began to diminish," she wrote. "The satisfaction of a day's work also began to vanish." The essay concluded with a quiet benediction: "I don't know if I am heading toward heaven or that other, dark place, but I know I have already lived in heaven for fifty years. Thank you, Provincetown" [Boston Globe, "In 'Provincetown,' poet Mary Oliver recalls quiet fishing town"](https://www.bostonglobe.com/lifestyle/2016/10/20/provincetown-poet-mary-oliver-recalls-quiet-fishing-town/AsfB3MJmRbCA7Vf0G9VziN/story.html). It is hard to imagine a more graceful exit from a tradition that had, by then, become indistinguishable from a life.

---

![Walden Pond and Cairn, circa 1890s — photograph by Alfred Winslow Hosmer showing the rock pile near Thoreau's cabin site, a tradition of stone-laying that continues today.](/api/blog/images/emerson_ecomyth_walden_cairn.jpg)
*Walden Pond and Cairn, circa 1890s. Alfred Winslow Hosmer, Concord Free Public Library. Courtesy of the William Munroe Special Collections.*

---

## V. The Ecomyths (2020–Present)

The poets now writing in New England are working in the wake of a difficult knowledge. They inherit Emerson's demand for "an original relation to the universe," Thoreau's practice of close observation, Dickinson's interrogative stance, Frost's farmer's realism, and Oliver's daily devotion — but they also inherit a landscape that is visibly changing in their own lifetimes. They are the first generation of New England nature poets for whom the nature in question has begun to send its regrets.

Megan Grumbling, who lives in Portland, Maine, published *Persephone in the Late Anthropocene* in 2020, a book that reframes the ancient myth of the goddess of spring for an era when spring no longer arrives on schedule. Persephone, in Grumbling's telling, "now comes and goes erratically, drinks too much, and takes a human lover in our warming, unraveling world" [Acre Books, Persephone in the Late Anthropocene](https://acre-books.com/titles/persephone-in-the-late-anthropocene/). The book interweaves "extreme weather, industrialized plenty, and ecological collapse" with the voices of its mythological figures. Grumbling won the Robert Frost Foundation Award for her earlier work, and teaches at Southern Maine Community College — a living connection between the tradition and its transformation.

Elizabeth Bradfield, a naturalist-poet on Cape Cod who lives in the same town where Mary Oliver walked for decades, has spent the last several years compiling a "feel guide" for the Gulf of Maine bioregion — a book that blends poetry, art, and natural history for the region from Cape Cod to Nova Scotia. The Gulf of Maine is one of the fastest-warming bodies of water on the planet, and Bradfield's project is an attempt to register what is disappearing. "Anyone who looks out from the inscape of the self and asks how they are connected to the world — air, trees, water, concrete, beetles, stars, seasons — in a full way is writing ecopoetry," she said in a 2025 interview [Terrain.org, Elizabeth Bradfield Interview](https://www.terrain.org/2025/interviews/inscape-elizabeth-bradfield/).

David Crews's *Mônadenok* project — the 408-line poem, the Abenaki names, the Emerson echo — is perhaps the most explicit act of literary archaeology in this new generation. Crews describes his method as a "revision of one Ralph Waldo Emerson published about the mountain in 1847," and the poem's sources include Thoreau's bird lists, the botanical surveys of Mount Monadnock, and the Pennacook and Cowasuck histories of the region. He is, in a sense, writing the same poem Emerson wrote, but with the additional knowledge of what arrived in the intervening centuries — Indian removal, industrialization, climate change, extinction. The poem occupies the same form. The world it describes does not [David Crews, Mônadenok](https://www.davidcrewspoetry.com/monadenok).

There is, too, the national movement of Poets for Science — born in 2017 when Jane Hirshfield wrote "On the Fifth Day" after climate information was removed from the White House website. The movement has since produced the *Dear Human at the Edge of Time* anthology (2023), which accompanies the U.S. Fifth National Climate Assessment, and the *Nature of Our Times* anthology (2025), published alongside the U.S. National Assessment of lands, waters, and wildlife. In November 2026, the Wick Poetry Center will convene a three-day Poets for Science Gathering, bringing together scientists and writers to ask what the humanities can contribute to the scientific understanding of ecological crisis [USA Today, "Finding hope in troubling times with poetry and science"](https://www.usatoday.com/story/lifestyle/columns/2026/05/24/merging-science-humanities-christensen/90173749007/).

---

## VI. The Forest That Taught Them (2100)

The ecological data from New England's forests is not ambiguous. The USDA Forest Service's *New England Forest Ecosystem Vulnerability Assessment* — a collaboration of more than thirty scientists and resource managers — projects that by the end of this century, the mean annual temperature across the region will rise by 3 to 8 degrees Fahrenheit. Boreal and northern species such as balsam fir, red spruce, and black spruce will lose suitable habitat and biomass. Southern species, including red maple, northern red oak, and black cherry, may expand their ranges northward [USDA Forest Service, NRS-173](https://www.fs.usda.gov/nrs/pubs/gtr/gtr_nrs173.pdf).

A separate assessment by Mass Audubon of forest carbon offset projects in central and western Massachusetts found that by 2050, half the trees in the study area will be vulnerable to dying from climate change, pests, or disease. The health of the surviving forest will depend largely on just two species — northern red oak and red maple — neither of which is reproducing adequately under current deer-browsing pressure [Mass Audubon, Assessment of Forest Vulnerabilities](https://massland.org/sites/default/files/resources/forest_vulnerability_assessment_mass_aud.pdf).

A 2024 study in *Frontiers in Forests and Global Change* modeled the distance tree species would need to migrate to find compatible climates: an average of 222 kilometers by the 2030s, 358 kilometers by the 2050s, and 662 kilometers by the 2090s — roughly three seed zones north for every species, every century [Frontiers, "Identifying climatically-compatible seedlots" (2024)](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/forests-and-global-change/articles/10.3389/ffgc.2024.1449340/full).

This is not merely an ecological story. It is a literary one. The sugar maple that turns the hills of Vermont red in October — the tree that Frost saw outside his window in Derry, that Dickinson watched from her window in Amherst, that Thoreau counted in the Concord woods, that Emerson used as a figure for the soul's relation to God — is projected to lose suitable habitat across much of its southern New England range. The red spruce that grows on the upper slopes of Mount Monadnock — the tree Emerson addressed in his poem, the tree Crews measures his lines against — is one of the species most vulnerable to warming temperatures.

When Crews stands on Monadnock and tries to see what Emerson saw, he is also trying to see what Emerson could not have seen: the end of the conditions that made his seeing possible. The "ecomyth," as the University of Maine honors thesis on Frost's poetry defines it, is "typically (1) oral and/or fluid in its telling, (2) saying something unknowable in terms of something knowable, (3) creating a momentary stay against confusion to therefore help us better understand the world around us, and (4) (attempting to) identify or represent a vital force as found in nature" [University of Maine, Frost's Ecomyth](https://digitalcommons.library.umaine.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1934&context=honors).

The tradition from Emerson to Crews is a tradition of creating such stays. And the question now is whether the staying will hold.

---

## VII. The Stubborn Song

The Dickinsonian scholar Martha Nell Smith once wrote that in Dickinson's poetry, "birdsong is arguably the most constant evanescent natural sound she recorded through writing in an age before the technologies of recording had been invented." The birds of the Connecticut River Valley, whose arrivals and departures Dickinson tracked for forty years, were "a waymark in an evanescent geography" [Dickinson's Birds, Unsilent Springs](https://manifold.umn.edu/read/a66e67c0-b299-47a5-9505-1ffe7f0ee1fe/section/a134e17a-e62b-4493-9899-91f0503a3a65).

Every poet in this tradition has been a recorder of evanescent geographies. Emerson recorded the feeling of spirit dissolving the boundaries of the body. Thoreau recorded the precise depth and temperature of Walden Pond. Dickinson recorded the date of the robin's return. Frost recorded the sound of a mowing scythe in a New Hampshire field. Oliver recorded the sight of a bear in the Truro woods. And now Grumbling records the erratic returns of spring, Bradfield records the warming water of the Gulf of Maine, and Crews records the mountain that he can see, as Emerson could, but that he might outlive in a form he would recognize.

Tradition is not inheritance. Tradition is something you choose, and then re-choose, every generation. The New England poets chose, again and again, to pay attention to the actual physical world in front of them — not the world of ideas, not the world of symbols, but the particular landscape of this specific place, with its specific mix of trees and birds and weather. That choice is now being re-made by poets who must attend to a world that is simultaneously the one they love and the one they are losing.

"We may trust a good deal more than we do," Thoreau wrote in *Walden*. "Nature is as well adapted to our weakness as to our strength."

We may need to trust it more now than ever. And New England's poets — the ones who came before, the ones writing now, the ones who will come after — will be the ones showing us how.

---

## Archival Visuals

**Photograph: Walden Pond, Thoreau's Cove, c. 1908**
- *Source:* Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Detroit Publishing Company Collection
- *Credit:* Detroit Publishing Co.
- *Rights:* Public domain
- *What it shows:* Thoreau's Cove at Walden Pond, Concord, Massachusetts, photographed more than fifty years after Thoreau left his cabin. The same shoreline he surveyed in 1846.

**Photograph: Walden Pond and Cairn, c. 1890s**
- *Source:* Concord Free Public Library, William Munroe Special Collections, Alfred Winslow Hosmer Collection
- *Credit:* Alfred Winslow Hosmer
- *Rights:* Courtesy Concord Free Public Library
- *What it shows:* The rock cairn marking Thoreau's cabin site, with visitors adding stones — a tradition that continues today. The cairn began with stones brought by early admirers within a decade of Thoreau's death.

---

## Source Notes

- [Emerson, *Nature* (1836)](https://archive.vcu.edu/english/engweb/transcendentalism/authors/emerson/essays/naturetext.html) — Primary source: the founding text of American Transcendentalism.
- [Thoreau, *Walking* (1862)](https://gutenberg.org/files/1022/1022-h/1022-h.htm) — Primary source: Thoreau's manifesto for wildness.
- [Thoreau, *Walden* (1854)](https://henrythoreau.org/walden/chapter01a-economy.html) — Primary source: Thoreau's account of his two years at Walden Pond.
- [Dickinson's Birds, Adagia](https://birds.adagia.org/project/about-overview) — Scholarly digital project documenting Dickinson's avian references.
- [Chen, "Coda: Natural Messages," Dickinson Electronic Archives](https://www.emilydickinson.org/emily-dickinson-lyrical-ecologies-forays-into-the-field/coda-natural-messages-and-aesthetic-pleasure-in-emily-dickinson-s-nature-writing) — Scholarly analysis of Dickinson's nature writing.
- [Harvard Thesis, Frost's Ecopoesis](https://dash.harvard.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/7312037d-ca0c-6bd4-e053-0100007fdf3b/content) — Academic thesis on Frost as ecopoet.
- [Paton, "Robert Frost and the American Landscape"](https://files01.core.ac.uk/download/pdf/61163255.pdf) — Scholarly article on Frost's landscape poetics.
- [Library of Congress, Mary Oliver Papers](https://hdl.loc.gov/loc.mss/eadmss.ms024014.3) — Primary source: finding aid for Oliver's papers, including 130+ notebooks.
- [Boston Globe, Oliver on Provincetown (2016)](https://www.bostonglobe.com/lifestyle/2016/10/20/provincetown-poet-mary-oliver-recalls-quiet-fishing-town/AsfB3MJmRbCA7Vf0G9VziN/story.html) — Primary source: Oliver's own retrospective essay.
- [Cape Cod Times, Oliver Obituary (2019)](https://www.capecodtimes.com/story/news/2019/01/18/person-in-community-people/6252584007/) — News account with Oliver's direct quotes.
- [Poetry Foundation, Mary Oliver Review](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/articles/69656/mary-oliver-and-the-nature-esque) — Critical review of Oliver's work.
- [David Crews, Mônadenok](https://www.davidcrewspoetry.com/monadenok) — Primary source: Crews's own description of his 408-line poem.
- [Megan Grumbling, *Persephone in the Late Anthropocene*](https://acre-books.com/titles/persephone-in-the-late-anthropocene/) — Primary source: publisher's description and reviews.
- [Terrain.org, Elizabeth Bradfield Interview (2025)](https://www.terrain.org/2025/interviews/inscape-elizabeth-bradfield/) — Primary interview source.
- [USA Today, Poets for Science (2026)](https://www.usatoday.com/story/lifestyle/columns/2026/05/24/merging-science-humanities-christensen/90173749007/) — News article on the Poets for Science movement.
- [USDA Forest Service, NRS-173](https://www.fs.usda.gov/nrs/pubs/gtr/gtr_nrs173.pdf) — Primary government report on forest ecosystem vulnerability.
- [Mass Audubon, Forest Vulnerability Assessment](https://massland.org/sites/default/files/resources/forest_vulnerability_assessment_mass_aud.pdf) — Primary source: on-the-ground forest assessment.
- [Frontiers in Forests and Global Change (2024)](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/forests-and-global-change/articles/10.3389/ffgc.2024.1449340/full) — Peer-reviewed paper on forest assisted migration.
- [University of Maine, Frost's Ecomyth Thesis](https://digitalcommons.library.umaine.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1934&context=honors) — Academic thesis defining "ecomyth."
- [Concord Free Public Library, Walden Images](https://concordlibrary.org/special-collections/walden/list) — Primary visual archive of Walden Pond historical photographs.
- [Walden Pond Historic Photo, Library of Congress](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Walden_Pond.jpg) — Public domain image via Wikimedia Commons.

---

*This article was researched using primary sources — original essays, poems, archival collections, government reports, and peer-reviewed science — rather than secondary news aggregation. All factual claims are linked to their source inline.*

post.content:
# The House That Breakfast Built: New Hampshire's Bed and Breakfasts Through Two Centuries

**On the porch of the Philbrook Farm Inn, at the hour when the White Mountains turn from granite to gold, the rocking chairs face the Presidential Range as they have since 1861. The screen door creaks; someone inside is beating eggs. Nothing here has changed, which is, of course, the whole point — and also, quietly, the miracle.**

<!-- IMAGE: [/api/blog/images/new-hampshire-bed-and-breakfasts_philbrook_porch.jpg] Philbrook Farm Inn porch with rocking chairs facing the Presidential Range at sunset. -->

---

In a state where tourism generates $7.5 billion in annual visitor spending and supports more than 70,000 jobs, bed and breakfasts occupy a peculiar and outsized niche [NH Division of Travel & Tourism 2026 Economic Impact Report](https://www.visitnh.gov/getmedia/a10ac1f0-45aa-41df-9cd6-63577fe08043/2026EconomicImpact.pdf). They are not the largest accommodation segment — that honor belongs to the chain hotels and resorts that ring the interstate exits — but they are the most enduring, the most personal, and, in many ways, the most New Hampshire. Of the 208 B&Bs operating in the state as of 2026, 85.58 percent are single-owner properties, which is to say that roughly 178 of them are someone's home, someone's life savings, someone's magnificent second act [SmartScraper B&B Report for New Hampshire](https://rentechdigital.com/smartscraper/business-report-details/united-states/list-of-bed-and-breakfasts-in-new-hampshire). The modern B&B industry nationwide generates $2.0 billion in annual revenue, with an average of six rooms per property, and 95 percent are run by owners for whom hospitality is a second career [Kentley Insights B&B Market Report](https://www.kentleyinsights.com/bed-and-breakfast-inns-industry-market-research-report/)[VerticalIQ B&B Industry Report](https://verticaliq.com/product/bed-and-breakfast-inns/). New Hampshire's version of this story reaches back farther than most: some of the buildings housing B&B guests tonight were already old when Abraham Lincoln was a young lawyer, and one suspects they will be old long after the last chain hotel has been converted into something else entirely.

![New Hampshire bed and breakfasts by ownership type — 85.6% are single-owner operations.](/api/blog/images/new-hampshire-bed-and-breakfasts_ownership_structure.png)
*Source: Rentech Digital / SmartScraper, April 2026.*

## The Farmhouse That Became an Inn

The origin story of the New Hampshire bed and breakfast is, in nearly every case, the origin story of a farmhouse. The **New London Inn** began in 1792 when Ezekiel Sargent built a farmhouse on what was then a rough road through the woods; it became a hotel called The Elms in 1870, when Herman Currier saw that the railroad might bring people who would pay for a bed [New London Inn History](https://www.thenewlondoninn.com/history). The **Inn at Pleasant Lake** was built in 1790 as a private residence by Caleb Segur and opened as an inn in 1868 by Colonel William Messer, who called it the Red Gables Inn — a name that would survive for more than 150 years of hospitality [Inn at Pleasant Lake History](https://www.innatpleasantlake.com/history). The **Wolfeboro Inn** started as an 1812 farmhouse built by Nathaniel Rogers; the railroad arrived in 1871, bringing tourists, and the building became a guesthouse in the 1920s, later known as the Carr House [Wolfeboro Inn Story](https://www.wolfeboroinn.com/about/our-story).

<!-- IMAGE: [/api/blog/images/new-hampshire-bed-and-breakfasts_inn_at_pleasant_lake.jpg] The Inn at Pleasant Lake, a white clapboard inn on the lakeshore. -->

The pattern is so consistent it functions almost as a law of regional economics: build a farmhouse in the late 18th or early 19th century, watch the railroad arrive in the 1870s, and retrofit the building for guests. The **Sugar Hill Inn** was built in 1789 as a farmhouse and now offers fourteen rooms and cottages [NH Magazine: Bed & Breakfast and Beyond](https://www.nhmagazine.com/bed-breakfast-and-beyond-2/). The **Pinestead Farm Lodge** in Franconia was built in 1852 by Henry Whitney and opened to the public in 1899 by Joe and Mary Sherburn, who met arriving guests at the train station with a horse-drawn carriage [Pinestead Farm Lodge History](https://www.pinesteadfarmlodge.com/history). It remains family-run today — the Sherburns' descendants are still the ones meeting the guests, though the carriage has been replaced by something with an engine and the horses by something with a reservation system.

The **Blue Bear Inn** in Francestown traces its roots to 1765, when Thomas Quigley settled the land. James Wilson, a Revolutionary War veteran, built the home in 1794, and the current brick structure dates to 1822. It served as a stop on the Underground Railroad before becoming the Inn at Crotched Mountain in the 1970s and, after a 2021 rebranding, the Blue Bear Inn [Blue Bear Inn History](https://bluebearinn.com/history/). The **Three Chimneys Inn** in Durham pushes the story back even further: its original homestead was built in 1649 by Valentine Hill, making it one of the oldest buildings in New Hampshire. It served as a merchant homestead, a Victorian estate, fell into ruin, and was restored in 1997 [Three Chimneys Inn History](https://www.threechimneysinn.com/history). One might say that in New Hampshire, a building has to try several lives before it discovers it was always meant to be an inn.

## The Philbrook Century

If there is a single property that embodies the New Hampshire B&B tradition, it is the **Philbrook Farm Inn** in Shelburne, and its story deserves the telling.

The building began as a farmhouse around 1834, in the Androscoggin Valley, with views of the Carter-Moriah and Presidential ranges — views that would prove worth more than any crop ever grown in their shadow. The Philbrook family began taking guests in 1861, the first summer of the Civil War, and never stopped. For more than 120 years, it was the oldest hotel in the United States operated by the same family at the same site, passing through five generations of Philbrooks before being listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1984 [NRHP Nomination: Philbrook Farm Inn](https://npgallery.nps.gov/NRHP/GetAsset/NRHP/84002804_text).

<!-- IMAGE: [/api/blog/images/new-hampshire-bed-and-breakfasts_philbrook_exterior.jpg] Philbrook Farm Inn exterior, a white clapboard farmhouse against the Presidential Range. -->

The Philbrook survived what killed most of the grand White Mountain hotels: the automobile. When guests could drive anywhere, the logic went, why would they stay in one place? The grand hotels of the nineteenth century — the Profile House, the Crawford House, the Glen House — burned, were demolished, or simply faded from memory. The Philbrook endured, not by competing with the new resorts but by refusing to become one. It remained small, personal, and unmistakably itself. Inside, it holds an extensive collection of White Mountain memorabilia — a museum of the landscape that surrounds it, curated by the family that has watched that landscape change and learned that the one thing a mountain cannot do is hurry.

The Philbrook's story is not unique in its broad shape, only in its duration. The same impulse — a farmhouse, a scenic view, an extra room, a paying guest — animates dozens of properties across the state. The **Wolfeboro Inn**, the **Inn at Pleasant Lake**, the **New London Inn**: each represents a variation on the same theme, a family deciding that hospitality is a better crop than hay. The lesson is one that commerce has somehow never quite learned: that the most reliable income is the one that arrives with a suitcase and leaves asking for the breakfast recipe.

## The Hospitality Virus

The path to becoming an innkeeper in New Hampshire rarely runs straight. National data shows that 95 percent of B&B owners enter the industry as a second career [VerticalIQ B&B Industry Report](https://verticaliq.com/product/bed-and-breakfast-inns/), and New Hampshire's innkeepers fit the profile with almost comedic precision.

**Steve Allen** ran a shipping business before buying the Sugar Hill Inn. He traded logistics for linens, spreadsheets for scones, and discovered that running an inn requires many of the same skills as running a supply chain — inventory management, scheduling, customer relations — plus the ability to make a perfect omelet [NH Magazine: Bed & Breakfast and Beyond](https://www.nhmagazine.com/bed-breakfast-and-beyond-2/).

**Denis Swords** arrived at the Follansbee Inn on Lake Sunapee with an even more dramatic career arc. He trained and worked as a geologist, then earned a law degree and practiced law, before deciding that what he really wanted to do was run a bed and breakfast. "I was looking for a change of pace," he said, with the magnificent understatement of a man who has changed everything except his capacity for understatement [Denis Swords, Innkeeper, Follansbee Inn](https://follansbeeinn.com/denis-swords-innkeeper-follansbee-inn-new-hampshire/).

<!-- IMAGE: [/api/blog/images/new-hampshire-bed-and-breakfasts_sugar_hill_inn.jpg] Sugar Hill Inn, a white farmhouse with guest cottages in autumn. -->

The pattern recurs so often it might as well be a recognized career path. It goes like this: corporate or professional career, followed by burnout or boredom, followed by the purchase of an inn in a scenic location, followed by the unnerving discovery that hospitality is harder than it looks, followed — for those who last — by the slow acquisition of a competence that resembles nothing they brought with them. The B&B industry is, in this sense, a vast machine for recycling the talents of lawyers, bankers, and shipping executives into breakfast service, reservation management, and the delicate art of telling the same guests the same directions to the same waterfall without betraying that you have told them a hundred times before. It is a profession that rewards the skills of middle management and the soul of a butler, and it attracts precisely the people who thought they had escaped both.

## The Regulatory Architecture

What distinguishes a bed and breakfast from any other lodging establishment in New Hampshire is, strictly speaking, a matter of law. The state defines a B&B as the owner's personal residence where breakfast is the only meal served, which exempts the property from certain commercial kitchen requirements [NH Admin Code He-P 2308.02](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-hampshire/N-H-Admin-Code-SS-He-P-2308.02). This is a regulatory distinction with real consequences: it means the eggs are cooked in a home kitchen, the dining room doubles as a family room, and the line between public accommodation and private residence is deliberately, legally blurred. No other industry has ever been so precisely defined by what it is allowed to cook for breakfast.

The **New Hampshire Bed and Breakfast Association**, formed on February 22, 2002, includes roughly 40 member properties across seven tourism regions [NHBBA About](https://www.staynh.org/About/). Membership requires a food service license, a New Hampshire Meals & Rentals Tax license, that the owner lives on the premises, and that breakfast is included in the room rate [NHBBA Membership Information](https://www.staynh.org/About/Membership-Information.html). These requirements codify the tradition: a B&B is not a hotel, not a short-term rental, not a restaurant with rooms. It is a house where someone lives, and where that someone feeds you breakfast. The law has succeeded in doing what philosophy has not: it has given a clear definition to the act of being made to feel at home.

The financial architecture is equally precise. New Hampshire's **Meals & Rentals Tax** applies at 8.5 percent to both rooms and meals, generating approximately $448.5 million in fiscal 2023, a figure that was trending 3.6 percent above estimate for fiscal 2025 [NHBR: Will Canada Chatter Cool NH's Tourism?](https://www.nhbr.com/will-canada-chatter-cool-nhs-tourism/). The Accommodation sector contributes **$2.16 billion** to the state's GDP [FRED: NH Accommodation GDP](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/NHACCOMDNGSP). For every dollar the state invests in tourism marketing, it receives $15 in return [NH Division of Travel & Tourism Economic Impact Report](https://www.visitnh.gov/getmedia/a10ac1f0-45aa-41df-9cd6-63577fe08043/2026EconomicImpact.pdf). The return on investment is extraordinary by almost any measure — though the B&B owner sees none of that $15 directly, only the guests it helps lure up the driveway. The economy, like a good innkeeper, works best when no one notices it working.

![New Hampshire Accommodation GDP, 2020–2024 — a steep post-COVID recovery from $670.9M to $2.16 billion.](/api/blog/images/new-hampshire-bed-and-breakfasts_accommodation_gdp.png)
*Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, FRED.*

![New Hampshire Meals & Rentals Tax revenue, FY2020–FY2024 — steady growth from $310M to $458.5M.](/api/blog/images/new-hampshire-bed-and-breakfasts_meals_rentals_tax.png)
*Sources: NH Department of Revenue Administration; NH Business Review.*

## The Chains, The Platforms, The Canadians

For all their charm, New Hampshire's bed and breakfasts operate in an increasingly competitive environment, and the forces arrayed against them have names.

**The chains.** After the 2008 financial crisis, hotels from the major chains — Hilton, Hampton, Best Western — began moving into the White Mountains, a region that had previously been the preserve of independent lodgings. Ed Butler of the Notchland Inn watched this happen with the uneasy sense that something fundamental was shifting: the same brands that lined the interstates were now appearing on scenic highways, offering predictable rooms and loyalty points that no B&B could match [NPR/StateImpact: White Mountains Innkeeper Struggles](https://stateimpact.npr.org/new-hampshire/2012/06/26/getting-by-getting-ahead-white-mountains-innkeeper-struggles-with-shifting-economic-landscape/). The modern traveler, it seems, prefers the comfort of knowing exactly what they will get over the adventure of discovering something they did not know they wanted.

**The platforms.** Airbnb and its competitors have redefined what a traveler expects from a short-term stay. The same guest who might once have sought out a B&B for its character and local knowledge can now rent an entire house through an app, never speak to a host, and feel no obligation to eat breakfast at a communal table. For B&Bs, this is an existential challenge: they must compete not only on price and location but on the increasingly intangible value of human interaction, at a moment when many travelers are voting, with their booking dollars, for its absence. Younger travelers — Millennials and Gen Z — say they value authentic local experiences and unique character, but they also expect smooth digital booking and the option to be self-guided with on-demand support [Frictionless Guest: What Gen Z and Millennials Expect](https://frictionlessguest.com/post/what-gen-z-and-millennials-expect-from-independent-lodging-experiences). The B&B, which has historically traded on the presence of the innkeeper, must now learn to offer that presence without making it feel like a requirement. It is a trick that would defeat most philosophers, yet the innkeepers are expected to manage it before check-in.

**The Canadians.** Canadian visitors have historically accounted for 5 to 10 percent of New Hampshire's tourism traffic. In 2025, border crossings dropped 17 percent, driven by tariff disputes and unfavorable exchange rates [WMUR: NH Tourism Summit, Canada Tariffs](https://www.wmur.com/article/new-hampshire-tourism-summit-canada-tariffs/64770284). For B&Bs in the northern parts of the state — the North Country, the Great North Woods, the lakes region near the border — this decline is not an abstraction. It is the reservation that did not come through, the empty room in August, the polite voicemail explaining that this year, sadly, they will be vacationing closer to home. International diplomacy, it turns out, has a direct line to the breakfast table.

Meanwhile, proposed budget cuts to the state's tourism marketing budget — reductions of 30 percent or more — could result in a $68 million loss in tax revenue, according to industry estimates [InDepthNH: Tourism Industry Concerns Over Budget Cuts](https://indepthnh.org/2024/11/14/new-hampshire-tourism-industry-voices-urgent-concerns-over-proposed-budget-cuts/). The math is straightforward: less marketing means fewer visitors means emptier rooms. And emptier rooms, for a B&B, means the difference between a property that survives and one that goes back to being just a house. The state, one might observe, has yet to discover the elegant economy of spending money to make money — a principle the innkeepers understand in their bones, because they have to.

## The Next Breakfast

What comes next for New Hampshire's bed and breakfasts depends on how well they can hold two contradictory ideas at once: that their strength lies in tradition, and that tradition alone will not save them. This is the sort of paradox that would paralyze a lesser industry, but innkeepers have been living inside contradictions since the first paying guest asked for an extra blanket.

The trends are not uniformly grim. The rise of remote work means that some guests now stay for weeks rather than weekends, treating a B&B as a temporary office with better views and superior baked goods. The demand for chef-driven, farm-to-table breakfasts — accommodating special diets, sourcing locally, serving meals that guests photograph — has elevated the culinary expectations of the industry and, in doing so, raised the barrier to entry for new innkeepers [NH Magazine: Bed & Breakfast and Beyond](https://www.nhmagazine.com/bed-breakfast-and-beyond-2/). The eggs have never been more scrutinized, and they have never been better.

But the challenges are structural. The average B&B has six rooms. The average owner is in their fifties or sixties, having arrived via a mid-life career change, which means that a wave of succession is coming — innkeepers who bought their properties in their forties and fifties are now approaching retirement, and the question of who takes over has no obvious answer. The industry's demographics mirror the state's: aging, experienced, and without a clear pipeline of younger owners ready to inherit the business of making strangers feel at home. The B&B, which has always been about the transfer of comfort, now faces a crisis in the transfer of itself.

And there is the deeper question of what a B&B is for in an age of frictionless accommodation. If a guest can rent a house, order groceries for delivery, and never speak to another human being, what is the value proposition of a place that requires conversation, a shared breakfast table, and the presence of the owner? The answer, for those who remain in the business, is that the value is precisely what cannot be automated: the innkeeper who knows which hike to recommend based on the guest's boots, who remembers that the couple from Boston prefers the blueberry pancakes, who sits on the porch at sunset and points out the peaks as the light drains from the sky. That is not a service. It is a way of life, and it cannot be scaled. It cannot even be franchised. It can only be lived, one breakfast at a time.

## The Porch at Dusk

The sun has finished its work on the Presidential Range. The peaks go dark, then go gray, then go quiet. On the porch of the Philbrook Farm Inn, the rocking chairs have been pulled inside for the night, but the view remains — the same view that five generations of Philbrooks have watched from this same hill, the same view that has greeted every guest since 1861, through wars and depressions and pandemics and the slow encroachment of a world that has less and less use for a rocking chair on a porch, and yet cannot quite bring itself to abandon one.

The screen door creaks. Inside, someone is setting the table for breakfast. The eggs will be fresh. The coffee will be hot. The innkeeper will ask how you slept, and will mean it. In an age of algorithms and automated everything, sincerity remains the one thing that cannot be outsourced.

In an industry measured in billions of dollars and millions of visitors, the bed and breakfast persists because it refuses to be measured in anything larger than the individual. Not the market. Not the segment. Not the channel. Just the room, the breakfast, the view, the kindness. Two hundred years of that, and still going. It is, when you think about it, a rather good return on investment — especially when you consider that the only capital required was a house, some eggs, and the nerve to open the door to a stranger.

---

*Sources: 1) NH Division of Travel & Tourism 2026 Economic Impact Report. 2) SmartScraper B&B Report for New Hampshire. 3) Kentley Insights B&B Market Report. 4) VerticalIQ B&B Industry Report. 5) NPR/StateImpact: White Mountains Innkeeper. 6) NH Magazine: Bed & Breakfast and Beyond. 7) NRHP Nomination: Philbrook Farm Inn. 8) NHBR: Will Canada Chatter Cool NH's Tourism? 9) InDepthNH: Tourism Budget Cuts. 10) WMUR: NH Tourism Summit Canada Tariffs. 11) Frictionless Guest: Gen Z and Millennial Expectations. 12) NHBBA About and Membership Information. 13) NH Admin Code He-P 2308.02. 14) FRED: NH Accommodation GDP. 15) Three Chimneys Inn History. 16) Blue Bear Inn History. 17) New London Inn History. 18) Inn at Pleasant Lake History. 19) Wolfeboro Inn Story. 20) Pinestead Farm Lodge History. 21) Follansbee Inn Innkeeper Profile. 22) Cornell Legal Information Institute.*
