post.content:
# The Art of Sauntering: 150 Years of Walking in New England

*In 1876, a handful of Boston gentlemen founded the Appalachian Mountain Club. A century and a half later, 16.9 million people walk the trails they built — and the philosophy that started it all has never been more urgently needed.*

---

On a Saturday morning in July 2025, a young woman from Somerville, Massachusetts, parked her Subaru at the Lincoln Woods trailhead in New Hampshire's White Mountain National Forest, laced her boots, and began walking. She followed the East Branch of the Pemigewasset River for 2.7 miles, crossed a suspension bridge, and started climbing. The trail steepened. Roots crossed the path like knuckles. The air thinned. By the time she broke treeline on Mount Flume, the temperature had dropped fifteen degrees and the view had opened across the Pemigewasset Wilderness — ridge after ridge of northern hardwood and spruce-fir, folding into a hazy blue distance that suggested, with the persuasive dishonesty of all beautiful views, that the world had no end.

She was, in one sense, merely one person walking in a forest. In another, she was the latest expression of a tradition of organized hiking in New England that is, in 2026, exactly 150 years old.

The Appalachian Mountain Club, the oldest outdoor recreation and conservation nonprofit in the United States, celebrates its sesquicentennial this year. Founded on January 8, 1876, in a lecture room at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the AMC began as a gathering of "thirty or forty gentlemen" interested in "exploring the mountains of New England and the adjacent regions, both for scientific and artistic purposes" [AMC History](https://www.outdoors.org/about/history/). Their first outing, that July, drew 175 people to the White Mountains via the Crawford Notch train. They climbed Mount Willard, admired the view of the notch, and returned to Boston with the satisfied air of people who had invented something whose name would not arrive until they needed it.

They had invented, without quite realizing it, the American framework for mass participation in wilderness recreation. A century and a half and an almost incomprehensible increase in scale later, the full shape of their invention has finally come into view.

---

![Mount Lafayette and the Greenleaf Hut in the White Mountains of New Hampshire — an AMC hut that has sheltered hikers since the early 20th century.](/api/blog/images/new_england_greenleaf_hut.jpg)
*Mount Lafayette and the Greenleaf Hut. Photo by Ken Gallager, August 2004. Public domain.*

## I. The Boston Gentlemen Who Walked Into History

The AMC was not, at first, a conservation organization. Its early members were amateur scientists, topographers, and mountain enthusiasts — the sort of late-Victorian New Englanders who believed that a proper education demanded both the ability to identify a schist formation and the moral fortitude to climb a peak before breakfast.

The club's first major project was building trails and huts in the White Mountains, which had become a summer destination for Boston's elite via the newly completed railroad through Crawford Notch. In 1888, the AMC built its first hut at Madison Spring — a stone shelter at 4,800 feet that could accommodate a dozen hikers [AMC Hut History](https://www.outdoors.org/about/history/). It was the beginning of a system that now includes eight huts along a 56-mile stretch of the Appalachian Trail in New Hampshire, capable of sleeping nearly 1,000 hikers per night — a lodging network that has somehow made the wilderness feel both pristine and almost civilized.

But the club's most consequential early act was not building — it was buying. In the 1890s, logged-over hillsides and clearcut slopes had become common sights in the White Mountains, and the AMC, unlike many of its contemporaries, recognized that scenic beauty could not survive market logic. In 1893, the club established a New Hampshire Forestry Fund and began purchasing land. One of its first acquisitions: thirty-six acres along Snyder Brook in Randolph, New Hampshire, protecting a remnant of old-growth forest from imminent logging [AMC Land Trust History](https://www.outdoors.org/resources/amc-outdoors/conservation-and-climate/in-land-we-trust/).

This was, in retrospect, the moment the AMC ceased to be merely a walking club and became something more consequential. A group of people who loved a landscape had decided to pay real money to stop other people from destroying it — a concept almost too simple to mention, and so radical that it is still being litigated, a hundred and fifty years later, in courtrooms across the country.

---

## II. The First Footpath

In 1909, a Vermont educator named James P. Taylor found himself on the summit of Stratton Mountain, waiting for the clouds to clear. He was, by most accounts, lost — a condition that has given rise to more useful ideas than clarity ever has. Somewhere between the fog and the frustration, an idea formed: a footpath running the length of the Green Mountains, from the Massachusetts line to the Canadian border — a "long trail" that would make "the Vermont mountains play a larger part in the life of the people" [VTDigger](https://vtdigger.org/2021/06/20/then-again-james-taylor-father-of-the-long-trail-had-plenty-of-help/).

On March 11, 1910, Taylor convened a meeting at the Van Ness Hotel in Burlington. Twenty-three people attended. The Green Mountain Club was founded. Its treasury held $100. The goal: clear a 270-mile path through some of the most rugged terrain in New England.

Work began on October 1, 1910. Club members scouted routes, hacked through undergrowth, and cut trail with hand tools. By the fall of 1911, they had cleared 29 miles from Camel's Hump north to Smugglers Notch. The Long Trail was completed in 1930 — the first long-distance hiking trail in the United States, and proof that a great deal can be accomplished with hand tools, optimism, and a complete disregard for the probable [Green Mountain Club](https://www.greenmountainclub.org/the-long-trail/).

The Long Trail is not merely a historic footnote. It is the direct ancestor of the Appalachian Trail, which shares 100 miles of its route through southern Vermont. Benton MacKaye, the visionary forester who conceived the AT, studied the Long Trail in detail before publishing his 1921 proposal in the Journal of the American Institute of Architects. He adopted its shelter system, its white-blaze marking system, and its cooperative management model — lessons learned from a trail that had been built, as one early member put it, "by a handful of men with axes and a great deal of optimism" [VermontBiz](https://vermontbiz.com/news/2012/august/16/vermont-had-significant-role-development-appalachian-trail).

What a handful of people with axes had demonstrated was that a long trail could exist as a cooperative venture — maintained by volunteers, supported by members, and held in trust for everyone. It was an idea so durable that it has now been replicated across thousands of miles of footpath on every continent — which is how one knows it was built for love, not for profit.

![AMC's Carter Notch Hut, one of eight high huts in the White Mountains chain, has hosted hikers since 1914.](/api/blog/images/new_england_carter_notch_hut.jpg)
*AMC's Carter Notch Hut. Photo by Petersent, August 2006. Public domain.*

---

## III. The Law That Saved the Mountains

The same year the Green Mountain Club began cutting the Long Trail, the White Mountains were being cut to pieces. Logging had accelerated so rapidly that visitors to Crawford Notch could hear the saws from the hotel verandas. The watersheds were eroding. The hillsides, stripped of their hardwood cover, looked, in the words of one Boston journalist, "like a battlefield after the fight."

What saved them was the Weeks Act of 1911 — a piece of legislation that the AMC had lobbied for relentlessly over the preceding decade. Allen Chamberlain, a former AMC president and a prolific journalist, wrote article after article for Boston newspapers, hammering the message that eastern forests needed federal protection. The AMC organized exhibits at the Boston Sportsman's Show, mobilized members to write Congress, and sent delegations to Washington. When the bill finally passed, on March 1, 1911, President William Howard Taft signed it into law, authorizing the federal government to purchase private lands for the protection of watersheds — and, incidentally, creating the mechanism that would establish the White Mountain National Forest [AMC Weeks Act History](https://www.outdoors.org/resources/amc-outdoors/history/the-legislation-that-saved-the-white-mountain-region/).

The scale of its impact resists easy summary. Nearly 20 million acres of forestland have been protected under the Weeks Act, including more than 40 national forests across the eastern United States. The White Mountain National Forest alone — 800,000 acres of hiking trails, ski slopes, trout streams, and old-growth stands — exists because people who walked in the mountains arrived at a rare conclusion: that walking alone, however satisfying, does not preserve what one walks through. One must also fight for it.

![Lake of the Clouds and the summit of Mount Washington, circa 1900 — the alpine landscape that the Weeks Act helped preserve for future generations.](/api/blog/images/new_england_lake_clouds_historic.jpg)
*Lake of the Clouds and the summit of Mount Washington, circa 1900. Detroit Publishing Company, Library of Congress. Public domain (published before 1929).*

---

## IV. The Numbers That Defy the Imagination

In 1876, the AMC could count its members in the hundreds. The trails they walked were measured in miles, not thousands of miles. The notion that anyone would bother to count visitors to a footpath would have struck them as absurd — a category error, like counting visitors to the sky.

In 2025, the Appalachian Trail Conservancy and the National Park Service released the first-ever accurate visitation estimate for the Appalachian Trail: 16.9 million recreation visits in a single year [ATC Visitation](https://appalachiantrail.org/protect/trail-management/visitor-use-management/visitation/). The sections managed by the National Park Service accounted for 6.2 million of those visits, making the Appalachian National Scenic Trail the ninth most visited unit in the entire National Park System — ahead of the Grand Canyon, ahead of Yosemite, behind only the Blue Ridge Parkway and the Golden Gate National Recreation Area — a ranking that its founders, who could scarcely have imagined the Grand Canyon as a tourist destination, would find more bewildering than flattering [The Trek](https://thetrek.co/appalachian-trail/thanks-to-a-new-counting-method-we-finally-know-how-many-people-actually-use-the-appalachian-trail-each-year/).

The New England states alone account for a significant share: New Hampshire recorded 2.88 million visits to the AT (second only to Virginia, which has far more miles of trail); Massachusetts, 1.08 million; Connecticut, 535,000; Vermont, 533,000; Maine, 85,000. The White Mountain National Forest, meanwhile, draws approximately six million visitors per year — more than Yosemite or Yellowstone National Parks [UNH News](https://www.unh.edu/news/2025/08/whos-visiting-new-hampshires-white-mountains).

The numbers would baffle the AMC's founders. The impulse behind them would not: the same desire to walk into a landscape and be altered by it, now multiplied by millions and enabled by the infrastructure those founders began building with their own hands.

---

## V. The Philosophy of the Footpath

Why do they do it? The question is older than the AMC — older, in fact, than most of the trails its members walk. It was being asked the first time a New Englander walked into the woods for reasons other than survival.

Henry David Thoreau, who died in 1862, fourteen years before the AMC was founded, wrote the region's definitive answer in his essay "Walking," first delivered as a lecture in 1851. "I wish to speak a word for Nature," he began, "for absolute freedom and wildness, as contrasted with a freedom and culture merely civil — to regard man as an inhabitant, or a part and parcel of Nature, rather than a member of society" [Thoreau, Walking](https://gutenberg.org/files/1022/1022-h/1022-h.htm).

Thoreau derived the word "sauntering" from the medieval "Sainte-Terrer" — a Holy-Lander, one who walked to the Holy Land. "For every walk is a sort of crusade," he wrote. But his insight was not merely etymological. He understood that walking was a form of thinking — that the rhythm of the feet freed the mind from its usual circuits. "The saunterer, in the good sense, is no more vagrant than the meandering river," he wrote. "He who sits still in a house all the time may be the greatest vagrant of all."

Modern science has spent the last four decades confirming what Thoreau knew before he had finished his first paragraph. The Attention Restoration Theory, developed by environmental psychologists Rachel and Stephen Kaplan in the 1980s, proposes that natural environments — with their "soft fascination," their gentle sensory engagement — restore directed attention in ways that urban environments cannot [Frontiers in Public Health, 2025](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1700325/full). A 2017 randomized crossover trial published in PLOS One found that three hours of mountain hiking produced significantly greater improvements in mood, activation, and calmness than the same duration of indoor treadmill walking — and significantly reduced anxiety and fatigue [PLOS One, 2017](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0177719). A 2024 systematic review of 17 studies confirmed that nature-based walking interventions improve mood, optimism, and mental well-being while reducing stress, anxiety, and negative rumination [ResearchGate, 2024](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/373236134_Effectiveness_of_nature-based_walking_interventions_in_improving_mental_health_in_adults_a_systematic_review).

The biophilia hypothesis — the evolutionary argument that humans have an innate affinity for natural systems — adds another layer. We are, the theory suggests, a species that evolved in savannas and forests, and our nervous systems have not fully adapted to a world of concrete, screens, and fluorescent light. Walking in the woods is not, in any serious sense, a leisure activity. It is a homecoming — a return to an environment our nervous systems still recognize as home, even if our calendars insist otherwise.

But the deeper answer may be simpler still. The walker on the trail is not, despite appearances, escaping meaning. She is creating the conditions under which meaning has room to arrive on its own. The path becomes a kind of template: follow it, and the mind follows its own hidden contours. The 19th-century AMC members, climbing Mount Willard in stiff collars and hobnailed boots, understood this even if they lacked the vocabulary for it. They walked because walking was the most direct route to a kind of attention that modern life — with its genius for interruption — had rendered impossible indoors.

---

## VI. The Weight of 150 Years

The AMC of 2026 is a very different organization from the one that met in the Rogers Building in 1876. Its operating budget runs into the tens of millions. It manages more than 114,000 acres of conservation land in Maine alone. Its All Out plan — the club's current five-year strategic vision — calls for protecting an additional 30,000 acres of Maine's 100-Mile Wilderness, building accessible "all persons trails" in southern New England, and cutting operational greenhouse gas emissions by 45% [AMC All Out](https://digitalcommons.dartmouth.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2148&context=appalachia).

And yet the core of its work has remained stubbornly, almost defiantly, unchanged. It still builds and maintains trails. It still educates people about the natural world. It still fights to protect the landscapes its members love. To mark its 150th anniversary, the club organized a 2,000-mile relay from Virginia to Maine — a walking procession that traced the spine of the Appalachians and honored the people and places that shaped the club's legacy [AMC 150th](https://www.outdoors.org/about/history/).

And the people still come. On any given summer weekend, the trailheads of the White Mountains fill by dawn. The Franconia Ridge trail counter — an electronic monitor embedded in the alpine zone — recorded days exceeding 900 visitors in 2024, a 300% increase from a decade earlier [Mountain Steward](https://www.mountainsteward.net/2025/06/25/the-numbers-game/). The parking lot at the Lincoln Woods trailhead overflows onto the Kancamagus Highway by 8 a.m. The AMC's eight White Mountain huts — which require reservations months in advance — serve 40,000 guests per season, each of whom has discovered that the finest hotel in New Hampshire is a hut you have to walk to.

What Thoreau called "the art of Walking" has become, in the aggregate, a regional economic engine. New England's outdoor recreation industry supports 432,000 jobs and generates $51.6 billion in consumer spending annually [Wildlands & Woodlands](https://www.wildlandsandwoodlands.org/sites/default/files/The%20Economic%20Case%20for%20Conservation.pdf). The Bureau of Economic Analysis reports that the outdoor recreation sector contributed $696.7 billion to national GDP in 2024 — 2.4 percent of the entire economy [BEA 2024](https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/outdoor-recreation-economic-statistics-us-and-states-2024). Massachusetts led the nation in growth at 6.9%, generating $14.6 billion for the state's economy [Mass.gov](https://www.mass.gov/news/new-report-massachusetts-leads-us-in-growth-of-outdoor-recreation-contributing-over-146-billion-to-states-economy). New Hampshire's outdoor recreation sector contributed $4.2 billion, supporting 33,000 jobs [NH Business Review](https://www.nhbr.com/federal-data-outdoor-recreation-generates-4-2b-for-nh-economy/).

The numbers have grown so large that they risk obscuring the simplicity of the act that generates them: one person, putting one foot in front of the other, on a path through the woods. Every statistic in this article traces back to that single motion — one foot after the other — repeated until it became an economy.

---

## VII. The Trail Ahead

The challenges facing New England's trail system are formidable, which is a polite way of saying they are deeply alarming. Climate change is shortening winter recreation seasons and stressing alpine ecosystems. Invasive species — the hemlock woolly adelgid, the emerald ash borer — are rewriting the forests that the trails pass through. The surge in post-COVID visitation has placed unprecedented pressure on trail infrastructure and on the volunteer networks that maintain it. The White Mountain National Forest's most recent visitor use survey, conducted in 2025, may confirm that the pandemic-era explosion in outdoor recreation was not a spike but a permanent shift [NHPR](https://www.nhpr.org/nh-news/2025-09-22/they-want-to-what-youre-up-to-in-the-white-mountain-national-forest).

But the tradition that began on a January evening in 1876 has proven resilient before. The AMC has survived two world wars, the Great Depression, the decline of the railroad, the rise of the automobile, the invention of Gore-Tex, the digitization of everything, and a pandemic. It has outlasted the industries that seemed, in their time, like permanent features of the New England landscape. It has done so by treating its methods as negotiable and its purpose as sacred: to help people know and love the outdoors, and to protect the places they walk.

The woman from Somerville, standing on the summit of Mount Flume, did not arrive there by accident. The trail beneath her feet was scouted by AMC volunteers in the 1920s, maintained by generations of trail crews, and protected by legislation that the club helped pass more than a century ago. The suspension bridge she crossed was built with donations from people she will never meet. The alpine zone she stood in — fragile, treeless, older than the country itself — exists because people who came before believed that some things are worth more than the timber that could be cut from them.

She may not have known any of this. The trail does not offer plaques explaining its own history. It offers something better: the clean white blaze on a tree, pointing the way forward; the sound of wind through spruce; the hard, satisfying work of climbing. The tradition is invisible only because it has been so thoroughly absorbed into the earth beneath her feet.

Perhaps that is the truest monument to what the founders built. A trail that has been walked for 150 years no longer needs to explain itself. It simply is. And the people who walk it — whether for an afternoon or a season or a lifetime — become part of something they may never fully name.

"The saunterer," Thoreau wrote, "is no more vagrant than the meandering river." One hundred and seventy-five years after he wrote it, sixteen million people a year prove him right. They are not lost. They are finding their way — one step at a time, the only method by which anyone has ever truly arrived anywhere.

---

*Source note: All factual claims in this article are linked to their primary sources via inline URLs. Primary sources include the Appalachian Trail Conservancy, National Park Service, U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, the Thoreau Project Gutenberg edition, the Appalachian Mountain Club, the Green Mountain Club, federal land management agencies, and peer-reviewed research published in Frontiers in Public Health, PLOS One, and other academic journals.*

# The Four-Season Economy: North Conway by the Numbers

---

**North Conway, New Hampshire** — On a Saturday in mid-August, the parking lot at Settlers Green fills by 10 a.m. with Massachusetts, New York, and Quebec license plates, each having traveled a considerable distance to prove that a bargain is worth any amount of time spent acquiring it. Up at Cranmore Mountain, mountain bikers queue for the chairlift, which is to say they queue for the pleasure of returning to where they started. At the 1874 train depot, the Conway Scenic Railroad loads a vintage coach for a slow crawl through Crawford Notch — a journey that derives its charm from going nowhere in particular, and therefore pleases everyone. Meanwhile, on West Side Road, hikers set out for the 10.2-mile semi-loop up North Moat Mountain, hoping to beat the afternoon thunderheads — a hope as old as hiking itself, and about as often rewarded.

This is North Conway in the summer of 2026 — a village of roughly 2,300 year-round residents absorbing a seasonal population that, at peak, can feel ten times that size. The scene looks effortless, as it has for nearly 150 years, though an effortless appearance maintained over a century and a half generally requires a great deal of strenuous effort behind the scenes. But the data beneath it tells a more complicated story — one of a small town that has reinvented its economy four distinct times since 1765, and now manages the tension between record tourism revenue and a permanent population that is aging, housing-constrained, and increasingly income-split.

![The North Conway Depot, built in 1874 in an eclectic Russo-Victorian style, remains the village's architectural anchor.](/api/blog/images/north_conway_depot.jpg)

## The $3.56 Billion Engine

The White Mountains region, anchored by North Conway, generates an estimated **$3.56 billion** in annual tourism economic impact [Tourism Stats](https://tourismstats.website/region/whitemountains). At the state level, New Hampshire's tourism industry produced **$7.5 billion in visitor spending** in fiscal 2024 from **14.6 million visitors**, returning roughly **$380 million** in rooms and meals tax revenue [NH Division of Travel & Tourism 2026 Economic Impact Report](https://www.visitnh.gov/getmedia/a10ac1f0-45aa-41df-9cd6-63577fe08043/2026EconomicImpact.pdf). Every dollar the state invests in tourism promotion generates **$15 in revenue** — an extraordinary return, provided one does not examine too closely who earns it and who merely passes it along [SMARInsights, cited in NHBR](https://www.nhbr.com/winter-wonderland-white-mountains-north-country-reporting-a-rise-in-season-visitors/).

The White Mountain National Forest alone draws about **6 million visitors annually** — more than Yellowstone (4.7M) or Yosemite (4.1M) — driven largely by its proximity to major Northeast population centers [UNH News](https://www.unh.edu/news/2025/08/whos-visiting-new-hampshires-white-mountains). The 2020 survey documented a **60% surge in overall WMNF visitation** during COVID and a **nearly 300% increase** in designated wilderness area use, a spike researchers are still analyzing for long-term trends [NHPR](https://www.nhpr.org/nh-news/2025-09-22/they-want-to-what-youre-up-to-in-the-white-mountain-national-forest). It appears that when civilization becomes slightly less comfortable, a great many people discover a sudden passion for the wilderness.

## Employment: Who Works Here

The largest employment sectors in the Conway area tell you everything about the town's economic structure — and nothing that a casual visitor could not guess. According to NH Employment Security's 2024 QCEW data, the town of Conway's **total covered employment** stands at **8,347 workers** across all industries, down slightly from 8,802 in 2014, but with average weekly wages rising from **$607 to $961** over that decade [NHES GraniteStats](https://www2.nhes.nh.gov/GraniteStats/SessionServlet?city=000205&cityName=Conway&page=Community.jsp). A nearly sixty percent wage increase sounds like progress, though it depends rather a lot on whether one's wages were the ones that increased.

Carroll County as a whole posted **20,156 covered employees** in September 2025, with **average weekly wages of $973** — a 4.2% year-over-year increase [BLS QCEW](https://data.bls.gov/maps/cew/NH?chartData=2&distribution=1&geo_id=33000&industry=10&neg_color=orange&ownerType=0&period=2025-Q3&pos_color=blue&showHideChart=show).

![Employment by industry sector in the North Conway area — retail and hospitality dominate the local economy.](/api/blog/images/north_conway_employment.png)

| Industry | Employed |
|---|---|
| Retail Trade | 568 |
| Arts, Entertainment, Recreation, Accommodation, Food | 387 |
| Educational Services, Health Care, Social Assistance | 291 |
| Construction | 205 |
| Professional, Scientific, Management, Admin Services | 156 |
| Finance, Insurance, Real Estate | 134 |
| Public Administration | 108 |
| Manufacturing | 43 |

*Source: USZip.com, 03860 ZIP code data, 2024 ACS 5-year estimates.*

The top five employers in the area reflect this mix: **Memorial Hospital** (250–499 employees), **Cranmore Mountain Resort** (250–499), **Conway School District** (274), **Eastern Slope Inn** (110), and big-box retail including **Walmart** (est. 1999) and **Market Basket** (opened 2023) [NHES Community Profile](https://www2.nhes.nh.gov/GraniteStats/SessionServlet?city=000205&cityName=Conway&page=Community.jsp). The town's largest employers, one notes, are the hospital to patch up the visitors, the resort to entertain them, the school district to educate the children of those who serve them, and the retailers to sell them things they did not know they needed.

## The Settlers Green Effect

When **Settlers Green** opened in February 1988 on the site of the former White Mountain Airport, it was the first outlet shopping center in New Hampshire. It had three anchor tenants — J.Crew, Eddie Bauer, and Banana Republic — in 89,000 square feet [Settlers Green Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Settlers_Green). It was, in short, a temple to the proposition that one should pay less for things one does not truly want.

Today, the complex spans **500,000 square feet** across four interconnected zones, with more than 60 stores and an estimated **$125 million in annual sales** [Settlers Green Leasing Package](https://www.settlersgreen.com/assets/documents/OVP-Management-Inc.-Leasing-Package.pdf). The 2023 expansion brought a **70,000-square-foot Market Basket**, along with new-to-market brands like Cotopaxi (its first-ever outlet store) and Swix (its first U.S. operation) [Settlers Green 2023 Highlights](https://www.settlersgreen.com/news/2023-leasing-and-development-highlights).

New Hampshire's **lack of sales tax** is a structural advantage that no amount of marketing could replicate. For Canadian families and Northeastern bargain hunters, Settlers Green is a destination in itself — a place where the absence of a tax feels almost as good as the presence of a sale. Since 1988, the center has donated more than $1.5 million to local nonprofits [Laconia Daily Sun](https://www.laconiadailysun.com/news/state/settlers-green-turns-35-outlet-village-adding-new-concepts/article_113b173a-6446-11ed-894e-f385548678be.html).

## Skiing: The Original Winter Economy

Before the outlets, there was the snow train. The Boston and Maine Railroad operated the first official **snow train** in 1931, and by 1932 trains were delivering skiers directly to North Conway [Cranmore Timeline](https://bigpicture.cranmore.com/pages/timeline). At the peak in the early 1940s, as many as **five trains would arrive on a Sunday**, carrying up to **4,000 skiers** for day trips from Boston — a system that delivered New Englanders to the mountains at a time when the only thing easier than getting there was falling down them.

The resort that caught them was **Cranmore Mountain**, founded by North Conway native Harvey Dow Gibson in 1937. With a **$15,000 WPA grant** (equivalent to ~$324,000 today), Gibson cleared 200 acres of Lookout Mountain and renamed it Cranmore. The **Skimobile** — a sit-car lift on a wooden trestle, invented by local mechanic George Morton — could carry as many as **122,000 passengers per season** before its removal in 1990 [Cranmore Timeline](https://bigpicture.cranmore.com/pages/timeline).

![The Skimobile at Cranmore Mountain in 1939 — a one-of-a-kind sit-car lift on a wooden trestle that carried up to 122,000 passengers per season.](/api/blog/images/north_conway_skimobile.jpg)

By 1939, Gibson had used his influence to secure the release of Austrian ski pioneer **Hannes Schneider** from Nazi Germany. Schneider's arrival cemented North Conway's identity as the "birthplace of American skiing" — a claim the village still makes, and with rather more justification than most such claims possess [New Hampshire Magazine](https://www.nhmagazine.com/navigating-north-conway/). In 2024, USA Today readers named North Conway **"Best Ski Town"** in its 10Best Readers' Choice Awards [NH Business Review](https://www.nhbr.com/the-changing-face-of-cranmore/).

Today, New Hampshire ski areas recorded **2,424,587 visits** in the 2024–25 season, a **3% increase** over the previous year and **6% above the 10-year average** [SKI NH / InDepthNH](https://indepthnh.org/2025/06/10/ski-industry-reports-past-season-up-3-percent-honors-individuals/). Under the Fairbank Group, which purchased Cranmore in 2010, more than **$65 million** has been invested in snowmaking, lifts, and summer attractions including a mountain coaster and downhill mountain bike park. A lift ticket that cost **$29 in 2000** now runs **$134** — an increase that seems steep until one remembers that $29 in 2000 bought a kind of innocence about what skiing would eventually cost [NewEnglandSkiHistory.com](https://www.newenglandskihistory.com/NewHampshire/cranmore.php).

## The Other Three Seasons

North Conway's economy is described as "four-season," and the visitor data bears that out — though it also reveals that some seasons are more equal than others.

![Seasonal occupancy rates and average daily rates for short-term rentals in North Conway show the dramatic swing between peak summer and shoulder seasons.](/api/blog/images/north_conway_seasonal_str.png)

**Summer** (June–August): Peak hiking season. Short-term rental occupancy can exceed **75–80%** in July and August, with average daily rates of **$333–$362** [StaySTRA](https://staystra.com/location/new-hampshire/north-conway/). The 2025 July 4th weekend saw **81% of businesses** reporting "good" or "great" performance in a Mt. Washington Valley Chamber of Commerce survey [Patch](https://patch.com/new-hampshire/across-nh/businesses-report-steady-july-4th-mt-washington-valley-fewer-canadian-guests). Eighty-one percent is encouraging, though one suspects the remaining nineteen percent had opinions worth hearing.

**Fall** (September–October): Foliage season drives some **3.7 million visitors** statewide, spending an estimated **$1.8 billion** [Laconia Daily Sun](https://www.laconiadailysun.com/real_estate/fall-foliage-fuels-new-hampshire-s-economy/article_aa06c4c3-18be-4f2d-a198-3962bd428a92.html). October occupancy for short-term rentals sits around **47%**, with ADRs of **$361** — high for a shoulder month, which is to say that New England's leaves command a premium that its weather could never quite justify.

**Winter** (December–March): Ski season is the economic backbone. February occupancy for STRs hits **56%**, with the highest ADRs of the year at **$392** [StaySTRA](https://staystra.com/location/new-hampshire/north-conway/). The 2023–24 winter advertising campaign spent **$538,000** and produced an estimated **64,000 trips** generating **$83 million in visitor spending** [NHBR](https://www.nhbr.com/winter-wonderland-white-mountains-north-country-reporting-a-rise-in-season-visitors/).

**Spring** (April–May): The true shoulder. April occupancy drops to **25.9%** and ADR falls to **$315**. Revenue per rental unit in April averages just over **$2,000**, compared to **$6,800** in August — a swing of more than 3x (The August figure reflects observed StaySTRA data; the stated summer occupancy range of 75–80% would suggest a higher theoretical value, indicating that data sources and aggregation methods may differ.) [StaySTRA](https://staystra.com/location/new-hampshire/north-conway/). It is the season that tourism officials speak of hopefully, and that everyone else endures.

## The Demographic Paradox

Here is where the numbers get uncomfortable — and, for those who enjoy a paradox, rather interesting.

North Conway's permanent population in 2026 is estimated at **2,271 residents** by World Population Review, down from a modeled 2020 estimate of 2,410. (The official 2020 Decennial Census recorded 2,116.) The year-over-year decline from 2025 to 2026 was -0.22% [World Population Review](https://worldpopulationreview.com/us-cities/new-hampshire/north-conway). The wider town of Conway, by contrast, grew slightly to **10,296** in 2024, up from 9,822 in 2020 [U.S. Census QuickFacts](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/conwaytowncarrollcountynewhampshire/PST045222).

The **median age in North Conway** is **61.8 years** — nearly 23 years older than the national median of 38.9. In the town of Conway, **35.1% of residents are 65 or older** [U.S. Census QuickFacts](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/conwaytowncarrollcountynewhampshire/PST045222). The under-18 population is just **12.4%**. This is a community growing older faster than it attracts young families — a demographic trajectory that resembles a retirement party no one thought to end.

The **median household income** in North Conway is **$71,198** — about 90% of the national median. Per capita income is **$54,337**, slightly above the state average [World Population Review](https://worldpopulationreview.com/us-cities/new-hampshire/north-conway). But the **poverty rate is 15.65%**, nearly double New Hampshire's statewide rate of 7.3% [Census Reporter](https://censusreporter.org/profiles/16000US3353860-north-conway-nh/). That is a striking figure for a community at the center of a $3.56 billion tourism economy — though perhaps not so striking when one considers that tourism economies are designed to move money through a place, not to leave it there.

**Housing data** tells part of the story. Of the **1,816 housing units** in the North Conway CDP, roughly **38.6% are vacant** at any given time, and **34.3% are seasonal or vacation properties** [NeighborhoodScout](https://www.neighborhoodscout.com/nh/conway/north-conway). This is not blight — it is a resort housing market. But it means that more than a third of the village's physical plant sits empty for large portions of the year, contributing to an affordability squeeze for year-round workers. It is, in short, a housing crisis dressed up as real estate appreciation.

## What the Numbers Don't Show

The data captures flows — visitors, dollars, workers, housing units. It is less good at capturing the structural tensions of a four-season resort economy, perhaps because tensions are harder to count than dollars.

**Canadian visitation**, which historically made up a significant share of North Conway's summer and fall traffic, has remained "soft" since the pandemic. In the 2025 July 4th Chamber survey, **nearly half of businesses** reported seeing fewer Canadian travelers than in previous years [Patch](https://patch.com/new-hampshire/across-nh/businesses-report-steady-july-4th-mt-washington-valley-fewer-canadian-guests). The gap has not been fully closed by increased visitors from New York and New Jersey — a reminder that even the most successful resort economy depends on the willingness of other people to cross borders.

**Infrastructure strain** is another persistent concern. Businesses cited **traffic** as the most frequent visitor complaint, followed by **parking shortages** and **restaurant wait times** [Patch](https://patch.com/new-hampshire/across-nh/businesses-report-steady-july-4th-mt-washington-valley-fewer-canadian-guests). The village's road network — essentially two-lane NH Route 16 / US 302 — was not designed for peak foliage weekend volumes, which is to say it was designed for a time when people had more patience and fewer places to be.

**Climate volatility** poses a longer-term risk. Cranmore's average annual snowfall of **86 inches** varies dramatically — from a low of **29 inches in 2015–16** to a high of **141 inches in 2016–17** [OnTheSnow](https://www.onthesnow.com/new-hampshire/cranmore-mountain-resort/historical-snowfall). The 2023–24 season brought 102 inches; 2024–25 delivered just 66. Snowmaking infrastructure has made the resort more resilient, but warmer winters remain the industry's central unspoken anxiety — the thing everyone discusses in terms of "investment in snowmaking capacity" when what they mean is "we are hoping the planet cooperates."

![Cranmore Mountain annual snowfall by season, 2012–2025. The average of 86 inches masks dramatic swings from 29 to 141 inches.](/api/blog/images/north_conway_snowfall.png)

## The Long Arc

What makes North Conway's economy unusual is not the numbers themselves but the durability of the pattern. The village has been a tourism destination since the 1820s, when newspaper engravings of the Wiley Slide avalanche drew the first summer visitors. It became an **art colony** in the 1850s when Benjamin Champney bought a house on what is now Main Street; more than **400 artists** passed through over the following decades, their White Mountain School paintings serving as de facto tourism advertising — which is to say that art, even then, was pressed into the service of commerce, and bore it remarkably well. The **railroad arrived in 1872** and the depot — that Russo-Victorian confection designed by Nathaniel J. Bradlee — opened in 1874. **Skiing arrived in the 1930s** via Cranmore and the snow trains. **Outlet retail arrived in 1988** with Settlers Green [New Hampshire Magazine](https://www.nhmagazine.com/navigating-north-conway/).

Each wave built on the previous one. The artists advertised the landscape. The railroad made it accessible. The ski industry added an entire winter season. The shopping center added a reason to come even when the weather was marginal. Today, North Conway is one of the few places in New England where a visitor can plausibly spend a long weekend skiing, hiking, riding a scenic railroad, and buying discounted Patagonia jackets — all within a 3-mile radius. It is a place that solved the problem of what to do with a landscape by giving people an endless variety of ways to consume it.

The numbers will continue to evolve. The 2025 White Mountain National Forest Visitor Use Monitoring survey, conducted by UNH researchers, will provide fresh data on whether the COVID-era visitation surge has normalized or reset baseline demand [NHPR](https://www.nhpr.org/nh-news/2025-09-22/they-want-to-what-youre-up-to-in-the-white-mountain-national-forest). The state's "Wildly Responsible" campaign, launched in 2025, represents an attempt to manage the environmental footprint of record crowds — an admirable goal, and one that sits in the same uneasy relationship with tourism as moderation does with appetite.

But the underlying structural reality appears stable: a small, aging permanent population serving a much larger transient one, generating billions in economic activity while grappling with housing shortages, infrastructure limits, and the quiet precarity of a model that depends, every season, on the weather, the exchange rate, and the willingness of 4 million people a year to get in the car and drive north. It is a system that works beautifully, provided one does not examine it too closely — which, to be fair, is true of most beautiful systems.

---

*Images: 1) North Conway Depot / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY). 2) Skimobile at Cranmore / Library of Congress, Marion Post Wolcott (1939). 3) Employment by industry chart / original data from USZip.com ACS 2024. 4) Seasonal STR chart / original data from StaySTRA 2024–2025. 5) Cranmore snowfall chart / original data from OnTheSnow.*

# The Bench Economy: What the IPL Pays Its Invisible Men

---

Mumbai, April 2026. In a hotel room somewhere in the city's satellite belt, a 24-year-old fast bowler sits on the edge of a bed that cost more than his parents' first car. The television is on, tuned to the match he is not playing in. His teammates are on screen, chasing 185 under lights at Wankhede. He is in full cricket kit because the rules require him to be ready for a moment that will only arrive through another man's misfortune. He is the standby. The reserve. A player whose career advances only when someone ahead of him collapses.

His contract says he earns ₹30 lakh this season — the new base price for uncapped players in IPL 2025, raised from ₹20 lakh in previous cycles [IPL Governing Council, 2024](https://sportstar.thehindu.com/cricket/ipl/ipl-news/ipl-auction-rules-overseas-players-earnings-cut-base-price-hiked-capped-uncapped-categories-details/article68698420.ece). If he plays every match, he collects another ₹7.5 lakh per game — ₹1.05 crore on top, as per the match fee system introduced by BCCI secretary Jay Shah in September 2024 [ESPNcricinfo](https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/ipl-2025-bcci-introduces-match-fees-for-players-1453001). If he never takes the field — and roughly 40% of contracted players see zero or near-zero game time any given season — he gets the ₹30 lakh and nothing else. The league pays him for his availability. Whether he is ever needed is a question the contract declines to answer.

The IPL is a league of 10 teams, each permitted to carry between 18 and 25 players [Sporting News, 2024](https://www.sportingnews.com/in/ipl/news/ipl-2025-mega-auction-rules/3793968cadf1a875f79a8515). That is roughly 230 contracted cricketers per season. On any given match day, 110 take the field (including the Impact Player substitute). The rest watch. Some of them are millionaires, like Krishnappa Gowtham, who was paid ₹9.25 crore by CSK in 2021 to play zero matches [Times Now, 2021](https://www.timesnownews.com/amp/sports/cricket/ipl/article/from-anrich-nortje-to-robin-uthappa-strongest-playing-xi-for-players-who-didnt-play-single-match-in-ipl-2021/755836). Some of them are young men from towns like Rewa, Madhya Pradesh, who signed their first IPL contract and became overnight the most famous person in a 50-kilometre radius. What unites them is a peculiar transaction: they are paid, sometimes handsomely, to be invisible.

This is the bench economy of the IPL — a parallel financial system within cricket's richest league, where the commodity being traded is not performance but presence. It raises a question the league's celebratory narrative prefers to ignore: what is the actual cost, measured in years and careers and the slow attrition of promise, of being the 18th man in a 25-man squad?

---

## The Mathematics of Exclusion

The arithmetic has a quiet cruelty about it. Before the introduction of the Impact Player rule in 2023, each match consumed 11 players from a squad of up to 25. That left 14 on the bench. The Impact Player rule — which allows teams to substitute one player mid-match — expanded the match-day group to 12, narrowing the theoretical bench to 13 [IPL Governing Council, 2024](https://www.iplt20.com/news/4109/ipl-governing-council-announces-tata-ipl-player-regulations-2025-27). In practice, the bench is often larger on game day because teams carry additional reserves and net bowlers.

Over a 14-match league season, a franchise will typically use 16 to 18 players. The remaining 7 to 9 — roughly a third of the squad — will have minimal or no on-field participation. Some of these players go entire seasons without stepping onto the field. Some go multiple seasons.

Nishant Sindhu was part of the Indian Under-19 World Cup-winning squad in 2023, bought by Chennai Super Kings at the auction. He spent three consecutive IPL seasons — 2023, 2024, and 2025 — on the books of CSK and later Gujarat Titans. He has never played a single IPL match [CricTracker, 2025](https://www.crictracker.com/cricket-appeal/3-players-who-were-bought-multiple-times-but-never-played-a-single-ipl-match-4428/). Kyle Mills, the New Zealand pacer, was bought twice — once by Kings XI Punjab in 2008 and again by Mumbai Indians in 2009. Zero matches [CricTracker, 2025](https://www.crictracker.com/cricket-appeal/3-players-who-were-bought-multiple-times-but-never-played-a-single-ipl-match-4428/). Pavan Deshpande was signed by Royal Challengers Bengaluru in 2018 and again in 2020. He never played [CricTracker, 2025](https://www.crictracker.com/cricket-appeal/3-players-who-were-bought-multiple-times-but-never-played-a-single-ipl-match-4428/).

These are not fringe cases. They are structural outcomes of a system where squad size exceeds match-day capacity by more than 100 percent.

---

## What the Bench Pays

In 2022, N Jagadeesan sat in Chennai Super Kings' dugout for two complete seasons before making his debut. He had been bought at his base price of ₹20 lakh in 2018. "Being on the bench definitely made me doubt myself, a hundred percent," he told Wisden India [Wisden, 2022](https://www.wisden.com/cricket-interviews/exclusive-jagadeesan-being-on-the-bench-at-csk-made-me-doubt-myself-i-would-keep-thinking-if-i-was-good-enough). "I would keep thinking if I was good enough and if I would be capable of playing."

The doubt vanished the night he finally played — 33 runs off 28 balls against Royal Challengers Bangalore in Dubai, 2020. But he played only six more games for CSK. In 2021, he was back on the bench full-time. Then he was released. "On a personal point of view, yes, I could only wish that I had a lot more game time," he said. But he added, speaking of CSK's stacked lineup and his role as a wicketkeeper-batter, "I knew for a fact that the combination was not going to suit me."

Jagadeesan's story captures a paradox at the heart of the bench economy. A player can understand the logic of his exclusion perfectly and still be hollowed out by it. Reason and self-doubt do not share a dressing room. The doubt returns every practice session when the XI is pinned to the board and his name is not on it.

Arjun Tendulkar experienced the same paradox across five seasons with Mumbai Indians. Signed in 2021 at ₹20 lakh, re-signed in 2022 at ₹30 lakh, and again in 2025 at ₹30 lakh, he played exactly five matches in five years — four in 2023, one in 2024, zero in 2025. Asked in 2026 whether he felt he deserved more opportunities, he did not equivocate. "Who doesn't feel that?" he told Shubhankar Mishra's podcast [Times Now, 2026](https://www.timesnownews.com/sports/cricket/no-one-wants-to-sit-on-bench-arjun-tendulkar-breaks-silence-on-not-playing-enough-for-mumbai-indians-article-153973103). "No one wants to sit on the bench."

The bluntness of that line — "no one wants to sit on the bench" — is striking precisely because it states aloud what the league prefers to leave implied. The IPL bench is not a finishing school or a development incubator, though franchises often frame it that way. It is a holding pen. Players are acquired, stored, and occasionally deployed. The ones who never get called up absorb the season in hotel rooms and practice nets, kept match-fit for a moment that may never arrive.

Adam Zampa, the Australian leg-spinner who took 6 for 19 on his IPL debut for Rising Pune Supergiant in 2016, described the experience in starker terms. "I went through all kinds of emotions, right from how good it is just to be a part of it to I am sick of this. Just get me home. I am not playing" [The Final Word Cricket Podcast, reported by SportsTak, 2024](https://thesportstak.com/cricket/indian-premier-league-22-mar-2024/story/i-am-sick-of-this-just-get-me-home-not-playing-adam-zampa-ipl-experience-rues-not-getting-multi-million-dollar-3054143-2024-08-11).

Zampa's frustration carried a specific sting. After his six-wicket haul, he expected to be a regular. He was not. Rajasthan Royals had R Ashwin and Yuzvendra Chahal in the spin department. There was simply no room. "I never got a multi-million dollar payday from the IPL," he said.

---

## The Financial Gradient

The bench economy operates on a steep financial gradient, and the gradient is what makes the arrangement tolerable — or at least negotiable.

At the top: a capped Indian player retained for ₹18 crore who sits out half the season earns ₹18 crore anyway. The contract is the contract. The IPL salary system states plainly that a player available for the full season is entitled to their full salary "regardless of the number of matches they play or are selected for" [Times of India, 2024](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/sports/cricket/ipl/top-stories/ipl-salary-system-explained-10-key-points-you-need-to-know/articleshow/115626093.cms). A franchise that releases a player before the contract expires must pay the full term.

At the bottom: an uncapped player at the minimum base price of ₹20 lakh (raised to ₹30 lakh in 2025) who sits the entire season takes home ₹20 lakh. That is life-changing money for a 22-year-old from a tier-2 cricket city. It is also roughly what a Ranji Trophy regular earns over a full domestic season of match fees — ₹40,000 to ₹60,000 per day, across 8 to 10 four-day matches, plus List A and T20 tournament fees [Gully Cricket, 2026](https://gully.cricket/indian-cricket-player-salary-breakdown/). A top domestic-grade player might earn ₹8 to ₹20 lakh in annual retainer under the MCA's new domestic contract system introduced in April 2026 [GK365, 2026](https://gk365.in/current-affairs-articles/sports/mca-domestic-player-contract-system-2026/).

The IPL bench, even unpaid a single match fee, doubles that domestic income — for two months of work, most of it spent watching.

This is the bargain. The player trades match practice, career development, selection leverage, and the irreplaceable experience of performing under pressure for a cheque that changes his family's financial trajectory. It is a rational choice. It is also, in the long run, a costly one.

![Earnings comparison: bench vs. playing XI vs. domestic cricket](/api/blog/images/ipl_bench_earnings_gap.png)
*Figure 1: Annual earnings comparison for an uncapped IPL player at base price — bench only (₹30L), regular playing XI (+₹1.05Cr in match fees), and a senior domestic Ranji cricketer (₹16–24L per season including retainers). Sources: [ESPNcricinfo, 2024](https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/ipl-2025-bcci-introduces-match-fees-for-players-1453001), [Gully Cricket, 2026](https://gully.cricket/indian-cricket-player-salary-breakdown/), [Sportstar, 2024](https://sportstar.thehindu.com/cricket/ipl/ipl-news/ipl-auction-rules-overseas-players-earnings-cut-base-price-hiked-capped-uncapped-categories-details/article68698420.ece).*

---

## The Opportunity Cost of the Bench

Shardul Thakur, now a senior India international, spent IPL 2016 on the bench at Kings XI Punjab before being released mid-season. He was Mumbai's highest wicket-taker in the Ranji Trophy that year but did not play a single match in the IPL. "It is frustrating because if you ask anyone in the squad, I was working as hard as anyone else in the training sessions," he told ESPNcricinfo [ESPNcricinfo, 2016](https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/feeling-of-being-left-out-hurts-me-shardul-thakur-1010975). "It is the feeling of being left out which is hurting me."

What stung most was not the lack of match time but the absence of explanation. Pawan Negi, bought by Delhi Daredevils for ₹8.5 crore in 2016 — making him one of the most expensive Indian buys that year — faced the same silence. "I still don't know. I kept wondering why wasn't I given more opportunities. And the team management didn't tell me the reason either," he told Sportskeeda [Sportskeeda, 2016](https://www.sportskeeda.com/cricket/pawan-negi-speaks-disappointing-ipl-9). He bowled nine overs in eight matches that season.

Venkatesh Iyer, who joined Royal Challengers Bengaluru in 2026 after being part of KKR's 2024 title-winning campaign, brought a more philosophical perspective. "It's not easy. But it's extremely important to stay motivated because you can easily get desperate," he told Rediff [Rediff, 2026](https://www.rediff.com/cricket/report/ipl-2026-venkatesh-iyer-spills-secrets-on-rcb-bench-life-and-comeback/20260422.htm). "You can easily lose out on your work ethic. So, I train my mind in such a way that I'm going to play every game."

But Iyer also admitted what no training regimen can fix: "It's something that you can't prepare for."

The data bears out the cost. Colin Ingram, the South African batter who played only 3 of 14 matches for Delhi Daredevils in 2011, told ESPNcricinfo that season: "I did feel a little left out and had to try and remind myself to stay sharp so that I would be ready when my time came. There were times when it was frustrating" [ESPNcricinfo, 2011](https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/south-africa-s-fringe-talent-spurned-at-the-ipl-518273). Ingram and five other South African players — including a young Faf du Plessis, who did not play a single match that season — missed the last round of South Africa's domestic first-class fixtures to sit on IPL benches. They became richer. They lost irreplaceable game time.

---

## The Impact Player Paradox

Introduced in 2023 and retained through at least 2027, the Impact Player rule was sold as an opportunity-expander — a way to involve more players in each match. Instead, it has shrunk the space for all-rounders and concentrated opportunity among specialists [The Hindu, 2026](https://www.thehindu.com/sport/cricket/impact-player-rule-ipl-team-balance-all-rounders-analysis/article70821215.ece).

A synthetic control analysis from Columbia University found that the Impact Player rule added an average of 12.3 runs per innings to IPL scores above global T20 trends. But the more significant finding was structural: the number of overs bowled by top-order batsmen dropped 38%, from 11.2 per match before the rule to 6.9 after [Columbia University Working Paper, 2026](https://www.cs.columbia.edu/~misra/impact-player-2026.pdf). Teams no longer need part-timers. They can carry a specialist batter who never bowls and swap him for a specialist bowler.

Rahul Dravid, India's head coach during the rule's introduction, told Sportstar he was "not particularly fond" of the Impact Player rule from a national team perspective [Sportstar, 2025](https://sportstar.thehindu.com/cricket/ipl/ipl-news/rahul-dravid-ipl-allrounders-impact-player-rule-rajasthan-royals/article69425777.ece). "As a coach, you want to develop all-rounders, and under the old 11 vs 11 format, certain players would have had more opportunities to bat or bowl in different situations."

Rohit Sharma put it even more directly on the Club Prairie Fire podcast in 2024: "I am not a big fan of the Impact Player. It is going to hold all-rounders back" [Wisden, 2025](https://www.wisden.com/series/ipl-2025/cricket-news/ipl-2025-why-the-impact-player-is-not-really-a-villain-for-indias-all-rounders).

For the bench player, the Impact Player rule creates an additional barrier. Not only are there 13 spots on the bench instead of 14, but the strategic logic that once justified carrying an all-rounder — "he gives us balance" — has been weakened. A specialist is now more valuable than a utility player. The bench, counter-intuitively, becomes more specialized and harder to break into.

---

## The Culture Shock

For players arriving from small-town India, the bench experience is compounded by a disorientation that has nothing to do with cricket. Ishwar Pandey, the fast bowler from Rewa, Madhya Pradesh, who played for Pune Warriors in 2013 and later Chennai Super Kings, described checking into his first IPL hotel room and encountering a bathtub. "Pehle jankari yeh le gayi, ke hai kya yeh cheez?" he told the Indian Express in 2026 [Indian Express, 2026](https://indianexpress.com/article/sports/cricket/inside-the-ipl-culture-shock-bathtub-glamour-ishwar-pandey-10597634/). "I just didn't know what it was. Do I have to bathe in it or sit in it?"

The air conditioning had buttons he could not decipher. He had to call for help. "Coming from Rewa, I had never stayed in such rooms in my life. It feels like we are in heaven."

But heaven, Pandey discovered, has its own disorienting logic. The glamour of the IPL — the celebrity owners, the after-parties, the hotel lobbies packed with fans and agents — can mask the precarity underneath. "There comes a phase where you get scared," he said. "Whether I am saying the right thing or wrong. Language is a problem."

Pandey watched the next generation of small-town arrivals go through the same cycle. "They think this is life. They don't know where their career is going and where they're going."

The culture shock is not incidental to the bench economy. It is a feature. The league recruits aggressively from India's vast domestic talent pool — 1,224 uncapped players registered for the IPL 2025 mega auction alone, alongside 320 capped players and 30 from Associate nations [Times of Sports, 2025](https://www.timesofsports.com/cricket/ipl/squad-2025-players-list/). Many of these players come from towns with no history of producing IPL cricketers. For them, the contract itself is proof of arrival. The bench is where that proof gets tested.

![Squad structure: 25 players, 11 spots, 13 on the bench](/api/blog/images/ipl_squad_structure_bars.png)
*Figure 2: For every match, 25 contracted players yield 12 match-day participants (including the Impact Player). The remaining 13 — often more than half the squad — do not take the field. Sources: [IPL Governing Council](https://www.iplt20.com/news/4109/ipl-governing-council-announces-tata-ipl-player-regulations-2025-27), [Sporting News](https://www.sportingnews.com/in/ipl/news/ipl-2025-mega-auction-rules/3793968cadf1a875f79a8515), [CricTracker](https://www.crictracker.com/cricket-appeal/3-players-who-were-bought-multiple-times-but-never-played-a-single-ipl-match-4428/).*

---

## The Unspoken Calculus

The franchises are not being irrational. The squad of 25 is an insurance policy for a high-variance, injury-prone sport played in extreme heat. A death bowler pulls a hamstring in the third over — the replacement needs to be IPL-ready. A top-order batter goes for a duck three matches running — the franchise wants options. The bench absorbs shocks.

But the bench also serves a financial function that franchises do not advertise. By stockpiling talent at base prices, teams ensure that rival franchises cannot access those players. An uncapped Indian player bought for ₹20 lakh and benched all season is not available to the team that might actually play him. It is a form of talent hoarding, enabled by a salary cap that makes bench-warmers cheap.

And the players know this. Tymal Mills, bought by Royal Challengers Bangalore for ₹12 crore in 2017, played a few games, got injured, and never fully recovered his IPL career. The price tag became a burden. "I feel getting bought for that much money hurt my reputation a little bit, because I didn't perform to those standards," he told the Times of India [Times of India, 2025](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/sports/cricket/news/exclusive-tymal-mills-on-the-rs-12-crore-price-tag-with-rcb-in-2017-and-the-baggage-it-brought/articleshow/117634023.cms). "If I would have had the same results but I was only bought for 3 or 4 crore, then the perception would have been a bit different."

Even now, Mills said, every year during the IPL auction, "I'm getting tagged and tweeted and mentioned as one of the worst buys ever."

---

## What Remains

In Rewa, Ishwar Pandey is still the man who made it. Builders arrive with brochures. Local politicians visit. Strangers make requests he does not know how to handle. "Many don't know me by face but the whole town thinks that there is an India cricketer from this place and they can get anything done through me."

He played for Pune Warriors, Chennai Super Kings, and Rising Pune Supergiant. He was part of the Indian squad but never played for India. The bathtub, he figured out eventually. The rest took longer.

"Players have to keep in mind that their focus should be on the game," Pandey said. "If we don't focus on the game, we won't get what we are getting."

But the game, for so many of them, is the thing they are not getting. Every April, a new cohort arrives — 230 young men spread across 10 teams, in 10 cities, carrying contracts that make them richer than they have ever been. Some will become stars. Some will play a handful of matches. Some will sit through entire seasons, watching, waiting, being paid to be available.

And every April, a boy from a new small town checks into a hotel room, sees a bathtub he does not know how to use, and wonders if he is good enough.
