post.excerpt: ![A jellyfish of the genus Cassiopea pulses slowly on the seafloor at night. It has no brain. It still sleeps.](/api/blog/images/sleep_cassiopea_jellyfish.jpg)
post.content:
# The Necessity Puzzle: Why Every Creature That Sleeps Risks Everything for Rest

![A jellyfish of the genus Cassiopea pulses slowly on the seafloor at night. It has no brain. It still sleeps.](/api/blog/images/sleep_cassiopea_jellyfish.jpg)

On a tropical seafloor, the upside-down jellyfish *Cassiopea* spends its life reclining on its bell, tentacles waving upward like a crown that rules nothing. It has no brain — no central nervous system at all, merely a diffuse nerve net. It cannot plan, remember, or dream. And yet, when night falls over the coral reefs it inhabits, *Cassiopea* performs an act that science once considered impossible: it goes to sleep.

Its pulsing rate drops by a third, from about 58 contractions per minute to 39. Lift the jellyfish from the seafloor at night, pull away its platform, and the animal drifts in the water column for up to five seconds before it "wakes" and swims to safety. During the day, the same jellyfish rights itself in under a second. When scientists from Caltech kept *Cassiopea* awake by squirting jets of water at it every 20 minutes, the jellyfish was 17 percent less active the following day — sluggish, sleepy, unmistakably in need of rest it had been denied [Nath et al., 2017, *Current Biology*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2017.08.014).

If a brainless jellyfish sleeps, then sleep is no luxury of the cerebral cortex. It is not a byproduct of complex cognition, nor a quirk of the mammalian line. Sleep appears to be a property of neurons themselves — perhaps of life itself. And that raises a puzzle so fundamental that scientists still cannot agree on the answer: why would any organism evolve to spend a third of its existence in a state of helpless vulnerability, unable to eat, mate, or defend itself, unless the return on that investment justified every danger it incurred?

## The Great Sleep Gap

The first lesson of comparative sleep science is that there is no normal amount of sleep. The "average" adult mammal sleeps 11.7 hours per day, according to the Phylogeny of Sleep Database — a compendium of 178 studies covering 127 species assembled by researchers at Boston University and the Max Planck Institute. But that average conceals a range almost grotesque in its spread [McNamara et al., 2008, *The Open Sleep Journal*](https://benthamopen.com/contents/pdf/TOSLPJ/TOSLPJ-1-11.pdf).

The donkey sleeps three hours. The armadillo sleeps twenty. The big brown bat packs nineteen hours of daily sleep, while the giraffe gets by on four and a half. The horse's sleep cycle — the time it takes to move from NREM sleep through REM and back again — runs sixty minutes. The chinchilla's runs six. These differences do not obey evolutionary order: primates as a group possess no characteristic sleep signature to distinguish them from rodents or insectivores. Within the same order, closely related species can spend wildly different amounts of time asleep [Siegel, 2005, *Nature*](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature04285).

![Total daily sleep time across 71 mammal species, with carnivores, herbivores, and omnivores plotted separately. Humans cluster at the low end, alongside other large-bodied omnivores.](/api/blog/images/sleep_mammal_hours.png)

For decades, sleep researchers sought to explain this variation by tying it to some functional purpose. Bigger brains demand more REM sleep, the theory ran — time to process information and consolidate memories. Higher metabolic rates require more sleep for energy conservation. The altricial young of certain species need extra REM for brain development. These explanations possessed a satisfying logic: sleep must serve a purpose commensurate with the organism's needs.

But when Isabella Capellini and her colleagues at the University of Bristol applied rigorous phylogenetic methods to the largest mammalian sleep dataset ever assembled — controlling for laboratory conditions and evolutionary history — the traditional correlations collapsed. Brain size did not predict REM sleep duration. Basal metabolic rate correlated *negatively* with sleep time, not positively. The only robust predictors of how much a mammal sleeps were ecological: how safe its sleeping site, what it eats, and how much time it must spend foraging [Capellini et al., 2008, *PNAS*](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0712043105) [Lesku et al., 2006, *The American Naturalist*](https://doi.org/10.1086/506973).

The herbivore, forever chewing and digesting, sleeps little. The carnivore, with its rich diet and fewer meals to pursue, sleeps long. The animal that dozes in an exposed burrow sleeps less than the one tucked into a safe tree hollow. Social sleepers — species that bed down together — sleep less than solitary ones, perhaps because more eyes watch for danger. These patterns suggest that sleep time is not primarily determined by how much sleep an animal *needs*, but by how much it can *afford*.

Here, then, is the first paradox at the heart of the necessity puzzle: the animal kingdom's sleep patterns are shaped less by the supposed benefits of sleep than by the costs of staying asleep. If sleep were not essential, evolution would have eliminated it in species that cannot afford it. And yet no species has.

## The Riddle of REM

![Sleep in the platypus: REM sleep occurs with a moderate-voltage EEG — a primitive feature linking monotremes to the earliest mammals. The platypus spends more time in REM than any animal on Earth.](/api/blog/images/sleep_platypus_rem.jpg)

If total sleep time is puzzling, REM sleep is positively confounding. Our most vivid dreams occur during this state of high brain activation and near-total muscle paralysis. But REM is no human invention, nor even a mammalian one in any straightforward sense. Its distribution across the animal kingdom defeats every simple explanation.

The platypus, a monotreme that diverged from other mammals some 166 million years ago, spends between 5.8 and 8 hours per day in REM sleep — more than any animal ever measured. That is roughly 40 percent of its total sleep time, and it occurs while the platypus's electroencephalogram shows a moderate- to high-voltage pattern, unlike the low-voltage, wake-like EEG that characterizes REM in placental mammals [Siegel et al., 1999, *Neuroscience*](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0306-4522(98)00588-0). The echidna, the platypus's fellow monotreme, occupies an even stranger position: it appears to combine aspects of REM and NREM sleep into a single, undifferentiated state, its brainstem activated while its forebrain generates slow waves. Siegel and his colleagues have argued that this represents the ancestral condition — that the two distinct sleep states we know today did not evolve sequentially, but instead *differentiated* out of a primitive precursor state that held the seeds of both [Siegel et al., 1998, *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B*](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.1998.0272).

If REM sleep evolved to serve some specific cognitive function — memory consolidation, say, or emotional regulation — then one would expect animals with more complex brains to have more of it. They do not. Birds, which have densely packed, neuron-rich brains and demonstrate sophisticated cognition, have remarkably little REM sleep — often less than 30 minutes per day, in brief bursts averaging under 10 seconds each [Roth et al., 2006, *Journal of Sleep Research*](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-2869.2006.00559.x). The great frigatebird, during its 10-day foraging flights over the open ocean, sleeps for an average of 42 minutes per day, often with only one cerebral hemisphere at a time. REM sleep episodes in flight are vanishingly rare [Rattenborg et al., 2016, *Nature Communications*](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms12468).

Dolphins and other cetaceans present an even more extreme case. Many researchers believe that dolphins do not experience REM sleep at all — or at least not in any form that resembles the REM sleep of terrestrial mammals. Instead, they engage in unihemispheric slow-wave sleep, one half of the brain at a time, which allows them to swim, surface for air, and remain vigilant continuously. If REM sleep were essential for brain function in mammals, the dolphin — with its large, complex brain — should need it most. Instead, it may have eliminated it entirely [Lyamin et al., 2008, *Sleep Medicine Reviews*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.smrv.2007.08.006).

Siegel has proposed that REM sleep may have a thermoregulatory function: brain temperature drops during NREM sleep and rises during REM, and REM sleep time across species correlates negatively with body and brain temperature. The monotremes, with lower body temperatures, have more REM. The birds, with the highest body temperatures among endotherms, have the least. Under this view, REM sleep is not primarily about dreaming or memory — it is about warming the brain back up after the deep cool of slow-wave sleep [Siegel, 2005, *Nature*](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature04285).

## The Dreaming Animal

But if REM sleep serves a thermoregulatory function, that cannot be its only role. The evidence that animals dream — that they replay their waking experiences during sleep — is now overwhelming, and it points to a cognitive function that cannot be dismissed as a mere byproduct.

In a landmark 2001 study, Matthew Wilson and his colleagues at MIT recorded the firing of hippocampal place cells in rats as they ran a circular track for food rewards. Each neuron fired when the rat was in a specific location, creating a distinctive sequence of neural activity that mapped the animal's journey. Later, during REM sleep, the same sequences replayed — but at a slower speed, approximately in real time, as if the rat were mentally rerunning the maze. The researchers found that memories of a sequential experience were reactivated during REM sleep, and that the reactivation was robust even 24 hours later, suggesting that REM sleep was involved in the long-term storage of memories [Louie & Wilson, 2001, *Neuron*](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0896-6273(01)00186-6).

A follow-up study, published the next year, found that the same replay occurred during slow-wave sleep as well — but in a very different form. Brief memory sequences corresponding to single laps on the track were replayed in compressed bursts of 100 to 200 milliseconds. A four-second run through the maze was condensed into a neural snapshot. Unlike REM replay, this SWS replay appeared only in the sleep period immediately following the behavior, suggesting it was part of the initial encoding of memory rather than long-term consolidation [Lee & Wilson, 2002, *Neuron*](https://news.mit.edu/2002/dreams).

More recent work has shown just how central this replay is to memory. In a 2024 study published in *Nature*, researchers recorded from the CA1 region of the rat hippocampus during sleep and during periods of sleep deprivation. They found that while sharp-wave ripples — the neural events that carry replay — continued to occur at normal or even elevated rates during sleep deprivation, the actual *content* of the replay was diminished or completely abolished. The brain produced the machinery of memory consolidation, but without sleep, it could not use it [Giri et al., 2024, *Nature*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07538-2).

If rats replay their mazes during sleep, do they dream in the way we do? Wilson, asked this question, answered with characteristic caution: "A lot of things suggest there is an extensive re-experiencing of the awake state during sleep. If we want to call that dreams, I'm perfectly comfortable with that description" [quoted in National Geographic, 2022](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/animals-dream-too-heres-what-we-know).

## The Octopus's Gif

The question of animal dreaming took an unexpected turn in 2021, when Sylvia Medeiros of the Federal University of Rio Grande do Norte published video evidence of sleeping octopuses changing color. *Octopus insularis*, a species found off the coast of Brazil, cycles between two distinct sleep states. In quiet sleep, the octopus is pale and motionless, its pupils narrowed to slits. Then, every 30 to 40 minutes, it transitions to an active sleep phase: its skin darkens, textures shift, colors race across its body, its eyes dart, and its suckers contract. These active bouts last about 40 seconds [Medeiros et al., 2021, *iScience*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2021.102332).

The resemblance to mammalian REM sleep is striking — and deeply puzzling, because octopuses and vertebrates last shared a common ancestor roughly 550 million years ago. Two-stage sleep, with a quiet phase alternating with an active, wake-like phase, appears to have evolved independently in cephalopods and vertebrates. A follow-up study in *Nature* in 2023 recorded direct neural activity from octopus brains during sleep and found that the active phase was accompanied by patterns resembling wakefulness in the superior frontal and vertical lobes — brain regions associated with learning and memory [Pophale et al., 2023, *Nature*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06202-1).

"If they are dreaming, they are dreaming for up to a minute," Sidarta Ribeiro, a co-author of the study, told NPR. "It should be more like small video clips, or even gifs" [NPR, 2021](https://www.npr.org/2021/03/25/980944495/sleeping-octopuses-may-have-dreams-but-theyre-probably-brief).

The independent evolution of REM-like sleep in a lineage separated from our own by half a billion years suggests that the phenomenon is not a contingent evolutionary accident, but an emergent property of complex nervous systems. When a brain reaches a certain threshold of complexity, it may *need* to produce an active sleep state — regardless of the evolutionary path that built it.

## The Human Exception

Among primates, humans are outliers — and not in the direction one might expect. We sleep less than any other primate that has been studied. Using phylogenetic prediction methods that control for body mass, brain size, diet, predation risk, and foraging needs, David Samson and Charles Nunn found that humans ought to sleep about 9.55 hours per day based on our biological characteristics. Instead, we average about 7 hours — the lowest total sleep time recorded among 30 primate species [Nunn & Samson, 2018, *American Journal of Physical Anthropology*](https://doi.org/10.1002/ajpa.23444).

But we are not simply sleeping less. We are sleeping differently. Humans pack a higher proportion of REM sleep into their shorter nights than any other primate. Our REM-to-NREM ratio is about 22:78, compared to 5 to 10 percent REM in many other primates. We achieved this not by increasing REM duration, but by dramatically reducing NREM — especially the lighter stages of sleep. We evolved, in other words, to sleep less but deeper [Samson & Nunn, 2015, *Evolutionary Anthropology*](https://doi.org/10.1002/evan.21464).

Why? The leading hypothesis, which Samson calls the "social sleep hypothesis," proposes that when our early ancestors descended from the trees to sleep on the ground, they faced new threats from predators and hostile conspecifics. The costs of sleep — the time spent vulnerable and unproductive — rose sharply. At the same time, the benefits of wakefulness — learning, social bonding, toolmaking, cultural transmission — became more valuable than ever. The solution was not to eliminate sleep, which remains mandatory, but to compress it: to obtain the same essential rest in less time, by sleeping more intensely [Samson, 2021, *Annual Review of Anthropology*](https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev-anthro-010220-075523).

The hunter-gatherer populations studied by Samson and his colleagues — the Hadza of Tanzania, the San of Namibia, the Tsimane of Bolivia — sleep 5.7 to 7.1 hours per night. They do not use electric light. They do not set alarms. And yet they sleep less than people in industrial societies, not more. The human sleep pattern is not a modern artifact of smartphones and blue light. It is an ancient adaptation — the signature of a species that traded sleep time for social time, and apparently came out ahead on the deal [Yetish et al., 2015, *Current Biology*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2015.09.046).

## The Ancient Constant

If down-to-earth hominins and soaring frigatebirds and deep-sea octopuses all sleep — if even the brainless jellyfish, pulsing on its ancient seafloor, shows a sleep-like state — then when did sleep begin?

The evidence from *Cassiopea* pushes the origin of sleep back to at least the emergence of neurons, more than 600 million years ago. Cnidarians, the phylum that includes jellyfish, were among the first animals to evolve tissue-level organization and differentiated cell types including neurons. Their nerve nets are diffuse and decentralized, lacking a brain of any kind. Yet they show all the behavioral criteria of sleep: a quiescent state, reduced responsiveness to stimuli, and homeostatic regulation — the "sleep rebound" that follows deprivation [Nath et al., 2017, *Current Biology*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2017.08.014).

The fact that melatonin — the same hormone that promotes sleep in humans — also induces quiescence in *Cassiopea* suggests that the molecular machinery of sleep is even more ancient than the behavioral state itself. The Caltech researchers who made the discovery tested several sleep-promoting compounds on the jellyfish. All of them worked [Caltech News, 2017](https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/surprising-ancient-behavior-jellyfish-79701).

This has led some researchers to propose that sleep's original function was metabolic, not cognitive. The earliest neurons may have needed periods of reduced activity to clear metabolic waste, manage oxidative stress, or conserve energy. Once that cellular function was established, it became a platform on which later evolutionary elaborations — memory consolidation, synaptic pruning, dreaming — could be built [Anafi et al., 2019, *Nature Reviews Neuroscience*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41583-018-0098-9).

Under this view, the difference between a jellyfish's night of quiet pulsing and a human's vivid, narrative dream is a difference of degree, not of kind. The same fundamental process — a cellular housekeeping function that no nervous system can do without — has been co-opted and elaborated by evolution into the rich internal theater we experience each night.

## The Puzzle Remains

After decades of research and hundreds of studies, sleep science has arrived at a remarkable conclusion: we still do not know, with any certainty, why we sleep. The leading hypotheses are not mutually exclusive, and none explains all the data. Sleep conserves energy, but some animals that need energy conservation most sleep the least. Sleep consolidates memory, but animals with extraordinary cognitive abilities — birds, dolphins — get by on astonishingly little REM sleep. Sleep clears waste from the brain, but we do not know if this is its primary function or a secondary benefit.

What the comparative evidence makes clear is that sleep is not a single thing serving a single purpose. It is a bundle of functions — metabolic, cognitive, thermoregulatory, restorative — woven together over hundreds of millions of years of evolution. Different species, facing different ecological pressures, have emphasized different aspects of the bundle. The platypus dreams for eight hours. The dolphin may not dream at all. The frigatebird catches micro-naps while circling in rising air currents at three thousand meters. The jellyfish slows its pulse on the reef at night.

All of them are solving the same problem in their own way: the necessity of sleep is absolute, but the form it takes is endlessly adaptable. We still do not know what the necessity is — only that no animal that has ever lived has found a way around it.

---

*— Source note —*

*This article draws primarily on peer-reviewed primary research. Key sources include the Phylogeny of Sleep Database (McNamara et al., 2008); Siegel's comparative sleep reviews in Nature (2005) and the UCLA Sleep Research Center; the Capellini et al. phylogenetic analysis in PNAS (2008); Samson and Nunn's primate sleep studies (2015, 2018); the Wilson and Lee rat replay studies in Neuron (2001, 2002); the Giri et al. sleep deprivation and replay study in Nature (2024); the Medeiros et al. octopus sleep studies in iScience (2021) and Nature (2023); the Rattenborg et al. frigatebird flight sleep study in Nature Communications (2016); the Nath et al. jellyfish sleep study in Current Biology (2017); and the AASM normative human sleep guidelines.*

post.content:
# The Unknown Continent: What Lies Beneath the World's Oceans

*The ocean covers 70 percent of the planet's surface and contains 90 percent of its living space. Its average depth is 12,080 feet. We have visually explored less than 0.001 percent of it. The deep ocean is not merely a feature of our planet. It is our planet, and we have treated it like a stranger at our own table.*

---

It begins with a descent into darkness.

At 200 meters, sunlight surrenders. The blue fades to indigo, then to a black so absolute that the human eye cannot distinguish up from down. At 1,000 meters — the bathypelagic zone — the pressure reaches 100 atmospheres. At 4,000 meters, the abyssal plain stretches across 70 percent of the ocean floor: a landscape of sediment and silence, interrupted only by seamounts the size of the Alps and trenches deeper than Everest is tall. At 6,000 meters, the hadal zone begins — a region of crushing pressure, perpetual cold, and life that has evolved to treat eight tons per square inch as routine.

The descent takes about two and a half hours in a submersible. It is a journey from the familiar to the alien, from the mapped to the imagined, from the world we know to the one we have only begun to suspect exists.

And the unsettling truth is this: we have better maps of the surface of Mars than we do of the ocean floor. Humanity has always found the distant more compelling than the immediate. Mars is a far more romantic subject than mud.

---

## I. The Atlas of Ignorance

As of April 2026, exactly 28.7 percent of the global seafloor has been mapped to modern high-resolution standards — an area of approximately 104 million square kilometers, roughly two-thirds of Earth's land surface [Seabed 2030, April 2026](https://seabed2030.org/2026/04/20/global-seabed-mapping-reaches-new-milestone-as-five-million-square-kilometres-added-in-a-year/). This represents a considerable acceleration: in 2017, when the Nippon Foundation-GEBCO Seabed 2030 Project launched, only about 6 percent of the seafloor had been mapped at comparable resolution. To put it another way: in less than a decade, we have nearly quintupled our knowledge of the shape of our own planet's floor — and it is still less than a third.

The remaining 71.3 percent — roughly 260 million square kilometers — exists on maps derived from satellite altimetry, a technique that infers seafloor topography from subtle variations in the height of the ocean surface. These maps reveal the broad outlines of the seabed: the mid-ocean ridges, the major fracture zones, the largest trenches. But they miss almost everything smaller than a few kilometers. Seamounts a thousand meters tall go undetected. Submarine canyons vanish into the noise. Shipwrecks, hydrothermal vent fields, and the fine-scale habitat structure that determines where life can survive — none of it appears [NOAA Ocean Exploration](https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/ocean-fact/explored/). It is the cartographic equivalent of knowing a person's silhouette and nothing else.

The Seabed 2030 Project — a collaboration between The Nippon Foundation and GEBCO, itself a joint program of the IHO and the UNESCO Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission — intends to close this gap by the end of the decade. In the 2025–2026 reporting year alone, nearly five million square kilometers of new bathymetric data were added to the GEBCO grid — an area roughly the size of the European Union. Two hundred twenty organizations from 37 countries contributed data, including first-time submissions from Malaysia, Morocco, Papua New Guinea, and Saudi Arabia [IOC-UNESCO, April 2026](https://www.ioc.unesco.org/en/articles/seabed-mapping-global-public-good).

The pace has been remarkable, as these things go. Global mapping coverage grew from 6 percent in 2017 to 26.1 percent in 2024, 27.3 percent in 2025, and 28.7 percent in 2026 — an average of roughly 3.2 percent of total seafloor area added per year [Frontiers in Marine Science, 2025](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fmars.2025.1543885/full). At this rate, the entire seafloor could be mapped by approximately 2047 — well beyond the Seabed 2030 target, but still a revolution in human knowledge, assuming one does not dwell on the irony that "revolution" here means finally discovering the shape of one's own home.

Yet even a complete map is not exploration. A map tells you where things are, not what they are.

![Global seafloor mapping progress, 2017–2026: from 6% to 28.7%](/api/blog/images/ocean_mapping_progress.png)

"Explorers have seen less than 0.001 percent of the deep ocean seafloor," NOAA notes — roughly the area of Rhode Island [NOAA Ocean Exploration](https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/ocean-fact/explored/). The vast majority of what lies beneath the ocean surface has never been observed by any human eye, instrument, or remotely operated vehicle. We inhabit a planet whose primary geographical feature — the deep seabed — is almost entirely unvisited. A stranger living in your house would know more about your attic.

---

## II. The Architecture of the Abyss

The deep ocean floor is not a featureless plain. It is a landscape of extreme topography, shaped by tectonic forces that operate on scales both vast and minute.

The mid-ocean ridge system is the most extensive chain of mountains on Earth, stretching nearly 65,000 kilometers — long enough to wrap around the planet one and a half times. More than 90 percent of it lies underwater, rising from the abyssal plain to an average depth of 2,500 meters below the surface. Along the divergent plate boundaries that form the ridge system, new oceanic crust is created continuously as magma rises from the mantle. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreads at 2 to 5 centimeters per year — slow enough to produce a steep, rugged rift valley the depth and width of the Grand Canyon. The East Pacific Rise spreads at 6 to 16 centimeters per year, producing a smooth volcanic summit without a rift valley at all [NOAA Ocean Exploration](https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/ocean-fact/mid-ocean-ridge).

![The vertical structure of the ocean: depth zones, features, and the deepest points of each ocean basin](/api/blog/images/ocean_depth_zones.png)

Rising from the seafloor are seamounts — underwater volcanoes that never reached the surface. Data from satellite altimetry and ship-based sonar suggests the number of seamounts at least 1,000 meters tall exceeds 100,000. Despite their abundance, fewer than one-tenth of a percent have been explored [NOAA Ocean Exploration](https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/education/seamounts/). Each seamount is a potential island of biodiversity: currents flow around them, concentrating nutrients and creating habitats for corals, sponges, and fish that may exist nowhere else. On a single expedition in January 2024, Schmidt Ocean Institute discovered four previously unknown seamounts in international waters off Central America, the tallest rising 2,681 meters from the seafloor — higher than any mountain in the eastern United States [Schmidt Ocean Institute, February 2024](https://schmidtocean.org/four-new-seamounts-discovered-in-the-high-seas/). Four mountains, hidden in plain sight, on a planet we have the audacity to call explored.

The ocean's trenches are the reverse image of its mountains: long, narrow canyons where one tectonic plate plunges beneath another, reaching depths that invert the scale of terrestrial elevation. The Mariana Trench's Challenger Deep, at approximately 10,935 meters below sea level, is the deepest point on Earth — deeper than Mount Everest is tall [NOAA Ocean Exploration](https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/ocean-fact/ocean-depth/). Only a handful of people have ever visited it. The first descent was made in 1960 by Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh in the bathyscaphe *Trieste*. No one returned until James Cameron's solo dive in 2012. The Five Deeps Expedition, led by explorer Victor Vescovo in the submersible *Limiting Factor*, conducted the first systematic survey of all five of the world's ocean deepest points between 2018 and 2019, discovering at least 40 new species and 30 previously unmapped underwater features in the process [Five Deeps Expedition](https://fivedeeps.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/FDE-Challenger-Release-FINAL-5132019.pdf); [Smithsonian Magazine, September 2019](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/american-becomes-first-to-visit-five-deepest-spots-worlds-oceans-180973094/). The deepest places on Earth have been visited fewer times than the surface of the Moon.

---

## III. The Life That Should Not Exist

The hadal zone — the region of ocean trenches from 6,000 to 11,000 meters — was once considered virtually sterile. The pressure exceeds 1,000 atmospheres. No sunlight penetrates. Temperatures hover just above freezing. Nutrients are scarce. It was assumed that very little could survive.

That assumption has been demolished.

In 2025, the Mariana Trench Environment and Ecology Research (MEER) project published a trio of papers in *Cell* that revealed an ecosystem of staggering complexity. Metagenomic sequencing of 1,194 sediment samples generated a 92-terabase-pair dataset — the largest of its kind — and identified 7,564 microbial species, 89.4 percent of which had never been reported. The study found that environmental selection, not random drift, drives microbial community assembly in these extreme depths, and that hadal microbes operate under evolutionary pressures distinct from those in shallower waters [Cell, 2025](https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(24)01436-3); [Science, March 2025](https://www.science.org/content/article/oceans-deepest-trenches-are-home-incredible-diversity).

That same year, researchers aboard the Chinese manned submersible *Fendouzhe* discovered flourishing chemosynthetic communities at 9,533 meters in the Kuril-Kamchatka Trench — the deepest and most extensive chemosynthesis-based ecosystems known on Earth. Fields of tubeworms up to 30 centimeters long, bivalves, and other invertebrates stretched across a 2,500-kilometer zone along the trench floor, sustained by methane produced by microbes rather than by sunlight [Nature, July 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09317-z); [Phys.org, July 2025](https://phys.org/news/2025-07-deepest-animal-communities-km-sea.html). They do not need the sun. They never did.

A 2026 study published in *Science* described a previously unknown hard-substrate fauna at depths from 9,000 to 10,898 meters in the Kermadec and Mariana trenches. The researchers identified 32 species across six phyla — most of them new to science — dominated by heterotrophic foraminifera that feed on terrestrial pine pollen that has fallen to the deepest ocean floor. The study concluded that similar protistan-dominated communities likely thrive in hadal regions across Oceania, representing unrecognized carbon hotspots in the deepest parts of the global ocean [Science, May 2026](https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.aea7086). Life in the most remote places on Earth, sustained by pine pollen carried from continents above. The planet is more connected than we ever imagined, and it has nothing to do with us.

Nor is life confined to the trenches. In January 2025, an iceberg the size of Chicago — designated A-84 — calved from the George VI Ice Shelf in Antarctica, exposing 510 square kilometers of seafloor that had been covered by 150-meter-thick ice for centuries. Within days, a Schmidt Ocean Institute expedition deployed the remotely operated vehicle *SuBastian* and found flourishing ecosystems at depths up to 1,300 meters: large corals, sponges, icefish, giant sea spiders, and octopus. "The science team was originally in this remote region to study the seafloor and ecosystem at the interface between ice and sea," said Dr. Jyotika Virmani, Schmidt Ocean Institute's Executive Director. "Being right there when this iceberg calved from the ice shelf presented a rare scientific opportunity" [Schmidt Ocean Institute, March 2025](https://schmidtocean.org/thriving-antarctic-ecosystems-found-in-wake-of-recently-detached-iceberg/). The ice retreated, and life was already there — as though it had been waiting.

---

## IV. A Census of the Unseen

The scale of marine biodiversity — and our ignorance of it — is one of the great scientific stories of our time. It is also a rather good comedy of manners, if one has the detachment to see it that way.

The Census of Marine Life, completed in 2010 after a decade of international collaboration, documented approximately 250,000 known marine species (excluding microbes). But the Census estimated that the true total could exceed one million — meaning roughly 75 percent of marine species have yet to be formally described [Census of Marine Life](http://www.coml.org/media-resources/frequently-asked-questions-faq.html). We have lived on this planet for the entirety of human history and have named barely a quarter of its co-inhabitants.

The Ocean Census, launched in 2023 by The Nippon Foundation and Nekton, aims to accelerate this process dramatically. In its Year 2 Impact Report (April 2024 — March 2025), the program documented over 900 new species — increasing the global annual marine discovery rate by 38 percent [Ocean Census Year 2 Impact Report](https://oceancensus.org/ocean-census-year-2-impact-report/). By Year 3, the pace had accelerated further: 1,121 new species in a single year, a 54 percent increase over the baseline discovery rate [Discover Magazine, May 2026](https://www.discovermagazine.com/ocean-census-uncovers-1-121-new-marine-species-from-sea-caves-to-deep-trenches-49127).

These discoveries span the full range of ocean depths. A newly identified chimaera — a "ghost shark" that split from sharks and rays nearly 400 million years ago — was found in Australia's Coral Sea Marine Park. A carnivorous sponge nicknamed the "death ball," covered in microscopic hook-like structures that trap crustaceans, was discovered at 3,600 meters near the South Sandwich Islands. A bristle worm living inside the translucent silica skeleton of a glass sponge was found near volcanic seamounts off Japan at 800 meters. Even shallow Mediterranean sea caves off Marseille yielded an orange-striped shrimp new to science [Ocean Census, 2026](https://oceancensus.org/our-top-12-highlights-from-the-ocean-census-in-2025/). Every place we look closely enough, we find something that has never been seen.

The Schmidt Ocean Institute, operating the research vessel *Falkor (too)*, has been one of the most prolific contributors to this wave of discovery. Three expeditions to the Nazca and Salas y Gómez Ridges in 2024 documented over 150 previously unknown species, bringing the known species count in this portion of the Pacific from approximately 1,000 to over 1,300. The expeditions also captured the first-ever footage of a live *Promachoteuthis* squid — a genus so elusive that most known specimens were collected in the late 1800s — and documented a Casper octopus in the Southern Pacific for the first time [Schmidt Ocean Institute, August 2024](https://schmidtocean.org/expeditions-chapter_8-2024/); [Ocean Decade, August 2024](https://oceandecade.org/news/20-suspected-new-marine-species-arise-from-sois-nazca-ridge-expedition).

Off Argentina, a 2026 expedition along the entire continental shelf documented the largest-known *Bathelia candida* coral reef — covering at least 0.4 square kilometers, nearly the size of Vatican City — along with 28 suspected new species and the first deep-water whale fall observed in Argentine waters [Schmidt Ocean Institute, February 2026](https://schmidtocean.org/argentinas-deep-sea-is-more-biodiverse-than-scientists-thought/). Off Uruguay, an expedition discovered thriving cold-water coral reefs built by *Desmophyllum pertusum*, a species recently listed as vulnerable to extinction, along with at least 30 potential new species [Schmidt Ocean Institute, September 2025](https://schmidtocean.org/vibrant-coral-reefs-discovered-in-historic-exploration-of-uruguays-deep-sea/).

These are not isolated findings. They are the first systematic glimpses of ecosystems that cover 70 percent of the planet. The Ocean Census now involves more than 1,000 scientists across 400 institutions. The Ocean Biodiversity Information System (OBIS) — the global repository for marine species observations — has surpassed 177 million occurrence records for 204,000 species, drawn from 7,201 datasets [OBIS](https://obis.org/). The database grows by millions of records each year, contributed by scientists in 99 countries.

And still the estimate holds: roughly 90 percent of marine species remain unknown.

![Marine species discovery acceleration: 1,121 new species in a single year, but 90% remain undiscovered](/api/blog/images/ocean_species_discovery.png)

---

## V. The Vessels That Take Us There

The tools for exploring this hidden world are as remarkable as the world itself — which is fortunate, because the world itself is remarkably unforgiving.

The human-occupied submersible *Alvin*, operated by the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, has been the workhorse of American deep-sea research for six decades. As of December 31, 2025, *Alvin* had completed 5,340 dives, totaling more than 11 million meters of vertical descent — equivalent to descending from sea level to the bottom of the ocean and back more than 500 times. Over its 60-year career, the submersible has carried 16,020 people to the seafloor, supported the publication of thousands of peer-reviewed studies, and spent a cumulative 37,290 hours submerged [WHOI Alvin Dive Statistics](https://www.whoi.edu/what-we-do/explore/underwater-vehicles/hov-alvin/dive-statistics/).

The submersible has been upgraded repeatedly. Its most recent overhaul, completed in 2022, extended its depth range from 4,500 to 6,500 meters — putting 99 percent of the ocean floor within reach. The new titanium personnel sphere, improved imaging systems, and enhanced manipulator arms represent more than a decade of engineering. "Alvin's recent upgrade opens new possibilities for deep-sea research," wrote the science verification team, noting that the sub can now access the abyssal and upper hadal zones — some of the least-understood regions on Earth [Phys.org, February 2025](https://phys.org/news/2025-02-alvin-ocean-depths.pdf); [WHOI, Alvin 60](https://www.whoi.edu/alvin60).

In the Pacific, the Chinese manned submersible *Fendouzhe* — "Striver" — has pushed even deeper. Capable of reaching the deepest parts of the ocean at nearly 11,000 meters, *Fendouzhe* conducted 33 dives in the Mariana Trench and neighboring regions between August and November 2021, collecting 1,648 sediment samples and generating the most comprehensive hadal ecological dataset ever assembled. The submersible's 2024 dives in the Kuril-Kamchatka and Aleutian trenches revealed the deepest chemosynthetic communities ever documented, at depths exceeding 9,500 meters [Cell, 2025](https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(24)01436-3); [Nature, July 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09317-z).

Meanwhile, a new generation of autonomous and remotely operated vehicles is expanding the reach of ocean exploration. The Schmidt Ocean Institute's *ROV SuBastian*, deployed from the research vessel *Falkor (too)*, can operate at depths of 4,500 meters and has conducted hundreds of dives across the Pacific, Atlantic, and Southern oceans, streaming live video to shore-based scientists and the public. NOAA's *Okeanos Explorer* has mapped hundreds of thousands of square kilometers of seafloor, discovering deep-sea coral habitats and hydrothermal vent fields. Environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling, integrated into regular operations aboard *Okeanos Explorer* in 2021, has opened a new window into deep-sea biodiversity by detecting genetic traces of organisms that conventional sampling methods miss entirely [NOAA Ocean Exploration, May 2026](https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/news/from-seawater-to-sequences-exploring-noaas-new-deep-sea-environmental-dna-dataset/). The water itself gives away its secrets.

At the deepest extremes, NASA and WHOI have developed the Orpheus autonomous underwater vehicles — small, pressure-tolerant robots designed to explore the hadal zone in swarms, capable of navigating the narrow, rocky terrain of ocean trenches autonomously [WHOI Hadal Zone](https://www.whoi.edu/ocean-learning-hub/ocean-topics/how-the-ocean-works/ocean-zones/hadal-zone/).

---

## VI. The Lure of the Seabed

The deep ocean is not only a site of scientific discovery. It is also a repository of mineral wealth — and a new frontier for geopolitical competition. One might almost call it a gold rush, if gold rushes were conducted through intergovernmental organizations with 170 member states.

Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the international seabed beyond national jurisdiction — known as "the Area" — belongs to no single country or corporation. It is managed by the International Seabed Authority (ISA), an autonomous intergovernmental organization established in 1994, with 170 member states, charged with regulating mineral-related activities "for the benefit of all humankind" [ISA, 2024 Annual Report](https://isa.org.jm/secretary-general-annual-report-2024/). One admires the idealism, while noting that "all humankind" has never been a phrase that survived first contact with valuable resources.

The resources in question are extraordinary. Polymetallic nodules — potato-sized concretions rich in manganese, nickel, cobalt, and copper — cover vast areas of the abyssal plain, particularly in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone (CCZ) of the central Pacific. The ISA has estimated that some 5.4 billion tons of metal-bearing nodules exist in reserved areas alone, though data quality varies significantly across the survey regions [ISA Policy Brief, July 2024](https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/Policy_brief_Current_status_of_reserved_areas_with_ISA.pdf). Cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts coat the slopes of seamounts in the western Pacific. Polymetallic sulfides — deposits rich in copper, zinc, gold, and silver — form around hydrothermal vents along mid-ocean ridges.

As of 2024, the ISA has issued 30 exploration contracts to 21 contractors, covering polymetallic nodules (19 contracts), polymetallic sulfides (8 contracts), and cobalt-rich crusts (5 contracts). Contractors include national agencies from China, India, Russia, South Korea, France, Germany, Japan, and Poland, as well as private companies and entities from developing states and small island nations including Nauru, Tonga, Kiribati, Cook Islands, and Jamaica [ISA Exploration Contracts](https://isa.org.jm/exploration-contracts/). These contracts grant exclusive exploration rights for 15-year periods, during which contractors are required to collect environmental baseline data, train personnel from developing states, and relinquish portions of their exploration areas at periodic intervals.

The tension between mineral extraction and environmental protection has intensified as scientific understanding of deep-sea ecosystems has grown. The 2025 discovery that chemosynthetic communities thrive across a 2,500-kilometer swath of the northwestern Pacific trench system — far more widespread than previously recognized — raises urgent questions about the potential impact of mining on ecosystems that may prove to be both fragile and extensive [Nature, 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09317-z). Contractors have invested an estimated $414 million in environmental baseline studies as of 2024, and the ISA is developing regional environmental management plans for the CCZ, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, and the Indian Ocean [ISA Environmental Baseline Policy Brief](https://isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/ISA-Environmental-Baseline-Policy-Brief-SSKI_2025.pdf). The irony is almost too neat: we are discovering what we would destroy in the same motion.

In June 2025, the ISA launched the Deep-Sea Biobank Initiative (DBI) on the margins of the UN Ocean Conference in Nice, establishing a global repository of biological samples and genetic data from the international seabed area, designed to promote equitable access to deep-sea research, particularly for developing states [UN Geneva, July 2025](https://www.ungeneva.org/en/news-media/news/2025/07/108752/deep-dive-international-seabed-authority-why-it-matters-now).

---

## VII. What Remains

After two and a half centuries of systematic exploration — from the *HMS Challenger* expedition of 1872–1876, which first discovered polymetallic nodules in the Pacific, to the 2025 discoveries of thriving ecosystems beneath Antarctic ice shelves — the deep ocean remains, by any honest measure, largely unknown.

The ocean's average depth is 3,682 meters, yet our knowledge of what lives below 200 meters is fragmentary. The global ocean has a total volume of approximately 1.332 billion cubic kilometers [NOAA NCEI World Ocean Volumes](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/sites/g/files/anmtlf171/files/2023-01/World%20Ocean%20Volumes.pdf). The volume that has been biologically sampled — with nets, cores, ROVs, or submersibles — is minuscule. The fraction that has been visually observed is infinitesimal. We are like a person who, having glanced at a single page of a library, declares himself well-read.

"We have only assessed under 30 percent of the samples collected from this expedition," said Dr. Michelle Taylor, head of science at Ocean Census, after a single expedition to the South Sandwich Islands that yielded 30 new species, speaking of the backlog that every deep-sea biologist knows: the rate of sample collection far exceeds the rate of analysis [ABC News, October 2025](https://abcnews.com/International/dozens-new-species-including-carnivorous-death-ball-sponge/story?id=126986681). The average time between collecting a specimen and formally describing it in the scientific literature is 13.5 years. There are an estimated 175,000 undocumented new species sitting in museum collections and institutional sample banks — already collected, already preserved, already known to exist, and waiting. The discoveries have already been made. They are simply waiting to be noticed.

"The deep sea may have served as an 'ecological refuge' during environmental changes caused by dramatic temperature and oxygen fluctuations," the MEER project researchers noted — a suggestion that the hadal zone has functioned as a sanctuary for life during past mass extinctions [Science, March 2025](https://www.science.org/content/article/oceans-deepest-trenches-are-home-incredible-diversity). If that is true, then the deep ocean is not merely a place of discovery. It is a library of survival — a record of how life persists through planetary crisis.

And we have read almost none of it.

---

The descent ends, eventually, with an ascent.

The submersible releases its ballast weights and begins to rise. The pressure decreases. The black fades to indigo, then to blue, then to the dazzling white of sunlight on the surface. The hatch opens. The crew blinks in the light. The voyage that took two and a half hours to descend lasted perhaps ten hours on the bottom, but it will take years — or a lifetime — to interpret everything they saw.

There are more seamounts on Earth than there are people who have visited them. There are more undiscovered species in the ocean than discovered ones. We have mapped less than a third of the seafloor, and seen less than a thousandth of it. The planet has a hidden continent, and we are still learning where its boundaries lie. The greatest age of discovery is not behind us. It is beneath us.

---

*Source notes: This article draws on primary sources from the Nippon Foundation-GEBCO Seabed 2030 Project, NOAA Ocean Exploration, the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, the Schmidt Ocean Institute, the International Seabed Authority, the Ocean Census, the Census of Marine Life, the Ocean Biodiversity Information System (OBIS), and the peer-reviewed journals Nature, Science, and Cell. All citations are to original institutional reports, datasets, and journal articles, not secondary news coverage.*

# The $21.5 Billion Trinket

## How souvenir shops became the stealth economic engine of small-town America

The smell arrives before the decision to enter. Paraffin wax from a rack of cinnamon-scented candles. Old paper. The faint metallic tang of cast-iron key chains stamped with the name of a town you would not have known existed had the highway not insisted. In the back, a wire basket holds polished stones labeled with single words — "Breathe," "Hope," "Wander" — beside a spinning carousel of postcards showing the same covered bridge at four different times of year, none of which look entirely real. The register crouches near the door, surrounded by bins of maple candy, miniature snow globes, and refrigerator magnets shaped like the state.

This is the American trinket shop. It inhabits the storefronts that pharmacies abandoned, the spaces between the coffee roaster and the real estate office, the ground floors of nineteenth-century brick buildings with pressed-tin ceilings and windows that bow outward onto sidewalks lined with painted benches. There are roughly 22,000 of these establishments across the United States, carrying the formal government classification NAICS 453220: Gift, Novelty, and Souvenir Stores. [U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, via FRED, IPUHN453220T300000000](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IPUHN453220T300000000)

In 2024, they generated $21.55 billion in sectoral output — the current-dollar value of everything they sold, adjusted for the usual inventory arithmetic. [U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, FRED, 2024](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IPUHN453220T300000000) That figure is a 54% increase from the pandemic trough of $14.01 billion in 2020 and a 10% rise from the $19.58 billion recorded in 2021, when the country was still blinking its way out of lockdown. [FRED, IPUHN453220T300000000](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IPUHN453220T300000000) In real terms — after removing the polite fiction that inflation is not happening — output rose 7% in 2024 alone. [U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Real Sectoral Output, IPUHN453220T011000000](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IPUHN453220T011000000)

These numbers are striking not because they are enormous — the total U.S. retail sector is measured in trillions, and a billion is a rounding error when viewed from sufficient height — but because they describe an industry that the prevailing narratives of American commerce have spent thirty years pronouncing dead.

![Twenty-one billion dollars' worth of things no one needed — bought by everyone who passed through.](/api/blog/images/trinket_sectoral_output.png)

## A half-century of contraction — and a stubborn persistence

To understand the trinket shop's present, one must first measure the scale of what was lost. The Bureau of Labor Statistics has tracked employment in gift, novelty, and souvenir stores since January 1990. The all-time high arrived in December 2000, when the industry employed 294,900 people across the country. [U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Employment Statistics, via CEIC; all-time max Dec 2000](https://www.ceicdata.com/en/united-states/current-employment-statistics-employment-non-farm-payroll/employment-nf-rt-gm-sh-os-gift-novelty--souvenir) By February 2026, that number had fallen to 119,800 — a decline of roughly 59%, as though two out of every three souvenir sellers had simply vanished into the landscape they once sold as a postcard. [BLS CES, Feb 2026, via CEIC](https://www.ceicdata.com/en/united-states/current-employment-statistics-employment-non-farm-payroll/employment-nf-rt-gm-sh-os-gift-novelty--souvenir) The Bureau's Industry Productivity program tells a story only marginally less stark: 145,200 jobs in 2024, down from 147,500 in 2022 and 146,500 in 2023, with the employment index (2017 = 100) sitting at 86.9 — meaning the industry employs roughly 13% fewer people than it did eight years ago, a steady erosion that continued even while the rest of the economy pretended nothing was amiss. [BLS via FRED, IPUHN453220W200000000](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IPUHN453220W200000000); [BLS via FRED, IPUHN453220W010000000](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IPUHN453220W010000000)

![The souvenir workforce, 1990–2026: a long staircase that stopped descending just before it reached the ground.](/api/blog/images/trinket_employment.png)

A 2016 BLS retrospective on gift-related retailers covering 2001–2014 documented a 38% decline in the number of gift, novelty, and souvenir establishments and a 37% decline in employment over that period alone. The only retail category that grew? Electronic shopping — up 373% in establishments and 226% in employment. [U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, "Sweets for the sweet," The Economics Daily, 2016](https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2016/sweets-for-the-sweet-establishments-and-employment-of-gift-retailers.htm)

The forces behind the contraction are well understood. The rise of big-box retailers like Walmart — the subject of a landmark 25-year Iowa State University study tracking the retailer's impact on small-town retail — drew shoppers away from Main Street with the promise of lower prices and wider aisles. [Iowa State University, "Revisiting Wal-Mart's Impact on Iowa Small Town Retail: Twenty-Five Years Later"](https://dr.lib.iastate.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/0066e3be-2fad-4298-939a-bbbc499b1d4a/content) Then came e-commerce, offering infinite shelf space and overnight delivery, quietly rendering obsolete the very act of browsing. The five-and-dime, the trinket shop's direct ancestor, largely collapsed: F. W. Woolworth closed its last U.S. stores in 1997, having spent 118 years teaching Americans how to buy small things, only to be out-taught by better technology. [Encyclopedia of American Studies, Johns Hopkins University Press](https://eas-ref.press.jhu.edu/view?aid=154)

But the graph does not descend to zero. The line flattened, then lifted. In 2024, real sectoral output grew 7%. [BLS via FRED, IPUHN453220T011000000](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IPUHN453220T011000000) Employment stabilized in the 145,000 range after the pandemic crash — it was 126,700 in 2021 and was trending upward through 2022 and 2023. [BLS via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IPUHN453220W200000000) Something kept the lights on. And that something, as it turns out, was feeling.

## The five-and-dime's long shadow

The trinket shop is no recent invention. Its lineage runs through the general stores that provisioned frontier America, the "racket stores" of the late nineteenth century — so named for the clanging of pots and pans on peddler carts — and most directly through the five-and-dime empire of Frank Winfield Woolworth. [Library of Congress, "Woolworth's Five and Dime," This Month in Business History](https://guides.loc.gov/this-month-in-business-history/february/woolsworth?loclr=blogadm); [Kansas Historical Society, "Duckwall's: A Kansas Five and Dime Story," 2004](https://khri.kansasgis.org/photos_docs/185-37_11.pdf)

Woolworth opened his first five-cent store in Utica, New York, in 1879. It failed. He opened a second in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, this time adding ten-cent items. It succeeded — proving that the difference between failure and fortune is sometimes merely five cents. By 1912, his company had grown to 596 stores across 37 states. [Library of Congress, Woolworth guide](https://guides.loc.gov/this-month-in-business-history/february/woolsworth) When he died in 1919, the chain had 1,081 stores and annual sales of $119 million. At its peak, Woolworth operated roughly 3,000 stores worldwide. [Encyclopedia of American Studies](https://eas-ref.press.jhu.edu/view?aid=154) Frank Woolworth had built his business on a maxim recorded by his biographers: "Small profits on an article will become big if you sell enough of that article." [U.S. Women's Bureau Bulletin No. 76, "Women in 5- and 10-Cent Stores," 1929, via FRASER/St. Louis Fed](https://fraser.stlouisfed.org/title/women-5--10-cent-stores-limited-price-chain-department-stores-5384/fulltext) He understood, decades before the age of mass retail, that the accumulation of tiny transactions is the quietest path to wealth.

The five-and-dime was never merely a store. It was a civic institution — the place where Americans bought their first goldfish, their Christmas ornaments, their spools of thread, their bottles of Evening in Paris perfume. It was also where they sat at the lunch counter: a counter that, in Greensboro, North Carolina, in February 1960, became the stage for a sit-in that reshaped the nation, proving that even the most ordinary places can hold extraordinary significance when history decides to make use of them. [Library of Congress, Carol M. Highsmith photograph, LC-DIG-highsm-43826](https://www.loc.gov/item/2017880730/)

When the Woolworth chain finally dissolved, the storefronts it left behind did not remain vacant for long. Independent operators moved in. The model persisted — not as a national chain, but as a local one, or none at all. The Vermont Department of Labor's ELMI Business Finder, drawing on Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages data, lists 126 active gift, novelty, and souvenir employers in the state as of 2026, the vast majority with 1–4 or 5–9 employees. [Vermont DOL, ELMI Business Finder, NAICS 459420](https://www.vtlmi.info/employer.cfm?cty=000&lvl=6&naics=459420&sort=listaddr&start=1&stfips=50) In Woodstock, Vermont — population 3,000 — a single block of Central Street contains Danforth Pewter, Fossilglass, Primrose Garden, R T Home, and the Unicorn. None employ more than nine people. It is a revolution conducted at the scale of a front porch.

## The nostalgia mechanism

Why does a rational consumer — equipped with a smartphone, an Amazon Prime account, and the entire apparatus of modern comparison shopping — walk into a small store and cheerfully pay $12 for a refrigerator magnet she could have ordered online for $4?

The answer, according to a landmark study published in the *Journal of Consumer Research* in 2014, lies in the emotional architecture of nostalgia. The researchers — Jannine D. Lasaleta, Constantine Sedikides, and Kathleen D. Vohs — conducted six experiments demonstrating that feeling nostalgic weakens a person's desire for money. [Lasaleta, Sedikides, & Vohs, "Nostalgia Weakens the Desire for Money," *Journal of Consumer Research*, Vol. 41, No. 3, October 2014, pp. 713–729](https://doi.org/10.1086/677227)

The mechanism, they found, is social connectedness. When participants were primed to feel nostalgic — by writing about a meaningful memory or viewing a nostalgic advertisement — they subsequently valued money less, were willing to pay more for products, parted with more in charitable giving, and drew smaller coins from memory. The nostalgic state made them feel socially connected, and that feeling quietly eroded the psychological importance of money. [Lasaleta et al., JCR, 2014](https://doi.org/10.1086/677227)

"Nostalgia may be so commonly used in marketing because it encourages consumers to part with their money," the authors wrote. A press release from the University of Chicago, where one author was based, put the finding with admirable bluntness: "We're more likely to spend money when we're feeling nostalgic." [University of Chicago, "The nostalgia effect," via Phys.org, July 22, 2014](https://phys.org/news/2014-07-nostalgia-effect-consumers.html)

The trinket shop is a physical engine for this psychological effect. Every element of the experience — the wooden floorboards, the handwritten price tags, the vintage signage, the scent of cinnamon and old paper — is a nostalgia trigger. The products themselves are physical anchors for memory: a postcard of a place you visited, a magnet shaped like a state you drove through, a polished stone stamped with a word that meant something to you on that trip. The shop does not merely sell souvenirs. It sells the permission to believe, however briefly, that the past is not entirely behind you.

A 2021 study published in the *Journal of Outdoor Recreation and Tourism* tested this relationship in a rural tourism context, surveying visitors to a Portuguese schist village. The researchers found that nostalgia directly triggered more intense sensory experiences, and those sensory experiences in turn increased the purchase of local products. [Kastenholz et al., "Nostalgia sensations and local products in rural tourism experiences," 2021](https://dspace.uevora.pt/rdpc/bitstream/10174/30182/1/Katenholz%20et%20al%20%282021%29%20Nostalgia%20sensations%20and%20local%20products%20in%20rural%20tourism%20experiences.pdf) The effect was strongest for tourists — those staying overnight — as opposed to same-day visitors. Nostalgia did not merely make them feel good. It made them buy things.

## The tourism pipeline

The trinket shop does not exist in isolation. It sits at the end of a pipeline that begins with a single decision — to go somewhere — and the numbers for small-town tourism in America are, by any standard, enormous.

In 2024, the National Park System recorded 331.9 million recreation visits, up 2% from 2023. [National Park Service, "2024 National Park Visitor Spending Effects," NPS/SR—2025/237, September 2025](https://www.nps.gov/nature/customcf/NPS_Data_Visualization/docs/NPS_2024_Visitor_Spending_Effects.pdf) Those visitors spent $29 billion in local gateway communities — the small towns that sit at the entrances to parks. [NPS, 2024 Report](https://www.nps.gov/orgs/1207/national-park-visitor-spending-contributed-%2456-billion-to-the-u-s-economy-in-2024.htm) The NPS explicitly tracks "Retail (e.g., souvenirs, sporting goods, and other retail purchases)" as one of eight spending categories. In 2024, retail generated roughly $1.2 billion in economic output from park visitor spending alone. [NPS, Table 3, 2024 Report](https://www.nps.gov/nature/customcf/NPS_Data_Visualization/docs/NPS_2024_Visitor_Spending_Effects.pdf) The lodging sector led at $11.1 billion, followed by restaurants at $5.7 billion — and then came everything else, including the shops selling arrowhead keychains and "I [Heart] [Park Name]" hats.

![Park visitors spent $29 billion in gateway towns. Much of it went toward objects smaller than the memory they were meant to preserve.](/api/blog/images/trinket_nps_spending.png)

The same dynamic plays out on Main Streets across the country. Main Street America, the national network of downtown revitalization programs, reported that its 1,172 designated communities generated $7.65 billion in local reinvestment in 2024 alone. The network helped open 6,324 net new businesses, facilitated the creation of 33,835 net new jobs, and rehabilitated 10,126 historic buildings. The return on investment: for every dollar a local Main Street program spent on operations, $21.73 of new investment flowed back into the downtown. [Main Street America, "2025 Designated Communities & 2024 Reinvestment Statistics Collective Impact," May 2025](https://es.mainstreet.org/the-latest/news/main-spotlight-announcing-the-2025-main-street-america-designated-communities-and-collective-impact-of-local-programs-in-2024)

Since 1980, the cumulative impact of the Main Street movement has reached $124.67 billion reinvested locally, 188,583 net new businesses created, 852,443 net new jobs, and 356,424 buildings rehabilitated. [Main Street America, Collective Impact Statistics](https://es.mainstreet.org/our-network/collective-impact) A 2023 study from Virginia Main Street found that since its inception in 1985, the state's program had generated more than 8,200 new or expanded businesses, 27,485 jobs, and over $2.6 billion in public and private investment. [Virginia Main Street, "2023 Impact Review," March 2024](https://virginiamainstreet.com/2024/03/11/the-numbers-are-in-2023-main-street-impact-review/)

![Every dollar a Main Street program spent returned twenty-two. Nostalgia, it turns out, has excellent credit.](/api/blog/images/trinket_main_street.png)

These are not solely trinket shops. But trinket shops are a visible and disproportionately important component of the mix. They require relatively low startup capital. They can operate in small spaces. They benefit directly from foot traffic generated by other Main Street businesses — the coffee shop, the bookstore, the farm-to-table restaurant. And they are, in a very real sense, the last stop before a visitor leaves town.

## The micropolitan boom

The towns where these shops matter most are not urban centers. They are the places the Census Bureau classifies as "micropolitan statistical areas" — municipalities with populations between 10,000 and 50,000, along with their surrounding economic zones. Heartland Forward, a policy research organization based in Bentonville, Arkansas, analyzed 527 such micropolitans in its 2024 "Most Dynamic Micropolitans" report. Seven of the top ten, the researchers found, rely on tourism as their primary economic driver. [Heartland Forward, "Most Dynamic Micropolitans 2024," August 2024](https://heartlandforward.org/research/most-dynamic-micropolitans-2024/)

Branson, Missouri — a town of roughly 12,000 in the Ozark Mountains — made the most dramatic leap, vaulting 359 spots to rank 119th overall. [Heartland Forward, 2024 Report, PDF](https://heartlandforward.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/Most-Dynamic-Micros-2024.pdf) Branson's entire economy is built on tourism: live music theaters, theme parks, outlet malls, and the shops that sell the souvenirs. Other tourism-dependent micropolitans in the top 25 included Jackson, Wyoming (gateway to Grand Teton and Yellowstone); Heber and Cedar City, Utah; Key West, Florida; Breckenridge, Colorado; Fredericksburg, Texas; Spearfish, South Dakota (gateway to the Black Hills); Kalispell, Montana (gateway to Glacier National Park); and Nantucket, Massachusetts. [Heartland Forward, 2024 Top 25](https://heartlandforward.org/research/most-dynamic-micropolitans-2024/)

The report's authors concluded that tourism had become "the dominant theme" of post-COVID economic growth in small-town America. [Heartland Forward, Executive Summary](https://heartlandforward.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/Most-Dynamic-Micros-2024.pdf)

A separate 2024 economic impact analysis from Pennsylvania found that 201.6 million visitors spent $49.9 billion in the state, with recreation leading all spending categories at 6.4% year-over-year growth. [Tourism Economics for Pennsylvania, "Economic Impact of Visitors in Pennsylvania," 2024](https://assets.simpleviewinc.com/simpleview/image/upload/v1/clients/poconos/Economic_Impact_of_Visitors_in_PA_Counties_2024_CLIENT_PRELIMINARY_9_17_25_da371832-2d3a-45dd-bbd5-cda98ae229b2.pdf) Tennessee reported $30.6 billion in direct visitor spending in 2023, with retail accounting for 11% — approximately $3.4 billion. [Tennessee Department of Tourism, "2023 Economic Impact," via Tourism Economics](https://www.tn.gov/content/dam/tn/tourism/documents/2024_Economic-Impact-Share.pdf) Missouri's FY2024 report counted 42.4 million visitors spending $12.5 billion, sustaining nearly 145,600 jobs. [Missouri Division of Tourism, "FY2024 Economic Impact," Tourism Economics](https://mdt-visitmo-cdn.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2025/05/FY2024-Missouri-Tourism-Economic-Impact.pdf)

The through line is clear: visitors arrive for the landscape, but they spend their money in the shops. And the shops exist because the town has a Main Street program, a historic building stock, a tourism board, and a critical mass of other small businesses that make the downtown worth walking through.

## A persistent storefront

The trinket shop is easy to mock. It sells what the industry calls "low-consideration goods" — items no one needs, which is precisely why they matter. The decision to buy a $6 magnet or a $12 candle is not a rational calculation of utility. It is an emotional transaction: an attempt to hold onto a moment, a place, a feeling for which the reasonable world has no adequate vocabulary.

The numbers suggest this is not a marginal behavior. The Bureau of Labor Statistics recorded $21.55 billion in output for the sector in 2024. The National Park Service counted $29 billion in total gateway spending, of which retail — mostly souvenirs — was a significant and tracked component. Main Street America documented $7.65 billion in local reinvestment, much of it flowing through small retail storefronts. The *Journal of Consumer Research* found that nostalgia makes people willing to pay more — and these stores are, in a very real sense, nostalgia distilleries, converting sentiment into revenue with the efficiency of a well-designed machine.

There are roughly 120,000 people still working in this industry as of early 2026. [BLS CES, Feb 2026](https://www.ceicdata.com/en/united-states/current-employment-statistics-employment-non-farm-payroll/employment-nf-rt-gm-sh-os-gift-novelty--souvenir) That is fewer than at the peak — much fewer — but it is not zero. The five-and-dime is gone. The Woolworth Building still stands in New York, no longer the world's tallest, converted largely to offices, a monument to an empire that dissolved into the very thing it once sold: memories. But the small stores — the ones with the pressed-tin ceilings and the paraffin candles and the bins of polished stones — are still open. They are not what they were. But then, neither are we.

---

*Data-driven feature article. All figures sourced from primary government datasets (BLS, FRED, Census Bureau, National Park Service, state tourism offices), peer-reviewed academic journals (Journal of Consumer Research, Journal of Outdoor Recreation and Tourism), and institutional research reports (Main Street America, Heartland Forward, Iowa State University). No secondary or tertiary sources used.*
