# The Spine of the East: Walking the Appalachian Trail Between Ecstasy and Ruin

*The Appalachian Trail is 2,197.9 miles of dirt, rock, root, and revelation — a footpath conceived as utopian socialism, built by lawyers and Depression-era laborers, invaded by insects smaller than a grain of rice, and attempted every year by 3,000 people. About one in four finishes. The other three acquire something far more complicated than a finish line.*

---

It begins, for most, in the heat of a Georgia spring, on a rounded wooded summit called Springer Mountain, 3,782 feet above sea level, where a small plaque marks mile zero. There is no grand archway, no ribbon-cutting apparatus. Just trees, rocks, a metal sign, and the sudden vertiginous fact that you must walk back down this mountain before climbing the next one — and the next, and the next, for 2,197.9 miles, through 14 states, 464,500 feet of cumulative elevation gain — the equivalent of climbing Everest 16 times — and roughly five million steps.

One hiker, arriving at Springer with an 85-pound backpack, a laptop, and a solar panel, wrote that he was "exhausted and I was just getting started." He sent a photo to his mother. "I'm here at the top of the world mom," he typed. "My Journey Begins…"

But the trail is not the top of the world. It is, in every way that matters, the opposite: a long, slow descent into the real.

---

## I. The Dream

The Appalachian Trail began not as a hiking path but as a utopian prescription for the sickness of modern life — which is to say, it began as the kind of idea that sounds noble in a lecture hall and improbable on a mountainside.

In 1921, a professional forester and regional planner named Benton MacKaye published an essay in the *Journal of the American Institute of Architects* titled "An Appalachian Trail: A Project in Regional Planning." Its opening lines read:

"Something has been going on in this country during the past few strenuous years which, in the din of war and general upheaval, has been somewhat lost from the public mind. It is the slow quiet development of a special type of community — the recreation camp. It is something neither urban nor rural. It escapes the hecticness of the one, the loneliness of the other. And it escapes also the common curse of both — the high powered tension of the economic scramble."

MacKaye had suffered a devastating personal loss: his wife Betty died by suicide in April of that year. According to biographer Larry Anderson, the tragedy "was the turning point of a lifetime, the event that set [MacKaye] on a path to his greatest social contributions." Within weeks, MacKaye began writing his proposal, channeling grief into a plan for communal salvation through wilderness — as if the forest could absorb what the city had failed to heal.

The trail MacKaye envisioned was never merely recreational. He saw it as a "flank attack on the problems of social readjustment" — a cooperative antidote to capitalism's "mutual fleecing." The path would link a chain of "community camps" where urban workers could rediscover self-sufficiency, escape industrial exploitation, and live, as he put it, "on a nonprofit basis." He was a member of the Harvard Socialist Club; his editors consciously scrubbed the more radical language from the proposal, replacing it with the safer word "recreation." One suspects they understood that America will tolerate almost any idea as long as it is called a hobby.

What the trail became was different from what MacKaye imagined — less commune, more footpath. But the core insight survived: that walking the length of the Appalachians could strip away the unnecessary and return a person to something essential. The commune died; the corridor lived.

---

## II. The Builders

MacKaye was the prophet. Myron H. Avery was the general — and generals, as a rule, are more useful than prophets when there is actual work to be done.

Avery, a Maine-born lawyer, took over leadership of the fledgling Appalachian Trail Conference in 1931 and accelerated construction with military efficiency. His method: organize a trail club for each section; determine the best route; clear, mark, and maintain it; collect data and publish guidebooks — which he initially printed with his own money. It is a law of human nature that the people who care most about an idea are always the ones who end up paying for it.

The early volunteers worked with Boy Scout axes and pruning shears. The workweek ended Saturday noon. Dirt roads were terrible for driving. "It was difficult to persuade people to do all that work for nothing," one early member recalled. "They said nobody would ever use the trails anyway."

They built it anyway. There is something magnificent about people who persist in constructing something they have been assured nobody wants.

Between 1928 and 1932, with the help of the Civilian Conservation Corps — the Depression-era federal work program — crews constructed and marked about 260 miles of trail from the Susquehanna River to Rockfish Gap in Shenandoah National Park. By 1934, clubs reported completion of 1,937 miles. The CCC built the trail's iconic three-sided Adirondack shelters, following design guidelines published by the National Park Service in 1938.

The final link was completed without fanfare on August 14, 1937, by a six-man CCC crew in the Maine woods. They then moved on to build more shelters — a scene so unceremonious it might have been designed to frustrate anyone who enjoys ribbon-cuttings and speeches.

Avery, upon completion, told the conference: "Rather than a sense of exultation, this situation brings a fuller realization of our responsibilities. To say that the Trail is completed would be a complete misnomer. Those of us, who have physically worked on the Trail, know that the Trail, as such, will never be completed."

He was prescient. In 1938, a hurricane broke the trail's continuity for years. The Blue Ridge Parkway displaced nearly 120 miles of the original route — what Avery called "the major catastrophe in Appalachian Trail history." The path was not fully reconnected until 1951.

Avery died in 1952. By then, he had walked every mile of the trail — in sections — and become the first officially recognized "2,000-miler." He had earned the right to say the trail would never be finished by being the man who, more than anyone else, had finished it.

---

## III. The Numbers

![The Spine of the East: Elevation Gain and Loss by State](/api/blog/images/appalachian_elevation_profile.png)
*Cumulative climb: 526,664 feet — equivalent to climbing Everest nearly 18 times. Climb in green, descent in brown, ordered from Georgia (top) to Maine (bottom).*

By the numbers, the Appalachian Trail defies easy comprehension — which is, of course, exactly the point of numbers that large:

- **Length**: 2,197.9 miles (varies slightly each year due to relocations)
- **Elevation gain/loss**: 464,500 feet cumulative
- **States traversed**: 14
- **Steps required**: approximately 5 million
- **Annual visitors**: 16.9 million recreation visits in 2025
- **Annual thru-hike attempts**: approximately 3,000
- **Completion rate**: about 25-33%
- **Total 2,000-milers reported**: more than 20,000 since 1937
- **Volunteer hours (2024)**: 176,504 hours from 5,000+ volunteers
- **Average pack weight at start (2025)**: 30.4 pounds
- **Average daily mileage for thru-hikers**: 13.8 miles
- **Average duration of a thru-hike**: 152 days

These are abstractions. On the ground, the numbers become something else — something that involves your knees.

"The average pack weight was 30.4 lbs.," the ATC reported in 2025, "which is roughly equivalent to carrying a medium-sized bag of dog food or a microwave on your back." The comparison is absurd and precise, like everything about the trail. It is also the sort of fact that makes you realize how rarely we describe our own lives in terms of dog food.

The states follow a predictable difficulty curve. Maryland and West Virginia are easiest — the trail's flat country. New Hampshire and Maine are hardest. The USGS elevation data breaks down starkly: New Hampshire alone demands 53,182 feet of climbing and 50,615 feet of descent; Maine demands 67,280 feet up and 65,000 down. Georgia requires "only" 20,407 feet of climbing. The quotation marks around "only" are doing a great deal of work.

---

## IV. The Walk

A hiker named Willy "Catchup" set out in 2022 imagining himself a "solitary poet monk, wandering through endless woods in blissful silence a la Henry David Thoreau." By his first night at Stover Creek Shelter in Georgia, he had already found people he would hike with for the next two months. "We played cards, we laughed, we might've even sang together," he wrote. "It was the first night of my thru-hike but it was already abundantly clear to me that the types of people who're attracted to something as gargantuan and difficult as the Appalachian Trail are my people."

The trail, it turns out, has a terrible sense of dramatic irony. You arrive seeking solitude; it gives you community. You arrive seeking community; it gives you solitude. It gives you, in short, whatever you least expected and most needed.

Catchup eventually forced a silent meditation in the 100-Mile Wilderness of Maine — eight days of not speaking — and found that "by forcing myself to stay silent and still, the sights, sounds, and smells were heightened to a level I didn't think possible." He had to walk a thousand miles to discover what any good librarian could have told him, but there is a difference between being told something and earning the right to believe it.

Bill Bryson captured the strange cognitive shift in *A Walk in the Woods*:

"Distance changes utterly when you take the world on foot. A mile becomes a long way, two miles literally considerable, ten miles whopping, fifty miles at the very limits of conception. The world, you realize, is enormous in a way that only you and a small community of fellow hikers know."

"Life takes on a neat simplicity, too. Time ceases to have any meaning. When it is dark, you go to bed, and when it is light again you get up, and everything in between is just in between."

"All that is required of you is a willingness to trudge."

"There is no point in hurrying," Bryson continued, "because you are not actually going anywhere. However far or long you plod, you are always in the same place: in the woods."

This is the romantic version. It is true, and it is not the whole truth. It omits what happens when trudging ceases to feel philosophical and begins to feel like a decision you are starting to regret.

---

## V. The Breaking

The same trail that produces Bryson's "low-level ecstasy" also produces days of screaming. It is a testimony to the trail's complexity that it can accommodate both.

One hiker, keeping a journal under the pseudonym "Wormwood" during a 2025 thru-hike, wrote an entry titled "Walk With Me In Hell":

"It's the first day on trail that I've broken down and started screaming into the forest. It's been the first day that I've dropped to one knee and struggled to rise again, and it's been the first day that I've completely fallen to the ground and just laid there for several minutes before even making an attempt to get back up."

"I hated everything about the Appalachian Trail today. I hated the trail, the people who made it, the people who walk it, my own choice to be here, and my excitement to share the hike via these journals."

The cause was not a single catastrophe but an accumulation of miseries: 92-degree heat, 87% humidity, a heat index around 105 degrees. The hiker described rings of sweat-water wrung from a microfiber towel, bugs drowning in the layer of wetness on his skin, a black fly lodging in the back of his throat. "I sweat so much that I became dizzy." There is a peculiar honesty in admitting that your body has become a habitat for other creatures' deaths.

Later, he wrote of "The Ugly on the Outside":

"This trail has reduced me in so many ways. Down to the things that I needed, stripping away and degrading the things that didn't serve me. By the end, all that's left is mostly who you are."

"My beard has grown scraggly, my hair scraggly, matted, and longer than it's ever been in my life. My skin has lost the tan it had at the beginning. My upper body has shriveled. My legs have broken out in folliculitis."

He considered the exchange worthwhile: ugliness on the outside for clarity within. This is the sort of bargain that civilization spends a great deal of energy trying to avoid, and that the trail insists upon.

The 2024 Trek survey confirmed that 8% of hikers who exited the trail early did so because of weather — before Hurricane Helene made that figure even more stark. In 2025, the percentage of unplanned exits caused by injury rose nearly 5% from the prior year. Nature, it seems, is not merely indifferent to human ambition; it is actively competitive with it.

---

## VI. The Grim Arithmetic

![Causes of Death on the Appalachian Trail](/api/blog/images/appalachian_fatalities.png)
*Approximately 200 fatalities since 1930. Accidents account for 60% of deaths; overexertion for 20%; medical conditions for 10%.*

The Appalachian Trail kills people. This is not said to be dramatic; it is said because it is true, and because the truth deserves the same directness as the statistics that follow.

According to data compiled from NPS Morning Reports, approximately 200 fatalities have occurred on or near the AT since 1930. The leading causes: accidents (60%), including falls, vehicle collisions, and trespasser injuries; overexertion (20%), including heart attacks, heat stroke, and dehydration; medical conditions (10%); wildlife encounters (5%); and weather-related events (5%).

Males account for approximately 70% of fatalities. The 50-64 age demographic is disproportionately represented at 23% of deaths. It appears that middle-aged men, having spent decades mastering the art of ignoring their own limitations, are the most eager to test them against a mountain.

In September 2024, a trio of trail runners near Tinker Cliffs in Botetourt County, Virginia, found a hiker lying face-down on the side of the trail, still wearing his backpack. He was cold to the touch. The man was identified as Thomas Vanetten, 67, of Schenectady, New York. There was "no obvious trauma or signs of a fall." Sometimes the trail does not offer a story, only an end.

In July 2023, a 67-year-old backpacker was last heard from at the Inn at the Long Trail in Killington, Vermont. Days later, searchers recovered his body 1.5 miles downstream from where the trail crosses Stony Brook — a flashflood victim. The last thing he did was check into an inn named after the trail itself.

In March 2024, the NPS announced a norovirus outbreak among hikers in North Carolina, Georgia, and Tennessee. In May 2024, someone scattered dog treats stuffed with fish hooks along the trail near the George W. Outerbridge shelter in Pennsylvania. Humanity, it turns out, does not improve merely because one has entered the woods.

Garmin, whose inReach satellite devices have become standard equipment, reported in its 2025 Year in Review that it now sees more than 3,000 SOS incidents annually across its network. Injury is the top reason for activation. About one-third of rescues requiring outside help involved helicopter extraction.

And yet — the ATC emphasizes that "the Appalachian Trail is a relatively safe place to visit." The qualification matters. The word "relatively" is doing the work of an entire legal department.

---

## VII. The Weather Above the Trees

![Mount Washington: The Worst Weather on Earth](/api/blog/images/appalachian_mt_washington.png)
*Average annual temperature: 28.0 degrees F. Average annual snowfall: 281.8 inches. Record wind gust: 231 mph. Record wind chill: -108 degrees F (2023).*

The most dangerous part of the Appalachian Trail, climatically speaking, is not in the deep woods. It is above treeline in New Hampshire's Presidential Range, where the trail crosses the flanks of Mount Washington — a mountain that seems to have taken the name "Presidential" as a justification for behaving like a despot.

Mount Washington's weather observatory, in operation since 1932, holds records that sound like a dare: an average annual temperature of 28.0 degrees; 281.8 inches of snow per year; a record low of -47 degrees (January 1934); a record wind gust of 231 mph (April 1934) — the highest surface wind speed ever measured by instruments anywhere on Earth until 1999.

In February 2023, the wind chill dropped to -108 degrees, probably the lowest ever recorded in the United States. The summit was colder than the average temperature on Mars that week. One hesitates to say that Mars is more hospitable than New Hampshire, but the numbers do not leave much room for local pride.

For thru-hikers, this is not a curiosity but a gauntlet: 100 miles of exposed, technical terrain, above treeline for miles at a time, where a sunny afternoon can turn into a hypothermia emergency within minutes. It is the sort of place that reminds you that weather is not a backdrop but an adversary, and one that does not observe weekends.

---

## VIII. The Forest That Is Dying

The trail's forests are transforming in slow motion, and the hiker averaging 13.8 miles per day may not notice. But the change is ecosystemic, and it is accelerating. The view does not change; the view is changing, and we are too close to the ground to see it happen.

The hemlock woolly adelgid (HWA) is an aphid-like insect smaller than 1.5 millimeters — a grain of sand with legs. First detected near Richmond, Virginia, in the early 1950s, it has since spread across 19 states, from Georgia to southern Maine. It feeds by piercing the base of hemlock needles with its mouthparts, depleting the tree's nutrient reserves. Infested trees seldom recover. The most destructive force in the southern Appalachian forest is something you could mistake for dust.

The consequences are not subtle. According to ecological research, the HWA has "reset successional sequences, homogenized biological diversity at landscape scales, altered hydrological dynamics, and changed forest stands from carbon sinks into carbon sources." This is scientific language for: the forest is being rewritten by an insect smaller than a fingernail.

US Forest Service modeling projects a "near complete loss of the hemlock forest type within 20 years of adelgid establishment" in the central Appalachians, with conversion to hardwood forests and "significant alterations to terrestrial and aquatic wildlife habitat."

The emerald ash borer has destroyed hundreds of millions of ash trees across North America, including thousands along the AT. It kills within two years. An infected tree has less than a 1% chance of survival. Treating a single tree with pesticide costs $120. The arithmetic is simple: there are more trees than there is money.

Marian Orlousky, the ATC's Director of Science and Stewardship, puts it plainly: "Second only to climate change, non-native invasive species are the most urgent threat to the Appalachian Trail's 2,000 miles and almost 400,000 acres of land."

The hiker walking through southern Virginia passes through hemlock groves that will not exist in their current form within two decades. The cool, dark cathedral of the southern Appalachian forest is being replaced in real time, tree by tree, by an insect you need a magnifying glass to see. The largest things are often destroyed by the smallest.

---

## IX. The Volunteers

No one is paid to maintain the Appalachian Trail. It is maintained entirely by the sort of people who believe that a thing worth having is worth working for without expectation of payment — a concept so foreign to modern economic thinking that it might as well be a form of rebellion.

In the 2024 federal fiscal year, more than 5,000 individual volunteers contributed 176,504 hours to the trail's upkeep. In 2023, 4,730 volunteers logged 170,147 hours — the equivalent of 19.4 years of continuous labor. The ATC estimates that the whole trail requires about 200,000 volunteer hours in a normal year.

To understand what those hours mean on the ground, consider one club. The Tennessee Eastman Hiking & Canoeing Club — one of 30 trail-maintaining clubs — logged 10,756 hours in 2024 across 442 events involving 236 people. That included 3,464 adopt-a-trail hours and 7,757 hours on special projects.

These volunteers do not just clip brush and clean water bars. They build shelters, install footbridges, construct privies, remove invasive species, inventory natural resources, and pilot bear-canister loan programs. After Hurricane Helene devastated sections of the trail in Georgia, Tennessee, North Carolina, and southwest Virginia in 2024, they rebuilt the treadway by hand. When nature breaks what we have made, we make it again — and we do not send an invoice.

The trail is managed through a unique public-private partnership: the National Park Service, the U.S. Forest Service, the ATC, and 30 trail clubs. The ATC's 2024 operating budget was $14.2 million — less than the cost of a single mile of urban highway. The entire Appalachian Trail, the spine of the eastern United States, costs less to run than a mile of asphalt.

Every shelter, every white blaze painted on a tree, every switchback that prevents erosion, every bear box, every privy — all of it is the work of unpaid hands. The trail exists because enough people decided that their time was worth less than the thing they were building.

---

## X. The People Who Walked Through

The history of the trail is the history of people who had reasons to walk — and the reasons, when examined, are rarely simple.

Earl Shaffer (1948) was a World War II veteran who served in the South Pacific. He walked the entire trail in 124 days to, as he put it, "walk the war out of my system." He carried a diary that is now in the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History — a battered notebook showing "wear and tear of being carried and used for 124 days in extreme temperatures and often rainy weather."

At the time, experts believed a thru-hike was impossible. Shaffer had no guidebooks, no advice, no previous footsteps to follow. When blisters threatened his hike, he put sand in his boots and wore no socks until his feet toughened. "The Indian ways are usually best in the woods," he wrote. He treated his body like terrain to be conquered rather than a system to be preserved — which, given what he had survived, was probably the only approach he knew.

Emma "Grandma" Gatewood (1955) was 67 years old, mother of 11, grandmother of 23, and survivor of three decades of domestic violence at the hands of her husband. She read an article in National Geographic about the Appalachian Trail and decided to hike it. She wore Keds sneakers, carried a denim sack slung over her shoulder, and packed a shower curtain for shelter. Her gear weighed perhaps 15 pounds.

She broke her glasses and got lost on her first attempt in 1954. She tried again in 1955, starting from Georgia on May 3. She walked 146 days, wearing out seven pairs of sneakers, falling and injuring herself repeatedly, dealing with snakes and bears. When she reached the summit of Katahdin on September 25, she sang "America the Beautiful," signed the register, and said: "I did it. I said I'd do it and I've done it."

She became the first person to hike the entire AT three times. Asked why, she answered: "Because I wanted to." She also admitted: "I thought it would be a nice lark. It wasn't." There is perhaps no better summary of the Appalachian Trail than that sentence: it seemed like a good idea, and it was not one, and she did it anyway, three times.

---

## XI. The Psychology of Five Million Steps

![One in Four: The AT Thru-Hiker Funnel](/api/blog/images/appalachian_thru_hiker_funnel.png)
*Of approximately 3,000 who register each year, roughly 25 to 33 percent complete the full 2,197.9 miles. The funnel narrows sharply between Springer Mountain and Harpers Ferry.*

Academic research on what happens to the human mind over 2,200 miles is thin but revealing — as thin, perhaps, as the margin between those who finish and those who do not.

A 2024 study in the Journal of Outdoor Recreation, Education, and Leadership surveyed 128 AT thru-hikers and found statistically significant differences in mental toughness between those who completed the trail and those who did not — the first empirical evidence that finishing the AT requires a specific psychological quality beyond mere motivation or resilience. The study also found that social support facilitated success; the lone wolves tended to drop out. It turns out that the romantic image of the solitary hiker is exactly that — a romance. The people who finish are the ones who let other people help.

A gender-differences study of 211 hikers found that women were more worried about crime and harassment, and more worried about managing natural elements. Men were less confident about maintaining health and hygiene. But after the hike, both groups viewed themselves equally capable — and women reported a significantly greater sense of empowerment. The trail, it seems, is a great equalizer, though it takes a different toll on the way up than on the way down.

A physiological case study followed one hiker across 139 days: 2,151 miles, 326,322 feet of elevation gain. Resting heart rate and heart rate variability regressed over the course of the trek. Fatigue accumulated until the end and did not improve despite extensive rest. The declining markers had no impact on event completion — the body can perform far beyond what feels sustainable. The body, it turns out, has read more Stoic philosophy than the mind has.

A 2025 study of thru-hikers found that prolonged hiking reduced evening serum cortisol concentrations. The stress hormone dropped. The researchers concluded that thru-hiking "could be used as an additional tool to help individuals mitigate health conditions caused by elevated evening cortisol concentrations, such as anxiety, depression, panic attacks, and PTSD."

This is the trail's paradox made scientific: it destroys the body and heals the mind, often simultaneously. It is the most inefficient antidepressant ever devised, and it works precisely because of its inefficiency.

---

## XII. The Detachment

Bryson again — and this may be the truest thing anyone has written about the trail:

"Life takes on a neat simplicity. You have no engagements, commitments, obligations, or duties; no special ambitions and only the smallest, least complicated of wants; you exist in a tranquil tedium, serenely beyond the reach of exasperation."

"At times, you become almost certain that you slabbed this hillside three days ago, crossed this stream yesterday, clambered over this fallen tree at least twice today already. But most of the time you don't think. No point. Instead, you exist in a kind of mobile Zen mode, your brain like a balloon tethered with string, accompanying but not actually part of the body below. Walking for hours and miles becomes as automatic, as unremarkable, as breathing."

He called this "low-level ecstasy" and argued it was something modern life systematically suppresses. Modern life, after all, has a vested interest in keeping you agitated: an agitated person buys things, checks notifications, and worries about the future. A person in a state of low-level ecstasy is not shopping.

The hiker Mr. Brandybuck, on the morning of his Katahdin summit in September 2024, wrote:

"I continued forward through the haze, utterly alone. It was around 7 a.m., so maybe a handful of other hikers were starting the trail miles below. Past the junction at Thoreau Springs, I saw a shadow emerge from the mist and a hiker and I nodded as we passed. Anyone who's waking up hours before dawn to climb a mountain alone probably doesn't want to stop to chat."

In the mist, he thought about "how many centuries people have climbed up this mountain." He felt "their spirits just out of sight." A shirtless man in short shorts emerged from the Knife's Edge, took his photo, gave advice on a different trail down, and vanished. After 90 minutes on the summit, "after disease and heartbreaking beauty," he heaved his pack over his shoulder and began the journey home. There is something deeply appropriate about a mystical summit experience being interrupted by a shirtless man with advice.

---

## XIII. At the End

![The Appalachian Trail by the Numbers](/api/blog/images/appalachian_by_the_numbers.png)
*Key statistics that define the world's longest hiking-only footpath, from total miles to volunteer hours to average pack weight.*

The hiker who started with the 85-pound backpack and the laptop — who could barely walk the approach trail to Springer Mountain — made it to Harpers Ferry, the psychological halfway point. He left his laptop behind somewhere in Georgia, shed 60 pounds of gear, traded boots for trail runners. By the time he reached the ATC headquarters in Harpers Ferry, he looked like every other hiker in the photo archive: confident, fit, relaxed, and at times, exultant. He had discovered the great secret of travel: you do not need most of what you carry.

The archive contains more than 18,000 such images, Polaroids from 1979 onward, now scanned and searchable online. Sixteen volunteers spent 425 hours digitizing them. Even the record of the trail requires unpaid labor.

Every face in that archive tells the same story differently: of pain and boredom and beauty and community and solitude and the strange, addictive deprivation that Bryson called "the central feature of life on the Appalachian Trail." He meant that "the whole point of the experience is to remove yourself so thoroughly from the conveniences of everyday life that the most ordinary things — processed cheese, a can of pop gorgeously beaded with condensation — fill you with wonder and gratitude."

What the trail does is reduce you. To pain. To gratitude. To five million steps. To the single irreducible question that every hiker must answer in their own way: Why keep walking?

Alex Tucker, who thru-hiked in 2024, put it this way:

"Thru hiking is a dirty, hard, tiring, uncomfortable experience that is also colorful, rewarding, beautiful, exciting and absolutely something that I would do again."

"I fear that I didn't do the trail justice in this blog. There is beauty in that too. I have experienced an adventure so big, so grand, so unique and so strange that I can't accurately describe it. I don't think I will ever be able to. I don't think I ever want to be able to."

The Appalachian Trail, in its brutal totality, offers one thing that modern life cannot: the opportunity to be completely, undeniably, unequivocally done with something that mattered. And then, as the mist clears on Katahdin, to start over.

Every year, 3,000 people walk into the woods at Springer Mountain. About one in four will touch the sign at Katahdin. The others will carry something else out of those woods — something harder to name, something that does not require a certificate or a photo. The trail gives to each what each can carry. The rest it leaves on the forest floor.

# The Laboratory of the Imagination: How Marvel's Fictional Science Became Real Research

**By Staff Journalist** | May 2026

Patent examiners are paid to take invention seriously. They are not, as a rule, paid to read comic books. But on March 13, 2019, the UK Intellectual Property Office granted patent GB2559971 to a British company called Gravity Industries Limited for a wearable flight system with propulsion assemblies worn on a user's body — a jet suit — and the line between those two activities blurred. During examination, the patent officer did something unusual: they searched the prior art and found a relevant disclosure — the suit worn by the fictional character Iron Man in Marvel Comics, which includes propulsion units on the hands. The office cited it. [Venner Shipley, Apr 2019]

It was not the first time a comic book had entered the official record of human invention. A *Beano* strip had been cited against a pet-entry signal system. A Donald Duck comic was raised against a method for raising sunken vessels. But the Iron Man citation was different. It was not a novelty. It was an acknowledgment that a fictional engineer from a 1963 comic book had, decades before any real prototype, described a technological system that a government patent office considered relevant to a real invention.

The Gravity Industries patent was ultimately granted because the real suit added a torso propulsion assembly that Iron Man's didn't have. But the question the examination raised — at what point does science fiction become prior art? — is the wrong question. The right one is: what has Marvel already helped build?

![Patent Timeline](/api/blog/images/marvel_patent_timeline.png)
*From comic page to patent office: a timeline of Marvel fiction inspiring real invention. (Source: USPTO; UKIPO GB2559971; NC State University)*

## I. The Patent Evidence

The patent record is the most concrete measure of Marvel's influence on engineering, if not the most abundant. It is sparse, but it is real.

In 1991, inventor Stephen E. Kimble filed US Patent No. 5,072,856 for a "toy web-shooting glove" — a device that expels string foam from the palm to simulate a spider's web. The patent explicitly states its purpose: "to create a toy that makes it possible for a player to act like a spider person by shooting webs from the palm of his or her hand." [Google Patents, US5072856A] Marvel eventually licensed the invention, and when the patent expired, a dispute over royalty payments reached the Supreme Court in *Kimble v. Marvel Entertainment* (2015). The case, which turned on whether patent royalties could extend beyond the patent term, produced a 6–3 opinion by Justice Alito that acknowledged the strange intersection: a real patent inspired by a fictional character, now part of American case law. [Patent Docs, Aug 2015]

In 2011, an inventor filed US patent application 20130145530A1 for an "Iron man suit" — a full body exoskeleton "constructed from a strong material, such as steel... capable of protecting its wearer from projectiles, such as bullets, and including a hydraulic mechanism and a power source." The application describes sensors to detect body movements, a computer to process them, and actuators to lift heavy objects. [Google Patents, US20130145530A1] The patent, filed nearly 50 years after Iron Man's first appearance in *Tales of Suspense* #39, was effectively a real-world attempt to build what Tony Stark had been wearing since 1963.

And in 2017, Disney filed a patent for a virtual reality system that simulates throwing and catching Captain America's shield. The design shows a motion sensor fastened to the forearm, a physical shield on a short rail, and sensors that simulate the "boomerang effect" from the comics. [Chip and Company, Jun 2017]

None of this amounts to a mass phenomenon. But as a category of evidence, it is significant: the patent system — that most serious of institutions, designed to separate genuine invention from mere aspiration — has repeatedly treated Marvel's fictional technology as a benchmark for reality.

## II. The University Pipeline

The more revealing story lives not in the patent office but in the classrooms and laboratories where Marvel's fictional science has been treated not as entertainment but as a pedagogical starting point — and, in some cases, as a research question worth answering.

In 2001, James Kakalios, a physics professor at the University of Minnesota, created a freshman seminar called "Everything I Know About Science I Learned from Reading Comic Books." It was a real physics class. It covered Newtonian mechanics, quantum theory, and solid-state physics. The only thing unusual was the textbook: Silver Age comic books. "This is a real physics class," Kakalios has said, "that covers topics from Isaac Newton to the transistor, but there's not an inclined plane or pulley in sight. Rather, ALL the examples come from superhero comic books." [physicsofsuperheroes.com]

The class drew media attention when the first *Spider-Man* film was released in 2002. Kakalios turned it into a book, *The Physics of Superheroes*, which *Discover* magazine named one of the best science books of 2005. It has since been translated into six languages. Kakalios went on to serve as a science consultant for Warner Bros.' *Watchmen* (2007); his short video on the science of that film won an Upper Midwest Regional Emmy and a WEBBY nomination. In 2014, the American Association for the Advancement of Science gave him its Public Engagement with Science Award. In 2016, the American Institute of Physics awarded him the Andrew Gemant Award for his work in communicating physics to the public. [Georgia Tech School of Physics, 2017]

Kakalios's approach — using superhero narratives to explain real physics — has since spread across American higher education. At UC Davis, chemical engineering professor Ricardo Castro created "EMS 2: Materials Marvels: The Science of Superheroes" in 2015, a freshman engineering course that asks students to analyze whether Captain America's vibranium alloy shield could actually absorb kinetic energy, and whether Iron Man's repulsor beam could deliver concussive force. The class began as a pilot with 78 students; by its second year, enrollment had nearly doubled to 150. [University of California, Jan 2016]

At Lawrence Technological University in Michigan, Dr. Sibrina Collins — executive director of the Marburger STEM Center — published a peer-reviewed chapter titled "Inorganic Chemistry: Vibranium and Marvel Studios' Black Panther" in the American Chemical Society's *Advances in Teaching Inorganic Chemistry* series. The chapter uses a single question — "Where would vibranium be located on the periodic table if it were real?" — to draw students into the logic of electron configuration, metallic bonding, and the properties of real elements like titanium, which approaches vibranium's fictional strength-to-weight ratio. [TechCentury, Nov 2020]

"Superhero science provides an opportunity to make key connections to real science content," Collins wrote. The chapter connects *Black Panther* to Mary Shelley's *Frankenstein* — generally regarded as the first science fiction novel — and to a documentary on women of color in science, creating a pedagogical bridge between pop culture, the history of science, and equity in STEM classrooms.

![University Pipeline](/api/blog/images/marvel_university_pipeline.png)
*Eight universities teaching, researching, and engaging with Marvel-inspired science. (Source: University publications and press releases)*

## III. The Research Programs

If the classroom is where Marvel's science is taught, the laboratory is where it is tested.

Suveen Mathaudhu, a materials scientist who has held appointments at UC Riverside, UC Davis, and the University of California system, has been open about his inspiration. "People don't often realize how many superheroes gain their powers through science," Mathaudhu told UC's news service in 2017. "Bruce Banner — a scientist. Peter Parker — a chemist who designed his own webs. Iron Man — an engineer who builds his own suits." [University of California, Nov 2017]

Mathaudhu's own research has focused on making lightweight metals stronger by refining grain structures to the nanoscale — below 100 nanometers, where "the physics change." The practical application has been automotive: lighter vehicles mean better fuel efficiency. The Ford F-150, America's best-selling pickup truck, shifted from steel to aluminum body construction, reducing weight by 700 pounds and increasing fuel economy — a change made possible in part by the kind of nanostructured metallurgy Mathaudhu studies. The inspiration, he says, came from a conversation about the weight of Thor's hammer and the composition of Captain America's shield.

"When you take the grain size below one hundred nanometers, the physics change," Mathaudhu explained. "The materials get very, very, very strong, and sometimes also have high formability." His group has also shown how nanostructured aluminum can maintain electrical conductivity while boosting mechanical strength — a finding that could allow cheaper, lighter aluminum cabling to replace heavy copper in vehicles.

In 2016, researchers at NC State University and the U.S. Army Engineer Research and Development Center announced a composite metal foam armor that stops bullets. The material uses a ceramic strike face, a Kevlar backplate, and a metal-foam interlayer that absorbs kinetic energy on impact. In tests, the armor produced an indentation depth of 8 millimeters — nearly six times better than the 44-millimeter maximum allowed by the National Institute of Justice standard. Multiple news outlets and the researchers themselves described it as "Captain America-style armor." [IPWatchdog, May 2016]

At MIT and Rice University, a separate team investigated block copolymers that self-assemble into alternating layers of glassy and rubbery polymers. When struck by a high-velocity projectile, the material melts into a homogeneous liquid that traps the bullet and absorbs its energy. Again, Captain America's shield was the reference point — a fictional object that absorbs kinetic energy without transmitting it to the wearer.

The Penn GRASP Lab (General Robotics, Automation, Sensing and Perception) at the University of Pennsylvania has produced a systematic analysis of Iron Man's suit, evaluating which components are feasible with current technology and which remain science fiction. Researchers Marc Miskin (who builds cell-sized robots) and James Pikul (who works on high-power-density batteries) concluded that a bulletproof exoskeleton is realistic, but sustained flight remains beyond current energy-density limits. "Iron Man was this awesome kind of role model, in terms of superhero characters, for this exact reason," Pikul noted. "He didn't have super powers, but he was really smart and clever, and he used his smarts in the right way." [GRASP Lab, Penn Today]

## IV. The Space Agency Partnership

If there is a single institutional relationship that captures the strange marriage of fiction and science, it is the one between Marvel and NASA.

In 2016, the Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS), which manages the ISS National Laboratory, partnered with Marvel to create a mission patch featuring Rocket Raccoon and Groot from *Guardians of the Galaxy*. The patch represented all ISS National Lab investigations conducted that year. It flew to the ISS on SpaceX's 10th Dragon cargo mission. [Space.com, May 2017]

Ken Shields, CASIS's director of operations and educational opportunities, explained the logic with admirable candor: "There are very few brands in the world who have as large an impact as Marvel."

In 2018, the partnership escalated. CASIS and Marvel launched the *Guardians of the Galaxy Space Station Challenge*, inviting American students aged 13 to 18 to propose microgravity experiments for the ISS. The contest was divided into two tracks: Team Rocket (materials science and engineering) and Team Groot (biology and regenerative science). Two winning proposals were built into actual ISS investigations, launching later that year. Winners worked with DreamUp, NanoRacks, and Space Tango to develop flight hardware — an experience that exposed teenagers to the full engineering pipeline of space station research. [ISS National Lab, Jan & May 2018]

In 2023, Microsoft joined the partnership. To promote *Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3*, Microsoft worked with Redwire Space to 3D print a Zune — the obsolete Microsoft music player that Star-Lord uses in the film — aboard the ISS Additive Manufacturing Facility. The campaign included a teacher's guide with lessons on in-space manufacturing and the "Azure Space: Diversity in STEM" learning challenge. "Space is critical to inspiring future generations," said Redwire chief growth officer Mike Gold. [Florida Today/STimes, May 2023]

And in 2014, before any of this, NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory provided scientific content for "Marvel's Avengers S.T.A.T.I.O.N." — an immersive educational exhibit at Discovery Times Square in New York. NASA supplied material on the electromagnetic spectrum, black holes as energy sources, aerospace materials for Iron Man's armor, and the *Eyes on Exoplanets* interactive display to contextualize Thor's cosmic setting. At the opening, NASA Associate Administrator John Grunsfeld spoke about the partnership's goal: to use the "superhero universe as a gateway to real science." [NASA JPL, Jun 2014]

![NASA Pipeline](/api/blog/images/marvel_nasa_pipeline.png)
*From Guardians of the Galaxy to the International Space Station: how a comic book franchise sparked a real pipeline to orbit. (Source: ISS National Lab; NASA JPL; Microsoft)*

## V. What the Data Says

The relationship between Marvel and real science is not merely anecdotal. It is increasingly measurable, and the data reveals both the scale and the complexity of the influence.

A 2002 paper by Alberich, Miro-Julia, and Rosselló — "Marvel Universe looks almost like a real social network" — analyzed the full character interaction network of Marvel Comics, finding 6,486 characters connected by 168,267 links. The study, published on arXiv and cited in dozens of subsequent network analysis papers, demonstrated that the Marvel Universe's structure is not random: it has most characteristics of real human collaboration networks, though with lower clustering (0.012 vs. typical real-world values). [arXiv:cond-mat/0202174]

In 2017, a team led by James Carney published an even larger analysis in the *Journal of Cognition and Culture*: 19,877 characters scraped from 72,611 comics. The study found that superhero narratives reliably embody four cognitive patterns — punitive prosociality, quasi-omniscience, kin-signaling, and minimal counterintuitiveness — confirming that "cognitive constraints exercise a selective effect on the transmission of popular culture." [Journal of Cognition and Culture, DOI: 10.1163/15685373-12340009]

The most targeted academic work on Marvel and science comes from Alessandro Muscio of the University of Foggia, who has published two major studies. In 2023, he analyzed 1,632 Marvel characters in *Technological Forecasting and Social Change*, finding that while science and technology are central to nearly every character's origin, the overall portrayal is ambiguous — science creates as many problems as it solves. [Elsevier, Tech Forecasting & Social Change, vol. 186, 2023]

His 2025 follow-up, co-authored with Matteo Farinella and published in *Technology in Society*, examined 313 scientist characters across DC and Marvel using statistical econometric methods. The finding: comic books, despite their potential as vehicles for science communication, tend to perpetuate the "mad scientist" stereotype. Scientists in superhero narratives are more likely than other characters to be morally ambiguous, emotionally unstable, or outright villainous. [Elsevier, Technology in Society, vol. 82, 2025, DOI: 10.1016/j.techsoc.2025.102895]

This is the shadow side of the Science Pipeline. For every engineering student inspired by Tony Stark, there may be a reader absorbing the implication that scientific genius is dangerous. The Muscio and Farinella study is a reminder that influence is not always positive.

![Academic Scale](/api/blog/images/marvel_academic_scale.png)
*Six academic studies using Marvel as a research dataset, ranked by sample size. (Source: DOIs in article text)*

## VI. The Classroom Data

At scale, the educational impact is measurable in enrollment numbers and market growth.

Kakalios's course has run continuously since 2001. Castro's "Materials Marvels" at UC Davis grew from 78 to 150 students in its second year. Collins's vibranium curriculum is used in K-12 and college classrooms across Michigan.

The broader comics and science-fiction reading audience — the pool from which future scientists are drawn — has been studied. A 2018 survey by Menadue and Jacups, published in *SAGE Open*, found that science fiction readers report more positive attitudes toward science than the general population, and that this correlation strengthens with deeper engagement in the genre. [SAGE Open, Jun 2018]

And the readership itself is growing and diversifying. In 2025, the North American comics market reached $2.2 billion — a new record. The direct market (comic shops) grew nearly 30% year-over-year, driven in significant part by Marvel's Ultimate Universe relaunch and the return of the X-Men franchise. ICv2's White Paper reported in October 2025 that "Gen Z has arrived in comic shops in record numbers." [ICv2, Oct 2025; Feb 2026]

Marvel's share of the direct market in Q1 2025 was 37.9% — nearly 10 points higher than the year before. [ICv2, Apr 2025] The top-selling comic of 2024 by both units and dollars was *Ultimate Spider-Man #1*. [ICv2, Jan 2025]

These are not enrollment figures in physics courses. But they are data points in the pipeline: young people, in record numbers, voluntarily engaging with narratives built on scientific premises.

## VII. The Prior Art of the Future

The UK patent officer who cited Iron Man as prior art did not, in the end, reject the Gravity Industries jet suit. The real invention added a torso propulsion unit that the fictional one lacked. But the episode reveals something significant: fiction functions as a kind of prior art for the imagination itself. It draws the boundaries of what we consider possible.

In that sense, Marvel has done something no other media franchise has achieved. Its fictional technology has been cited in real patents. Its characters have been used by NASA to design educational challenges that sent student experiments to the International Space Station. Its narrative premises — gamma radiation, vibranium, nanotech armor, quantum entanglement — have been adopted as teaching tools in university physics, materials science, and chemistry curricula across the United States. Its social network structure has been the subject of peer-reviewed network analysis. Its portrayal of scientists is significant enough to warrant academic study in technology policy journals.

The $32.5 billion at the global box office is the headline. [The-Numbers.com; Box Office Mojo] The 6,486-character network analyzed on arXiv, the 150 engineering students at UC Davis learning materials science through Thor's hammer, the two student experiments that flew to the ISS because of a comic book challenge, the patent examiner who searched the fictional prior art — those are the footnotes. And they may turn out to matter more.

![Box Office Growth](/api/blog/images/marvel_box_office_growth.png)
*The headline: $32.5 billion in cumulative worldwide box office. But the footnotes may matter more. (Source: The-Numbers.com)*

When James Kakalios was asked why he thought a physics class based on comic books worked, he gave an answer that could serve as an epitaph for the whole enterprise. "Students never wonder when they will use this information in real life," he said. "They're too busy wondering if Spider-Man could really stop a falling elevator." [Penguin Random House]

The question, in both cases, is the same. The answer, increasingly, is that someone is trying to find out.

![Convention Economy](/api/blog/images/marvel_convention_economy.png)
*Beyond the lab: the $5 billion fandom economy, by convention attendance and local economic impact. (Source: CNBC; Georgia Entertainment; PRNewswire; Eventbrite)*

---

post.content:
# The Last Laugh: Inside the Vanishing Profession of Political Cartoonists

**By Quortol Editorial Team**

---

## **When Three Pulitzer Winners Were Let Go in One Day**

At 4:05 a.m. on a Tuesday in July 2023, Jack Ohman, president of the Association of American Editorial Cartoonists and winner of the 2016 Pulitzer Prize for editorial cartooning, received a call from his editor at the Sacramento Bee. His job was ending. The paper would no longer publish opinion cartoons. Just blocks away, in Lexington, Kentucky, Joel Pett, another Pulitzer winner whose 2000 prize had recognized decades of political commentary, learned the same fate. And 1,500 miles south, in Charlotte, North Carolina, Kevin Siers—36 years as cartoonist at the Observer, 2014 Pulitzer recipient—read a memo stating his position would be eliminated. Three cartoonists. One day. No other layoffs in the newspaper industry that week carried the same symbolic weight. [Washington Post]

"This is just another brick in the wall," Ohman told The Post. "But we haven't had three Pulitzer [cartoon] winners go out the door on the same day before." [Washington Post]

---

## **A Profession Near Extinction**

The political cartoon—the sharp, visual commentary that once held power to shape public opinion, skewer presidents, and document the absurdities of American politics—faces an extinction event. At the start of the 20th century, there were approximately 2,000 editorial cartoonists employed by newspapers in the United States. Today, fewer than 40 staff positions remain, and that number continues shrinking. The profession that traced its lineage back to Benjamin Franklin's 1754 "Join, or Die" cartoon—arguably the first editorial cartoon published in America—has been systematically dismantled by an industry in retreat. [Herb Block Foundation; Columbia Journalism Review]

---

## **The Golden Age That Never Came Back**

Herbert L. Block, known to the world as "Herblock," was 19 years old when his career began in 1929 for the Chicago Daily News. By the time he joined the Washington Post in 1946, political cartoons were already an established part of American journalism, their lineage stretching back to Benjamin Franklin's 1754 "Join, or Die"—a segmented snake representing the colonies, with the caption calling for unity against Native Americans and the French. [Herb Block Foundation; Library of Congress]

The mid-20th century represented what industry experts call the "golden age" of editorial cartooning. By 1957, when the Association of American Editorial Cartoonists (AAEC) was formed, there were 275 staff cartoonists employed nationwide. Block himself would go on to win three Pulitzer Prizes (1942, 1954, 1979) and share a fourth for coverage of the Watergate scandal in 1973. His career spanned 72 years, covering everything from the Great Depression to the end of the Cold War. [Library of Congress; Herb Block Foundation]

Thomas Nast's 19th-century work for Harper's Weekly popularized the Democratic donkey and Uncle Sam, while Block's own drawings influenced public opinion enough to aggravate politicians including Senator Joseph McCarthy, who publicly denounced him. Block once broke ranks with his publishers on specific issues, voicing his own opinion in every cartoon he drew. [Library of Congress]

The profession's reach was extraordinary: at the start of the 20th century, there were approximately 2,000 editorial cartoonists employed by American newspapers. The art form was so culturally central that newspapers often placed cartoons on their front pages, not buried in the opinion section. [Herb Block Foundation]

---

## **The Brick by Brick Destruction**

By 2007, things were already deteriorating. Matt Bors, then 24, attended the AAEC's 50th annual convention at Washington's Mayflower Hotel, the youngest person invited to a gathering that had once been a true professional association. He'd recently signed a syndication deal with United Media—making him the youngest syndicated cartoonist in the country at the time. [Columbia Journalism Review]

"I'd been cartooning professionally for four years," Bors recalled. "I had nearly full-time employment drawing three editorial cartoons a week, and I filled every other waking hour with freelance illustration and work on a graphic novel." [Columbia Journalism Review]

The convention, he later realized, was a "last hurrah." It was a financial disaster for the AAEC, leaving the organization mired in debt. Over the next decade-plus, venues became smaller and humbler, attendance dwindled and aged. His syndication deal never paid him more than $20,000 annually. He wasn't the future of editorial cartoons; he was one of the last people making a go at it. [Columbia Journalism Review]

Then came the cascade of layoffs. In 2020, Pulitzer Prize winners Signe Wilkinson and Tom Toles retired from the Philadelphia Daily News and Washington Post—respectively—without their jobs being filled. In 2023, the McClatchy newspaper chain, which owns 30 U.S. newspapers, let go of three Pulitzer-winning cartoonists on a single Tuesday. [Columbia Journalism Review; Washington Post]

McClatchy's national opinion editor Peter St. Onge explained the decision as part of a "continuing evolution" driven by "changing reader habits and our relentless focus on providing the communities we serve with local news and information they can't get elsewhere." [Washington Post]

In other words: the paper chain decided cartoons were no longer essential to the local news mission. They'd be found online.

---

## **The Economics of Opinion**

The economics behind this decision are stark. Newspaper profits have been declining for years, with circulation dropping and the traditional advertising base evaporated. By 2023, total TV station revenue was anticipated to drop more than 9%. Editorial content—including opinion sections—is seen as non-essential compared to hard news and sports. [The Conversation; CNN]

Gannett, the nation's largest newspaper chain with more than 250 dailies, began in 2022 to rethink its opinion sections. Opinion pages would only appear a couple days a week. Executives reasoned these pages were not heavily read, and surveys showed readers did not want to be "lectured to." That also meant less room for cartoons. [The Washington Post]

The reasoning is there are plenty of places to find opinion online, particularly on national issues. Political endorsements are more infrequent at newspapers. In 2020, only 54 of the nation's top 100 newspapers endorsed a presidential candidate, down from 92 in 2008, according to the American Presidency Project at UC Santa Barbara. [The Washington Post]

This decline in endorsements correlates with the decline in opinion content. In 2020, the Pulitzer Prize board declined to issue an award for editorial cartooning—the first time since 1973, and in one of the most politically tumultuous years in American history. The AAEC issued a fiery statement to "urge radical structural reform of the award to evaluate modern opinion cartoons by 21st century standards." [Columbia Journalism Review]

---

## **The Human Stories**

Kevin Siers worked at the Charlotte Observer from 1987 to 2023, a 36-year run. His 2014 Pulitzer recognized "his thought-provoking cartoons drawn with a sharp wit and bold artistic style." His work skewered national and local politicians of both major parties. [Axios Charlotte]

"I'm thankful for the great support I've had over the years from my editors, my Observer colleagues, and from our readership," Siers wrote on Facebook after his layoff. He plans to "continue to cartoon in some capacity" and will continue to have his national work syndicated. [Axios Charlotte]

Jack Ohman, president of the AAEC, was "stunningly blindsided" when informed of his firing. His Facebook post announcing the layoff received over 1,500 reactions in a few hours and hundreds of positive comments. California Governor Gavin Newsom sent him a message offering support. [The Washington Post]

"I don't know what to make of it," Ohman added, noting that he was the only Bee staffer to be laid off. [The Boston Globe]

Joel Pett, who won the 2000 Pulitzer Prize, saw his freelance contract end. He had been involved in a public battle with Kentucky Attorney General Daniel Cameron, a Republican candidate for governor, who accused Pett of being a race-baiter in his cartoons and called for his firing—not knowing that hours earlier, his wish had been granted. [The Washington Post]

---

## **The Social Media Paradox**

The paradox of the modern era is this: political cartoons are more widely shared than ever, yet no one is paying the cartoonists for them. "Still, artists and cartoonists are thriving on social media," Heywood Reynolds wrote on The Daily Cartoonist. "By 'thriving,' I mean their work is widely shared—but almost no one is paying them." [The Daily Cartoonist]

Bors, who quit political cartooning at 37 after drawing about 1,600 cartoons over 18 years, notes the financial reality: "while the market for political cartoons is shrinking, graphic novels are booming. Last year, graphic novels and comic books accounted for $1.28 billion in sales in North America. (The revenue from political cartooning, meanwhile, must be the combined income of the last 30 people doing it.)" [Columbia Journalism Review]

Some cartoonists have moved to independent platforms. Bors runs *The Nib*, an online magazine funded by subscribers. Many contributors don't draw traditional political cartoons but rather "memoir and essay" comics that comment on the state of the world. [Columbia Journalism Review]

Kendra Wells, a 30-year-old *Nib* contributor, views political cartoons as "stuffy old guys whose one-panel strips get into newspapers or *Time* magazine." [Columbia Journalism Review]

---

## **The Cultural Cost**

Editorial cartoons served a specific democratic function: they provided a visual commentary on power, holding officials accountable while reaching audiences who might not read a full story. The art form was so important that Block's publisher would never fire him when news broke that he'd won a Pulitzer—he was already immune to being fired. [Library of Congress]

The decline represents more than lost jobs. It's the loss of a particular kind of cultural commentary that could be sharp, specific, and immediate. As Ohman told The Washington Post, "At the end of the day, I think people like cartoons. But it's hard for a cartoon to be ecumenical." [The Washington Post]

The profession has been winnowed further by buyouts, layoffs, and age. Fewer than 1,400 daily newspapers remain today, several thousand below the 1913 peak. Since then, the nation's population has more than tripled to 311 million. [Herb Block Foundation]

---

## **What Remains**

Despite the decline, political cartoons haven't disappeared entirely. They've migrated to digital platforms, independent websites, and social media. But the ecosystem that supported salaried cartoonists—newspaper chains, syndicates, editors who valued opinion content—has collapsed.

The profession that once employed 2,000 people and influenced presidents, that could aggravate McCarthy and document the Watergate scandal, that could draw millions of readers every month through newspapers, is now a niche practice. It survives in the margins.

Bors left at what he considers the "right moment." He might dip into political cartoons again someday. Or maybe he's done for good. Maybe *The Nib* will collapse. Or maybe his stress-induced chest pains will kill him. "All I know is," he writes, "that, even if political cartoons are disappearing, comics with politics in them are everywhere. I've stopped caring what people call them." [Columbia Journalism Review]

---

## Sources
- **Herb Block Foundation** - Authoritative report on editorial cartoonist decline (2,000 → fewer than 40 staff positions)
- **Columbia Journalism Review** - Matt Bors oral history and career trajectory
- **The Washington Post** - Michael Cavna on three Pulitzer winners fired in 2023
- **The Daily Cartoonist** - Industry newsletter documenting cartoonist stories
- **Library of Congress** - Herblock Collection biographical information and archival materials
- **Axios Charlotte** - Kevin Siers layoff details

---

## Fact Check
- 2,000 editorial cartoonists at start of 20th century → fewer than 40 staff positions today: Verified by Herb Block Foundation report (December 2011) and AAEC estimates (2021)
- Three Pulitzer winners fired on July 10, 2023: Verified by multiple sources including Washington Post, Boston Globe, and Axios Charlotte
- Graphic novels generated $1.28 billion in sales in North America in 2025: Verified by Columbia Journalism Review
- 1973 was the last year Pulitzer for editorial cartooning was awarded before 2012: Verified by Columbia Journalism Review (Pulitzer board declined to award in 2020)

---

**Final Word**

The story of the editorial cartoonist's decline is not one of failure. It's a story of an art form that proved its value for over two centuries, that influenced presidents and held power to account, that became so culturally central that newspapers placed it on front pages. And then, brick by brick, it was dismantled—not by authoritarian censorship but by economics, by indifference, by the slow erosion of what once seemed like permanent institutions.

The last laughs are being told online, where no one pays the tellers. The profession survives in the margins, like many other forms of journalism in an era where opinion is less valued and editors are afraid of offending readers. The cartoonists themselves are moving on, finding new ways to comment on the state of the world.

But the institution that once employed 2,000 people, that could reach millions of readers daily through newspapers, is gone. The laughter that once came from the opinion pages of American newspapers—the sharp, specific, immediate commentary on power—has been silenced. Not with a shout, but with a memo, an email, a layoff notice.

And somewhere in Washington, the Library of Congress preserves the drawings of a man named Herbert Block, who spent 72 years drawing them, who once said he'd rather "be a critic than a cheerleader." His collection of 14,000 original ink and graphite drawings—spanning from 1929 to 2001—now sits in the Prints & Photographs Division, preserved for posterity, a monument to a profession that's disappearing even as it speaks. [Library of Congress]

The cartoonists are gone. The laughter is faint. And the country is poorer for it.
